title: [Bugfix][KV Connector][ROCm] MoRIIO: accept kernel-block-split MLA/indexer KV views
summary: ## Summary If a backend's kernel block sizes exclude the manager block size, `create_kv_cache_views` gives connectors a **kernel-block-split** 4-D view (leading dim in kernel blocks, `r = num_states / N`). MoRIIO's 4-D branch only accepts `r == 1`, so registration fails with `Unsupported MoRIIO MLA cache shape`. Affected on `main`: DeepSeek-V3.2-style models on ROCm (e.g. GLM-5.2). `ROCM_AITER_MLA_SPARSE` and `DEEPSEEK_V32_INDEXER` support kernel blocks `[1, MultipleOf(16)]`, so a `--block-size` that isn't 1 or a multiple of 16 (e.g. 8) is split to kernel block 1. **Change** (`moriio_layout.py`, `get_layer_transfer_geometry`): - Accept split views for single-head caches (MLA latent, indexer); group them with `group_kernel_blocks` so the geometry is in manager blocks. A dense single-head block is the same bytes for any kernel block size, so P and D may differ. - Multi-head splits stay rejected (byte order depends on the layout). Bit-identical for `r == 1`; no wire or metadata change. +17/−5 in one source file. GLM-5.3-Flash no longer needs this since #57169 (packed layout, never split group-wide). ## Validation All runs on MI300X. GSM8K: `lm_eval` 5-shot, full 1319, strict-match. NIAH: needles found / 10 at 2K / 8K / 32K words, seeds 0 / 1 / 2. | Model | Setup | Tree | `--block-size` | GSM8K | NIAH 2K / 8K / 32K | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | GLM-5.2-FP8 | 1P1D, EP8 per node, MoRIIO WRITE | `main` `5d35ce3934` | 1 | 94.01 ± 0.65; 94.84 ± 0.61 | 10/9/10, 10/10/10, 10/10/10 | | GLM-5.2-FP8 | same | this PR `501baf943f` | 1 | 94.09 ± 0.65 | 10/10/10, 10/10/10, 10/9/9 | | GLM-5.2

title: [Perf][KV Offload] Report tiering lookup metrics once per request
summary: ## Overview The tiering manager looks up a request's prompt one chunk at a time, and for every chunk it records a query count, a hit count, and a sync-delay histogram sample. On a 128k-token prompt that is 8192 samples sent to the API server per request. This PR adds them up per request and reports one total per tier, when the request is scheduled or finishes. title: [MRV2][Spec Decode] Cap dummy-run requests by their draft slots
summary: ## Overview With draft-model speculative decoding, engine startup fails with an `AssertionError` whenever `max_num_seqs * 2 > max_num_batched_tokens`, e.g. `--max-num-batched-tokens 256` with the default `max_num_seqs`. `_dummy_run` keeps `num_reqs = min(num_tokens, max_num_reqs)` and then takes one draft slot per request out of the token budget, which can leave fewer tokens than requests. This caps `num_reqs` the same way #65270 capped warmup. ## Claims - draft_model starts and generates at 256/256, 128/128 and 256/200 (`max_num_batched_tokens`/`max_num_seqs`), which crash on main. Configs that already started are unchanged. ## Validation - `pytest tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_model_runner_v2.py`: the new test fails 2 of 5 cases on main. title: [Perf][Model] Gemma 4: remove trailing image padding to enable FlashAttention in vision SDPA
summary: ## Summary Gemma 4's image processor pads every image to `max_soft_tokens × 9` patches. The padding is represented by a trailing block at `(-1, -1)`, which the Hugging Face vision tower converts into a boolean attention mask. When an attention mask is present, PyTorch SDPA cannot use the FlashAttention backend and falls back to the memory-efficient backend. On RTX 5090 with this shape, that is about 3.6× slower per attention call. This PR removes the trailing padding before the vision encoder, allowing SDPA to select FlashAttention, then pads the encoder output back to the processor's original length before pooling. The change is 35 lines in `gemma4_mm.py` and does not add a new kernel. ## Performance On an RTX 5090 with `nvidia/Gemma-4-26B-A4B-NVFP4` (main 08567505b0 + this diff only; `gemma4_mm.py` and the test file are identical to the PR base 0f112d1800; `--kv-cache-dtype fp8`, TRITON_ATTN, marlin MoE): | Prompt | main | PR | Δ | | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------: | ---------: | ---------: | | 1 image @280 (default), TTFT | 74.3 ms | 57.1 ms | **−23.2%** | | 16 images, mixed sizes @280, TTFT | 1019 ms | 747 ms | **−26.7%** | | 16 images @70, TTFT | 221 ms | 206 ms | **−6.8%** | | 46 images @560 (~25k tokens), TTFT | 7703 ms | 5022 ms | **−34.8%** | | `vllm bench serve`, 6 images/request @560, max-concurrency 1, median TTFT | 942 ms | 592 ms | **−37.2%** | | Same benchmark, throughput | 1.01 req/s | 1.56 req/s | **+54%** | The two server runs for each arm differed by ≤1%. title: [RFC]: Resource bound for the `/tokenize` endpoint
summary: ### Motivation. `/tokenize` is a vLLM-specific endpoint. Its request models currently build tokenization parameters with `max_total_tokens=None`: ```python TokenizeParams( max_total_tokens=None, ... ) ``` `VLLM_HTTP_MAX_REQUEST_BODY_SIZE` limits the serialized body (default 32 MiB), but in an isolated test an approximately 18 MiB synthetic prompt tokenized to 4,404,015 tokens, so a body within that limit can still expand to millions of tokens. We investigated an API-server availability incident and believe this path is a plausible contributor, but the evidence is partly indirect: - The exact production request body was not retained, and per-write historical thread IDs were not retained, so the triggering request and the write-lock holder cannot be identified. - A tokenizer worker was observed blocked in `do_user_addr_fault -> rwsem_down_read_slowpath -> down_read`. Its stack matched `TokenizersBackend._encode_plus` and the list comprehension in Transformers' `_encode_plus`, which builds a Python token list. - A register value at that point (`RDX=0x2001f68` = 33,562,472) equals the pointer-array size of a Python 3.12 list with 4,195,309 elements (appending one more element grows it to 37,757,824 bytes). This is consistent with, but does not prove, a multi-million-element token list being built. - During the same period the API server stopped serving health, metrics, logs, and requests for about 9 minutes 34 seconds; the container stayed running, with no restart and no OOM kill. We have not established a direct causal link between the blocked worker and the full outage. - In

title: WIP [RFC]: SupportsReload, a single post-load contract and reload verifier (follow-up to #59502)
summary: ## TL;DR #59502 makes reload cheap and safe for **quant methods**. The weakest part of reload is everything **around** them: - model-level `process_weights_after_loading` (PWAL) hooks that reload never calls; - `load_weights` code that writes params directly; - weight-derived tensors that nobody owns; - a global reload flag that every PWAL has to branch on. On main, each of these silently serves stale or wrong weights. This RFC proposes one small contract with a fixed place for every kind of post-load work. Model authors implement it, and the framework can **verify** it before an update starts: | Kind of work | Where it goes | Runs | |---|---|---| | Per-shard transform (TP narrowing, permutation, layout scatter, `-exp(A_log)`) | the param's `weight_loader` | on every load | | Per-module checkpoint → kernel conversion | module PWAL: **always transform, build once** | on every load, as the module completes | | Weight-derived values held by kernels (alphas, `1/a_scale`, bmm scales) | kernel `refresh()`, **called by the framework** | after every load, cold start included | | Cross-module derived values (mHC broadcast, DSpark stacks) | `SupportsReload.refresh_model()` | after every load, cold start included, last | | Non-weight setup (compile, device placement, geometry) | `post_load_setup()` | cold start only | Four consequences: 1. **No global reload flag.** The `reload_mode()` / `is_reloading()` flag from #59502 goes away. 2. **No model-level weight hook.** The free-form model `process_weights_after_loading()` stops doing weight work. 3. **One sanctioned pattern** for model-s

title: [Bugfix][UMBP] Restore Mamba hybrid prefixes at boundaries inside attention blocks
summary: <!-- markdownlint-disable --> ## Overview A Mamba hybrid that checkpoints its state inside an attention block never restores from UMBP at that checkpoint, so a returning prompt resumes from an older boundary or is computed again. Store the attention page with each state page core hands off at such a boundary, keyed at the same boundary, as the finished-tail path already does. Default `enable_partial_hash_hits` to true for Mamba "align" hybrids whose `prefix_match_unit` is finer than the scheduler block, since only hash-granular lookups reach those checkpoints. An explicit setting still wins, and other models keep `false`. The fix adds the pages to the entries `_add_boundary_state_plans` already turns into store plans, so plan construction and its checks stay in one place. The default is a separate commit and is documented in `docs/features/umbp_store_connector_usage.md`. ```bash pytest -v -s -rs tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_umbp_hybrid.py -k "restores_every_byte or partial_hash_hits_default" pytest -v -s -rs tests/v1/kv_connector/umbp_integration/test_mori_token_e2e.py -k hybrid ``` Commits: `4997a1d593` (fix) and `b0d03d9e22` (default), on nightly `9bc16ae6a3`. ## Claims - A Mamba hybrid restores from UMBP at the same boundary as a local GPU prefix hit, with identical tokens and logprobs. Granite 4.0-H 350M: 0 → 832 restored tokens of an 840-token prompt. - Nemotron-H-8B keeps its GSM8K accuracy with 98.8% of the prompt tokens restored from UMBP. - Kimi-K3.1-Pro on one MI355X node: 13,910 → 16,824 tok/s/GPU (+21%), prefix hit 90.7% → 94.1%, TTFT p90 5.45 → 3.03 s. ## Va

title: [RFC]: Expose EPLB expert topology and per-expert token load metrics
summary: ### Motivation. EPLB makes two pieces of information operationally important but currently opaque: 1. **Which logical experts are resident on which GPU / physical slot.** 2. **How many tokens each physical expert processed over a load window.** Today the only EPLB observability is the optional `log_balancedness` scalar/log line, which reports an aggregate `avg/max` ratio. That is useful for detecting imbalance but cannot answer questions such as: - Which GPU is the hotspot for a given MoE layer? - Is a popular logical expert replicated on the right ranks? - Did a rearrangement actually move the hot experts, or only reshuffle cold ones? - Which physical replicas absorb traffic after a routing-placement change? - How does expert-level load correlate with TTFT/TPOT or link utilization? The existing EPLB RFC (#30696) covers instance-level balancedness and rebalancing state. This RFC is narrower and complementary: it proposes exposing the physical expert placement plus per-physical-expert token load, so operators and researchers can reason about actual expert-level hotspots. ### Proposed Change Add an opt-in EPLB config flag: ```json {"enable_expert_metrics": true} ``` When enabled, EPLB emits expert placement, per-phase token load, and timestamp/event metrics. #### `vllm:eplb_expert_topology` Gauge, labels: - `model_name`, `engine` (standard vLLM labels) - `model` (target or draft model name) - `layer` - `ep_rank` (`physical_expert // num_local_experts`) - `physical_expert` Value: the logical expert id currently held by that physical slot. The label set is stable across rearran

title: [Bugfix][DSA] Split FlashInfer sparse MLA calls above the 65535 gridDim.z limit
summary: ## Purpose `FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE` returns garbage, with no exception, for any step that sends 65,536 or more tokens through sparse MQA. For example, GLM-5.3 with `--max-num-batched-tokens 65536` returns HTTP 200 with wrong output for every prompt of 64K tokens or more. `_forward_mqa_kernel` passes each query token to trtllm-gen as its own request (`q.unsqueeze(1)`), so the kernel batch equals the step's token count. trtllm-gen uses the batch size as `gridDim.z` (`numCtasZ = params.mBatchSize` in FlashInfer `fmhaKernels.cuh`), and CUDA caps `gridDim.z` at 65,535. A larger launch fails with `CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_VALUE`, but FlashInfer's `cuErrCheck` only prints it. The kernel never runs, and the output tensor is left uninitialized. This also makes TTFT look faster than it is. This PR splits the trtllm-gen call into chunks of at most 32,768 query rows. Rows are independent: each token carries its own top-k list. Steps of 32,768 tokens or fewer, including every decode and CUDA graph batch, still make exactly one call and skip the `torch.cat`. Why 32,768 rather than 65,535: vLLM's FlashInfer autotune tunes power-of-two token buckets up to `max_num_batched_tokens` and rounds calls up to a bucket (`kernel_warmup.py`). The 65,536 bucket's profiling launches of `trtllm_batch_decode_mla` fail the same way (`CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_VALUE` during startup with a 65,536 budget), so a 65,535-row call would run with a tactic picked from failed launches. 32,768 is the largest power of two under the limit. title: [Core] Bounded-memory streaming sessions: retention, in-place KV eviction, consolidation
summary: ## Purpose Draft implementation of RFC #51948: give a long-running streaming-input session (#28973) a constant memory footprint, no matter how long it runs. Nothing here activates unless a request sets `streaming_retention` in `SamplingParams.extra_args` - requests that don't take none of the new paths. **Size, before anything else.** The diff looks large, so here is where the lines actually are. The first two commits are #53861 and #53871. The feature commit itself is 5,573 lines, of which 4,029 are tests. **What it does.** Each session's context is tracked as segments (a pinned anchor = system prompt + first turn; content segments; reply segments). When a session goes over its budget, the oldest unpinned segments are evicted in place while the session keeps running: KV blocks freed through the #53871 primitive, encoder-cache entries released, and every per-token array compacted by exactly the block-aligned range the KV manager reports back. **Positions: survivors keep theirs.** After an eviction the position space has gaps. Cached K stays rotationally consistent with no kernel changes and no re-rotation. We also built the alternative (compact survivors to new positions and re-rotate cached K, which is what #43374's design delegates to an out-of-tree runner) and benchmarked both on the same model and harness: keeping positions was clearly ahead on accuracy at identical latency. **Shared mechanics for text and multimodal sessions**: mRoPE models carry a per-token position tensor, extended each chunk from `max_cached_position + 1` and sliced on eviction. title: [KV Offload] Explain EFAULT from a full /dev/shm in _madvise_populate_write
summary: ## Overview When `/dev/shm` runs out while the CPU KV offload shared region is pre-faulted, `MADV_POPULATE_WRITE` fails with `OSError: [Errno 14] Bad address`, which does not point at `/dev/shm`. With data parallelism this happens with offload sizes that fit one engine at a time but not all of them together. Each region's creator checks `/dev/shm` free space and then calls `ftruncate`, which reserves nothing on tmpfs, so engines starting together all pass the check. Pages are only claimed when `MADV_POPULATE_WRITE` faults them in, and on a full tmpfs `madvise` reports that as `EFAULT`. On main (`642c18d6`), 8× RTX 4090, Qwen3-8B, `--data-parallel-size 8 --kv-offloading-size 32` and a 251.9 GiB `/dev/shm`: all 8 engines loaded the model, then 6 failed with `Bad address` and the server exited. This PR makes the existing `_madvise_populate_write` helper turn that `EFAULT` into an error that names `/dev/shm`. Nothing else changes. ## Claims - In `_madvise_populate_write`, an `OSError` with `errno.EFAULT` is re-raised as a new `OSError(errno.EFAULT, …)`, chained from the original. From the 64 MiB reproduction below: *"Pre-faulting the mapping failed with EFAULT, most likely because the memory backing it ran out. If it is in /dev/shm (now 0.00 GiB free of 0.06 GiB), note that /dev/shm is shared by every process that uses it, including other data-parallel engines; increase its capacity or reduce the host buffer size"* - The free/total figures come from `shutil.disk_usage("/dev/shm")`; if that call fails, they are left out and the error is still raised. - `EINVAL` (which selects th

summary: ## Overview Follow-up to #62444, which moves the CPU copy of a GPU prefix hit to the MRU end at admission. title: [Bug][Watermarking]: `deduplicate_contexts="all"` misses repeats across the prompt boundary under speculative decoding
summary: ### Describe the bug With `deduplicate_contexts="all"`, a token is sampled without the watermark when its context (the previous `context_width` tokens) already occurred earlier in the prompt or the output. Under speculative decoding this check misses contexts whose earlier occurrence starts in the prompt and ends in the output. Those tokens are watermarked, while non-speculative decoding samples them without the watermark, so the two paths can produce different text. The default `single_turn` and `none` are not affected. ### Example Take `context_width=2` and count one token per word. The prompt ends with `... say it twice: bye`. The model has answered `bye` so far, and the drafter proposes `bye` again. | Position | 0 (prompt) | 1 (output) | 2 (draft) | 3 (next token) | |---|---|---|---|---| | Token | `bye` | `bye` | `bye` | ? | The token at position 3 has context `(bye, bye)` from positions 1-2. - **Non-speculative decoding** with mode `all` searches the prompt too. It finds `(bye, bye)` at positions 0-1, the last prompt word followed by the first output word. The context is a repeat, so the token is sampled without the watermark. - **Speculative decoding** checks the n-grams that end at the last committed token or at a draft through the contexts of the earlier rows in the same verification block. The earlier row stores its context as `(-1, bye)`, because context positions inside the prompt are written as -1. `(bye, bye)` does not match `(-1, bye)`, so the token is watermarked. title: [Bugfix] Skip FP8-dequant fast paths for PP-missing layers in GLM-5.3-Flash load
summary: ## Purpose Fixes #55725. GLM-5.3-Flash crashes at weight load on multi-node (2×8 H100) with `KeyError: 'layers.11.self_attn.fused_qkv_a_proj.weight'` on every second-node worker, while single-node runs fine. ## Root cause With 2 nodes the run is pipeline-parallel (PP=2), so layer 11's params exist only on stage-0 ranks. The attached log (`layer11.log`) shows all `Worker_PP1_TP0..7` crashing; PP0 is clean. The normal load path guards every weight with `is_pp_missing_parameter` (glm5next/common/model.py), but the two FP8-dequant fast paths bypass it and index `params_dict` directly: - `_try_load_fp8_attn_proj` → `params_dict[target_w]` (the traceback in the issue) - `_try_load_fp8_indexer_wk` → `params_dict[fused_name]` (same class of hole) On a PP rank that doesn't hold the layer, `params_dict` has no such key → KeyError before the normal path ever gets a chance to skip the weight. ## Fix In both fast paths, return `False` when the target param is absent from `params_dict`, so the weight falls through to the normal path, which skips it via `is_pp_missing_parameter`. The indexer-wk guard is placed *before* buffering, so PP ranks also don't accumulate fp8 tensors that nobody loads. title: [Perf][UMBP] Ask the other ranks only about objects the first rank holds
summary: <!-- markdownlint-disable --> ## Overview A hash-granular UMBP lookup asks every rank about its own copy of every probed object, although callers only use whether all ranks hold an object and most probed positions hold nothing. On an 8-rank Kimi K3 deployment a long prompt sends tens of thousands of keys per lookup, and in embedded mode the scheduler asks the ranks' lookup sockets one after another, so a synchronous lookup blocks scheduling for the sum. Ask the first rank about every object, then the other ranks only about the objects it holds. Keep each object's own key count, since a TP-replicated group stores one key per object where the other groups store one per rank. Leave an object the first rank cannot answer for unknown (`None`), as one query would. Use this for the request lookups, async and synchronous, and for the residency checks before storing a restored prefix and before emitting KV events. The lazy-offload residency check still asks every rank: it must see an unavailable rank before it stores the window, and its confirmed-key cache keeps it small. Embedded mode makes the same per-rank requests with fewer keys; standalone mode makes a second call when the first rank holds anything. ```bash pytest -v -s -rs tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_umbp_core.py -k "first_rank or two_phase" ``` Commit: `92c994d1e0`, on nightly `9bc16ae6a3`. ## Claims - The same lookup results with about an eighth of the keys at 8 ranks when most probed positions miss. - Kimi-K3.1-Pro on one MI355X node: +2.7% throughput at the same hit rate together with #67942 (hybrid restore) and #6794

title: [Feature][Model Loading] Add --verify-weights flag to detect corrupted checkpoint tensors
summary: ## Purpose vLLM's safetensors weight loading pipeline performs **no content-level validation** on weight tensors. The only checks are: 1. safetensors header JSON can be parsed (Rust level) 2. data_offsets don't exceed file size (Rust level) 3. tensor shape matches model expectation (Python level) 4. weight name completeness for non-quantized models (Python level) If a checkpoint file is corrupted during transfer (network errors, storage failures, incomplete copies) but the header and shape are still valid, vLLM **silently loads corrupted weights** and produces incorrect inference results without any error or warning. ### Real-world impact A customer deploying Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-w8a8 had a corrupted `quant_model_weights-00008-of-00010.safetensors` (sha256 mismatch, 4.28GB). vLLM loaded the corrupted weights without error, causing intermittent tool call argument truncation. Normal chat worked fine, making the issue extremely hard to diagnose. ### Proposed solution Opt-in `--verify-weights` flag that checks each loaded floating-point tensor using a single `abs().max()` reduction (30x faster per-tensor than separate isnan+isinf+max passes; NaN propagates through max, so one pass covers all three cases): - **NaN** → raises ValueError, blocks startup - **Inf** → raises ValueError, blocks startup - **All-zero** (tensors > 1024 elements) → logs warning (small biases/norms may legitimately be zero) ### Limitations Cannot detect valid-but-incorrect values (e.g. bit flips changing `weight_scale` from 0.5 to 50.0). External sha256 verification is still recommended for full integrity check

title: [Model Loader] Direct reload of online-quantized modules
summary: <!-- markdownlint-disable --> Direct weight reload (`VLLM_RELOAD_MODE=direct`, #64336) now supports online quantization on a BF16 checkpoint. Part of #54477 (F4). This revision replaces the earlier layerwise-staging approach: no module is staged on meta, buffered, or re-quantized at `finish`. Online quantization in direct mode is a pre-quantized checkpoint method whose loaders quantize on arrival. The diff against main is 10 files: about +200/-10 of source, plus tests and docs. ## Problem `VLLM_RELOAD_MODE=direct` refuses online quantization. Online methods create BF16 parameters on the meta device and quantize them in post-load processing. A direct reload writes in place into the kernel tensors, and those cannot hold BF16, so there is nothing to load the update into. ## Design The only place a high-precision tensor can become a quantized one is the place it arrives: the weight loader. - **Only in direct mode.** With `VLLM_RELOAD_MODE=direct` (and not for requantization), `OnlineQuantizationConfig.get_quant_method` returns the method of the matching pre-quantized checkpoint for a convertible scheme. Every other mode keeps the online classes, so behavior there is unchanged from main. - **Online scheme = checkpoint method + quantize-on-load.** - `quantize_on_load` wraps the weight loaders once and permanently. Each arriving tensor is quantized, then its values and scales are written through the original loaders. - Cold start and direct reload therefore load and post-process exactly like that checkpoint. There is no layerwise staging. - The full unsharded tensor is quantized b

summary: ## Overview Follow-up to #64869. `WeightsMapper` runs `weights_transforms` on the raw checkpoint stream, before `AutoWeightsLoader` skips the layers on other PP stages and the MoE `weight_loader` skips the experts on other EP ranks. When a rank reads the full checkpoint, it runs the transforms on weights it later skips. That's cheap for a rename, but not for a transform that decodes tensors, like the CSF scale transform in #64312. This adds `RankLocalTransform`, a wrapper that marks a transform as safe to run on only the weights its rank loads. When every transform in the mapper has it, `load_weights` maps each raw name first and drops the weight before the transforms if it falls in a `PPMissingLayer` or `StageMissingLayer`, or names an expert that its MoE layer leaves to another EP rank. Now that #64312 is on main, this also wraps its CSF scale transform. ## Claims - Wrapping is opt-in. It's only safe when dropping one layer's or one expert's inputs leaves every other output unchanged, and each output's mapped name stays in the same layer and expert as its inputs. A transform that takes a max over a layer's experts breaks the first; one that merges experts breaks the second. A transform must not turn a non-input-scale weight into an input scale, since some MoE methods need every expert's input scales. - Once per `load_weights` call, each `MoERunner` gets a filter built from the expert map, quant method and global input scale rule that `weight_loader` uses, so it only drops expert weights `weight_loader` would skip. title: [Bugfix][Responses API] Order in-flight tool call tail before post-tool content in split_delta

title: [Bugfix][Frontend] Replace invalid tool call names by a placeholder in the Mistral renderer history
summary: <!-- markdownlint-disable --> ## Disclosure AI assistance was used. The changes were reviewed and tested manually. ## Overview **Fixes blocking broken tool calls with Mistral Large 4 that block harness with `BadRequestError`, instead of allowing the harness/agent to recover.** With `--tokenizer-mode mistral`, `mistral-common==1.13.1` rejects a tool call whose name is not `[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}`, and vLLM fails the whole request with an HTTP 400: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/157e42a76267566b2e232f47e67d70cbe98fdb9f/vllm/renderers/mistral.py#L25-L49. title: [Bugfix][Kernel] Fix FlashInfer MXFP8 linears for N not divisible by 8 or 32
summary: ## Overview On SM100/SM103, MXFP8 linears whose per-rank output size N is not a multiple of 8 silently compute garbage, and those not a multiple of 32 crash if they reach the CUTLASS kernel. Tensor parallelism produces such N in hybrid Mamba models, for example in the Mamba `in_proj`: - `nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Nano-4B-BF16` at TP8: 2188 per rank - `nvidia/Nemotron-H-4B-Instruct-128K` at TP4: 4124 per rank With `--quantization mxfp8`, both score about 0 on GSM8K. ## Claims - `FlashInferCutedslMxfp8LinearKernel` declines N % 8 != 0. `mm_mxfp8(backend="cute-dsl")` stores its 16-bit output with TMA, which needs 16-byte aligned rows. FlashInfer doesn't validate N and launches anyway, so these layers returned garbage (relative error 1.4 to inf at M ≥ 64). - `FlashInferCutlassMxfp8LinearKernel` pads N to a multiple of 32 at weight prep and slices the output back. Selection now falls back to it for the layers above. FlashInfer's SM100 CUTLASS MXFP8 GEMM requires N % 32 == 0 and raises otherwise, yet `can_implement` accepted such N on SM100/103. - Every other layer selects the same kernel as before, and padding is a no-op when N % 32 == 0. No configuration that works today changes. ## Validation GB300 (SM103) with these versions: - vLLM `cab3f26ab` (precompiled wheel), as main and with this patch applied - FlashInfer 0.7.4 (the pinned version) - torch 2.14.0+cu132 **Unit tests.** The new GPU test fails on main and passes with the fix: ``` $ pytest -q -rf tests/kernels/quantization/test_flashinfer_mxfp8_linear.py main: 11 failed, 5 passed PR: 16 passed ``` <details><summary>main: f

title: [Bugfix] Drop num_stages for MLA decode with fp8 KV cache on small-smem GPUs
summary: ## Summary `_decode_grouped_att_m_fwd` already guards against shared-memory overflow by falling back to `num_stages=1`, but the condition only fires for `BLOCK_DMODEL >= 1024`. MLA with `D_QK=576` pins `BLOCK_DMODEL=512` and `BLOCK_DPE=64` earlier in the same function, so the guard never applied to it. With a bf16 KV cache that tile still fits. With an fp8 KV cache the extra dequant staging pushes it past the 101,376-byte opt-in limit found on consumer and workstation Blackwell parts, and every MLA decode dies on the first generated token with `triton.runtime.errors.OutOfResources`. Fixes #53748. ## Measurements Shared memory required by the stage-1 grouped kernel, read from `JITFunction.warmup(...).metadata.shared` on GB10 (sm_121, `shared_memory_per_block_optin = 101,376`), triton 3.7.0, torch 2.12.0+cu130: | KV dtype | `num_stages` | shared memory | vs limit | |---|---|---|---| | bf16 | 1 | 59,392 | fits, 41,984 spare | | bf16 | 2 | 63,488 | fits, 37,888 spare | | fp8 | 1 | 83,968 | fits, 17,408 spare | | **fp8** | **2** | **102,400** | **1,024 over — launch fails** | ## Why not simply `or is_mla` The issue suggests widening the guard to `BLOCK_DMODEL >= 1024 or is_mla`. The table above shows the bf16 MLA path has 37,888 bytes to spare at `num_stages=2`, so that condition would drop a pipeline stage it does not need to. It would also drop it on datacenter parts, whose opt-in limit accommodates the fp8 tile comfortably. title: [Bugfix] Don't route TOWER/CONNECTOR LoRA mappings to the language wrapper
summary: ## Summary With `enable_tower_connector_lora` on, `_set_adapter_mapping` routes a TOWER or CONNECTOR `LoRAMapping` to the language-model punica wrapper whenever the model's `get_mm_mapping()` has no matching module prefixes — the dispatch falls through to the final `else`. Since `_execute_mm_encoder` emits a CONNECTOR mapping whenever `get_num_mm_connector_tokens` is present (and the `SupportsMultiModal` protocol supplies a default), a model with a tower but **no connector** gets an encoder-token-sized CONNECTOR mapping written over the language wrapper's decode-step metadata every step. title: [KV Offload] Bound staged loads by primary tier capacity
summary: > **Status: draft, superseded by RFC #66782.** Request-level promotions are now designed in #66782, which replaces the sketches discussed in this thread. Its core change (item 3) builds on #60128, which is planned to land first in its current state. title: [Bugfix][KV Offload] Handle split kernel blocks in canonical mappings
summary: ## Overview The canonical KV mapper expects cache tensors to use manager-sized blocks, but attention backends can store each manager block as several smaller kernel blocks. FlashInfer can select 64-token kernel blocks for 128-token manager blocks. The mapper does not recognize the resulting page count and shape, so it assigns a non-portable fallback mapping to an otherwise valid cache. This can cause canonical-layout validation to reject the cache and abort engine startup. For statically portable configurations, map all kernel blocks belonging to a manager block into its canonical page. Keep existing opaque mappings for topology-specific configurations so their persisted bytes remain compatible. ## Claims - Restores canonical offload initialization for statically portable attention configurations with split kernel pages. - Preserves canonical bytes, existing topology-specific fallback encodings, and unsplit layouts' transfer plans. ## Validation - Lightweight byte-mapping regressions: **12 failed before, 12 passed after**. The opaque-cache compatibility regression passes. Tests use CPU tensors and mocked configuration; no model loading or GPU is required. Full mapping suite: **48 passed**. Pre-commit passes. - Separate local model validation: SmolLM2/FlashInfer startup fails before and passes after; FS-reloaded outputs match direct offload. title: [Metrics] Add vllm:kv_admission_refusals counter
summary: Adds a per-engine Prometheus counter, `vllm:kv_admission_refusals{reason}` (`vllm:kv_admission_refusals_total`), for waiting requests the scheduler refuses KV cache blocks, labeled by the check in `allocate_slots` that refused them. ## Overview When `allocate_slots` returns `None` for a waiting request, the request stays at the head of the queue and everything behind it waits. Today nothing says why. The pool may be too small for the request, free blocks may be short, or blocks may be free but held back by the `--watermark` headroom or by the reserve for in-flight async KV loads. `vllm:kv_cache_usage_perc` and `vllm:num_requests_waiting` show that requests wait, not what blocks them, and the remedies differ: more memory, a lower watermark, or fewer concurrent P/D loads. This PR records the reason at the point `allocate_slots` refuses, most fundamental first: | `reason` | Refused because | |---|---| | `exceeds_pool_capacity` | the request needs more blocks than the pool has | | `insufficient_free_blocks` | not enough free blocks | | `watermark` | it would fit without the watermark headroom | | `inflight_load_reserve` | it would fit without the blocks reserved for in-flight prefills (`reserved_blocks`, async KV load admissions) | ## Claims - `vllm:kv_admission_refusals_total{reason}` counts waiting requests refused KV cache blocks, labeled by the check in `allocate_slots` that refused them. - Each request is counted at most once per reason while it waits. title: [Metrics] Add vllm:kv_token_slots gauge
summary: Adds a per-engine Prometheus gauge, `vllm:kv_token_slots{kv_group,kind}`, for how the token slots in the KV cache blocks of running and loading requests are used: filled, tail slack in each request's last block, and slots reserved for lookahead and speculative tokens. ## Overview KV cache memory is allocated in whole blocks. A request's last block is usually only partly filled, and blocks allocated for lookahead slots and speculative tokens hold no KV yet. `vllm:kv_cache_usage_perc` counts whole blocks, so this internal fragmentation is invisible. It grows with the block size: with `block_size=128` (common on TPU) or 256, each request wastes up to 127 or 255 slots in its last block. This PR exports, per KV cache group: | `kind` | Meaning | |---|---| | `filled` | computed tokens still held, including the tokens scheduled this step (tokens in null blocks a sliding window released are excluded) | | `tail_slack` | unused slots in each request's last computed block | | `reserved` | slots in blocks allocated past them (lookahead and speculative tokens) | `tail_slack / (filled + tail_slack)` is the fraction of held KV memory lost to partial blocks. ## Claims - `vllm:kv_token_slots` reports the three kinds above for running requests and every request in `kv_holding_waiting` (async loads in flight, and finished loads not yet admitted), per token KV cache group. title: [Perf][MiniMax-M3] Two-shot fused MoE finalize + all-reduce + norm + MXFP8 up to 512 tokens
summary: <!-- markdownlint-disable --> > **Depends on #65433**. This branch contains its 5 commits; this PR's own change is the last 3 commits. title: [Perf][MiniMax-M3] Raise the fused MoE finalize + all-reduce cap from 32 to 128 tokens
summary: <!-- markdownlint-disable --> ## Overview This extends MiniMax-M3's existing fused MoE finalize (`FUSED_MOE_FINALIZE_MAX_TOKENS = 32` on `main`) to decode steps of up to 128 tokens. On NVIDIA (SM100 family, TP without EP, NVLink multicast), MiniMax-M3 leaves a decode step's MoE top-k finalize to the next layer's input norm. A fused kernel there does the finalize + shared-expert add + TP all-reduce (one-shot multicast Lamport) + Gemma RMSNorm + MXFP8 quantization of the `qkv_proj` input. On `main` this applies only up to 32 tokens. Above 32 tokens, each MoE layer runs a slower tail: - the MoE's own finalize; - a separate shared + routed add; - FlashInfer's two-shot all-reduce + RMSNorm; - a separate MXFP8 quantization. This PR raises the cap to 128 tokens at TP ≤ 4 (64 at TP8, see Details). That covers decode steps of up to 16 requests with 7 speculative tokens (MiniMax-M3.1 Flash's DSpark recipe), or 32 requests with 3. The kernel and its numerics are unchanged; only the cap, its scaling with TP, a batch-invariance guard and the test move. ## Claims - **Cheaper per-layer MoE tail on GB300, TP4.** The whole tail was measured in situ: from the end of the routed fc2 to the start of the next `qkv_proj` GEMM, covering finalize, shared add, all-reduce + norm and MXFP8 quantization. title: [Perf] Reduce peak memory in MiMo audio residual quantization
summary: ## Summary MiMo's audio tokenizer produces discrete audio codes for the multimodal input path. Its residual vector quantizer keeps the previous decoded frame tensor alive during the next codebook lookup and decodes the last set of indices even though only the codes are returned. Release the decoded tensor after subtracting it and skip the final residual update. This preserves the sequence of residuals consumed by every selected codebook, including partial selections. ## Validation Ran the original and patched vLLM `ResidualVectorQuantization.encode` with the published XiaomiMiMo/MiMo-Audio-Tokenizer dimensions (width 1280, 20 codebooks sized 1024, 1024, then 18 × 128). Both used identical seeded FP32 weights and inputs, PyTorch 2.14.0, and the model implementation from base `2ab8e2f`. Tested RTX 3080 and A10 separately. | Input frames | Peak additional allocated CUDA memory before | After | |---:|---:|---:| | 256 | 8.51 MiB | 7.26 MiB | | 4096 | 76.05 MiB | 60.59 MiB | | 16000 | 297.06 MiB | 236.69 MiB | Code indices matched exactly at all three lengths on both GPUs. Five additional comparisons covered a single codebook, partial ranges, all codebooks, and a stop beyond the available layers. Each timing used a warmup followed by 11 synchronized measurements. At 16000 frames the median was 35.00 to 34.56 ms on RTX 3080 and 48.24 to 47.63 ms on A10. These are tokenizer-component measurements with synthetic features. End-to-end audio quality, full-model serving memory and request latency were not measured. - [x] AI assistance was used during the creation of this PR.

summary: ## Summary Fixes #67692 by enforcing an `allowed_peers` admission policy in the P2P secondary KV-offload tier (`vllm/v1/kv_offload/tiering/p2p/`) and its ZeroMQ control transport. title: [Bugfix] Pin long-lived host buffers at their exact size
summary: ## Overview torch's caching host allocator, which `pin_memory()` and `pin_memory=True` go through, rounds every block up to the next power of two. That's fine for short-lived staging buffers. But for buffers that live as long as the process the cache doesn't buy anything, and a buffer just over a power of two pins up to twice its size in page-locked memory the OS can't reclaim. This adds a small `empty_pinned()` helper (`vllm/utils/pinned_memory.py`). It allocates exactly the requested size with `cudaHostAlloc` / `hipHostMalloc` through the existing `CudaRTLibrary` wrapper and frees it once the last view is gone. I've used it in the two GiB-sized places that don't already have an open PR: - The private per-tensor CPU KV offload tier. CUDA normally uses one exactly registered region (#50094), but ROCm has been on the private tensors since #57160, so the rounding from #53042 is back there. Fixes #53042 on ROCm. - CPU-resident weights, which is what the prefetch weight offloader leaves on the host (CUDA and ROCm). Two places allocate those: the offloader's own copy, and `device_loading_context`, which moves a CPU weight to the GPU for `process_weights_after_loading` and then copies it back into a new pinned tensor. The second copy is the one that stays, so both have to change. XPU keeps torch's allocator. ## Claims - The CPU KV tier on ROCm pins exactly what it asks for instead of rounding each tensor up to a power of two. In my repro that's 4.25 GiB less page-locked memory for a 4.75 GiB tier, with identical output. - CPU-offloaded weights are pinned at their exact size too.

title: [ROCm][MiniMax-M3] Fuse qkv_proj's per-token FP8 input quant into the input RMSNorm

title: [Tracking][Spec Decode] Context Aware Sparse LM Head Tracker
summary: Tracking issue for context-aware sparse draft LM heads: the drafter computes exact logits only for a static token list plus rows picked per draft token from its hidden state, instead of reading the target's full lm_head for every draft token. ## Motivation An MTP drafter reads the target's full lm_head for every draft token. On Qwen3.8-Flash-Next that is 248,320 x 2,560 in BF16, about 1.27 GB per draft token, and at MTP k=3 on DGX Spark (GB10, 273 GB/s) these reads take 20 to 30% of the decode step. A static list of frequent tokens (FR-Spec, #58578) cuts the bytes but misses the context-specific tail: a 32k list alone loses 5.7% of average acceptance length and 33% on multilingual prompts. The context-aware part: per draft token, a rank-256 projection of the lm_head (built from its weights at load time, no calibration data) scores the rows outside the list, and the best ones get exact logits. The target verifies with its full head, so outputs are unchanged. Measured on one DGX Spark, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4 + MTP (k=3), SPEED-Bench qualitative, same-node pairs: - BF16 rows (32k list + 16k context-picked rows): +13.8% decode at c=1, +7.7% at c=4, average AL +0.1%. - NVFP4 rows: +23.3% at c=1 over the full BF16 head. - **On top of an already quantized head** (sparse head with NVFP4 rows vs the full NVFP4 draft head, same node, c=1, MTP k=3 to 8): +5.5 to 7.9% on Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (NVFP4 copy from #59973), +8.0 to 13.7% on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and +5.5 to 12.2% on Qwen3.8-27B (checkpoint NVFP4 heads). At c=4: +0.5 to 6.7%, +4.2 to 6.9% and +3.2 to 10.3%. The gain grows with draft

summary: ## Overview The full-sequence admission gate (`allocate_slots(..., full_sequence_must_fit=True)`, which the scheduler uses whenever `scheduler_reserve_full_isl` is on, the default) checks the prompt alone. title: [Perf][Model Runner V2] Skip no-op staged-write flush of BlockTables.num_blocks
summary: ## Summary / motivation `BlockTables.apply_staged_writes()` ends with an unconditional `num_blocks.copy_to_uva()` on every step, but `num_blocks.np` is written only in `append_block_ids`. On decode steps where no block was appended (the common case between block-boundary crossings), the flush re-copies an unchanged buffer. On platforms with mapped pinned host memory each `copy_to_uva` is a cheap CPU-side memcpy, but on the fallback path — no mapped pinned memory, which is the common case on non-CUDA platforms such as Ascend — every flush issues a real H2D copy with per-call launch overhead. A decode step that appended no blocks therefore pays one wasted pinned-buffer memcpy plus one wasted H2D copy per step. This PR tracks a dirty flag set by `append_block_ids` and makes the flush a no-op when clean. Steps that append blocks flush exactly as before; data flow, values, and flush ordering are unchanged. The same dirty-flag pattern is already used upstream by `ThinkingBudgetState._budget_dirty`. Scope note: the equivalent guard for the `Sampler` staged-write flush already exists in `add_requests` (guarded by `scheduled_new_reqs`, landed with the `update_states` refactor #32562 and #36824), so this PR is limited to `BlockTables.num_blocks`. Relation to the downstream plugin: vllm-ascend carried this as a monkey patch (vllm-ascend#20135); its maintainer asked to move the optimization into vLLM upstream instead of maintaining a downstream patch, hence this PR. title: [RFC] Declarative metrics hooks, metric levels, and a runtime level control plane
summary: ## Summary We would like upstream discussion on a small observability control plane that lets deployments: 1. **Add metric points declaratively** (YAML symbol hooks + handlers), without editing scheduler / model-runner business code for each new series. 2. **Gate expensive metrics by level** (`basic` / `detail`), so the default path stays cheap. 3. **Change the active level at runtime** (config hot-reload and/or an HTTP / utility-RPC command that reaches every EngineCore and worker). vLLM Ascend has a working prototype of (1)–(3) on top of **MS Service Metric** (`ms_service_metric`). Parts of the control plane currently require an Ascend-side monkeypatch because vLLM lacks a stable extension point. We want to upstream the *shape* of the design (and eventually drop the patch), not dump Ascend-specific handlers into core as-is. **Related prototype:** https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-ascend/pull/19776 **MS Service Metric docs:** https://gitcode.com/Ascend/msserviceprofiler/blob/master/ms_service_metric/README.md --- ## Motivation - Production dashboards need a **small always-on set** of metrics; debug / deep profiling needs **opt-in, higher-overhead** series (per-step histograms, high cardinality, host-side work). - Shipping every new series as a hard-coded edit in scheduler / runner does not scale across backends (CUDA / Ascend / …). - Operators need a **safe runtime dial** (raise level while debugging, lower it again) that reaches **all processes**, including pipeline stages that do not run the same file-reload path as the wave head. summary: ## Overview Run empty-chat validation inside the existing pre-admission KV cleanup wrapper. title: [Bugfix][EPD] Clear ECMooncakeConnector local cache on reset_encoder_cache
summary: ## Purpose Resetting the encoder cache on the prefill/decode (PD) instance can break the next request that uses the same image. ``` A -> A -> succeed (HTTP 200; the model answered "Gray.") A -> reset PD -> A -> fail (Encoder cache miss / EngineDeadError / HTTP 500) -> PD EngineCore shutdown ``` The PD engine has already dropped the embedding, but the Mooncake connector still thinks it is local, so it does not load the embedding from the Encoder again. The engine then hits an empty cache and raises an unhandled `RuntimeError: Encoder cache miss`. EngineCore treats this as a fatal error, the request returns `EngineDeadError` (HTTP 500), and the PD API server shuts down EngineCore. The root cause is a bookkeeping gap. `Scheduler.reset_encoder_cache()` only called `encoder_cache_manager.reset()`, which clears EncoderCacheManager hashes without populating `freed`. The connector's `_local_cache` is only discarded later, in `build_connector_meta`, via `free_encoder_mm_hashes`. After a reset that path never runs, so `_local_cache` stays stale. On the next identical multimodal request, `ensure_cache_available()` sees `mm_hash in _local_cache` (and/or a READY transfer) and skips Load. This PR adds `ECConnectorBase.reset()` (default no-op), calls it from `Scheduler.reset_encoder_cache` after the EncoderCacheManager is cleared, and implements it for Mooncake. The contract is cache bookkeeping only: after reset, the connector must not treat the already-cleared local Encoder Cache as a hit, and must not schedule an already-consumed transfer. - Clear `_local_cache` and related scheduler b

title: [Bugfix] Exit EngineCore and workers when their parent is SIGKILLed
summary: ## Purpose When the process that owns an `LLM` or an engine is SIGKILLed (OOM killer, `kill -9`, a scheduler tearing a job down), `VLLM::EngineCore` and its `VLLM::Worker_*` keep running and keep their device memory; this arms `prctl(PR_SET_PDEATHSIG)` in both so they exit with their parent. EngineCore is not a daemon process, and a worker only watches its death pipe once `WorkerProc.__init__` returns, and that pipe is never closed if the engine core itself was SIGKILLed, so today nothing reaps them. The kernel signal goes to a handler that checks the parent is really gone, because `PR_SET_PDEATHSIG` also fires when the thread that started the process exits while the parent lives on; a parent that died before the call took effect is caught by re-checking right after it. Linux only; a no-op elsewhere. Prior art: #34816 (same two entry points, arming `SIGTERM` directly without either check) was closed by the stale bot. #40935 (open draft) covers EngineCore but not the workers, adds macOS/Windows watchers, and on Linux arms `SIGTERM` directly and only checks for a reparent to pid 1. The control rows below show what each check catches. ## Test Plan ```bash pytest tests/utils_/test_system_utils.py -k test_set_parent_death_signal ``` Three cases, each in a real `multiprocessing` child: the parent is SIGKILLed (child must exit), the thread that started the child exits while the parent lives (child must survive), and the parent exits before the child arms (child must exit). title: [Core] Stop re-queuing waiting requests that max_loras blocks
summary: ## Overview Once `max_loras` adapters are scheduled, the waiting loop in `Scheduler.schedule()` pops and re-queues every waiting request for another adapter on each step that reaches the waiting queue, so step time grows with the blocked queue. Under the FCFS policy this change defers those requests without running the per-request checks on them, and leaves them in place when no request behind them needs those checks. This matters for a multi-LoRA server with more adapters in demand than `max_loras` and a backlog of queued requests. I haven't seen a report of it, and the numbers below are scheduler CPU time on a synthetic case, not end-to-end serving. ## Claims - FCFS with 64 running requests on 2 adapters (`max_loras=2`) and 5,000 waiting on 50 other adapters: `schedule()` plus `update_from_output()` drops from 3.72 to 0.60 ms per step on CPU. That is the best case, where no waiting request can be admitted. In a smaller case (2 long requests on both adapters, `max_num_seqs=4`) with 3,000 admittable requests behind 5,000 blocked ones, the blocked ones are still popped and re-queued on the way, and the step drops from 1.85 to 0.59 ms. - Priority keeps main's scan and its cost: 8.20 ms (main) vs 8.10 ms (this PR) per step in the same case. The previous head was 2 to 3% slower here, because the scan's `max_loras` check had become a call per request; that check is main's code again. - Without LoRA, and with LoRA when one blocked request heads the queue and nothing behind it can be skipped, step time is within run-to-run spread of main (table below). - One shape is slower: reque

title: [RFC]: Incremental MoE Expert Offloading — GPU Cache + Async Pipeline
summary: ## Summary Dynamic MoE expert weight offloading for vLLM. Expert weights live in CPU pinned memory; a fixed-size GPU cache holds the hottest experts; LFRU eviction and cross-layer prediction minimize cache misses. Models that exceed GPU VRAM can run on smaller hardware. **PR 1 is open:** [#37190](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/37190) (~980 LOC Python, passing CI). This RFC covers the full 3-PR architecture and provides production data from [tinyserve](https://github.com/e1n00r/tinyserve), an independent implementation of the same techniques (30 tok/s decode on 8 GB GPU, 550+ tests). ## Motivation Large MoE models (DeepSeek-V3 671B, Qwen3.5-122B) don't fit in a single GPU. Only a small subset of experts activates per token (e.g., 8 of 256), so most expert weights sit idle. Moving cold experts to CPU and caching hot ones on GPU lets these models run on hardware that would otherwise OOM. ### Prior art in vLLM | PR | What it does | Limitation this RFC addresses | |---|---|---| | [#34535](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/34535) (merged) | Static CPU weight offload | No runtime migration — offloaded weights stay on CPU permanently | | [#29941](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/29941) (merged) | Async H2D prefetch for non-MoE weights | Pattern reused for expert prefetch in PR 2 | | [RFC #33869](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/33869) / [#31938](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/31938) | Monolithic MoE offload (cache + CPU kernels + DBO + prefetch) | Closed — too large to review/pass CI. title: [Bugfix][Quantization] Keep fp32 weight_scale during batch-invariant FP8 dequantization
summary: ## Overview When `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1` takes the BF16 dequantization fallback (`not fp8_scaled_mm_is_batch_invariant(self.fp8_linear)`), `Fp8LinearMethod.apply`, `Fp8PerTensorOnlineLinearMethod.apply`, and `Fp8PtpcOnlineLinearMethod.apply` cast `layer.weight_scale` from `float32` to `bfloat16` (or `x.dtype`) before multiplying by `layer.weight`. When this fallback runs eagerly without Inductor (for example under `--enforce-eager`, `TORCH_COMPILE_DISABLE=1`, `-O0`, or compilation mode `NONE`), it double-rounds weights through `RN_bf16(w * RN_bf16(s))` instead of computing the product in `float32` and casting it once to `bfloat16` (`RN_bf16(RN_fp32(w * s))`). title: [RFC][HiSparse] On-Demand KV Gather and Layerwise Two-Slot Reuse for Sparse-MLA (DSA) Prefill
summary: ### Motivation. HiSparse already offloads large sparse-MLA (DSA) main KV to CPU memory, keeps lightweight indexer KV on GPU, and resolves decode KV on demand from top-k indices. However, as noted in the [HiSparse design doc](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/55aa0cab78dedbb018ad4f4ea649f2d3d5e1c2a8/docs/design/hisparse.md#L219-L220), *"prefill and mixed prefill/decode batches retain per-layer staging."* This proposal builds on HiSparse's CPU offload framework to complete prefill data loading and buffering. Long-context prefill requests typically fall into two patterns. **Short-append requests** (common in multi-turn agent and coding workloads) hit long CPU-cached prefixes with only a few new tokens; per-layer compute is brief, so H2D history loading dominates latency. **Large-chunk requests** (such as later chunks in chunked prefill or long appends after a CPU prefix hit) have longer per-layer compute windows, while concurrency and long sequences put heavy pressure on GPU memory capacity. In practice, the scheduler frequently batches both request types together. For short-append requests, indexer KV stays on GPU and produces top-k indices before main KV is loaded, yet [HiSparse's current prefill path](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/55aa0cab78dedbb018ad4f4ea649f2d3d5e1c2a8/vllm/v1/hisparse/runtime.py#L785) builds a full-history staging layout and reads every non-resident history row from CPU. title: [Frontend][Performance] Reuse tokenized text across session turns
summary: ## Review guide This PR adds tokenization reuse for text chat sessions. Each page links to its incremental code. If you prefer reviewing everything together or as stacked PRs, I can switch. ## Overview Successive chat turns often resend a long conversation with only a small addition. This PR avoids tokenizing the unchanged text again by retaining the previous rendered prompt and token IDs for each session. Clients continue to send complete requests; an agent hint—the existing `session_id` field—selects the previous prompt to compare, and text comparison determines what can be reused. See [RFC #63359](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/63359). ## Claims - Opt-in reuse of tokenized text across session turns, with a configurable CPU memory budget; disabled by default. - In a synthetic replay of growing chat histories, frontend CPU time per request decreased **25.1%** and mean time to first output decreased **19.7%** across four pairs of runs. End-to-end request latency decreased about **1.0%**. Short independent requests did not show a consistent benefit. ## Validation Qwen3-0.6B on an RTX 3090, FP16, four concurrent clients, with prefix caching, chunked prefill and CUDA graphs enabled. title: [RFC]: Opt-in online quantization of the target model LM head
summary: ### Motivation. Would the vLLM community be interested in a general, opt-in mechanism to quantize the **target model's output LM head** online? In some comparatively smaller models, the vocabulary projection can be a meaningful portion of decode work and memory traffic. We evaluated a 27B model on Ascend and observed close accuracy and lower TPOT in our measured workloads. TTFT improved in some workloads, but not all; these results are platform- and workload-specific. Some existing quantization backends already support quantized heads, and targeted online quantization exists for supported module families via [#51285](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51285). We would like feedback on how to extend or integrate these mechanisms for `ParallelLMHead`, including mixed checkpoints where the body is pre-quantized but the head is floating point. This is a proposal for discussion, not a claim that vLLM has no quantized-head support today. Related: [#50281](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/50281) and [#40999](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/40999). vLLM already supports opt-in draft LM head quantization in Model Runner V2 for eligible MTP/EAGLE drafters that would otherwise share the target head, via `draft_lm_head_quantization` ([#59973](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/59973)). It gives the drafter a private quantized head while the target retains its original head for verification. This RFC focuses on quantizing the target head itself, and asks how the two features should interact. ### Proposed Change. - Provide an opt-in way to select onli

title: [Spec Decode] Broaden NVFP4 draft LM-head validation beyond GB10: Memra results and Blackwell/model matrix
summary: ## Context Thanks for landing #59973. I wanted to connect its DGX Spark / Qwen3.8-Flash-Next results to independent, earlier measurements in [Memra](https://github.com/avifenesh/memra), and suggest a broader evaluation of **draft-only LM-head quantization** across Blackwell GPUs, model families and speculative workloads. This is **not a request to replace or reimplement #59973**, nor a claim that the two implementations have identical benchmarks. The point is to make the optimization useful beyond the one GB10/model combination, and to share reproducible evidence. ## Independent results and lessons from Memra Memra's published [draft-regime documentation](https://github.com/avifenesh/memra/blob/main/docs/DRAFT-REGIME.md) reports that quantizing the MTP draft head to **NVFP4** incurred *no measurable acceptance penalty versus Q5_K* in its tested configuration, with approximately one-quarter of the head bytes. This was established before the vLLM merge and is a separate observation from FR-Spec vocabulary trimming. The [trimmed-draft builder](https://github.com/avifenesh/memra/blob/main/tools/make-trimmed-draft.sh) records an end-to-end Qwen 27B draft configuration at **101 tok/s, 85.2% acceptance (K=3)** versus a previous daily draft at **99.6 tok/s, 83.3% acceptance**. **That is a combined draft-artifact comparison, not an isolated NVFP4-head A/B**, so it should not be quoted as a quantization-only speedup. The [Ornith-1.5-35B-A3B artifact/receipts](https://github.com/avifenesh/memra/blob/main/research/ornith15-st-nvfp4-20260819/RECEIPTS.md) document another family using NV

title: [Mamba] Declare prefill checkpoint alignment once per layer
summary: ## Overview Each Mamba layer declares the token alignment of the prefill checkpoints it can export from inside a forward pass once, in `MambaBase.get_prefill_checkpoint_alignment()`. `MambaBase.get_kv_cache_spec` derives `num_prefill_checkpoint_blocks` and `prefill_checkpoint_alignment` from it. Mamba2 (#57329), GLM-5.3-Flash KDA (#56960) and Kimi-K3 KDA (NVIDIA and AMD) drop their `get_kv_cache_spec` overrides. Split out of #60050. ## Claims - Spec fields are unchanged when every Mamba layer of the model declares an alignment, which holds for all Mamba2 and KDA models: Mamba2 `1`, FlashKDA `16`, ROCm fused KDA `KDA_CHECKPOINT_ALIGNMENT`. Mamba layers that declare none still get no checkpoint fields. - Four copies of the same `replace(spec, num_prefill_checkpoint_blocks=..., prefill_checkpoint_alignment=...)` override become one, so the two fields can no longer disagree. A checkpoint block reserved without an alignment would cache a state that is never written. - The platform gets one place to read a layer's checkpoint grid. #60050 (merged) reads it to keep align-mode blocks on FlashInfer GDN's 64-token grid, and with this PR the KDA layers' alignments feed the same rule. That has no effect for FlashKDA (`16`). title: [RFC]: Octave KV, a native 3-bit KV cache for AMD GPUs
summary: PR: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/59774 ### Proposal to improve performance ## Where this comes from We serve Qwen3.8-27B (GPTQ W4A16) on boxes with four RX 7900 XTX, 96 GB in total, with tensor parallel 4 and MTP. Our users send long prompts: whole repositories, long documents, agent sessions that run for hours. With an fp16 KV cache and 8 GB per GPU for it, a box holds about 446k tokens, so one long request fills it. On ROCm today the options below 8 bits are TurboQuant, UltraQuant (#57057, gfx950 only) and KVarN (#46613, CUDA-first). We tried TurboQuant first, since it is merged and its idea (random rotation plus a Lloyd-Max codebook) is the right one. On our hardware three things got in the way: - With MTP on (`qwen3_next_mtp`, k=3) every preset produced garbage, and GSM8K fell to around 1%. Without MTP it was correct. - Its multi-token path copies between host and device per layer, so it cannot be captured in CUDA graphs. - Its Triton kernels are slow on RDNA3. At 380k tokens the first token took 621 s, against 371 s with fp16. So we wrote our own backend: same family of ideas, a few changes to the format, and every kernel in HIP. Against TurboQuant on the same hardware it comes out ahead on all three things we care about. It holds as many tokens or more at each size: at about 200 bytes per slot the two hold 2.07M and 2.05M tokens, and our 216-byte format holds 6% more than TurboQuant's 230-byte one. It loses less: 2.5× less excess NLL at 380k at the same size, and GSM8K stays at fp16 level (91.8-92.4 against 89.8). And it is faster: per layer at 380k, deco

title: [Perf][Kernel] Add bias + GELU + NVFP4 quant to the SM120 NVFP4 GEMM epilogue
summary: ## Overview With #65578, the FFN of NVFP4 BERT-style encoders still writes the up projection's 4x-wide output in 16 bits and reads it back for the bias add + GELU + NVFP4 quant of the down projection's input. BERT calls it through `maybe_fused_mm_act_quant`, the GEMM-level counterpart of `maybe_fused_act_quant` (cf. `fused_gemm1` in MiniMax-M3), via a custom op that keeps #65578's kernels below 128 tokens, where one 128-row tile is mostly padding. title: [Spec Decode] Measure the Dynamic SD table instead of writing it by hand
summary: # [Spec Decode] Measure the Dynamic SD table instead of writing it by hand Towards #62740. ## Why this is needed **What vLLM supports.** PR #32374 added the Dynamic SD hardcoded table. PR #57053 makes V2 honor the runtime K. This PR builds on both. It writes the table that #32374 reads. **What is missing.** The values of the table. The #32374 branch drafted an offline profiler which was removed before merge. The docs tell the user to write the table by hand. **Why that matters.** The documented example works on some dense models but on a MoE model it loses up to 18% throughput. The failure is silent, as reported in https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/49548 and https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/49986. No user can tell which case their model is in. The best fixed K loses 12.7% at some load on the same setup where a measured table loses 3.4% — so the table mechanism pays, but only with the right values. **Relation to adaptive verification.** AV does one job: it decides how many drafted tokens to verify. It does not set how many tokens the engine drafts. The Dynamic SD table sets that number. The two features do different jobs, and they compose: the table caps drafting at each batch size, and AV trims verification inside that cap. **This is where production systems are going.** DeepSeek does the same in production: their [DeepInfer](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepinfer) inference stack, built on vLLM, drafts 5 tokens per step with DSpark and schedules verification from a profiled hardware throughput curve ([their deployment Q&A](https://github.com/deepseek

summary: ## Overview Add daemon-to-daemon weight seeding to the preload stack: a second replica's daemons fill their shards from an already-loaded replica instead of reading the checkpoint again. title: [Model] Support sequence parallelism with pipeline parallelism for Qwen3-Next, Qwen3.5 and DeepSeek-V2/V3
summary: <!-- markdownlint-disable --> ## Overview Enable sequence-parallel MoE (SP) with pipeline parallelism (PP) for Qwen3-Next, Qwen3.5, and models using `DeepseekV2DecoderLayer`: DeepSeek-V3/R1, Kimi-K2, DeepSeek-V2, Mistral Large 3, and the DeepSeek MTP drafter. With DP > 1, TP > 1, and EP, these models keep token shards on each TP rank between layers. They currently disable this optimization under PP because the next stage expects full-token tensors replicated across TP ranks. This PR restores that layout with an all-gather at each non-last stage's exit, then re-shards where needed in the next stage, following DeepSeek-V4 (#65766) and MiniMax-M3 (#65537). Credit to @AceCoder0 for first enabling this combination in #53191 (last updated 2026-08-21). This PR also covers `vllm/models/qwen3_5/nvidia/model.py` and keeps SP enabled for small batches. #53191 added a small-batch all-reduce fallback for Qwen3-Next after observing NaNs on Ascend; on CUDA, Qwen3-Next and Qwen3.5 match the SP-off baseline in concurrency-1 GSM8K without that fallback. ## Claims - Enable SP under PP for Qwen3-Next, Qwen3.5, and DeepSeek-V2/V3 with DP > 1, TP > 1, and EP. - GSM8K scores are within run-to-run noise of PP1 with SP. Prompt-logprob differences from PP1 are no larger than those of PP2 on main. - Qwen3.5 throughput is comparable to main. DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Qwen3-Next decode throughput is about 4% lower than main; DeepSeek-V2-Lite shows a similar SP decode cost at PP1, so PP now has the same trade-off as PP1. - Qwen3.5 MTP under PP with SP achieves comparable GSM8K accuracy and acceptance length

title: [DeepSeek-V3.2] Support sequence parallelism with pipeline parallelism
summary: <!-- markdownlint-disable --> ## Overview Enable sequence parallelism (SP) with pipeline parallelism (PP) for DeepSeek-V3.2 on NVIDIA GPUs, fixing incorrect results on `main` when PP > 1, DP > 1, TP > 1, and expert parallelism (EP) are enabled. That path also incorrectly scales the MoE output by the TP size. ## Claims - DeepSeek-V3.2 with PP > 1, DP > 1, TP > 1, and EP now uses the same SP path as PP = 1. - GSM8K accuracy matches PP1 at 0.955, and mean NLL is comparable: 0.928 versus 0.932 at PP1. On `main`, this configuration yields GSM8K accuracy of 0.858 and mean NLL of 1.511. - With one token per decode step (requests sent one at a time), PP2 produces the same tokens and logprobs as PP1. title: [V1] Fix KV cache capacity discrepancy between cold and warm starts under torch.compile (#54383)
summary: ### Purpose Resolves #54383. ### Root Cause When booting under `torch.compile` on a cold start, JIT compilation occurs during `model_runner.profile_run()` inside `Worker.determine_available_memory()`. Transient compiler scratchpads and Triton workspace inflate the peak activation snapshot, permanently reducing the allocated KV cache pool by ~5% (e.g. 5,408 tokens on Qwen3-32B AWQ) compared to subsequent warm boots. ### Solution - Under `torch.compile` (`compilation_config.mode != CompilationMode.NONE`), trigger an initial compilation pass ahead of memory profiling. - Purge compiler scratchpad buffers via `gc.collect()`, `torch.accelerator.empty_cache()`, and `torch.accelerator.synchronize()`. - Added unit tests in `tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_worker.py` parameterized over `CompilationMode` to verify that warmup execution and accelerator cleanup fire strictly when compilation is enabled and are skipped in eager mode. ### Scope Clarification This change strictly isolates the cold-start profiling memory inflation under `torch.compile`. It does not touch memory pooling logic, startup plan persistence, or allocator split limits. ### Community Impact & Reproduction Verified with independent reproduction on dual RTX 4090s (@vitalyrodnenko in #54383) and A100-80GB, restoring 100% cold/warm KV cache token parity. ### Testing - `uvx ruff check`: 0 errors, 0 warnings. - `uvx ruff format --check`: clean formatting. - Unit tests: CPU-first simulation in `tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_worker.py::test_compilation_warmup_before_memory_profiling`.

title: [Bugfix][MRv1] Decouple async Mamba align D2H counts from InputBatch row shifts (#51571)
summary: ### Purpose Fixes #51571: In ModelRunner V1 (`MRv1`) with hybrid models (Mamba / GatedDeltaNet) and speculative decoding (MTP), accepted token counts get out of sync when requests finish and batch rows shift, leading to repeated/corrupted tokens. ### Root Cause 1. **Async Mode (`use_async_scheduling=True`):** Step N copies accepted token counts over D2H asynchronously. Meanwhile, Step N+1 runs `_update_states()` on CPU (`condense()`, `swap_states()`). If D2H writes straight to `InputBatch.num_accepted_tokens_cpu_tensor`, the in-flight DMA races with CPU row moves, and gathering through `prev_positions` in `_prepare_inputs()` permutes the counts twice. 2. **Sync Mode (`use_async_scheduling=False`):** In sync mode, execution finishes before row moves, so `InputBatch` naturally moves counts with requests. As @amittell and @WonkaRed pointed out, doing an unconditional 1:1 copy from the runner buffer in `_prepare_inputs()` overwrites the newly moved rows with stale Step N indices (`[2, 4, 1]` regressed to `[5, 4, 3]`). ### Solution - **Async mode (`use_async_scheduling=True`):** D2H copies to `self.num_accepted_tokens.cpu` (runner buffer). In `_prepare_inputs()`, `_sync_num_accepted_tokens()` remaps counts through `prev_positions` and updates `input_batch`. - **Sync mode (`use_async_scheduling=False`):** D2H copies to `self.input_batch.num_accepted_tokens_cpu_tensor` directly. We also sync `num_accepted_tokens_event` at the start of `_update_states()` so the copy finishes before requests are removed or condensed. title: [V1 Scheduler] Fix Priority Queue Preemption Re-admission (#41951)
summary: Fixes #41951 (supersedes #41952, #56843) ### Why this change is needed In v1 with `scheduling_policy="priority"`, `PriorityRequestQueue` sorts waiting requests using `Request.__lt__`, which only compared `(priority, arrival_time)`. When a running request got preempted due to KV memory pressure, it was pushed back into the heap. If a fresh request with the same priority arrived earlier but hadn't started yet, the heap popped the fresh request first. This left the preempted request sitting idle while incoming requests overwrote its partially computed KV blocks, wasting GPU work and forcing a full recompute once re-admitted. ### What changed 1. **Sort preempted requests ahead of fresh ones (`vllm/v1/request.py`)**: Added a `sort_key` property on `Request` and routed `__lt__` through it, boosting preempted requests with `-min(num_preemptions, 3)`. Capping at 3 gives re-admission priority without letting repeatedly preempted requests starve incoming queries. 2. **Anti-thrashing in victim selection (`vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py`)**: Updated the preemption victim key to `(r.priority, -min(r.num_preemptions, 3), r.arrival_time)` so the scheduler victimizes least-preempted requests first instead of repeatedly thrashing the same request. 3. Consolidated this fix with @Aravind0403 (who diagnosed the original issue in #41951) and incorporated their unit tests with co-authorship. This only touches `priority` mode; default FCFS queues and speculative decode paths are unaffected. ### Testing - `pytest tests/v1/test_request.py -k "test_request_priority_comparison"` (passes) - `pytest t

Finer hits cache more blocks per request, so they can lose hits when the KV cache is nearly full, which is why this is opt-in. The video budget, frame count and profiling dummy are sized from image settings, while the processor resizes video frames with `video_min_pixels`/`video_max_pixels`. This PR sizes them from the video pixel limits, so startup profiles the largest admitted video: the engine either reserves enough memory for it or fails at startup. Follows #66608 (merged). The video encoding itself is unchanged. ## Claims - On one A100 80GB at 16384 and 24576, main runs out of memory in the vision encoder on the first admitted video (a 4,645-token prompt). With this PR all tested videos complete, including full-budget ones (15,569 / 23,941 prompt tokens); inputs are random-pixel frames at the sizes listed below. - Profiling now covers the largest admitted video, so it reserves more: 5.57 / 8.87 GiB for transient activations and 173,056 / 64,512 KV cache tokens at 16384 / 24576 (main: 0.68 / 1.27 GiB, 323,584 / 312,320 tokens). At 32768 a full-budget video does not fit on 80 GB, and startup fails with `No available memory for the cache blocks`, where main starts and then crashes on an 11,581-token video. Video size hints in `limit_mm_per_prompt` shrink the profiled video (below). - With default settings the per-item video budget equals the profiled video at every context length checked (8192 to 131072), also under `max_pixels`/`video_max_pix

title: [Perf][Mamba] Optimize prefill splits for mid-block resume (3 forward passes to 1)
summary: ## Overview For hybrid (Mamba "align") prefix caching: when a request resumes from a prefix hit in the middle of a Mamba block and its prompt ends in the next block, main runs it in up to 3 steps (stop at the block boundary, stop at the checkpoint, then the rest). This PR runs it in 1 step by letting the checkpoint state be written into the block the request resumed from, in its block table. Builds on #67717, which keeps blocks a mid-block resume ran past from getting the full-block hash; this PR relies on that to put the checkpoint in the resumed block. ## Motivating example Kimi K3.1, one aggregated instance with TP8 + DCP8 (2 × 4 GB300), `--enable-prefix-caching --prefix-match-unit 128`, `--max-num-batched-tokens 16384`. The block size is 1280 tokens, and prefix-cache hits land on 128-token boundaries. Two requests in one conversation: - **Request 1** has a 1,984-token prompt. Its cached Mamba state is at 1,920, the last 128-token boundary, which is in the middle of block 1 (tokens 1,280–2,560). - **Request 2** continues the conversation: request 1's prompt and answer plus a new user turn, 2,880 tokens. It hits the cache at 1,920 (`cached_tokens: 1920`), so 960 new tokens remain. Its prompt ends in block 2. **main**: 3 forward passes for request 2's prefill (`--enable-logging-iteration-details`): ``` Iteration(76): 1 context requests, 640 context tokens # 1920 -> 2560: stop at the block boundary Iteration(77): 1 context requests, 256 context tokens # 2560 -> 2816: stop at the checkpoint Iteration(78): 1 context requests, 64 context tokens # 2816 -> 2880: the rest ``` **T

title: [Perf][Qwen4Exp] Drop the defensive zero fill from the QSA output path
summary: <!-- markdownlint-disable --> ## Overview Remove the defensive `output.zero_()` from the real QSA forward path for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (Qwen4Exp), and strengthen tests for the kernel’s output-write contract. This is the QSA equivalent of the merged GDN change in [#64419](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/64419). ## Claims - Eliminate one full padded-output zero fill per QSA layer during inference. - Preserve bit-identical actual-row outputs: the attention kernels are unchanged and overwrite every actual row. - Enforce write coverage with a NaN-poisoned output buffer in the kernel correctness test. ## Validation On B300 (`sm_103`): ```bash python -m pytest tests/models/qwen4_exp/test_qsa_reference.py tests/models/qwen4_exp/test_qsa_prepare.py -x -q ``` Result: **98 passed in 119s**. - The modified correctness test uses a NaN-poisoned output buffer and covers both dispatch arms: Triton split-K and the Blackwell fp8 decode kernel. title: [Kernel][MoE] Batch every per-expert MoE weight prep loop (TRT-LLM FP4/MXINT4/FP8/BF16, CUTLASS MXFP4)
summary: ## Purpose Part of #54477. Direct reload reruns cold-start post-load processing on every update, so MoE weight prep runs once per update. Several prep paths worked one expert at a time: a Python loop of small gathers, interleaves or swizzles per expert, often byte by byte. Every per-expert loop in MoE weight prep now runs as one batched operation. Permutations depend only on the per-expert shape, so each is computed once and applied to all experts in one gather (`gather_rows` in `quant_utils`), moving whole rows in the widest word that divides a row: - **DeepSeek-V4 MXFP4 (TRT-LLM):** the w3/w1 interleave is folded into the shuffle permutation, so each tensor is gathered once. - **gpt-oss MXFP4 (TRT-LLM):** the w1/w3 swap is folded into each permutation; the scale interleave runs once over `[E, N, K]`. - **NVFP4 static prep (TRT-LLM)** (`prepare_static_weights_for_trtllm_fp4_moe`): one gather per tensor, one scale interleave over all experts. - **MXINT4 static prep (TRT-LLM)** (`prepare_static_weights_for_trtllm_mxint4_moe`): one gather per tensor; the weight gather also writes the block layout (`gather_rows(..., block_k)`). - **FP8 per-tensor (TRT-LLM)** (`rotate_weights_for_fi_trtllm_fp8_per_tensor_moe`): the gated-activation row reorder and the shuffle are composed into one index, applied in place. - **BF16 block layout (TRT-LLM)** (`convert_moe_weights_to_flashinfer_trtllm_block_layout`): experts are gathered in chunks of ~1 GiB instead of one at a time, still in place. - **CUTLASS MXFP4 scale swizzle** (oracle `_swizzle_cutlass_mxfp4_scales`, compressed-tensors W4A4 MX
