title: [Feat] hicache: opt-in exclusive L2->L3 tiering, dedup cache-mode L3 writes through the existence cache
summary: ## Motivation With `--hicache-storage-backend` in cache mode, storage (L3) is written at L2 admission: every page that enters the host pool is also written to storage. L3 therefore always holds a superset of L2 and adds no reusable capacity. A prefix that is evicted from host is only in L3 if its write happened to complete, and a prefix that is still in host is fetched from host anyway. On a Mooncake store shared by several prefill workers this showed up as a store that turns over constantly (every L2 admission is a put) while the hit rate does not move. This PR adds an opt-in mode where L3 is written from the coldest host pages ahead of their eviction instead. The two tiers then hold different pages and L3 becomes an overflow layer for L2. Measured on Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-NVFP4, GB300, 3P:2D PD-disaggregated, AgentX closed-loop trace at concurrency 1000: 142.2K total TPS/GPU without a store, 152.2K with the store in this mode (+7%); host hit rate held at 93.1%. At concurrency 850, where the host pool alone already covers the working set, the extra write traffic costs about 1.5%, which is why the mode is opt-in. The second commit fixes write-side dedup in cache mode. A recompute after L2 eviction re-creates a node with `backuped=False`, so the node flag alone re-writes content that L3 already holds. `write_backup_storage` now skips spans the `StorageExistenceCache` covers, and beliefs are recorded on the storage ack from the full hash chain (not the `completed_tokens`-truncated one) so ranks cannot diverge in the write/skip decision. title: [Fix] [AMD] dsv4: Read preshuffled indexer keys in TileLang
summary: ## Problem #31563 made AITER's 16×16 preshuffled layout a paired writer/reader contract for the DeepSeek-V4 indexer cache: when `aiter_can_use_preshuffle_paged_mqa()` is true, the cache writers store each page's FP8 keys in tiles of 16 tokens × 16 bytes, and the AITER reader reads them back the same way. The TileLang reader (`SGLANG_OPT_USE_TILELANG_INDEXER=true`) was not updated. It still treats every 128 bytes of the page as one token's key, so each key it builds is stitched together from 16-byte pieces of 8 different tokens. Only 128 of the 8192 key bytes in a page are where it expects them. Every byte is still a valid FP8 value, so nothing crashes or turns NaN; the indexer just scores the wrong keys and picks the wrong top-512 blocks for sparse attention. Short contexts hide it: with at most 512 visible compressed blocks, top-512 selects all of them whatever the scores are. We replayed one saved long DeepSeek-V4-Flash request on CPU and compared the cached keys with reference keys recomputed from the compressor input: - Decoded with the 16×16 layout, they match (mean cosine similarity 0.9997 over 2124 keys; the gap is FP8 rounding). The writers store the right keys, in 16×16 tiles. - Read row-major, as the old reader does, they are unrelated to the reference (0.068). The bug is in the reader. - As a result, the block selection is close to random. When generating token 8191, the indexer has to keep 512 of about 2048 history blocks; only 26% of the blocks the old reader keeps are ones it should keep, and keeping 512 blocks at random would already get 25% right. ## When it

title: [Feat] kv-compression: Share encoded KV across P/D transfer and HiCache L2
summary: ## Motivation Related to #39740 — Pluggable KV Compression for Disaggregated Serving. This draft adds an optional shared KV compression layer to Mooncake P/D transfer and Prefill HiCache L2. The same encoded representation can be transferred, retained across requests, reused without re-encoding, and restored after GPU KV eviction. Attention continues to read the model's existing GPU KV layout and dtype. The contribution is lifecycle integration: sharing representations while preserving source protection, cache identity, request admission, transfer completion, and safe reclamation. LZ4 and ANS are reference lossless backends; this PR does not claim a serving speedup or a stable public plugin ABI. ## Design and Modifications ### Ownership boundaries HiCache owns prefix matching, backup and restoration admission, eviction, references, and cache publication. P/D owns transfer-range selection, protocol metadata, RDMA submission, and remote completion. The shared layer owns packing, encoding/decoding, representation compatibility, leases, and bounded execution resources. ```text Prefill GPU KV | Pack / Encode | Shared encoded objects / \ v v GPU wire buffer Prefill HiCache L2 | / \ Mooncake RDMA Restore Reuse for P/D | | without re-encoding Decode restoration v | HiCache adoption v | Decode GPU KV Prefill GPU KV ``` P/D compression can run with L2 disabled. Retained Host objects are gathered into an independent GPU wire buffer before transmission; this is representation reuse, not zero-copy Host RDMA. L2 residency is an in-process cache, not durable storage across worker restarts

title: [Scheduler] Add opt-in shared schedule/forward stream for the overlap scheduler
summary: ## What changes This PR adds an opt-in env flag, `SGLANG_SHARE_SCHEDULE_FORWARD_STREAM` (default off). Default behavior does not change. - **Before:** the overlap scheduler always keeps a separate schedule stream. Every decode step has GPU waits between this stream and the forward stream: the forward stream waits for its inputs, and the WAR barrier makes the schedule stream wait for the forward stream. On ROCm, each stream maps to a different hardware queue. On gfx950, a wait that is pending on one queue slows each kernel dispatch on the busy forward queue. With `SGLANG_FORCE_COARSE_WAR_BARRIER=1`, the WAR wait is pending for almost the whole forward step. In our traces this added about 0.6 µs to each forward kernel, or about 1.1 ms per MTP decode step (about 1,860 kernels). - **After, with the flag set:** the scheduler queues its own GPU work on the forward stream. Both waits are then in order on one stream, so no wait crosses hardware queues. With the coarse WAR barrier, the GPU order is the same as before, because the schedule work already waits for the whole forward. CPU/GPU overlap stays. The flag has no effect with pipeline parallelism. - **Who sees it:** only servers that set the flag. We measured it on AMD MI355X (gfx950) with GLM-5.3-Flash MXFP4, MTP, and the recipe's `SGLANG_ENABLE_WAR_BARRIER=1 SGLANG_FORCE_COARSE_WAR_BARRIER=1`. ### Measured The measurements ran on [salexspb/sglang@a87779a65c](https://github.com/salexspb/sglang/commit/a87779a65c6fe15936f2150c1949ded49a4c96ad) (upstream `e1f43c9a61` plus open GLM-5.3-Flash/HiSparse PRs). summary: ## Motivation `sglang:num_aborted_requests_total` counts abort dispatches rather than mutually exclusive request failures. title: scheduler: bound consecutive prefills to protect decode
summary: ## Problem `Scheduler.get_next_batch_to_run()` currently gives every eligible new prefill batch priority over the running decode batch. Under an ongoing prompt-heavy arrival stream, a new prefill remains eligible on every scheduling pass, so the fallback decode path may not run for an unbounded time. This is not only a tail-latency problem. A request that has completed prefill still needs a decode step before it can emit its first token, and in-flight streams need later decode steps for every subsequent token. Starving decode therefore raises both TTFT and inter-token latency, increases request residence time, and can self-amplify concurrency until aggregate decode throughput collapses. The production report in #32549 measured this effect under sustained chunked-prefill traffic with speculative decoding: 250+ active streams received roughly one decode batch every 24 seconds, even though KV-cache usage remained low and the engine was otherwise healthy. The strict prefill-first decision is the common cause; the report reproduced it with both DSPARK and EAGLE. Existing controls do not bound this starvation: - `--num-continuous-decode-steps` applies only after decode has already been selected. - Smaller prefill chunks reduce the duration of one prefill turn, but do not change its priority over decode. - Mixing prefill and decode is not the safe path for the affected speculative configurations. ## Solution Add the opt-in scheduler control: ```text --max-consecutive-prefill-batches N ``` - `N = 0` is the default and preserves current prefill-first scheduling. - With `N > 0`, afte

title: fix(hicache): square NVFP4 host-pool geometry + page-granular block-scale transport
summary: Closes #43239. ### The bug NVFP4 device pools store **packed** fp4 — one device row holds `row_dim / 2` **bytes** (`store_dtype=uint8`, e.g. `k_buffer[l]: (size, 2, 128)` = 256 B/token) — and keep per-block scales in **separate** tensors (`k_scale_buffer[l]: (size, 2, 16)`). The generic MHA host pool sizes host rows from device *element* counts (512 B/token), and HiCache JIT kernels take a single shared element size for both sides: - **H2D** views the 256 B device row as half of a 512 B element: token *i* lands at device rows `2*i`; the in-range guard truncates the rest (in-engine at production scale: a 56,704-index loadback wrote ~64 KB of 14.5 MB — the function returns having restored nothing). - **D2H** gathers 512 B spans off 256 B-stride rows, pairing two device tokens per host row. - **Scales never move at all** on the `kernel` path, so even a byte-correct payload dequantises with stale scales. With MTP draft KV packed behind the pool (#30393), every restored draft row is garbage: `spec_accept_length` silently pins to 1.0, throughput falls ~25% below the no-MTP baseline, target outputs stay correct, `/flush_cache` doesn't help, only a restart heals. Even without MTP, target-KV loadbacks are corrupted the same way (usually masked by re-prefill). Reproduced deterministically at cycle 0 (3/3) on v0.5.21; `pool_host/mha.py` on current `main` has the identical geometry (`get_size_per_token` at lines 217–222, selector at 1557). title: [RFC] Quantization module layout: Config, Scheme, backend kernels
summary: ## Summary Quantization methods in SGLang are currently written in two different shapes. Five of them follow a package layout with an explicit scheme split: - `layers/quantization/awq/`, `compressed_tensors/`, `gptq/`, `modelslim/`, `quark/` The rest are single files that hold config parsing, weight creation, post-load processing, and backend kernel dispatch together: - `fp8.py` (2765 lines), `modelopt_quant.py` (3050), `mxfp4.py` (2060), and 14 smaller ones. 17 top-level files define a `QuantizationConfig` subclass today. This RFC suggests finishing the migration so that every method follows the layout our own contribution guide already prescribes: ```text layers/quantization/<method>/ <method>.py # Config: parse, validate, select a scheme schemes/ <method>_linear.py # Scheme: weight create, load, post-process <method>_moe.py ``` with backend kernels under `hardware_backend/<plat>/quantization/<method>_kernels.py`, and scheme selection done explicitly through `get_linear_scheme` / `get_moe_scheme`. Nothing here is a new architecture. `docs/docs/developer_guide/quantization_contribution_guide.mdx` specifies this already, and #21126 (AWQ) and #26402 (GPTQ) are worked examples. This is a plan to take the rest of the directory there. The intent is incremental. Every existing import path keeps working through re-export shims, each PR is small enough to review in one sitting, and the directory is busy enough that nothing should depend on a long-lived branch: it took 46, 48, 49, 56, 70 and 84 commits in the last six months, 217 in the last 90 days. Please use English, otherwise it will be closed. ### Motivation `Scheduler.get_new_batch_prefill` walks the waiting queue in FCFS order and `break`s at the first `AddReqResult.NO_TOKEN`. When the queue head is a large request whose KV budget does not fit, nothing behind it is considered, even if smaller requests (or requests with a long prefix hit, which need almost no new KV) would fit right now. The pass ends with an empty or tiny prefill batch, the GPU idles for that round, and the head is retried next pass. On a prefill-only node (PD disaggregation) this is the dominant idle cause under long-prefix multi-turn load: admission is the only consumer of freed KV, requests are large, and the queue head is routinely blocked for many consecutive passes. title: [Bug] Eager hybrid target verify fails when TP padding breaks fixed-width request groups
summary: ## Describe the bug **Eager target verification can terminate hybrid-attention workers when TP/MLP-sync padding produces an incomplete fixed-width request group.** This was originally observed in GLM-5.3-Flash KDA and independently reproduced in Qwen3.5-35B-A3B GDN on a main-based source. The shared failure does not require the GLM DSA KPool path. The two layout requirements must hold together: - TP collectives require an aligned physical token count. - Fixed-width EAGLE/NEXTN verification requires complete groups of `D` tokens per request. The affected eager preparation aligns only to the attention TP size `A`: ```text L = B * D # real tokens P = ceil(L / A) * A # physical tokens after TP padding ``` For `B=38`, `D=6`, and `A=8`, this gives `L=228` and `P=232`. The 232 rows cannot be partitioned into complete six-token requests. On Qwen/GDN, all eight TP ranks failed with: ```text RuntimeError: shape '[38, 6, -1]' is invalid for input of size 237568 ``` `237568 = 232 * 1024`. The original GLM/KDA failure had the same geometry and a different channel width: `712704 = 232 * 3072`. ## Trigger and CUDA Graph boundary The demonstrated trigger is fixed-width hybrid target verify taking the eager path, with TP padding that leaves `P % D != 0`. Eager execution or padding alone is insufficient to cause this particular failure. CUDA Graph was enabled in the reproduction. A graph limit of 32 with a running-request limit of 64 allows batch 38 to fall back to eager naturally. title: [Feature] Distributed Weight Data Parallelism (DWDP) for Sparse MoE Models
summary: ## Summary Implement **Distributed Weight Data Parallelism (DWDP)** in SGLang — a parallelism strategy that distributes MoE expert weights across GPUs within a node while keeping attention weights fully replicated. Instead of using collective synchronization (AllReduce/AllGather), DWDP uses asynchronous peer-to-peer prefetches to pull remote expert weights before they are needed, eliminating synchronization barriers from the critical path. Inspired by NVIDIA's TensorRT-LLM DWDP implementation ([blog](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/blob/main/docs/source/blogs/tech_blog/blog19_DWDP_Distributed_Weight_Data_Parallelism_for_High_Performance_LLM_Inference_on_NVL72.md), [PR #12136](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/pull/12136)), which demonstrated **8.8% output TPS/GPU improvement at comparable TPS/user in the 20-100 TPS/user serving range under 8k/1k ISL/OSL** and **14.26% iteration latency reduction** on DeepSeek-R1 with GB200 NVL72. --- ## Motivation ### The Problem with Tensor Parallelism for MoE Current MoE inference in SGLang uses Tensor Parallelism (TP) or Expert Parallelism (EP), both requiring collective communication (e.g., AllReduce, AllGather) at synchronization barriers. As model sizes grow and batch sizes vary, these synchronization points become the bottleneck: - **Small batches:** Compute finishes quickly but all ranks wait at the barrier. - **Imbalanced expert routing:** Some ranks finish early but stall waiting for stragglers. - **NVLink bandwidth underutilized:** High-bandwidth peer links (NVL72: 1.8 TB/s bisection) are used only in bursts during co

title: [Tracking] Host allocator: page-aligned allocation with host-side bookkeeping
summary: ## Motivation The KV allocator keeps its source of truth on device, so freeing KV reads device state back: `torch.unique(free_index // page_size)` with a data-dependent output shape, and on the SWA side a `full_to_swa_index_mapping` gather plus its `> 0` liveness filter. Each forces a stream synchronization on the scheduler's stream. Under the overlap scheduler those syncs queue behind the WAR barrier, so the CPU parks until the in-flight forward drains -- a measurable throughput loss where requests finish every step. None of that information needs a device read; it is host-known at allocation time. Target design (validated end-to-end by the #31335 spike): - Allocation is planned host-side in whole pages; each request tracks a page-ceiled extent (`req.kv.kv_allocated_len`) with a single writer. - `free()` receives whole pages by construction -- no dedup, no liveness filter, no data-dependent shapes. `torch.unique` survives only behind a legacy API for truly scattered index sets. - Device tables (`req_to_token`, `full_to_swa_index_mapping`, `free_pages`) become write-only projections consumed by kernels; the scheduler never reads them back. ## Status The hybrid SWA free path is sync-free at every page size as of #38159: for the mapping-table `SWATokenToKVPoolAllocator` with the radix or chunk cache, no device read is left on the allocator free path. The remaining reads live in other allocators and caches (see "Remaining"). ## Landed **Host-side KV ownership (`req.kv`)** -- the bookkeeping the allocator reads instead of the device - #29427 / #29429 / #29432 -- `req.kv` contai

summary: ## Motivation Fix #42144 `XGrammarGrammarBackend._sanitize_structural_format` is intended to recursively normalize missing or `None` `json_schema` fields to empty schemas `{}`. title: [Perf] [NVIDIA] dsa: Run FlashInfer's fused SM120 indexer for DSA top-k
summary: ## Motivation On SM12x (RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell and the rest of the SM120/SM121 family), the DSA lightning indexer runs as two steps: 1. DeepGEMM's FP8 MQA logits write a `[rows, keys]` fp32 logits tensor. 2. A separate top-k transform reads those logits back to pick 2048 keys per row. At long context the second step reads every logit again. FlashInfer now ships a fused SM120 indexer, `flashinfer.dsa_indexer.dsa_indexer_det_topk(..., backend="sm120")` (flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#7085). title: [Perf] Gather the striped prefix KV for DSA extend under DCP (env-gated prototype)
summary: ## Motivation Under `--dcp-size c`, DSA (GLM-5.3 / DeepSeek-V3.2 style) extend chunks take the decode-style path: per layer, Q is all-gathered to all heads, each rank attends over its owned top-k slice, and the partial outputs + LSE are exchanged with an all-to-all. For an 8192-token chunk that is ~0.8 GB of NVLink traffic per rank per layer with no overlap. Measured on 4xB300 with GLM-5.3 NVFP4: DCP4 prefill runs at 14-15k tok/s vs 22-25k tok/s for plain TP4, and on the AgentX c48 point prefill batches take ~69% of wall time even at a 97% cache hit rate. ## Change Behind `SGLANG_ENABLE_DSA_DCP_EXTEND_GATHER_KV=1` (default off, no behavior change otherwise): DSA extend under DCP keeps the plain 16-head path, and inside the TRT-LLM DSA forward each layer all-gathers the striped latent prefix rows of the batch into a position-ordered scratch buffer that the sparse kernel reads directly (`dsa_dcp_gather.py`). One plan per extend batch (owned rows in position order, receive permutation, position page table, and a slot -> row map for the fused top-k output). title: [Feat] attention: Support sparse query positions in FlashInfer prefill
summary: ## Motivation Selective prefill can issue queries at positions `[0, 7, 16]` while retaining a 17-token KV sequence. The SGLang/LMCache CacheBlend integration needs explicit query positions while preserving full KV lengths. ## Modifications Add optional `SparseQueryMetadata` to `ForwardBatch` and use its request-local positions to plan FlashInfer paged prefill with a custom causal mask. For a single sparse request, prepack the mask with FlashInfer's parallel `packbits` API: the default segment packer uses one CTA per request, which is costly for long masks. Multiple requests retain the wrapper's segment packing. Limit this entry point to eager FP16/BF16 full self-attention, with explicit rejection of graph capture, speculative execution, context parallelism and other unsupported wrapper configurations. This exposes an attention primitive; normal scheduling does not enable CacheBlend or selective model execution. ## Accuracy Tests - CPU metadata contract: 3 tests pass, including inconsistent-layout subtests. - Existing GPU attention fixture now covers both one and two GQA requests, shuffled physical pages, non-contiguous query positions and changed selected inputs. title: [DSA] Fix top-k v2 emitting invalid indices under tie overflow / inf scores (IMA in FA3 sparse decode)
summary: (generated by claude) ## Motivation The nightly `test_glm52_fp8.py` perf test crashed with an illegal memory access on all three variants ([run](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/actions/runs/28986113304/job/86015497076)). The CUDA coredump shows the faulting kernel is **FA3 sparse decode** (`FlashAttnFwdSm90`, bs=1 decode right after an 8192-token prefill), and the faulting `LDGSTS` address is exactly `kv_pool_base - 1152B` (= one 576-elem bf16 DSA KV row) — i.e. FA3 dereferenced **KV slot index `-1`**. The `-1` comes from the fused top-k v2 kernel. FA3 reads exactly `min(seq_len, topk)` entries of the top-k output (`dsa_cache_seqlens = seq_lens.clamp(max=topk)`), so every one of those slots must hold a valid index. Two data-dependent extremes break that contract: 1. **Tie overflow**: the collect pass keeps at most `kMaxNumTie = 1024` candidates from the threshold bin. When the bin holds more (ReLU-degenerate indexer scores easily put thousands of positions on one exact value — the random-token perf workload hits this; short gsm8k requests never reach the sparse path, which is why accuracy passed) and `topk - above_count > 1024`, `handle_tie` pads the remaining slots with `-1`. Unit repro on H200: seq=8320, topk=2048, 100 winners + 8220 zeros → **924 invalid entries inside the valid prefix**. 2. **inf / >65504 scores**: `coarse_bin_lower_bound` computed NaN boundaries for bins touching the fp16 ±inf keys (their neighbors live in NaN key space), so the collect pass matched nothing; large-but-finite scores (>65504, which fp16-round into the inf bin) were dropped entirely

title: [Perf] diffusion quantization layer: fix 6 real perf/overhead bugs
summary: Reviewing the diffusion (`multimodal_gen`) quantization layer against a set of 7 reported perf-optimization claims turned up 6 confirmed, real bugs/overheads (verified by reading the code, reasoning about correctness, and confirming on a real GPU). Opening this to track the fix and request it be assigned to me. ## Confirmed and fixed 1. **ModelOpt NVFP4 scale TMA conversion does a GPU->CPU->GPU round trip.** `process_weights_after_loading` built the padded TMA-layout scale buffer with a device-less `torch.zeros(...)` (defaults to CPU), forcing a copy off and back onto the GPU every load. An on-device version of the same transform already exists (`_linear_nvfp4_scales_to_tma`); it just wasn't being called here. - Benchmarked on a T4: 1.3967 ms/call (old) vs 0.0535 ms/call (new), ~26x faster, bit-identical output. 2. **Dynamic NVFP4 recomputes `weight_scale_2.max()` every forward.** That value is fixed after loading; cache it once instead of reducing the tensor on every call. 3. **Comfy full-precision NVFP4 unswizzles scales on every forward.** The swizzled->linear scale conversion is load-time-fixed; do it once in `process_weights_after_loading` instead of in `apply()`. 4. **BnB 4-bit allocates and copies an output buffer for a single, unfused shard.** The common (non-fused) case doesn't need an intermediate buffer; call `matmul_4bit` directly and skip the copy. 5. **ModelOpt W8A16 scales the full `[out, in]` weight (an N*K elementwise pass) before every matmul, instead of scaling the much smaller `[*, out]` output.** It also rounds the scale to bf16 before using it, discard

title: [RFC #32321] Tiled paged prefill kernel for radix-prefix batches (MLX)
summary: ## Motivation RFC #32321, "Kernels and lowering": *Kernel tuning + benchmarking PR … paged prefill kernel for radix-prefix batches (currently the weak kernel)*. **Stacked on #36164.** Until it merges, only the last commit (`548da75`) belongs to this PR. `radix_prefill_deferred` launches one 1024-thread threadgroup per (packed query token, q head), and each threadgroup walks its whole causal KV range alone. Nothing is reused across query tokens, so KV traffic is N·(P + N/2) per head. Profiling on an M4 shows that this traffic is the bottleneck: - At P=2048 the per-token kernel's time grows linearly with N, even for N ≤ 32 (log-log slope 0.98). A kernel that reuses each KV tile across 32 query rows stays flat there (slope 0.03). - Counting the no-reuse bytes, it runs at 120–190 GB/s, the memory ceiling (about 120 GB/s nominal). Counting each KV row once, it moves only 0.2–4.6 GB/s, so more than 96% of its reads are redundant. ## Modifications **`python/sglang/kernels/ops/attention/_deferred_radix_attention_mlx.py`** - New tiled prefill kernel. Each threadgroup owns 32 new-token rows of one request, for one q head and one KV split. Each 32-key K/V tile (16 keys for head_dim 256) is staged once in threadgroup memory and shared by all 32 rows. QKᵀ and PV use `simdgroup_matrix`, and the online softmax stays in registers (MLX steel-attention fragment layout). - Same contract as the per-token kernel: - the borrowed pool is read-only - prefix rows are read through `req_to_token`; new rows come from `current_k`/`current_v` - invalid slots are left out of the softmax - an invalid requ

title: [Fix] [SM120] dsv4: Keep the V4.1 indexer usable on SM12x
summary: Prerequisite for #47210 (SM120/SM121 dense FP8 native block32 DeepGEMM): without this change DeepSeek-V4.1 does not reach readiness on SM12x with either GEMM backend. The two PRs have zero file overlap and no code dependency in either direction. ## Motivation On SM120/SM121 the DeepSeek-V4.1 candidate indexer cannot start. The selection gate (`is_sm100_or_newer()`) compares the capability major against `>= 10`, so SM12x enters the candidate path, while the DeepGEMM capability flag is gated on `is_sm100`. Because the dense paged logits kernel is present on SM12x, the already implemented dense blocks backend works there. A SM120 sparse-table kernel exists on DeepGEMM's `nv_dev` branch (`#447`) but not in the pinned `sgl-deep-gemm` release builds, so it cannot be enabled from SGLang today. This change therefore fixes the failure at the capability check rather than unifying the two gates: narrowing `is_sm100_or_newer()` to match `is_sm100` would also fold SM100/SM103 into the dense path, where a missing sparse kernel means a broken install and should keep raising. Separately, `make_full_topk_indexer` derives `use_deep_gemm_decode` from `is_sm100_or_newer()` alone. title: [Perf] [AMD] all-reduce: prefer QuickReduce before CustomAllReduce
summary: ## Motivation When QuickReduce and CustomAllReduce are both eligible, the current out-of-place all-reduce dispatch selects CustomAllReduce first. This prevents an explicitly configured QuickReduce codec from being used for overlapping message sizes. This change gives eligible QuickReduce configurations priority while preserving the existing fallback chain. It also allows ROCm deployments that already enable AITER to use AITER's QuickAllReduce implementation without breaking launch scripts that still use the legacy SGLang environment names. ## Modifications - Change plain out-of-place all-reduce dispatch from: ```text CustomAllReduce -> QuickReduce -> PyMSCCL++ -> torch symmetric memory -> PyNCCL ``` to: ```text QuickReduce -> CustomAllReduce -> PyMSCCL++ -> torch symmetric memory -> PyNCCL ``` - Apply the same ordering in eager execution and the runtime `"auto"` resolver used by compiled and graph-replayed paths. - Include QuickReduce eligibility in the eager symmetric-memory shortcut guard so that shortcut cannot bypass an eligible QuickReduce communicator. - Add a QuickReduce factory that: - selects AITER QuickAllReduce when `SGLANG_USE_AITER=1`; - falls back to SGLang's bundled implementation only when the AITER import is unavailable; and - leaves constructor failures visible to the existing communicator setup error handler. - Wrap bundled and AITER communicators behind an SGLang-owned adapter instead of assuming the out-of-tree implementation exposes SGLang-specific state. - Close QuickReduce before destroying its process groups. - Translate legacy environment variables

title: [Fix] parser: Fail a DeepSeek-V4/V4.1 thinking turn that stops before </think>
summary: ## Motivation Fixes #48561. A DeepSeek-V4.1 thinking generation can hit EOS without emitting `</think>`. With the default deepseek-recipe output adapter, that turn finished as a successful response: the reasoning, empty content, no tool calls and `finish_reason: "stop"`. An agent client reads this as a completed turn that has neither an answer nor an action. DeepSeek-V4 (`dsv4`) runs through the same adapter, so this PR changes both. The cause is model behavior, not SGLang's parsing: - DeepSeek reproduced an EOS before `</think>` with similar prompts and passed it to the model team (deepseek-ai/deepseek-recipe#45). The hosted API also returns such a turn as a success with reasoning only. - vLLM sees the same with DeepSeek-V4 (vllm-project/vllm#48645), and a vLLM maintainer treats it as a model failure. SGLang cannot complete or reinterpret such an output. The unclosed text may be unfinished reasoning (this issue) or an answer the model gave without thinking (the vLLM report), and there is no reliable signal to tell the two apart. Moving the text to `content` would show unfinished reasoning as the answer. This PR therefore makes such a turn fail explicitly. An agent can then retry or surface the failure instead of taking an empty turn as complete. When an answer without `</think>` is the cause, the client loses that answer and has to retry the turn. Once the model closes its reasoning, the check never fires. The scope is narrow. title: [Fix] gdn: Keep a mixed batch's decode tail on the decode kernels under deterministic inference
summary: ## Motivation Fixes #46446. With `--enable-deterministic-inference` and `--enable-mixed-chunk`, Qwen3.5-9B's greedy output for a request changes when another request's prefill is mixed into one of its decode steps. `EagerRunner.execute` runs a MIXED batch as EXTEND, so the GDN layers process each running request's decode token as a 1-token sequence through the chunked prefill kernel (`chunk_gated_delta_rule`). Without mixed chunk, the same token goes through the recurrent decode kernel. The two are mathematically equal but not bitwise equal, and the difference stays in the recurrent state. In the issue's repro only one step is mixed (the 255-token intruder plus the target's 1-token tail at prefix 4120), and that step is enough to flip the target's greedy token about 100 tokens later. The full-attention layers (Triton, deterministic) do not need a change: with only the GDN layers fixed, the outputs match exactly. ## Modifications - `ForwardBatch.num_mixed_decode_reqs`: the number of running requests that `mix_with_running` appended to a MIXED batch, set in `init_new` from `mix_running_indices_cpu`. This is needed because the eager runner relabels the batch as EXTEND before the attention backends see it. TBO children set it to `None`. - `GDNAttnBackend`: under deterministic inference, `init_forward_metadata` cuts a mixed batch once per forward into its prefill rows and its decode tail (`build_gdn_mixed_decode_split`). `forward_extend` then runs the prefill rows through the unchanged extend path and the tail through `forward_decode`, the same path a decode step takes. title: [Feat] hicache: Expose host-tier occupancy and write-back blocking metrics
summary: ## Motivation HiCache exports the host tier's fill level (`sglang:hicache_host_used_tokens` / `sglang:hicache_host_total_tokens`), and L3 hits lost to a full host tier already show up as `sglang:storage_prefetch_unfulfilled_tokens_total{reason="host_capacity"}`. What is missing is *why* the host tier has no room, and two failure paths that leave no metric at all: 1. **What fills the host tier.** Under `write_through`, every token cached on the GPU keeps a host copy, so a host pool sized close to the GPU pool has little room left for storage hits. A hybrid-pool model (sliding-window or Mamba components) cannot shorten a storage hit to that room and drops it whole. Today this can only be inferred from the write policy, the GPU pool size and the host pool size. 2. **L3 prefetches skipped by the staging cap.** In cache host-memory mode, `HiCacheController.prefetch_rate_limited()` stops new L3 lookups once staging reaches `prefetch_capacity_limit` (half the host pool). The only trace is `_prefetch_outcome_stats["declined_rate_limited"]`, which is never exported. No lookup happens, so these never reach `storage_prefetch_unfulfilled_tokens_total`. 3. **Write-back evictions that stall.** When a write-back device eviction can neither back its victim up (no free or reclaimable host room) nor drop it (a node in the subtree is pinned), `_evict_device_walk` and `_evict_leaf_with_backup` only log `write_back: backup failed under host memory pressure but subtree drop declined`. title: [Bug] Simulator Replay startup eagerly imports optional AIConfigurator dependency
summary: ### Describe the bug SGLang Simulator eagerly imports `aiconfigurator` during startup, even when the Replay predictor is selected and `--max-total-tokens` is explicitly set. The hang appears to be on the device whenever a grammar-masked DSpark verify is batched with another request. One hypothesis: ranks disagree on accepted draft lengths under the grammar mask, which leaves mismatched collective sizes. We have not confirmed this. ### Reproduction We saw 3 hangs in 5 runs of the incident reproduction: 2 of 2 with the overlap scheduler, each within 1–3 minutes of overlap, and 1 of 3 without it. title: [Fix] scheduler: Relay multimodal requests to later PP stages without raw features
summary: ## Motivation Under pipeline parallelism, the first PP stage relays every newly received request to the next stage (`_pp_send_pyobj_to_next_stage(recv_reqs)` → `point_to_point_pyobj`, i.e. pickle + gloo send). Every later stage then rebroadcasts the object to its attention TP/CP peers and relays it again. With `mm_feature_transport=cpu`, `RequestReceiver._finalize_shm_features` has already materialized each image's raw feature tensor into the request object by that point. For example, a 1080p image is about 6 MB of CHW uint8. All of it gets serialized at every hop on the scheduler threads. Later stages never consume these tensors: - `prepare_mm_inputs` embeds multimodal inputs on the first PP rank only ("Non-first pipeline ranks consume proxy tensors and return no embeddings"). - The PP-capable models outside that routine (`gemma4_unified`, `cosmos3_edge`, the transformers backend) also embed on the first rank only. - On later stages the scheduler needs just the pad values, and those come from the item hash. So the relay is pure overhead, and it grows with images per request. Agent-style traffic that resends the conversation's screenshots every turn makes every PP iteration slower. The whole pipeline then queues up, and **text-only requests slow down as much as image requests**. ## Modifications - `mm_utils.strip_mm_features_for_pp_relay(reqs)`: returns copies of the requests in which multimodal items that already carry a `hash` drop `feature`. - Unhashed items keep their feature, because the next stage hashes it to derive the pad value. - The relaying stage's own request o

title: [Fix] rust-server: Reject Rust-only punctuation in stop regex capture names
summary: ## Motivation The Rust stop-regex validator admits `(?P<a.b>x)`, `(?P<a[b]>x)`, and `(?P<a]b>x)` with bound 1, but CPython's `re.compile` rejects all three as invalid group names. These patterns should fail request validation before being forwarded to Python. ## Modifications Reject Rust-only `.`, `[`, and `]` punctuation in Python-spelled capture names. Keep ordinary ASCII/Unicode names and escaped or character-class lookalikes accepted. This is a focused punctuation fix; it does not attempt to reconcile Unicode identifier tables across Python versions. This is independent of #46346, which addresses whitespace inside counted repetitions. ## Accuracy Tests - Before the fix, the new rejection regression fails; the positive controls pass. - A CPython differential check agrees on all seven new negative/positive patterns. - `rustfmt --edition 2024 --check rust/sglang-server/src/utils/regex.rs` and `git diff --check` pass. - `cargo test -p sglang-server --lib utils::regex --locked`: 14 passed in the real crate. - `cargo test -p sglang-server --lib message::sampling --locked`: 26 passed (caller-side normalization tests). - No GPU/model-serving or end-to-end scheduler run performed. ## Speed Tests and Profiling No inference benchmark. The added scan is limited to the capture-name header during stop-regex admission. AI-assisted implementation and local validation.

title: [Fix] scheduler: Honor pause_generation under PP and release aborted PD rooms and rejected sessions
summary: - **PD prefill: clear the bootstrap room of an aborted request.** A prefill request aborted after it left the bootstrap queue is retired through `release_prefill_sender(abort_sender=True)`, which only called `sender.abort()`. Nothing polls that request again, so its room stayed in `request_status`, `transfer_infos`, `req_to_decode_prefix_len` and `failure_records` for the life of the server (every `CommonKVSender` backend). `release_prefill_sender` now also calls `clear()`, in its own best-effort block so a failing `abort()` does not skip it, and `CommonKVSender.clear()` pops `failure_records` too (`failure_exception()` reads the reason before clearing). - **Streaming sessions: release the session when a turn is rejected.** `create_req` marks a streaming session in flight before the dLLM validation and the sampling-mask validation run. Both rejections returned without unmarking it, so every later turn of the session was refused with "Streaming session already has an active request" and closing it left the session registered. Both paths now call `session.abort_req()` (`Scheduler._release_rejected_session`). title: [Perf] [NVIDIA] gemma4: fuse the TP all-reduce with the layer epilogue and FP8 quant on NVLink multicast
summary: ## Motivation Every dense Gemma-4 layer ends its attention and its MLP with a TP all-reduce followed by RMSNorm → residual add (× `layer_scalar`) → RMSNorm → per-128 FP8 quant for the next block-FP8 GEMM. At TP4 on H200 with 4k-token extend chunks this chain is an NCCL all-reduce plus three epilogue kernels, ~301 µs per site, and it runs twice per layer. The existing FlashInfer all-reduce fusion does not cover Gemma's norm → add → norm order or an FP8 output, and is sized for decode batches. title: [Feat] kernels: Add out-of-tree dispatch for gated RMSNorm
summary: ## Motivation Out-of-tree platforms need a supported way to provide a gated RMSNorm implementation without monkeypatching SGLang internals. ## Modifications - Convert the FLA gated `RMSNorm` to `BaseFusedOp`. - Preserve the existing Triton and CPU paths. - Add a portable Torch reference implementation for supported gate activations and layouts. - Add unit coverage for gating, strided gates, and invalid layouts. title: [Fix] tbo: Capture routed experts at each child's parent rows
summary: ## Why With `--enable-two-batch-overlap`, `return_routed_experts` returns wrong ids. Both TBO children write the shared device buffer from row 0, while readback uses parent batch order, so one child overwrites the other and the remaining rows stay zero or stale. Generated tokens are not affected. Non-EP DP TBO (DeepSeek V4) has a second mismatch: its MoE captures every DP rank's padded rows, while readback uses the parent's DP offset. ## What - Pass `tbo_parent_token_range` through `ForwardContext` and write each child's real rows at that range. - For non-EP DP TBO, also pass this rank's parent offset (`tbo_parent_dp_offset`). Capture reads the rank's rows from the child's gather and writes them at that offset. Non-TBO paths are unchanged. ## Verification **DeepEP:** Qwen3-30B-A3B FP8, 2×H200, `--tp-size 2 --attn-dp-size 2`, 48 greedy tokens. Requests whose routes differ from TBO off, by rank load (token diff is 0 throughout): | Load | Before | After | |---|---|---| | `[32,32]` | 64/64 | 0/64 | | `[3,29]` | 32/32 | 16/32 | | `[1,31]` | 32/32 | 1/32 | | `[0,32]` | 32/32 | 0/32 | | `[8,8]` | 16/16 | 0/16 | "Before" ran on an earlier main (8884b4b421). Zero ids drop from about 37% to 1.13%, matching TBO off. The remaining `[3,29]` and `[1,31]` diffs are all in decode. TBO off shows the same pattern when only the batch layout changes (`[8,8]` vs `[32,32]`), so they look like numeric sensitivity to batch shape. That cause is inferred, not proven. **Non-EP DP:** DeepSeek V4 architecture with 8 layers and seeded dummy weights, 4×H200, `--tp 4 --attn-dp-size 4`, 249 requests pinned

title: [Feat] qwen4-exp: accept HMM devices for the file-backed PLE table
summary: # [Feat] qwen4-exp: accept HMM devices for the file-backed PLE table ## Motivation `--ple-offload-backend file` (#37068) keeps Qwen3.8-Flash-Next's 47.7 GiB FP8 N-gram table in a file-backed mmap that the gather kernel reads directly. That needs a GPU that can read pageable host memory, which CUDA reports as `cudaDevAttrPageableMemoryAccess`. The load-time check asks for `cudaDevAttrPageableMemoryAccessUsesHostPageTables` instead, which only ATS parts such as GB10 report: it says how the access works, not whether it works. For paged-experts (#42557, #48642), we are working towards serving models from disk that don't fit neither RAM, nor VRAM on consumer hardware. A discrete GPU on the open kernel modules (for example an RTX 50-series card, which runs only on them) reads pageable memory through HMM, where the driver mirrors the process's page tables: `PageableMemoryAccess` is 1, `UsesHostPageTables` is 0. The check refuses such a card, and the only way past it is `SGLANG_QWEN4_PLE_FILE_SKIP_DEVICE_CHECK=1`, which is documented for devices that cannot be queried and switches the check off entirely. Yet the file backend is useful there: on an RTX PRO 6000 it keeps the table out of locked memory (the cookbook asks for at least 64 GB of free RAM for the pinned table), and on smaller cards the table fits nowhere else. CUDA's [Unified Memory guide](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-programming-guide/04-special-topics/unified-memory.html) lists Linux HMM systems among those with full unified memory support, which "can directly access file-backed memory". summary: ## Motivation The shared MQA logits budget uses driver-visible free memory but does not count unused blocks held by PyTorch's caching allocator. A warmed server can report zero driver-free bytes while the allocator still has several GiB not occupied by tensors. title: [Bug] [mamba/hybrid] MambaPool.copy_from gathers all source temporal states into one temporary (n x state_size) - CUDA OOM under parallel admission bursts
summary: ### Summary On hybrid models with a mamba/KDA recurrent-state pool (e.g. GLM-5.3-Flash), `MambaPool.copy_from` in `python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/memory_pool.py` copies the temporal state with a batched index assignment: ```python # memory_pool.py, lines 1216 and 1222 (main, a133231d31): temporal[:, dst_indices] = temporal[:, src_indices] # and, in the sibling path: self.mamba_cache.temporal[:, dst_indices] = self.mamba_cache.temporal[:, src_indices] ``` The right-hand side gathers **all** source slots into one temporary (`[state_size, n_src]`) before the scatter — a single peak allocation of `n_src × per-slot state bytes`. The conv-state part of the same function already uses a fused per-slot copy (`fused_copy_conv_slots`, line 1205); the temporal gather is the remaining batched copy. ### When it bites Under an admission burst, radix-cache COW copies checkpoints for several cached requests in one scheduler step, so `n_src` reaches ~8–12. On GLM-5.3-Flash the temporal state is **34.0 MiB per slot per GPU** (TP=2), so one call spikes **~272–410 MB per GPU** on top of steady-state free memory. With `--mem-fraction-static` 0.965–0.98 the spike exceeds free VRAM and the step fails with `CUDA out of memory`, which the scheduler then retries (OOM-retry log lines + latency spikes for everyone in flight). ### Measured (GLM-5.3-Flash W4AFP8, TP=2, 2× H100 NVL 94 GB) | | value | |---|---| | temporal state per slot | 34.0 MiB / GPU (35,651,584 B) | | one 8-slot gather | 285,212,672 B spike / GPU | | free VRAM at burst time (mem-fraction 0.965–0.98) | ~192 MB | | unpatched, 12-request par

summary: ## Motivation MiniMax M3.1 Flash runs on H200 without speculation, so its low-batch decode is all small-M linears. On a TP8-shaped 12-layer proxy at batch 1, the block-FP8 linears take 39% of the GPU busy time per step (449 of 1149 us), all of it in DeepGEMM. #45828 added a GEMV for these behind `SGLANG_ENABLE_FP8_BLOCK_GEMV`, but it stops at K=4096. M3.1's q/k/v, index and gate/up projections have K=6144, so they stay on DeepGEMM with the flag on. The flag does move the TP8 shared-expert down projection (K=384), where the GEMV is slower. #48399 lists this flag as waiting on an H200 accuracy run. The full-model run below is on M3.1 at K=6144. M3.1 tracker: #46869. ## Modifications Only `use_hopper_fp8_block_gemv` changes. The kernel already sizes its slab from K. - K=6144 is admitted for M <= 8 and N <= 8192. Other K above 4096 stay out. - Odd K block counts above one (K=384, 640, 896, 1152, ...) go to DeepGEMM. title: [Perf] diffusion: Keep a folded Gemma-4 encoder's vocab table on the host
summary: ## Motivation When the Gemma 4 text encoder (LTX-2.5) is folded across ranks with `--encoder-parallel fold`, its `VocabParallelEmbedding` shard stays on the GPU. Layerwise offload deliberately skips sharded tables, because their gather feeds an all-reduce that needs device tensors. At fold 2 that leaves 1 GB of the 2 GB vocab table in VRAM on every rank. Without folding, the whole table lives on the host. The encoder's VRAM goes from 0.10 GB to 1.04 GB. On a 32 GB RTX 5090, that extra gigabyte breaks LTX-2.5 at Ulysses 2: - The breakable CUDA graph capture runs out of memory, so denoising falls back to eager mode. - On this host, eager mode is launch-bound at 0.81 s per step, against 0.45 s with graphs. - A later request then hits a CUDA OOM. ## Modifications `Gemma4UnifiedTextModel` builds its table through a new `_vocab_embedding()` helper: - **Unfolded** (TP world size 1): returns the existing `VocabParallelEmbedding`, unchanged. - **Folded**: every rank keeps the whole table as a plain `nn.Embedding`, loaded with the default weight loader. `host_resident_table_names` already names this table, so layerwise offload parks it on the host and gathers rows there, the same as for the unfolded encoder. The rows are the same: the sharded gather only adds zeros from the other ranks. Each rank holds 2 GB of host memory for the table instead of 1 GB of VRAM. ## Accuracy Tests New test in `test_gemma4_unified_layerwise_offload.py`: - When unfolded, the helper returns `VocabParallelEmbedding`. - When folded, it returns `nn.Embedding`. - Both give identical rows for the same weights.

title: [NPU] Fix packed MTP KV and Indexer transfers in HiCache
summary: ## Problem Enabling MTP with HiCache on Ascend can fail during MLA host-pool initialization because `NPUMLATokenToKVPool` does not expose CUDA-style `data_ptrs`. Bypassing that initialization alone is insufficient. For GLM-5.2, HiCache packs 78 target layers and one draft layer into a shared host pool. Draft device layer 0 must map to host layer 78, rather than host layer 0. The draft pool also contains Indexer state that needs its own host slots. ## Root Cause The existing implementation assumes that: - Every MLA device pool exposes a per-layer pointer table. - Device and host layers share the same index space. - Host Indexer allocation only needs to account for the target pool. NPU MTP uses separate target and draft device pools backed by continuous tensors. Their K/V layers and Indexer slots must be mapped independently into the packed host allocation. ## Fix - Skip CUDA-style packed device pointer construction on NPU. - Include draft Indexer slots and optional Indexer scales in host allocation and capacity accounting. - Add an NPU range-transfer helper with independent device and host layer offsets. - Back up and restore target and draft buffers using separate packed host regions. - Preserve the full host page stride when passing sliced buffers to the legacy NPU exchange and AscendC paths. - Preserve non-MTP transfer dispatch and non-NPU pointer-table construction. - Add CPU regression tests for packed allocation, target/draft mapping, Indexer isolation, and transfer metadata. The changes are limited to `mla.py` and a new regression test file. ## Dependency Depends on #

Each of these layers then launches a chain of small torch kernels: the pair-partner lookup with `roll` / `where` / `masked_fill`, the gathers from the pair-state ring, the norm and the stores. Static verify uses the fused `c1` / `c2` kernels instead. On 4x B300 at concurrency 16 and 64, the torch chain was the largest compact-only GPU cost in the verify graph. title: [Fix] InstantTensor: return load-time GPU memory to the KV cache
summary: ## Motivation With `--load-format instanttensor` (#40453), GPU memory after weight loading is higher than with the default loader, and the KV cache shrinks by the difference. On GLM-5.3 NVFP4, TP4 on B200, "Load weight end" mem usage was 108.89 GB against 106.88 GB for the default loader. That cost 812k KV tokens against 836k. There are two causes: 1. **A lazily created NCCL communicator.** InstantTensor all-gathers over `get_parallel().world_group.device_group`. SGLang never otherwise runs a collective on that group (its world-group uses are CPU-group object collectives and barriers), so the loader's first all-gather creates its NCCL communicator. That communicator's buffers then stay resident for the life of the process: 0.77 GB/GPU on H100 TP4 without NVLS, and more with NVLS. 2. **Allocator fragmentation from the clones.** `copy=True` clones every tensor, unsharded, through the shared caching allocator. Long-lived allocations made during and after loading (e.g. `post_load_weights`' `w_kc`/`w_vc`) are carved out of the freed blocks of the largest clone (the 1.8 GB embedding for GLM-5 dimensions). `empty_cache()` then can't return that segment: 1.74 GB/GPU in a synthetic run. ## Modifications `instanttensor_weights_iterator`: - When loading over the world group (the default load group), it creates a temporary NCCL group spanning the world, passes it to InstantTensor, and destroys it when iteration ends. Other load groups, such as a PP stage's TP group, keep using their own device group, since `new_group` must be called by every rank. - It pulls each tensor from InstantTen

title: [router] Disable reqwest's default 30 s TCP_USER_TIMEOUT on upstream sockets
summary: ## What changes **Before:** the router's shared upstream HTTP client inherits reqwest 0.12's default `TCP_USER_TIMEOUT` of 30 s on Linux. The kernel aborts a router-to-worker connection when the data the router sent stays unacknowledged for 30 s. This also happens when the worker is alive but reads a large request body slowly and advertises a zero receive window. **After:** the router does not set `TCP_USER_TIMEOUT` on upstream sockets. A worker that is slow to read a request body no longer loses the connection after 30 s. `request_timeout_secs` still bounds each request. **Who sees it:** router deployments where a worker reads large request bodies slowly. The clearest case is PD disaggregation with one decode engine under burst load. The decode HTTP process tokenizes each long prompt on its event loop. During a burst it stops reading sockets for more than 30 s. **Why it matters in PD mode:** `execute_dual_dispatch_internal` sends the prefill and decode requests concurrently and waits for the prefill. When the kernel aborts the decode socket, the router stores the decode error and keeps waiting. The prefill engine waits in its bootstrap queue for a decode engine that never got the request. The request hangs until `SGLANG_DISAGGREGATION_BOOTSTRAP_TIMEOUT` expires. Only then does the router log `Decode request failed ... error sending request`. **Measured evidence** (MI355X, 3 prefill engines and 1 decode engine at TP2 on two nodes, GLM-5.3-Flash MXFP4, agentic benchmark with long multi-turn prompts, concurrency 160, sglang-router 0.3.2 built with reqwest 0.12.28 and hyper-ut

summary: ## Motivation `--max-running-requests` may be larger than `--cuda-graph-max-bs-decode`; batches above the largest captured batch size are expected to fall back to eager execution. title: LoRA Async Pipelining Per Requeust Load
summary: ## Motivation Currently LoRA Loading for Per Request needs to first sequentially **load all the LoRA layers** before **beginning Pre-Fill**. This adds significant overhead in TTFT. If you are using the current overlap loading you can only get gain of Pre-Fill of the previous run with incoming LoRA. This enhances that with **current LoRA load** with **current Pre-Fill**. However, **Pre-Fill** is a layer by layer process and for large enough input tokens(**> 1000 tokens**) it is **longer than LoRA Loading time**. If we run **LoRA loading and Compute in separate streams(CUDA or otherwise)** we can hid significant part of the LoRA loading time with **Sync points** in each LoRA layer of the forward pass to make sure the LoRA layer is loaded. **This specifically complements Overlap Loading in SGLang** which was already implemented which starts early loading for the next request while the previous request is running compute. ## Modifications - Enhance Overlap loading to also Pipeline LoRA Loading with Forward Pass - **mem_pool** slice caching so **lora_a**/**lora_b** used cached weights. - **max-loaded-loras**: with overlap loading, defaults to **max_loras_per_batch** when unset. - Added unit tests in **test/registered/unit/lora/test_lora_overlap_loader_unit.py** -

summary: ## Motivation Falling off the end of the captured CUDA graph shapes is currently silent. When the decode batch exceeds the largest captured shape, decode falls back to eager execution; on a small model this is roughly a 4x per-token latency increase. Because arrivals are admitted directly into the running batch, the slowdown feeds back into the batch size via Little's law and the system settles into a second stable operating point — across 46 observed transitions, none recovered within the run. This is reachable with default settings. On an L40 at tp=1, `cuda_graph_max_bs` defaults to 32 while `max_running_requests` defaults to 4096, so the scheduler can admit far more concurrent requests than the fast path was captured for. See #33483 for the full measurements and controls. Today an operator has no signal that this happened. Throughput looks normal, `#queue-req` stays at 0, and median TPOT can still read clean if the transition occurs late in the workload. This PR makes the moment visible. ## Modifications Adds a one-time warning when the decode batch first exceeds the largest captured CUDA graph shape, naming both values and the two flags that control them. - `<model_runner.py>`: emit the warning at the point where the batch is found to exceed the largest captured shape, guarded by a boolean on the runner so it fires at most once per server lifetime. - No behaviour change. title: Fix DeepSeek-V4 mHC combine allocating transients in the NCCL symmetric pool
summary: ## Motivation Root cause of #33800 (DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 emitting corrupted output at DSpark draft depth 5 on SM120). The non-TileLang mHC combine fallback runs its y-combine reduction inside the `use_symmetric_memory` context, so the large intermediate (the `[m, hc_mult, k // hc_mult]` product) and the dtype cast allocate in the NCCL symmetric pool, not just the final `y`. Transients in that pool intermittently alias in-flight symmetric all-reduce buffers, and the corrupted values reach committed tokens. Depth 5 was never special to the code: its verify shape (m = bs x 6) just produced the pool occupancy pattern that made collisions land in output on our hardware. The same file already documents this exact hazard for the MoE path ("Only this final output enters the pool; intermediate buffers stay on the default allocator to bound pool occupancy") — this fallback predates that comment. ## Modification Compute the reduction on the default allocator; allocate only the final `y` in the pool and copy in. The downstream all-reduce still sees a symmetric input. summary: <!-- Thank you for your contribution! Please follow these guidelines to enhance your pull request. If anything is unclear, submit your PR and reach out to maintainers for assistance. title: [Spec][DSpark] Clamp per-request verify window to context/generation budget (fix #33454)
summary: ## Motivation Fixes #33454. DSpark allocates a full verification window for every request regardless of remaining model-context or generation budget. summary: ## Motivation `update_weights_from_tensor` indexes `serialized_named_tensors` by `tp_rank`, so an HTTP caller has to send one identical copy of the payload per rank. title: [decode] Spec-decode with large draft-token counts OOMs mid-traffic on the decode instance - no upfront capacity check (verify workspace vs KV pool is zero-sum)
summary: ## Summary When serving speculative decoding with a large draft-token window (DFlash num-draft- tokens = block-size >= 8) under PD disaggregation, the decode instance passes CUDA graph capture at startup but OOMs mid-traffic once both the spec-verify workspace and the KV pool are stressed. There is no upfront capacity check: the server starts "successfully" and requests fail in flight (HTTP 500, most of the batch stuck). ## Evidence (8xA800 80GB decode, TP8, mooncake RDMA; target 122B GDN/MoE, draft 6L) Four configurations, all failed under c8/c32 business traffic: | cuda-graph-bs | mem-fraction-static | outcome | |---|---|---| | 48 | 0.70 | KV pool 337K tokens, free 1.15GB -> verify workspace OOM | | 32 | 0.70 | free 1.8GB -> single 32MB allocation fails | | 32 | 0.58 | KV pool collapses to 22K -> cannot fit 61.6K concurrent tokens | | 16 | 0.70 | KV pool 677K, free 2.83GB, capture fully succeeds -> c8 still OOMs mid-run (297/300 requests stuck) | Single-node (same 8 GPUs, no PD) runs D=16 fine at 64.5GB peak - the PD decode-side budget is what turns it zero-sum. ## Root cause The spec-verify graph workspace (scales with draft-token count) and the KV pool share the same free memory on the decode instance. Startup only validates that capture fits; it never checks "workspace + worst-case live KV <= budget". Raising mem-fraction makes workspace OOM more likely; lowering it starves the KV pool. Otherwise, it will be closed. ### Describe the bug Since #35540 every HiCache host-pool sizing guard checks `requested_bytes > host_memory_budget_bytes()`, where the budget is `(psutil.virtual_memory().available - 10 GiB) // ranks_per_host()` (`python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/pool_host/base.py`). Splitting the free memory by the number of co-located ranks is only right for a reading taken before any of those ranks allocates. But each rank reads `available` at the moment it reaches the guard, and TP ranks reach it at different times: pinning a large host pool takes seconds and nothing synchronizes the ranks between pools. A rank that arrives after `k` peers have already pinned their pools sees `available` reduced by `k × pool` while still dividing by the full rank count, so the peers' pools are subtracted twice and the guard raises `ValueError: Not enough host memory available` on a host that has room for all of them. With a sidecar pool (DSA indexer, MiniMax index-K, mamba) the same happens again on the second guard, after the first pool has been pinned on every rank. title: [Proposal] Fuse static FP8 activation quantization into producer kernels (norm / activation / allreduce epilogue)
summary: ## Summary For checkpoints with static per-tensor FP8 dense linears (ModelOpt `modelopt_fp8` / `modelopt_mixed` — e.g. the Nemotron, Llama and Qwen FP8 exports, and Qwen3.5-V2), SGLang's CUDA path launches a standalone `_static_quant_fp8` kernel before every FP8 GEMM. On Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-NVFP4-V2 this amounts to **240 standalone quantization kernels per decode step per rank**. Profiling shows these kernels give back roughly **half of the FP8-over-BF16 GEMM benefit**. Because the scale is a load-time constant, static quantization can run as an epilogue of the kernel that produces the activation (RMSNorm / SiluAndMul / allreduce fusion) instead of as a standalone kernel. vLLM implements this at both the norm level and the allreduce level, and SGLang's own ROCm path already has a norm-level fusion; the CUDA path currently has neither. title: [Bug][PP] PP disaggregated prefill hangs: bootstrap queue history diverges across stages under abort storms (RCA + fix series)
summary: ## Summary On PP disaggregated prefill, a burst of client cancellations can make the per-stage bootstrap queues diverge: stages stop agreeing on which requests were admitted/aborted, subsequently select different microbatches, and the fixed PP P2P send/recv schedule deadlocks — each rank blocks in a *different* send/recv slot until the NCCL watchdog kills the server a full hour later. Requests keep returning 200 on `/health` the whole time. Environment where we hit it in production: PP=8 disaggregated prefill (TP=1) + Mooncake KV transfer, HiCache L2-only, 32K-token inputs with ~90% shared prefix, high-concurrency cancellations. This issue tracks the RCA and the fix series: - [ ] #34568 — fold HiCache prefetch readiness into the bootstrap consensus (prerequisite; closes the L3-storage readiness divergence gate) - [ ] #34569 — ordered immutable bootstrap decisions with exactly-once apply (main fix; closes the abort / local KV-failure / metadata-finalize gates) - [ ] #34570 — PD router: never auto-replay a request that may already be dispatched (stops the router from generating non-idempotent replays that amplify these races) ## Incident signature (how to recognize it) Align each rank's `Prefill batch` lines by order of appearance (**not** by timestamp — adjacent logical batches legally land in the same second across skewed stages). summary: ## Motivation This follows up #48977. That PR synced the trtllm DSA row plan fix, which plans on the per-token `seq_lens` the kernel reads. title: [Fix] health_check: Require completed inference for /health_generate, not any scheduler message
summary: ## Motivation A PD prefill engine whose model execution had stalled kept returning 200 from `/health_generate`, so the router kept re-admitting it. The handler passed whenever `tokenizer_manager.last_receive_tstamp` advanced, and every scheduler message advanced it: aborts, errors, control replies, and an empty `HealthCheckOutput` that the scheduler flushed from idle housekeeping (`on_idle`) and from `process_batch_result_disagg_prefill` regardless of whether any forward had finished. On a prefill engine successful requests send nothing to the tokenizer, so those synthetic signals were the only health evidence, and none of them required inference to complete. Health should stay failed while model execution is stalled even if HTTP, control messages, aborts, or errors continue, and recover only through fresh completed work. ## Modifications Health is now driven by a dedicated completed-inference acknowledgement. - **Scheduler** (`managers/scheduler_components/health_monitor.py`, new): `SchedulerHealthMonitor` registers every incoming probe and, at the very end of `Scheduler.process_batch_result` (after `process_batch_result_*` have synchronized and consumed the device results), sends `HealthCheckOutput(rid, incarnation, completion_seq, dp_rank)` to each pending probe when the batch did real work: a prefill chunk with `extend_num_tokens > 0`, a decode or verify step, with at least one non-aborted request. title: [UnifiedRadixCache] Bound SWA HiCache load-back to one sliding window
summary: ## Motivation With HiCache on a hybrid SWA model, load-back of a host-only SWA node restores the node whole, even when it is much longer than the sliding window. Attention only reads the last `sliding_window_size` tokens before the match end, so everything older is loaded into the device SWA pool and never read. `finalize_match` also charges that whole node to `swa_host_hit_length`, so the scheduler reserves device SWA for it too. This resolves the `TODO(hzh)` left in `components/swa.py` / `swa.rs` by #27391. This matters most when a match ends inside a long host node. The typical case is a prompt prefilled in one chunk (e.g. a PD prefill role): its whole prompt's SWA sits in one or two nodes, and a later request that branches inside it would reload all of it. In a CPU harness (W=128, page 16, 2048-token prompts, branch at 3/4 of the prompt), each load-back went from 1,536 SWA slots to 128, and the number of load-backs that fit in one batch went from 1/2/5/10 to 2/4/8/11 at SWA/full ratios 0.25/0.5/0.75/1.0. Requests that decoded before being cached see no difference, since their host nodes already hold about one window. Scope: this is read-side only. It changes device SWA usage per load-back and the matching admission charge. It does not change how much SWA write-through puts on host, which is decided on the backup path. The trimmed head is not on device after the load, so a later request that branches inside it does its own one-window SWA load-back instead of hitting on device; together such requests transfer no more SWA than one whole-node load. ## Modifications - New co

title: [Fix] dsv4: Keep trtllm-gen sparse MLA from reading lengths the launch right before it wrote
summary: ## Motivation The trtllm-gen sparse MLA kernels that `--dsv4-attn-backend trtllm` launches (`trtllm_batch_decode_sparse_mla_dsv4`) read `sparse_topk_lens` (and, on one warp role, `seq_lens`) **before** their `griddepcontrol.wait`. In the SASS of the FlashInfer 0.7.2 cubins, every warp role path loads these fields ahead of the PDL wait, for both the `fmhaSm100fKernel_*DenseDynamicTokenSparseP1*` variants and the `fmhaSm107aKernel_*` ones. The MMA warp has no wait at all. Under PDL a dependent launch has no visibility guarantee for its predecessor's stores until it executes that wait. On every indexed (ratio 1 / 2 / 4) layer, `pack_sparse_tail` writes the lengths and the FMHA runs right after it. If two warp roles of one CTA read different lengths, the producer warps decide that the CTA has no KV tile while the consumer warpgroups wait for one. That CTA never exits. We hit this as a decode hang on 4x VR200 (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, DEP4). A GPU core dump of the stuck rank showed a single resident FMHA CTA. Its producer warps had exited, both consumer warpgroups were spinning on their first full barrier, and the length registers of the two roles held 276 and 277. The other three ranks then timed out in Mega MoE's grid sync. On that build `pack_sparse_tail` released its dependents before it stored the lengths, which widens the window. On `main`, `pack_sparse_tail` is launched without PDL and never triggers early, so the FMHA can only start once the pack's CTAs have exited. title: [Perf] [NVIDIA] dsv41: Index-Q RoPE + fp4 pack runs one thread per fp4 block for prefill-sized calls
summary: ## Motivation `index_q_rope_pack_weights` (`index_q_kernel` in `fp4_indexer_rope.cuh`) applies RoPE and two-stage fp4 packing to the DeepSeek-V4.1 indexer query and also writes the head weights. It gives each (token, head) row of 128 bf16 to one warp, which per row means: - 4-byte loads; - four 16-lane max reductions and two shuffles; - two 1-byte payload stores per lane; - 4-warp CTAs. That shape was chosen from decode measurements and suits decode. At prefill sizes it runs far from memory bandwidth. On VR200 a 32768-token chunk with 32 index heads (1M rows, ~340 MB of traffic, ~26 us at HBM speed) took 251 us per indexer layer. ## Modifications - `index_q_block_kernel` gives each 32-element fp4 block to one thread: four threads per row, 256-thread CTAs of 64 rows. Warps 0-3 take the head blocks and warps 4-7 the RoPE blocks, so the RoPE branch is warp-uniform. Each thread does: - all of its loads before any math: the input block, plus its `freqs_cis` slice for the RoPE half, as `kMaxVecBytes` vectors (32 bytes on Blackwell); - the RoPE of its tail pairs; - both block absmaxes as trees seeded with 0; - the fake quant up to the e2m1 grid value, then the packer's exponent read from the grid amax's biased exponent (no division) and the e2m1 codes, with the two power-of-two scales folded into one multiply; - one 16-byte payload store and one byte of the row's little-endian scale word. The row's first thread writes the head weight. The current version of the kernel is @zcnrex's from review (about 10-23% faster than the first version, same bytes). - **Bitwise:** every fp4 stage

summary: ## Motivation Under pipeline parallelism, a later stage's `SWAKVPool` holds global layer ids, but it reports `start_layer = 0`. Code that reads the pool's first layer through `start_layer` then asks for a layer the stage doesn't have. For example, `TritonAttnBackend.__init__` reads `get_value_buffer(token_to_kv_pool.start_layer)` when the model isn't mambaish and the SWA and full value head dims match. title: [Fix] mamba: Make Mamba2 prefill batch invariant in deterministic mode
summary: ## Motivation Fixes #43413. In deterministic mode, a Mamba2 prompt can produce different outputs when other requests move it to a different offset in the packed prefill batch. Reusing a checkpoint produced by decode or a different scan reduction can also change the continuation. Related work: #48425 covers GDN's automatic cache strategy; #23128 discusses decay overflow. This change preserves neutral zero-dt padding and exact Mamba2 prefill checkpoints. ## Modifications - Pad packed requests with zero effective `dt` so each scan starts on its own chunk grid, then run the padded batch together. - Round scan boundaries to the cache precision and take checkpoints directly from the scan. Keep boundary copies separate from the varlen reduction for the ROCm compiler path. - Preserve the cumulative decay across zero-dt tails. With Falcon's large decay coefficients, FP32 scan roundoff can otherwise overflow the final cached state. Raw dt padding also uses the bias precision so cancellation stays exact. - Align chunked-prefill ends at absolute positions and reuse prefill checkpoints in deterministic Mamba2 mode. Shortest-prefill and dynamic chunk budgets leave room for the next scan boundary; insufficient memory defers the continuation. - Add regression coverage and a fixed-input split-state diagnostic that records the first differing stage and the selected Triton configurations. ## Accuracy Tests Rechecked on an RTX 4090 (24 GB, SM89), driver 595.71.05, PyTorch 2.14.1+cu130, Triton 3.8.0 and FlashInfer 0.7.2, integrated with main `db5cd6ba`. title: [Perf] eplb: Vectorize the static per-rank dispatch map
summary: ## Motivation With `ep_dispatch_algorithm=static`, every EPLB rebalance rebuilds the per-rank dispatch map in `compute_logical_to_rank_dispatch_physical_map`. For DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at DEP32 that is 40 x 384 x 32 calls, which take 250-290 ms on every rank on each rebalance while the whole DP group waits. ## Modifications - `_compact_candidates`: move each row's valid physical ids to the front, keeping their original order. - `_nearest_expert_dispatch`: pick the same-GPU replica, otherwise the same-node replica when it narrows the candidate set, using tensor ops over the replica slots. Rows with a single replica broadcast it. This is the same rule as `_find_nearest_expert`, which still serves the startup collapse in `_compute_logical_to_all_physical_map`. - Only the (layer, expert, rank) entries left unresolved still go through `_fair_choices` with the seeded `random.Random`, in the same row-major order. title: [Perf] kimi-k3: Fuse the decode MoE routing for 1-256 rows into one kernel
summary: [by Claude Code] Original authors: @nvpohanh, @kpham-sgl, @zcnrex ## Port of #48414 In every Kimi-K3 / K3.1 decode MoE layer, a serial chain of small kernels runs between the router and the routed experts. It is `route_quant_fused` (top-16 of 896 plus the MXFP8 quant), then the padded-row mask, then trtllm-gen's routing kernel inside `trtllm_fp4_block_scale_routed_moe`, which builds the expert-sorted permutation. #48414 replaces the chain with one kernel for 1-256 rows and any local expert range. The routed MoE then runs only its GEMMs, from that kernel's metadata, through FlashInfer's prepared-routing body. This PR ports that: the kernel with its op and test, the `route_quant_handoff` / `select_experts` / `KimiK3MoE` wiring, and the MXFP4 runner's prepared-routing entry. This PR differs from #48414 in three ways: - **Named for Kimi-K3, not K3.1.** K3 and K3.1 share the MoE that the kernel is specialized for: 896 experts, top-16 by sigmoid plus bias with no groups, a 3584-wide latent, and MXFP4 trtllm-gen SiTU experts. Their checkpoint configs differ only in K3.1's `dsa_config`. Both models run `KimiK3MoE`, so the fused path already ran on K3. `kimi_k31_fused_routing` is now `kimi_k3_fused_routing`, and the `K31*` symbols are now `KimiK3*`. - **No kill switch.** `SGLANG_K31_FUSED_ROUTING` is removed. Every case that the fused path cannot serve already falls back to the unfused chain. - **SM107 with FlashInfer < 0.7.3 keeps the unfused chain.** On SM107, FlashInfer 0.7.2 builds no FP4 tile-192 kernels and turns MoE PDL off, and #48414 mirrored both rules. summary: ## Motivation MoE model implementations such as Gemma4 own their routing semantics: they compute router logits, choose the top-k experts, and pass a `TopKOutput` to an expert executor. summary: ## Summary Four small fixes for requests that a pause, a memory release, an abort, or a PD role switch could leave in a broken state. ## Changes - **Beam groups on a retract pause.** `pause_generation(mode="retract")` now aborts live beam groups instead of requeueing their leaders. `retract_all` frees each leader's member rows before its KV is released and records the abort reason, which is the same path `ScheduleBatch.retract_decode` takes under KV pressure. title: [Fix] quantization: Apply each fused projection's own NVFP4 global scale in linear layers
summary: ## Motivation Fixes #48919. The NVFP4 linear GEMMs take one weight global scale per layer. For a fused layer (q/k/v, gate/up) whose projections store different global scales: - `ModelOptFp4LinearMethod` and `ModelOptNvFp4A16LinearMethod` keep the largest for every projection, so the others are dequantized too large (the NVFP4A16 method warns). - `CompressedTensorsW4A4Fp4`, the default for compressed-tensors NVFP4 on SM100 and SM120, keeps the largest with no check, and `CompressedTensorsW4A16Fp4`, used on SM80-SM90, refuses the checkpoint at load (#40022). `RedHatAI/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-NVFP4` and `RedHatAI/gemma-4-31B-it-NVFP4` have such q/k/v layers, so they fail to load on an H100 and are misread on a B200. A global scale is a factor on its projection's output columns. So the GEMM can run with the largest one, and each projection's columns can be multiplied by its own scale over that one. This is exact up to the rounding of the output, with no requantization. ## Modifications - `fp4_utils.fused_global_scale_ratio(global_scales, logical_widths, divisor=...)` returns the scale the GEMM runs with (the largest; `divisor` handles compressed-tensors' 1/scale convention) and the per-column ratio over this rank's output columns, or `None` when every projection stores the same scale. `apply_fused_global_scale_ratio` multiplies the output by it in fp32, before the bias. - Used by `CompressedTensorsW4A4Fp4`, `CompressedTensorsW4A16Fp4` (FlashInfer bf16 x fp4 and Marlin), `ModelOptFp4LinearMethod` (Marlin, W4A4, W4A16) and `ModelOptNvFp4A16LinearMethod`. title: [RFC] Integrate MindIE-SD as an Acceleration Library for SGLang Diffusion
summary: ## Summary and motivation This RFC proposes integrating MindIE-SD as an optional Ascend acceleration library in SGLang Diffusion, starting with dense quantized attention and sparse attention through the existing attention architecture. The intended role is comparable to FlashInfer at the library/inference-framework boundary: MindIE-SD provides reusable accelerated computation and execution APIs, while SGLang owns serving and framework orchestration. This comparison describes the integration model, not API compatibility or feature parity. The goal is broader than copying individual kernels into SGLang. Initial implementation discussions are in #46029 and #40580. This RFC asks maintainers to agree on ownership, dependency boundaries, validation and maintenance before expanding the integration. It does not imply those PRs or any particular SDK mode are already qualified or accepted. ## 1. Library positioning and scope MindIE-SD should provide public, versioned APIs for accelerated diffusion computation on Ascend. Initial scope: - Dense attention with explicitly qualified FP8/MXFP8/MXFP4 modes. - Sparse attention with independently configured sparse algorithm and numerical precision. - Quantization, Q/K rotation, packing, rearrangement and native execution required by those APIs. - Capability and compatibility information sufficient for integration-time selection. Potential follow-ups include fused layers/blocks and reusable execution planning where profiling demonstrates value. title: [Fix] dp-attention: Take single-node control-plane ports from a free block
summary: ## Motivation With DP attention, `PortArgs.init_new` derives six control-plane ports (tokenizer, detokenizer, rpc, metrics, scheduler input, load collector) from `--port + 233`. The real owner is the prefill server in another container: psutil reports `pid=None` for a socket held by a process in another PID namespace, and `psutil.Process(None)` is the calling process. On a single node without `--dist-init-addr`, nothing outside the server derives these ports, so they do not need to come from `--port`. This picks up the approach of #30833 by @luccafong (closed as a stale draft) on current main, with them as co-author of the commit. ## Modifications - `PortArgs.init_new`, single node, no `--dist-init-addr`: the launcher takes the block from the new `get_free_port_block`. summary: ## Motivation DeepGEMM's `mega_mhc` runs the DeepSeek-V4.1 shifted mHC seam in one launch: the post (new residual), the next sublayer's mix statistics and Sinkhorn, and its pre-collapse and RMSNorm, with bf16 and MXFP8 outputs. Standalone, it took 118 us at 8K rows and 427 us at 32K. That is 7.5 to 8.3 TB/s of the ~105 KB per row the seam must move, against a ~13.4 TB/s copy roofline.
