We progressively prune layers according to their effect on acceptance length to reduce the cost of packed drafting. Removing five of 36 layers retains over 99\% of mean acceptance length across three benchmarks with Qwen3-8B as the target. Across seven benchmarks, D3D averages 5.00times and 5.71times decoding speedup with Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B targets, compared with 4.03times and 3.67times for DFlash. On GSM8K with Qwen3-32B, speedup reaches 7.48times. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/fudan-generative-vision/D3D.

title: SpecOPD: Branch-Parallel On-Policy Distillation for Speculative Decoding
summary: Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates large language model inference by reducing the sequential cost of token-by-token generation. Advanced SD methods reduce proposal cost with parallel drafters that predict entire blocks in one forward pass, but overall speedup still depends on acceptance length. On-policy distillation (OPD) can push well-trained drafters beyond acceptance-length plateaus, yet conventional pipelines collect supervision through sequential draft-and-verify rollouts. Our key insight is that on-policy supervision need not inherit these dependencies: a draft block can be supervised using only its reference prefix and draft-sampled history. We propose SpecOPD, a branch-parallel OPD framework that parallelizes draft sampling and target supervision across independent branches drawn from the evolving drafter policy at reference anchors. We pack these branches into proposal trees to share target-prefix computation, using tree masks for full attention, branch-consistent indexer groups for sparse attention, and indexed state replay for linear attention to preserve each branch's history. We train the drafter with an E2E-TV surrogate that directly targets acceptance length. Our study spans 8B full-attention (GQA), 27B full-linear (GQA--GDN), and 125B sparse-linear (QSA--GDN) targets, three parallel draft architectures (DFlash, DSpark, and DFlash V2), and four task domains (dialogue, coding, mathematics, and agentic). SpecOPD achieves up to 41.45% higher mean acceptance length, 16.09times supervised-token throughput over sequential-rollout OPD under native configurations

title: The SIMPLE Law for Energy Cost of LLM Inference
summary: Generative AI is billed per token, yet tokens are not equally expensive. Each token enters the KV-cache and raises the cost of those that follow, so energy grows non-linearly along a sequence whose tokens look identical. No analytical model states what a token costs, and the most accurate SOTA model is a fit, not a law: it absorbs architecture into fitted coefficients, requiring per-LLM fitting. We derive closed-form expressions of the computational and memory-access complexity of LLM inference in terms of architectural hyperparameters, covering MHA and GQA, and compare a family of analytical models of increasing granularity. From these, we obtain the SIMPLE Inference Model to Predict LLMs Energy (SIMPLE), a four-parameter law that separates prefill from decode, and decode into KV-cache cost and next-token computation. Over traces of 13 dense LLMs from six families on NVIDIA H100 GPUs, it attains R2 = 0.969 and 11.97% MAPE, 3.1-3.5x below the SOTA, without per-LLM calibration. The SIMPLE law explains as well as predicts: prefill energy grows quadratically with the hidden dimension, so larger LLMs suffer most from long inputs; and more aggressive GQA KV grouping reduces the per-token energy by up to 3x relative to standard MHA. Increasing the reasoning token budget pushes output length beyond the analytically derived energy minimum, driving super-linear energy growth; although accuracy grows with the budget, energy grows faster, so Intelligence per Joule peaks at an intermediate budget and falls by up to 3.14x across a 4.0x reasoning-budget range. Agentic serving raises ener

title: NitroFusion2: Bringing Adversarial Loss to the Text Stream of Multimodal Diffusion Transformers
summary: Adversarial diffusion distillation has conventionally relied on image features for discrimination. We revisit this choice for multimodal diffusion transformers (MMDiTs), whose text stream becomes image-dependent through joint attention. We introduce Text-Stream Adversarial Distillation (TSAD), which exploits intermediate text-token states as a new adversarial representation. Because the text stream has already read the image while remaining tied to the text condition, changing that condition changes what information it extracts from the image. Building on this property, we introduce Aspect-Cued Discrimination (ACD), which conditions the discriminator on different aspects of the sample, such as typography, objects, or style, to steer which properties are emphasized during adversarial training. Building on the expert-discriminator design of NitroFusion, we integrate TSAD and ACD in NitroFusion2. NitroFusion2 brings few-step distillation from the conventional 4-8-step regime down to just 1-2 steps at comparable quality. At one step, it produces sharp rendered text and rich fine-grained details, making one-step generation practical rather than merely a stress test for distillation. At two steps, it remains competitive across the evaluated benchmarks. These results establish the MMDiT text stream as a powerful and steerable representation for adversarial diffusion distillation.

title: LoopVQ: Sub 1-bit KV Cache Quantization for Looped Transformers
summary: Looped transformers are a parameter-efficient alternative to standard transformers for language modeling. By reapplying the same layers across multiple loop steps, recent looped language models match the performance of non-looped models several times their size. While this architecture effectively reduces parameter memory, each loop step still stores its own keys and values, so the key-value (KV) cache grows linearly with the number of loop steps and becomes the main memory bottleneck. We observe that the KV cache of looped models is highly redundant along the loop axis and that the loop steps differ substantially in their sensitivity to quantization. Based on these observations, we propose LoopVQ, a KV cache vector quantization method for looped transformers that codes channels of multiple loop steps jointly, and fine-tunes the codebooks to match the output of the full-precision model. At 0.5 bits per element, LoopVQ outperforms existing KV cache vector quantization methods for standard LLMs on general, long chain-of-thought reasoning, and long-context retrieval tasks with Ouro and Huginn models. Its design is orthogonal to these methods, and combined with TaSQ, it retains much of the BF16 accuracy even at 0.25 bits per element. We also implement LoopVQ in SGLang, where it nearly halves the decode latency at a 32K-token context and raises the peak serving throughput by up to 4.3times and 6.1times on the 1.4B and 2.6B Ouro models compared to the BF16 baseline.

title: Multi-layer Indexer: Overlapping Selection and Attention in DeepSeek Sparse Attention
summary: Sparse attention cuts the cost of long-context inference by making the attention matrix sparse: each query attends only a subset of the sequence, chosen by a fixed pattern or, in recent production LLMs, learned per query. In DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA), the attention of DeepSeek-V3.2 and the GLM-5 family, every layer is preceded by a lightning indexer that scores the whole cache and keeps the k=2048 highest-scoring tokens for the layer to attend. At long context this indexer scan, not the sparse attention it feeds, is where the decode time goes. But adjacent layers select nearly the same tokens, so a layer can attend the selection of the previous indexer layer instead of its own. This removes the dependency: each indexer then runs concurrently with the attention of its layer. The resulting Multi-layer Indexer (MLI) needs no retraining and no new weights. Its default realization changes no kernel, running inside SGLang's production decode graph; an optional fused decode kernel accelerates it further on DeepSeek-V3.2. MLI composes with IndexCache (the cross-layer reuse GLM-5.2 ships as IndexShare): IndexCache drops the indexer from some layers, and MLI hides the scan on the rest. We serve DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5 under IndexCache's protocol at retentions 1/2 to 1/32 (the fraction of layers that keep an indexer) and contexts 10K to 195K. At equal retention the composition decodes faster than IndexCache: up to 14.5% faster on DeepSeek-V3.2 and 9.8% on GLM-5 at 1/2, and 7.9% and 5.1% at 1/4, largest where IndexCache keeps the most indexers and growing with context. At retenti

title: Ask, Don't Equip: Question-Driven Coding Agents for Deep Kernel Optimization
summary: LLM agents for GPU kernel optimization sit at two ends of a structure-freedom tradeoff. Scripted agents fix what the model does at each step, via a learned policy, an optimization menu, or fixed roles, and are sample-efficient where the recipe applies and stall where it does not. Open-ended agents let a self-directed model mutate a population of kernels and pay for the freedom in trials: thousands of evaluations, repeated edits, and wrong candidates. Both respond to hard targets by equipping the agent with more: parsed profiler output, disassembly analysis, retrieval over documentation and libraries, and stores of lessons. We argue that both lack direction, a hypothesis about where the remaining gap is, and that a short question asked at the right moment supplies it without narrowing what the agent may do next. We present KernelSeek, a question-driven agent that makes an existing CUDA kernel faster with no operator-specific knowledge and no faster implementation to imitate: a general-purpose coding agent, a minimal harness that enforces a verifiable goal, and questions at decision points, first from a human, then from a bank the agent applies to itself. On the same task, evaluator, hardware, and week, a tool-rich autonomous agent built in the prevailing style plateaued at 0.50x FlashAttention-3 after 133 model-driven steps; KernelSeek reached 1.13x. It then produced dependency-free FlashAttention forward kernels for Hopper and Blackwell, single CUDA files with no CUTLASS, CuTe, cuBLAS, or cuDNN, correct on all 182 scenarios per architecture and 1.16x FlashAttention-3 and 1.

title: [Feat] mem_cache: preserve branch and tail checkpoints for hybrid Linear reuse
summary: ## Motivation Hybrid prefix reuse requires Full KV and a recoverable Linear state at the same cached boundary. In the affected `extra_buffer` tracking path, choosing an interior branch in the final Prefill extend can leave its already-computed aligned prompt tail without a separate checkpoint. Subsequent tail continuations then resume from the earlier branch. This patch preserves both the branch and aligned prompt-tail checkpoints within one GDN prefill extend. It does not split the extend or add another model forward. The feature is experimental and defaults to disabled. ## Modifications - Add opt-in `SGLANG_EXPERIMENTAL_GDN_BRANCH_AND_TAIL`. Reserve at most one optional branch snapshot per batch, with native checkpoint headroom and collective TP fallback when any rank lacks a spare slot. - Capture branch convolution history and recurrent state at the same depth, copying the latter from native Triton `h`. Native tracking retains the aligned tail. Publish the independently owned branch after successful forward completion; release duplicate/discarded optional slots and clear Prefill-only metadata before Decode. - Reuse the existing unified cache publication and eviction paths. Add real-allocator cache tests, complete-state CUDA comparisons, TP1/TP2 model continuation tests and a pinned public AgentX replay script. Initial supported scope: `Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration`, CUDA Triton GDN, BF16 recurrent state, `extra_buffer`, eager unified serving, final Prefill extend. title: [Perf] paged-experts: optionally fuse copying missing experts with MoE kernels (Triton and Marlin)
summary: Any feedback is highly welcome! I'm a PhD student working on serving performance, but I'm new to contributing to sglang and open-source repositories in general. Please let me know if I've missed anything obvious! ## Motivation Paged Experts copies every missing expert into its GPU slot before the MoE kernel starts. That makes every expert wait for every transfer: resident experts cannot start until all copies finish, and each missing expert waits for the others to arrive. Fusing the host reads into the MoE kernel removes that dependency, so the GPU pipelines computation with transfers. This matters more as CPU-GPU interconnects get faster, as with NVLink-C2C on GH200, GB200/GB300 and (upcoming) Vera Rubin. ## Design Our goal is to extend the existing MoE kernels (Triton and Marlin) to pipeline loading missing experts alongside computing resident experts, without unnecessary dependencies between them. The host copies are variants of the existing Triton `fused_moe_kernel` and Marlin MoE kernel, chosen through their existing entry points; no other implementation in SGLang pages experts in from inside a MoE kernel. The kernel has to use as much of the interconnect bandwidth as it can for the whole launch, without taking every SM, so resident experts keep progressing. - How the kernel knows which experts to read from host memory: each layer has K GPU slots, and routed entries normally carry a slot id 0 to K − 1. title: [Feat] [Intel] disaggregation: Support PD incremental KV transfer on XPU
summary: [Feat] [Intel] disaggregation: Support PD incremental KV transfer on XPU ## Dependency https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/51211 ## Motivation With `--disaggregation-decode-enable-radix-cache`, the decode server reports the prefix it already holds (`decode_prefix_len`) and prefill sends only the KV pages after it. This saves KV transfer bytes and decode memory whenever requests share a prefix (multi-turn chat, shared system prompts). On Intel XPU this path did not work end to end: - NIXL `PackedKVSender` is hard-wired to CUDA (`cuda:{gpu_id}` buffer, `torch.cuda` streams) and builds its pointer table as a plain `int64` tensor, which rejects XPU addresses. - The decode deferred destination publish uses `torch.cuda.Stream/Event` and is gated on `torch.cuda.is_available()`, so it can never run on XPU. While measuring the feature, we also found that `kv_transfer_latency_ms` was not measuring the transfer. For senders that report their own latency (NIXL), it ended when the prefill scheduler *polled* and saw `Success`. A busy prefill polls once per forward, so the metric absorbed hundreds of milliseconds of poll delay. It barely moved when the radix cache cut bytes by 80%, and `kv_transfer_speed_gb_s` collapsed. ## Modifications **Commit 1: Support PD incremental KV transfer on XPU** - `nixl/packed.py`: `PackedKVSender` uses the current device and the buffer's device module, and builds its pointer table with `make_ptr_table`. - `decode.py`: deferred destination publish runs on `torch.get_device_module(...)` (stream, event, `current_stream`, `stream()`), enabled for `cuda`

title: [Fix] model_loader: Split checkpoint prefetch among each node's own ranks
summary: ## Motivation `--weight-loader-prefetch-checkpoints` splits the checkpoint's shards among a node's ranks, so that the node reads each shard once and the ranks' mmap loads hit the page cache. On multiple nodes, the split is wrong: - The split strides by `world_group.local_size or launch_world_size`. - On GPU, `LOCAL_SIZE` is never set, so the stride is the whole world size (`tp * pp`), while the offset `local_rank` is the GPU index. - With 4 nodes of 4 GPUs, every node prefetches the shards whose index `i` satisfies `i % 16 < 4`: the same quarter on every node. - The other three quarters are never prefetched on any node and are read through page faults during loading. ## Modifications The split now uses the number of ranks per node, `launch_world_size // nnodes` when `LOCAL_SIZE` is unset, and this rank's position on its node, `rank % ranks_per_node`. Ranks are numbered node by node. No option is added. Prefetch itself stays opt-in; #50342 (on by default) and #37806 (automatic on network filesystems) propose enabling it, and either would hit this bug on every multi-node run. ## Accuracy Tests Prefetch never changes which weights are loaded. Greedy completions of 5 prompts × 64 tokens were identical in every start below: - `Qwen/Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8`: sha `4ca5858b6ea52984` - `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro`: sha `cb1fb64ef757888e` ## Speed Tests and Profiling **Setup:** - 4 nodes × 4 GPUs, DP-attention plus EP16 (`--tp 16 --dp 16 --ep 16 --enable-dp-attention --weight-loader-prefetch-checkpoints`). - 920 GiB host RAM per node; checkpoints on a Lustre filesystem. - Every node's

title: [Fix] moe: Release the gate-up output alias before down GEMM
summary: ## Motivation In `_fused_moe_kernel_sequence`, the gate/up output is assigned to both `gemm1_out` and an intermediate-cache variable. After activation, `del intermediate_cache1` does not release the gate/up buffer because `gemm1_out` still owns a reference. This is an intra-call lifetime issue, not evidence of a progressive memory leak across requests. ## Modifications Delete the temporary `gemm1_out` alias immediately after the first GEMM invocation. title: [Perf] tokenizer_manager: Drop the prompt token list once a single request is dispatched
summary: ## Motivation `GenerateReqInput.input_ids` stays a Python `list[int]` for the whole request, because `ReqState.obj` holds the request until it finishes. With long agentic prompts (0.5-1M tokens) at high concurrency, the tokenizer manager process holds tens of millions of list elements in the young GC generations. Every gen0/gen1 collection walks all of them, about 8-9 ns per element, so the process stalls for 0.2-0.5 s per collection. Clients see these stalls as mid-stream gaps in the token stream. A PD decode gateway hits this hardest: it serves the full prompt of every in-flight request for the whole length of its decode. ## Modifications - `TokenizerManager.generate_request`, single-request path: after `_send_one_request`, a list `obj.input_ids` is swapped for the `array('q')` copy the tokenized request already carries. - The GC does not track an array, and the swap allocates nothing. - Nothing in the tokenizer manager reads `obj.input_ids` after dispatch except the finished-request log and the request dumps. - The request logger renders an array the same as a list, in both the text and JSON formats. - `scripts/playground/replay_request_dump.py` converts an array `input_ids` back to a list before posting a dumped request. A companion Dynamo change drops the handler's own references to the same list in disaggregated decode: ai-dynamo/dynamo#18895. The prompt list is freed by refcount right after dispatch only when the caller drops it too. ## Accuracy Tests No effect on model outputs: the scheduler already receives the `array('q')` copy. ## Speed Tests and Profiling DeepSe

title: [Perf] benchmark: Fix empty [32,32] search space in block-wise GEMM tuner
summary: ## Motivation Part of #50057. The block-wise W8A8 GEMM tuner could not tune a `[32, 32]` quantization recipe: `get_configs_compute_bound()` only produced `BLOCK_SIZE_K ∈ {64, 128}`, while `tune_on_gpu()` keeps only configs whose K tile divides `--block-k`. For `--block-k 32` every candidate was filtered out, and `tune()` then failed on a bare `AssertionError` **after** printing that the run had completed. This make the tuner support small block sizes and fail loudly and early when a block size genuinely has no valid tile. ## Modifications - New `python/sglang/benchmark/tuning_configs.py`: search-space construction moved here, torch/triton-free so it is CPU-testable. - `get_cuda_block_k_tiles(block_k)` keeps the historical `[64, 128]` K tiles whenever they divide `block_k`, and otherwise falls back to the largest supported tile that divides it (e.g. `32` for a `[32, 32]` recipe). Unsupported sizes raise a `ValueError`. - `get_configs_compute_bound(is_hip, block_k)` uses those tiles. - `benchmark/kernels/quantization/tuning_block_wise_kernel.py` - Passes the requested `--block-k` into the config generator. - Validates `--block-k` in `main()` before any device is initialized. - Replaces the bare `AssertionError` with a clear `RuntimeError`, and adds a clear `ValueError` if the filtered search space is empty. - Removed the now-duplicated local config generators. - `benchmark/kernels/quantization/README.md`: document the supported `--block-k` values. - New CPU unit test `test/registered/unit/bench/test_tuning_block_wise_kernel.py`. ### Behaviour preserved for existing recipes |

title: [Fix] [MUSA] kvcache: reuse public Triton store path
summary: ## Summary Route the MUSA KV-cache store through SGLang's existing public Triton cache-copy kernel. title: [Fix] dsa: Make metadata kernel batch size a runtime arg to avoid per-bs Triton recompiles
summary: ## Motivation Three Triton kernels in `python/sglang/kernels/ops/attention/dsa/metadata.py` declare the batch size as `bs: tl.constexpr`. The batch size changes from one step to the next: - `_fused_dsa_decode_metadata_kernel` - `_fused_dsa_target_verify_metadata_kernel` - `_fused_dsa_draft_extend_metadata_kernel` Because `bs` is a `tl.constexpr`, Triton specializes on it and compiles and caches a separate kernel for every batch size it sees. These kernels are not called during CUDA-graph capture. They run when a graph's metadata is filled on replay, with `bs` set to the padded graph batch size. So on main, the first decode step at each new padded batch size JIT-compiles up to three kernels inside the serving loop, and the Triton cache gets one entry per kernel per captured size. These kernels only use `bs` as a runtime bound: `offs_b < bs`, `row < bs`, `tl.range(0, bs)`, and `expanded_size = bs * next_n`. The compile-time tile shapes already come from `BLOCK_BS = next_power_of_2(bs)` and `BLOCK_EXPANDED`, so `bs` itself does not need to be a `constexpr`. For the same reason, `bs` is also added to each kernel's existing `do_not_specialize` list. Otherwise Triton's divisible-by-16 integer specialization would still compile a separate variant for batch sizes like 16, 32 or 48. This is the same bug as https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/33506, which @amd-mvarjoka fixed in another file. This PR applies that fix to the file below. ## Modifications - `python/sglang/kernels/ops/attention/dsa/metadata.py`: removed `tl.constexpr` from `bs` in all three kernels. `bs` stays in e

summary: ## Motivation **What** Mount the `FUSED_LINEAR_GELU` quality site on gfx1250 with a backend that keeps the FlyDSL GEMM and replaces aten's GELU with one bit-exact Triton launch, so the Wan2.2 FFN GELU stops taking 2.3 ms per block. **Why** `_input_independent_ok` rejects every arch >= 12.0 to keep the cuBLASLt epilogue off SM120, and gfx1250 reports 12.5, so the site never mounted on MI450. The FFN then runs `F.gelu(approximate="tanh")` on the [90000, 13824] bf16 intermediate: its byte offsets pass 2**31, so TensorIterator splits it into two launches that each reach only ~2.2 TB/s (1164 + 1131 us per block). hipBLASLt has no tuned gfx1250 kernels, so the cuBLASLt-style `_addmm_activation` is not an option; the gfx1250 backend runs `apply_unquantized_linear` (FlyDSL) and then the new kernel in place. title: [Feat] linker: support pipeline parallelism in linker
summary: ## Motivation Support pipeline parallelism (PP) in both `layer_wise` and `prefetch` modes of the unified cache external linker. Each rank queries its own storage shard, so backends only need to answer local lookups. The pipeline then agrees on a prefix that every stage can restore. ## Layer-wise loading PP0 issues a ticket with the request key and its local prefix position. Each rank queries the external store for the missing suffix and reports the page boundaries it can restore. A downstream stage can start its lookup before the request arrives. If its local device-cache prefix ends at a different position, it rechecks the suffix from its own pinned prefix. The ranks select the longest common boundary and use it during admission. Each stage then follows the existing layer-wise path, loading only its own layers into slots owned by the request. The restored KV enters the radix tree through the normal request insertion path. ## Prefetch and PP coordination Prefetch reuses HiCache’s ordered ticket broadcast and scheduler readiness relay. PP0 issues tickets in request order, and every rank queries its local backend. 1. PP0 sends its local hit upper bound through the readiness relay. Each stage reserves device slots up to that bound while slower local lookups can still be in flight. 2. Each rank builds a mask of the page boundaries its local query can restore and removes boundaries beyond its **actual reservation**. A single PP `MIN` all-reduce intersects these masks. title: [Feat] scheduler: Keep a reserve of KV and state slots for cached prefixes (--prefill-cache-reserve)
summary: ## Motivation On multi-turn agent traffic the prefix cache collapses once the sessions' contexts no longer fit next to the running requests. GLM-5.3-Flash NVFP4 on 2x B200 (TP2, the 0.9 split that was its default before #50018: 2,969,600 KV tokens, 419 state slots) with coding-agent sessions of about 75K tokens, `lru`: the hit rate is 0.91 at 16 sessions, 0.43 at 40 and 0 at 64. At 64 sessions 58 running requests hold 98% of the KV pool. A session that steps out for a tool call leaves its KV evictable, the next prefill takes it, and the session comes back to a full recompute. The extra prefill keeps decode waiting, so requests hold their KV longer and the next round loses more. The eviction order can't fix this: on the same setup (runs on #49430's branch, where `lru` is main's policy and the policy was still called `gds`; #49430 was reverted in #50118 and is now the opt-in `state_cost` in #50122) `lru` and `gds` both had a 0 hit rate at 64 sessions, since almost nothing is left to choose from. `--enable-session-radix-cache` (#29173) only evicts unreferenced KV first; with every session still open all of it is referenced, so I did not expect it to help and did not measure it. Admission can: a request that reuses little of the cache should wait for running requests to finish rather than take the room other sessions are about to come back to. This adds `--prefill-cache-reserve R` (off by default). summary: ### What this PR does / why we need it? `KVPoolWorker` requests `lazy_init` from the storage backend only for compressed models (`use_compress`, DSV4 `compress_ratios`) — the deferral introduced for that family in #9771. The gate therefore tracks the packed-path condition rather than the model family alone. summary: ### What this PR does / why we need it? Adds a reproducible single-layer GLM5Next KDA speculative verification benchmark on Ascend950DT_9581. The tuned kernel uses a contiguous convolution window throughout batches 1–80 and accumulates the decay prefix in Vector registers except at batch 2. The tuned TileLang schedule keeps weights on the owning core at batches 1, 3 and 5–10. At batches 11 through 80 it runs the two BF16 gate projections across the full token matrix with dense linear operators. The TileLang mixed kernel consumes the gate rows and performs convolution, state projection, recurrence and normalization. At batches 14, 17, 19 and 22 it retains the six-row input projection padding. The paired runner uses the same input tensors for the unfused baseline and tuned TileLang path. The serving change pads the merged input projection to 54 rows for full six-token RecoverSSM batches 6–8 on this SKU, then slices the projected tensor back to its valid rows before the state update. title: [RFC]: MoonEP redundant-expert load balancing for inference prefill
summary: ## Motivation ### Problem: MoE prefill is compute-imbalanced Expert-parallel MoE places each expert on exactly one rank. Every token is routed to its top-K experts, so a rank's work is set by how many routed rows land on the experts it owns. Real traffic is not uniform: in the workloads below the per-layer peak-to-average ratio (PAR, max expert load / mean expert load) is 1.7 on average for Qwen3-30B-A3B and reaches 2.53 on the hottest layer. Two effects follow: 1. The hot expert's owner rank runs a longer grouped GEMM while the other ranks idle. All-to-all and MC2 move the rows but cannot split the compute, so they do not fix the straggler. 2. With data parallelism, ranks advance in lockstep. A slow prefill rank stalls the whole DP step, which shows up directly as TTFT tail latency and, in a mixed prefill/decode run, as decode bubbles. ### What MoonEP changes MoonEP (MindSpeed-MM style) achieves balance by moving *weights*, not rows. Each rank keeps its `E/R` home experts and owns `B` redundant expert **slots** (`B = E/R` by default). Per MoE layer, a device-side planning kernel computes the global per-expert load, selects the `B` remote experts that each rank should host, and marks the rows that rank will compute locally. The rank prefetches those remote expert weights into its slots over SHMEM one-sided RMA, then runs a grouped GEMM over a zero-copy `[E/R + B]` weight alias. Rows for the prefetched experts stay local. Combine gathers the partial outputs and sums the top-K contributions with FP32 route weights. title: [BugFix][PCP] Compact decoder replay across PCP ranks on prefix hits
summary: ### What this PR does / why we need it? Fixes #22416. With prefill context parallelism (`PCP > 1`), prefix caching and `--swa-bounded-replay`, a cache hit can return an immediate EOS (`token_ids=[1]`) instead of the expected continuation. Cold prefills and PCP=1 hits are fine. Root cause: `DecoderReplayState._pcp_kept_lengths` decides whether the compact decoder replay saves rows by comparing the **global** kept row count with the **PCP rank-local** padded token extent: ```python num_padded = int(global_kept.sum()) # 128 if num_padded >= batch.num_tokens_after_padding: # 30 on PCP8 return None ``` A prefix hit schedules the hit's last replay window plus the uncached tail, and PCP spreads that query across ranks (e.g. 234 tokens -> 24-30 rows per rank on PCP8). The global window (128) is therefore larger than the local padded width (30), so the function returns `None`, the compact replay is skipped, and layers 21-39 run in the ordinary PCP main pass with the scheduler's replay floor instead of the compact replay floor. Cold prefills (local width ~1246) and PCP=1 hits (local width 234) take the compact replay, which is why only PCP>1 hits break. This PR compares against the global scheduled extent from the global batch instead. Compaction is a global decision; the rank-local padded width is not a valid proxy for it. ### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change? No. This is a correctness fix for an existing opt-in feature (`swa_bounded_replay` with `PCP > 1`). Prefix caching off and PCP=1 are inert: `DecoderReplayState` is only constructed when bounded replay is enabled

title: [RFC]: Eager-mode Sequence Parallelism (SP) with RS+GEMM/AG+GEMM Overlap
summary: ### Motivation. [#42770](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/42770) moves vLLM away from full-graph `torch.compile` fusion passes toward fusions expressed directly in eager/model code. [#43224](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/43224) tracks the concrete porting work for that effort and leaves two explicit open questions unanswered: 1. **Sequence Parallelism (SP)** — "We should decide whether to keep an SP path at all in the manual-fusion world." 2. **Async-TP** — "Not sure if this is possible to port to manual fusion." This RFC proposes an eager-mode answer to both open questions: - **Yes, keep SP** — expressed as a property of the model's own forward pass, not a compiler pass. - **Yes, Async-TP is portable** — as an opportunistic behavior of the same mechanism, which degrades gracefully to plain SP when it isn't available. **RFC Draft design:** https://docs.google.com/document/d/1yKH678I3_rcm6_IQzEbbMaGOwdDPS7Ri9YGLlutP5Bs/edit?tab=t.0 ### Proposed Change. ### Why SP needs a communication/GEMM boundary TP duplicates token-wise work like norms and residual adds. title: [Performance]: Quantize Humming per-token FP8 activations before AgRs dispatch
summary: ### Proposal to improve performance Humming indexed MoE experts currently defer dynamic per-token FP8 quantization until after AgRs gathers FP16/BF16 activations. Each receiving rank then quantizes the gathered rows before running the experts. This causes two avoidable costs: - AllGather transfers 16-bit activations even though the experts consume FP8. - The same activation rows are quantized separately on multiple receiving ranks. This can add communication and quantization overhead to prefill-heavy workloads using data parallelism with expert parallelism. I propose quantizing local activations with Humming’s existing producer before dispatch, transporting the FP8 activations together with their FP32 per-token scales, and reusing them in the receiving experts. Humming already has an input-scale path that skips repeated input quantization. The initial scope would be eligible eager execution with indexed Humming, dynamic per-token E4M3 activations, AgRs, TP=PCP=1 and DP=EP>1. Small batches may incur additional overhead, so an opt-in implementation would allow workload-specific use. ### Report of performance regression _No response_ ### Misc discussion on performance Related implementations: - #51332 enables pre-dispatch block-FP8 for Humming; the per-token path remains deferred. - #30014 moves FlashInfer FP4 quantization before AllGather. - #61962 proposes MXFP8 quantization before MoRI dispatch for AMD/AITER. This proposal targets Humming’s per-token FP8 path with AgRs. Reusing Humming’s own quantizer is important because the generic FP8 quantizer has different scale-floor

title: [Feature]: Support attention-only LoRA under MRV2 prefill context parallelism (PCP)
summary: ### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch MRV2 prefill context parallelism (PCP, #46570) currently rejects LoRA at startup. In `vllm/v1/worker/gpu/pcp_manager.py:175` (upstream main `898a7c68c2`): ```python if vllm_config.lora_config is not None: raise NotImplementedError("MRV2 PCP does not support LoRA yet.") ``` This makes PCP and multi-LoRA serving mutually exclusive. Those are exactly the two features that are most useful together: PCP is for long-context prefill, and LoRA is for serving many tenants from one base model. A user who needs both currently has to pick one. I would like to implement and upstream **attention-only LoRA under MRV2 PCP**, and I am opening this issue to confirm the scope before sending a PR. #### Why this is not just removing the guard Under PCP the model forward runs on rank-local chunks, but sampling runs on the restored global batch. LoRA has two different mappings and they must be built from different batches: - `token_lora_mapping` describes the tokens this rank actually computes, so it must stay rank-local. - `prompt_lora_mapping` describes the logits rows that the logits processor applies to (this is what `lm_head` LoRA uses). It must be built from the global batch's `req_ids`, `idx_mapping_np`, and `cu_num_logits_np`. Building it from the rank-local batch assigns an adapter id to the wrong row, and a request sampled on another rank can be missing entirely. MoE expert LoRA is a separate problem. PCP gathers MoE tokens across ranks before expert dispatch, so a rank's local token-to-adapter mapping does not describe the tokens its experts see.

title: [Bugfix][KV Offload] Defer block-reuse fences until the step is finalized

title: Optimize sliding window prefix cache hit search
summary: ## Summary Optimize `find_longest_cache_hit` in `SlidingWindowManager` to reduce lookup complexity from O(max_num_blocks) to O(max_num_blocks / stride) for low cache hit rate scenarios. ## Motivation The current implementation scans every block from right to left, costing up to `max_num_blocks` `BlockPool.get_cached_block` lookups even when the cache is cold. For a 128K-token request with a 4K window, this performs ~8192 lookups (block_size=16) although a hit only needs `cdiv(sliding_window - 1, block_size) = 256` contiguous blocks. ## Changes - **Stride-based probing**: Probe every `stride = sliding_window_contiguous_blocks` blocks from the right - **Right expansion on hit**: On a probe hit, expand right (at most `stride - 1` blocks) to verify - **Aligned jumps on miss**: After a miss at `idx`, resume at the next aligned edge below `idx - 1` - **Direct cached-prefix fallback**: Compute the cached-prefix fallback directly instead of full scan ## Performance From issue #62336 benchmarks: | pattern | main lookups | proposed lookups | main time | proposed time | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | cold cache | 8192 | 33 | 4.49 ms | 0.021 ms | | 1% random cached | 8192 | 33 | 4.61 ms | 0.021 ms | | tail hit / full cache | 256 | 257 | 0.23 ms | 0.23 ms | | adversarial (cached blocks on probe lattice) | 8192 | 128 | 4.63 ms | 0.11 ms | The worst case remains O(max_num_blocks), but the common low-hit-rate case becomes O(max_num_blocks / stride). ## Testing - Syntax verified with `python3 -m py_compile` - Existing tests should pass (will be verified in CI) --- <a href="https://app.blacksmi

title: [RL] Sharded RDT on the load plan
summary: ## Purpose Part of #64418 (tracker item **E1**). This PR moves the sharded RDT weight-transfer engine onto the load plan (`plan_loads`, `get_boxes`/`get_dest`) and direct reload. The load plan already knows where each weight lands, so RDT uses the plan rather than its own bake. - **Chosen:** flat buckets. title: [RFC]: Fault-tolerant sharded RDT weight sync: continue on surviving inference engines
summary: ### Motivation. With the sharded RDT weight-transfer backend (as redesigned on the load plan in #68038, part of #64418), one failed inference engine fails the weight sync for every engine. An engine crash fails the round within seconds. A lost RPC fails it only after the 300 s HTTP timeout or stall watchdog. RL rollout pools run on preemptible or shared capacity and see both kinds of failure. The sync should continue on the engines that are still healthy and let the failed ones rejoin later. This RFC lists the failure classes to handle, describes what happens today, and proposes a protocol. #68038 leaves this out of scope; it would be implemented in follow-up PRs. ### Proposed Change. #### Scope - **In scope:** failures on the inference side (an engine or a network path to it), before, during and after a sync. - **Out of scope:** trainer rank failures. A dead trainer rank ends training regardless of the transfer backend. #### Failure classes | # | Class | Example | What happens today (#68038) | |---|---|---|---| | F1 | Engine dead before the sync, still in the live set | replica crashed between steps | the sender's `start_weight_update` raises, then `_fail_producers`: **the sync fails for everyone**, quickly | | F2 | `start_weight_update` lost on the network, engine healthy | dropped HTTP request or response | same as F1; if the request did arrive, the engine is also left mid-reload | | F3 | `update_weights` lost **before** reaching the engine | dropped request | the engine is live and registered but never pulls. title: [RFC]: Token-Level Handoff for Encoder Disaggregation
summary: ### Motivation. The current Chat Completions EPD path can keep raw media off P/PD, but P/PD still renders the chat template, tokenizes the prompt, and reconstructs multimodal placeholders from model-specific metadata. E's multimodal processor has already computed that layout. We propose forwarding the layout E computed rather than the information needed to reconstruct it. Token-level Generate becomes the long-term worker interface for EPD. ### Proposed Change. #### Worker handoff 1. **Coordinator → E:** Send prompt token IDs with unexpanded media markers and the original media. 2. **E → Coordinator:** Return expanded prompt token IDs and per-item features: modality, cache identity, placeholder offset and length, the `is_embed` mask when needed, and CPU metadata the downstream model still reads. P/PD uses the supplied layout and loads embeddings through the EC connector, without receiving raw media or reconstructing placeholders. 4. **Coordinator → separate D:** Forward the same prompt layout and features with P's KV transfer parameters, not E's EC transfer parameters. The model's existing multimodal processor computes the layout; the coordinator treats model-specific metadata as opaque. Embeddings and KV still travel through their respective connectors. #### Multi-encoder fan-out Keep per-item routing and batch items assigned to the same encoder. title: [KV Offload] Prefetch secondary lookups on request admission
summary: ## Overview Start eligible secondary-tier metadata lookups when a request is admitted, so the lookup can overlap an already-running model step. With the EngineCore behavior from [#65466](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/65466), an `ADD` can be handled while EngineCore waits for the current worker output; this lets admission submit the probe before that step completes. The normal scheduler lookup still decides the hit boundary and starts promotion. ## Claims - Avoid waiting for the next `on_schedule_end()` to submit eligible FS/OBJ probes. - Reuse the async lookup state at scheduler lookup time, so a probe is not submitted twice for the same key. - Filter admission candidates against the current GPU/CPU cache snapshot and bound candidate count and outstanding prefetch batches. - Keep promotion and primary-tier slot allocation on the normal lookup path. This follows the request-arrival lookup timing used by the merged [Mooncake #61292](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/61292), adapted to `OffloadingConnector`'s tiered metadata lookup. Mooncake caches an async RPC result in its connector lookup client; this change reuses the FS/OBJ async lookup manager and filters GPU/CPU-resident chunks before probing secondary storage. It does not change the scheduler's final cache boundary or promotion decisions. Related work has a different scope: [#58198](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/58198) proposes a request-free CPU-to-GPU data load primitive, while this PR only starts secondary metadata probes for an admitted request. title: [Perf][Mamba] Export ShortConv (LFM2/LFM3) prefill checkpoints
summary: <!-- markdownlint-disable --> ## Overview Let the ShortConv layer of LFM2, LFM2-MoE and LFM3 (and their VL / Audio / Omni wrappers) export align-mode prefill checkpoints. With prefix caching on, the scheduler stops splitting a prompt at its last Mamba block boundary only if every Mamba layer can export a checkpoint. ShortConv declared none, so on CUDA and ROCm every long LFM prompt took an extra prefill step. No open PR covers this. #61462 only warms up the ShortConv prefill. ## Claims - In align mode, `ShortConv` declares checkpoint alignment 1. After its prefill conv it copies the conv window (the last `L_cache - 1` inputs) at each checkpoint, through the shared `MambaPrefillCheckpointExporter`, as Mamba2 does. PLE keeps exporting over all its non-spec rows. - When ShortConv layers in several KV cache groups share one metadata build, `update_block_table` re-gathers the checkpoint destinations for each group, as Mamba2 does. title: [Core] Session-based retention and lookup for the prefix cache
summary: ## Overview Requests that carry a `session_id` have the cached blocks they use evicted after all other cached blocks, and the session's next turn finds those blocks without a cache lookup per block. On by default with a 600 s TTL (`--session-cache-ttl`, `0` disables). It covers every KV cache group, so hybrid models keep their Mamba checkpoints. - **Lookup**: the session table records where the previous turn's blocks are. title: [Bugfix][KV Connector] Stop P/D transfers short of the last prompt token
summary: ## Purpose P/D decode recomputes the last prompt token. NIXL and Mooncake load all N prompt tokens and the scheduler then rewinds one token, but by then every group was laid out for position N. For a sliding window, prefill and decode both drop the block holding position N - W whenever N % block_size == block_size - 1, so the recomputed token N - 1 attends to the null block. With a zeroed null block this silently perturbs one window position for 1/block_size of requests; on DeepSeek-V4.1, whose null block is not zero, it corrupts the output (NaN logits at 1023/4095/8191 tokens, reported in #59197). The local prefix cache never has this problem: it caps a hit at N - 1 before allocation. Mamba P/D already avoided it with a Mamba-only backoff. This PR makes the backoff unconditional, so P/D follows the same rule as the local cache for every model. ## Changes - NIXL `_prefill_backoff()` and Mooncake P2P: the prefiller always stops at N - 1, and the decoder loads N - 1 tokens and computes the last one (multi-module MTP still backs off its lookahead). Both sides then lay out every group for the position decode resumes at. - NIXL bidirectional transfer: the prefiller pulls the decoder's KV from an earlier turn only if that KV ends before its last prompt token. The workers pair blocks from the end of the sequence, so a shorter pull (a prompt shorter than the decoder's context, e.g. a regenerated turn, or one the decoder's KV fully covers now that the prefiller stops one token short) shifted every block. - The cut never splits a multimodal item: if the prompt ends inside one, both s

summary: ## Overview This PR adds stream admission to persistent state ([RFC #65543](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/65543)). title: [Core] Persistent state: state pool, scheduling and release fence
summary: ## Overview This PR adds the lifetime of persistent state ([RFC #65543](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/65543)): a fixed pool of per-request state slots on the GPU, scheduling that binds one slot to a request across steps and across the inputs of a streaming-input request, and a release fence that returns a slot to the pool only after the worker has finished every write to it. title: [Bugfix][V1] Use the Mamba cache group's block size for align-mode chunk splitting
summary: ## Purpose Hybrid KV cache groups may have different token block sizes. `cache_config.block_size` is the **minimum over all groups** (set in `v1/engine/core.py` once the KV config is built) and represents a generic allocation geometry — it is not necessarily the Mamba recurrent-state block geometry. Using it in `_mamba_block_aligned_split` schedules chunk ends on a grid where the worker can never materialize a Mamba state. ## Reproduction Heterogeneous layout derived from a production deployment (Qwen3.8-27B hybrid + DFlash drafter, mamba align + prefix caching): - target FullAttention block 1648, drafter attention block **816** (page-size matching: 16 × 51), `MambaSpec.block_size` **1648**, hash unit 16, `cache_config.block_size = min(...) = 816`. Old scheduler stops chunks on the 816 grid; the worker (`postprocess_mamba`) checkpoints a state only where a chunk ends exactly on the 1648 grid. `816k == 1648m` only at the scheduler LCM (84048), so mid-prefill: - no state ever materializes, - the mamba group publishes **no** full-block prefix hash — or one claiming a boundary the slot never materialized (state-poisoning class from #43559) — - and a request repeating the same prompt **immediately** reuses nothing (hybrid reconciliation min = 0). The new tests in `tests/v1/core/test_mamba_align_chunk_split.py` reproduce this with real modules on current main (attention 816 + mamba 1648): they fail before this patch and pass after. ## Root Cause `_mamba_block_aligned_split` used the **generic** cache block size where the **Mamba state checkpoint geometry** is required. title: [Bug][Multimodal] Muse-Spark-Open: encoder profiling uses a 4-frame dummy while the model samples up to 600 — a single max-length video OOMs all TP ranks
summary: ### Describe the bug Muse-Spark-Open's profiling dummy builds its video with a hardcoded `num_frames=4` (`vllm/models/muse_spark/common/processor.py`, `MuseSparkOmniDummyInputsBuilder.get_dummy_mm_data`), while the model's video path samples up to `num_frames_per_video` = **600** frames per video (2 fps, the checkpoint's processor config). The encoder is therefore profiled at a ~150x smaller activation than a real maximum-length request, and no memory budget anywhere accounts for the real peak — the encoder-cache budget is token-based (76,800, correct), but the **activation** measurement comes from actually running the dummy. Compounding it, the `VideoDummyOptions.num_frames` override cannot raise the dummy either: `_get_dummy_videos` clamps with `num_frames = min(num_frames, overrides.num_frames)`, so a `num_frames: 600` override logs "exceeds the model's maximum number of frames (4)" and keeps 4. ### Impact — a user-triggerable, silent engine crash At default `gpu-memory-utilization` (and at 0.98), a single 5-minute video request (600 frames) OOMs **every TP rank** simultaneously and kills the engine: ``` torch.OutOfMemoryError: CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 886.00 MiB. GPU 1 has a total capacity of 184.31 GiB of which 813.31 MiB is free. ``` - Reproduced 5 times across two utilization settings; deterministic. - The EngineCore fatal **exits 0**, so pod restart-reason alerts do not catch it; each occurrence takes a serving pod out for ~5 minutes. - With cudagraphs (~9 GiB) plus the extensible KV cache's runtime growth, free memory converges to ~810 MiB regardless o

title: [KVConnector] Expose passive prefix hints for SimpleCPU and UMBP
summary: ## Overview Expose normally completed, reduced prefix-hit lengths from SimpleCPU and UMBP through a side-effect-free advisory getter. This supplies the missing connector adapters for the SPF proposal in https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/66705 without copying its scheduler implementation. ## Claims - Known zero is distinct from an unknown lookup; the hint includes the already-computed local prefix. - Reading a hint does not issue a query, consume a future, construct a load plan, pin CPU blocks, or refresh LRU state. - Allocation, request completion, and cache reset retire hints. Changed request identity, token length, hashes, or skipped external reads cannot reuse an old hint. - No throughput, latency, or cache-hit-rate improvement is claimed. ## Dependency and commit layout **Stacked on #66705; merge that prerequisite first.** Its original commits `d862580aac555dd452cf6bad663db1ef28b005db`, `61b2467842de84b6738a87a768acf17610e2a6e0`, and `b427c8b9594c2c97365cd3af1eae96ef2b39414e` are retained unchanged, including all original authorship, trailers, and commit IDs. Merge commit `e6dbc146fcdaff83b0b4f9fc8f1905fe4a6d1701` combines that exact SPF head with the adapter's existing main baseline `82c6b325b49ce361f5a295eb7d932e1b439e187d`. This retains newer UMBP fixes instead of reverting to the older SPF branch baseline. The only adapter implementation commit is [`acf0f5cf429de1f851a2e7e1a94d6e8676754947`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/commit/acf0f5cf429de1f851a2e7e1a94d6e8676754947), still 10 files / 265 additions. Review that commit for the connector-only change.

title: [RFC]: [KV Offload] Batched, serializable connector-manager interface
summary: ### Motivation. The offloading connector (`vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/offloading/`) and the offloading manager (`vllm/v1/kv_offload/`) share an interface that assumes both run in the same process, on the same thread, over shared mutable Python objects: - `lookup(key, req_context)` is **per key**. A cold 10k-chunk sliding-window group costs 10k calls per walk, and 20k for a full-attention plus sliding-window model over an absent store. Each call also polls finished jobs, reads the clock twice and records a metric sample. - `ReqContext` is **not a value**. Its counters delegate back into the connector (`_VllmReqContext._scheduler`), it carries a type-keyed `_state` scratch dict, and it carries `_offload_key_positions`, a per-request map the manager reads per key. - **Positions are connector-owned** data: `get_offload_key_position(key)` is a manager → connector call on the lookup and eviction paths. - **Four separate calls end a step** (`on_schedule_end`, `has_pending_work`, `take_events`, `get_stats`), each a crossing on its own. This blocks two directions: 1. A native (Rust) connector as in #66862. Every key is a Python↔Rust crossing, and every counter or position read is a reverse call into the connector. 2. An **external manager** over IPC, or a remote one. A per-key RPC is unusable, and `ReqContext` cannot be serialized: it holds a reference to the connector, arbitrary Python objects, and connector-owned state. ### Goals 1. One `lookup` call per ordered key slice. 2. `ReqContext` is immutable, call-scoped and serializable. 3. One call at the end of a ste

title: [Perf] DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash specialized decode for DEP2/4/8 on B300
summary: ## Overview This PR adds **DEP-specific fused EP communication for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on B300**: routing writes directly into dispatch buffers, expert finalize publishes to each request's owner, and one owner kernel combines reduction, local shared-expert output and mHC. It supports DEP2/4/8 at TP1. The executor, attention/indexer and Engram prefetch build on #61868 and #63921; main's TRTLLM W13/W2 kernels remain unchanged. The paired DEP2 measurements reduce full decode-step time by **8.7-16.1%**; earlier DEP4/8 prototypes reduce it by **6.2-25.5%**. **Benchmark setup:** Single-node B300, TP1 with DP=EP=2/4/8, DSpark5, **adaptive verification disabled**, and a **synthetic mean acceptance length of 3.51** in both arms. Each request uses **84Ki-648Ki input tokens (about 86k-664k)** and generates **3,000 output tokens**, with **2/4/8 concurrent requests per DP rank**. Inputs are prefilled before timing; results are three-run medians with FULL decode graph replay. **C denotes total concurrency across all DP ranks.** Each main/DEP pair uses identical prompts, lengths and rank assignments at the same concurrency. Each prompt starts with a distinct rank/request identifier, so shorter requests within a batch are not prefixes of longer ones. title: [Refactor][KV Cache] Remove EAGLE block dropping and default to lookahead hashes
summary: ## Purpose Lookahead block hashes are now used by core prefix caching and by every hash-keyed in-tree KV connector. With them, an EAGLE, EAGLE3 or MTP prefix hit already proves that the draft KV at the block boundary is reusable. The legacy approach drops the last matched block and compensates for it everywhere else. It is no longer needed, so this PR removes the drop and makes lookahead hashes the only behavior. #65448 (merged) enabled lookahead hashes for the remaining in-tree connectors. `supports_lookahead_block_hashes` now only marks connectors whose external hits ignore hash lookahead: Example, HF3FS, LMCache and FlexKV match by token IDs and report False. Core keeps lookahead hashes for them, and vLLM logs that spec decode acceptance may drop. More details: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1FaPogNcsjkYNgUORg1Scctj-9RDx7NTV3ZG6Gv84UdY/edit?tab=t.0 ## Implementation The drop changed what a hit length means. Every piece of code that predicts where a later request will hit therefore had to compensate: - lookup, with proof margins and convergence guards; - registration, with an extra proof block and wider SWA retention; - Mamba checkpoints, which back off one block; - a draft-group tagging chain; - and a copy of these rules in each connector. Lookahead puts the next L tokens into each block's hash, so a matched block already proves the boundary. With that, all of these compensations go away. The hand-written, drop-aware bounds collapse into one function: ``` get_reusable_prefix_length(N, a, L) = floor((N - max(1, L)) / a) * a ``` L is `num_hash_lookahead_tokens`: 1 for

title: [Bugfix][Muse Spark] Keep the FP32 RoPE tables in FP32
summary: <!-- markdownlint-disable --> ## Overview Muse Spark builds FP32 RoPE tables. `RotaryEmbedding.forward_cuda` (and `forward_hip`, which goes through it) calls `_match_cos_sin_cache_dtype`, which replaces an FP32 cos/sin table with a copy in the query's dtype (eager), or casts the whole table on every call or uses a BF16 copy (compiled). So Muse Spark's DSpark context-key precompute and the unfused attention branch of the AMD and NVIDIA attention rotated BF16 Q/K with a BF16 table, and the FP32 table was gone after the first call. Since #58838, `forward_cuda` runs the rotation through the vLLM IR ops `rotary_embedding` / `rotary_embedding_query_only`. On top of that, this PR changes three things: - **`rotary_embedding/base.py`.** `forward_cuda` passes `self.cos_sin_cache` to the IR op as is when it is on the query's device, and keeps the helper for an actual device mismatch. - **`kernels/vllm_c.py`.** The `vllm_c` provider no longer requires `query.dtype == cos_sin_cache.dtype`. The C++ kernels (`rotary_embedding`, `rotary_embedding_out`) dispatch on the Q/K dtype and the table dtype independently and compute in FP32. With the requirement, an FP32 table with BF16 Q/K falls back to the `native` provider. - **`muse_spark/{amd,nvidia}/dspark.py`.** The context-key precompute calls `self._rotary_emb.forward_cuda(positions, k, None)` instead of the module, as the Muse Spark attention already does. title: [CI][ROCm] Transcendental, reduction and MFMA bounds for specialized decode (T1 of #68016)
summary: ## TL;DR GPUs compute `exp`, `1/x`, `1/sqrt(x)` and matrix products approximately — the answer is close to the true one, never equal to it. To test code that uses them, you have to decide up front *how* close counts as correct. The usual shortcut is to run the code once and call whatever it printed the acceptable answer; that proves nothing, because it will still "pass" after someone breaks it in a way that moves the number only slightly. This PR tests AMD's DeepSeek-V4.1 decode kernels against limits worked out from the chip manual and from the arithmetic itself, **before** the kernels are run — so a test failing means the kernel is wrong, not that it drifted. 34 new tests, all passing on both the boards they target — MI355X in 24 seconds, MI300X in 15. ## Purpose Completes the primitive tier (T1) of #68016 for the AMD monokernels. #67135 checked the device helpers that have a closed form — roundings, packings, scale codes, data movement — and asserted them bit-exact. This adds the helpers that cannot be bit-exact: the hardware transcendentals, the wave reductions and the MFMAs. The point of the series is that comparing a monokernel against vLLM's own ops cannot localise a bug, because both sides reach for the same helpers and a shared bug cancels. The same argument applies to tolerances: a tolerance measured from the kernel it checks proves nothing. **Every bound here is derived a priori** — from AMD's documented instruction accuracy, from the helper's own source, or from the arithmetic of the accumulator — and is written next to the assertion that uses it. title: [Core] Resolve the Mamba block size from the KV cache specs of all pipeline stages
summary: <!-- markdownlint-disable --> ## Overview In align mode the scheduler aligns every Mamba group to one block size, but each worker sizes its Mamba blocks from the attention layers it holds, so under pipeline parallelism a stage of a hybrid model without attention layers keeps the default 64 while the other stages use the aligned size; with prefix caching, Nemotron-Nano-9B-v2 at PP=4 then fails on its first batch, and CPU KV offloading fails at startup. This PR resolves the Mamba block size once in the engine core from the KV cache specs of all workers, and every worker rebuilds its Mamba specs with it. Fixes #51752. Credit to @taking-lying-flat, who found the mismatch and proposed syncing the sizes chosen by the stages with attention layers in #51764; credited as co-author. ## Claims - Under pipeline parallelism, the Mamba KV cache specs of every stage use the Mamba block size of PP=1. title: [Core][Spec Decode] Give the DFlash/DSpark drafter's KV its own block pool
summary: ## Purpose **Stacked on #64109 (DFlash/DSpark drafter KV backs only its tail) and #64628 (`--max-num-inflight-kv-loads`)**, and builds on #63416 (NIXL pairs KV regions by layer, now merged). The branch merges #64109 and #64628; the rest of the diff is this PR. This PR adds `--draft-kv-pool`, which gives a DFlash or DSpark drafter's sliding-window KV its own block pool. With the hybrid KV cache manager every group draws from one pool, and every block is as large as the widest group's. A drafter group of a few sliding-window layers therefore pays a target-sized block for each of its blocks. RFC #59117 measures what this costs on a GDN target with a 5-layer DFlash drafter: 3-11x less KV capacity. In its own pool, a drafter block is as large as the drafter's layers. The pool is sized for the window each request keeps under #64109. ## Changes **Config:** `--draft-kv-pool` and `--draft-kv-pool-cache-fraction` (default 0.5). **Planning** (`kv_cache_planning.py`): - `get_global_kv_cache_groups` groups the drafter's `DFlashSlidingWindowSpec` layers on their own, in pool 1 (`KVCacheGroupSpec.pool_id`). - The pool holds the null block plus `(max_num_seqs + max_num_inflight_kv_loads) × (1 + cache_fraction)` requests at their admission cap. An async KV load holds drafter blocks without counting toward `max_num_seqs`, and #64628 caps those loads, so this bounds every request that holds drafter blocks. A KV consumer with the pool must therefore set `--max-num-inflight-kv-loads`; startup fails without it. The pool is sized from the specs alone, so every worker and the scheduler agree on it

title: [Bugfix][Frontend] Stop API workers and coordinator on parent loss
summary: ## Overview Stop Python API workers and the DP coordinator when their launcher dies, so an API-only head node cannot leave an old HTTP endpoint running. Addresses the API-only lifecycle case in #65096 ([scope note](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/65096#issuecomment-6615887947)). ## Claims - Locally owned API/coordinator processes detect loss of their original parent, request normal SIGTERM cleanup, then bound a stuck shutdown with self-exit. - The parent PID is captured before spawning, covering loss before initialization. - Separately owned engines are not terminated by the frontend's owner-loss handler. - EngineCore supervision and startup-handshake deadlines are unchanged. ## Validation Baseline process tests failed in all four requested start-method/SIGTERM cases: `API worker/coordinator outlived their launcher`. A real API-only deployment with tiny Llama weights also kept returning the configured model from `/v1/models` after launcher SIGKILL. The patched standalone probe exited all API-side processes while its separate headless launcher and engines stayed alive. The new real-server regression fails on base `37753d9` with four surviving API-side processes, then passes with the patch, including port rebind and separate-engine survival. title: [Feature] Add MXFP8 expert online quantization to DeepGEMM MegaMoE
summary: ## Overview Add an online quant mxfp8 path for DeepGEMM MegaMoE: BF16 expert shards are quantized to MXFP8 with canonical per-32 UE8M0 scales while loading, DeepSeek-V4 selects it automatically when the config requests dynamic MXFP8 experts. ## Claims - Add a dynamic MXFP8 quantization path for MoE experts: `DeepGemmMegaMoEExperts(..., online_quant=True)` quantizes each BF16 expert shard to `fp8_e4m3` with canonical per-1x32 UE8M0 scales while loading, so the checkpoint needs neither pre-quantized expert weights nor expert scales. - Enable MXFP8 MegaMoE for DeepSeek-V4: the model resolves `MEGA_MOE_MXFP8` with online quantization when `quantization_config.moe.weight` is dynamic MXFP8, and keeps the existing offline MXFP4 path for every other expert precision. - Accuracy: with BF16 dense layers, full GSM8K scores 0.9356 and 0.9378 with MXFP8 online experts versus 0.9439 with BF16 experts. ## Validation **Unit tests** ```bash python -m pytest tests/model_executor/layers/test_mega_moe_online_quant.py -v # 4 passed ``` Kernel test on SM100 — online loading of a BF16 expert shard writes exactly the values and scales that loading a pre-quantized MXFP8 shard writes: ```bash python -m pytest \ tests/kernels/moe/test_deep_gemm_mega_moe.py::test_deep_gemm_mega_moe_online_quant_matches_pre_quantized_loading -v # 1 passed ``` **Accuracy** DeepSeek-V4-Flash, full GSM8K test set (1319 questions), 5-shot, greedy. Dense is bf16, the two arms differ only in whether use mxfp8 megamoe or bf16 experts. | arm | GSM8K | | --- | ---: | | bf16 experts | 0.9439 | | mxfp8 megamoe | 0.9356 / 0.9378 |

title: [Perf][Kernel] Use FlashInfer cute-dsl NVFP4 linear for decode on SM120
summary: ## Purpose On SM120, use FlashInfer's cute-dsl NVFP4 GEMM for decode-sized inputs. `FlashInferCuteDslNvFp4LinearKernel` heads `_POSSIBLE_NVFP4_KERNELS` but is gated to sm_10x, even though FlashInfer's cute-dsl FP4 backend gained an SM12x runner in flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#5100 (included in the pinned 0.7.4). On SM120 that runner is faster than FlashInfer CUTLASS (today's default) up to 64 tokens and slower above, so this: - allows the kernel on SM120 when FlashInfer has the SM12x runner and torch is built for CUDA 13+, which that runner requires (`has_flashinfer_sm12x_cutedsl_fp4_gemm()`); - on SM120 dispatches per call inside a custom op (`sm120_cutedsl_nvfp4_mm`): cute-dsl when M <= 64 and the output is BF16 (the SM12x runner only writes BF16), FlashInfer CUTLASS otherwise. Both take the same swizzled + padded operands, so the weight layout is unchanged. Layers whose padded (N, K) the SM12x runner rejects (N or K not a multiple of 64, or N * K >= 2**31) use CUTLASS for every M; - compiles the cute-dsl kernels for M = 1..64 once per weight shape at load time. cute-dsl compiles one kernel per token-count bucket on first use (0.3-0.5 s each); without this, eagerly run layers such as `lm_head` on the sampled tokens compiled while serving and raised median TTFT by 14% at concurrency 32. SM100/103 behavior is unchanged. SM121 (GB10) is not measured and keeps its current selection. Not a duplicate: no open PR enables cute-dsl NVFP4 linear on SM12x (searched "cutedsl sm120", "FlashInferCuteDslNvFp4LinearKernel", "sm12x_cute"). Related: #67202 reorders b12x ahead of FlashInfer CUT

title: [Metrics][SpecDecode] Add draft-logits NaN statistics aligned with the verifier's read set
summary: ## What does this PR do? Extend the sampler NaN statistics to the **draft logits**, restricted to the read set of the speculative-decoding verifier. The existing probe (`VLLM_COMPUTE_NANS_IN_LOGITS` -> `get_num_nans`, reported per request as `num_nans_in_logits`) only covers the target side; this PR adds `get_num_draft_nans` and plumbs `num_draft_nans` alongside `num_nans` through the existing chain (`SamplerOutput` -> `ModelRunnerOutput` -> `EngineCoreOutput.num_draft_nans_in_logits`), gated by the same flag. ## Why is it needed? With speculative decoding, an acceptance collapse can come from either side: the target verification logits or the draft proposals. The current statistics are blind to the draft side, so a production failure cannot be attributed -- a real incident on DeepSeek V4.1-flash DSpark collapsed to all-placeholder output with acceptance 0 and no self-recovery, and the target-side probe alone could not disambiguate "target poisoned" from "draft poisoned". (The target-side chain was later confirmed by the nan_to_num fix in #14116.) The draft side also needs **more than a raw scan**: `draft_logits` is a persistent `[max_num_reqs, K, V]` cache whose inactive slots and unscheduled steps hold stale data. A full-buffer scan reports NaNs from cells the verifier never loads, and misattributes them to the current step. The statistics input set must equal the verifier's read set. ## Design The probe is restricted to the verifier's read set on three axes: 1. **Active (slot, step) pairs** -- the census gathers exactly the rows the verify kernels consume, indexed by the

title: [ROCm][Muse Spark] Support EPLB with FP8 and BF16 experts
summary: ## Overview Lets Muse Spark run with `--enable-eplb` on ROCm with Triton FP8 and BF16 experts; today it fails at init (`Muse Spark FP8 on ROCm does not support EPLB`). MXFP4 still rejects EPLB. On 8× MI300X, EPLB gives +2.2–6.5% throughput at 8k–16k input and concurrency 32–64, and is 3.5–5.2% slower at 1k input. Median TTFT is 11–27% lower at every 8k and 16k point. Changes: - `FusedMoEFactory` attaches its `EplbLayerState` to a caller-built router that has none, so the Muse router maps logical to physical experts and records load. The MoE block passes `enable_eplb` and `num_redundant_experts` to the experts. - The Quark FP8 Triton MoE method declares `supports_eplb`: the expert dim is outermost in every weight and scale. - The consolidated expert loader fills every initial physical replica from `EplbState.build_initial_global_physical_to_logical_map`, not only the first `num_logical_experts`. On ROCm, use `"communicator":"pynccl","use_async":false`. With async NIXL, rearrangements overlapped and serving was 9–68% slower than without EPLB; the model logs a warning. Synchronous steps on `main` still do up to five GPU→CPU syncs, removed by #66399; the numbers below are without it. ## Validation `amd/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-Quark-PTPC-FP8`, TP8 + EP, 8× MI300X, `vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:nightly-83c078d955` with this branch's files mounted. title: [Feature][KV Offload] Don't count transient tier I/O errors as back-pressure
summary: ## Overview Part of #54363 (item 4, classification only). Failed FS-tier jobs now carry their errno, and transient errors no longer push the tier into back-pressure. ## Claims - `JobResult.error_errno` holds the errno of a job's first failing operation (None if unknown). The FS tier sets it for stores and loads. - `tiering/io_errors.py` classifies errnos as CAPACITY, TRANSIENT, PERSISTENT or UNKNOWN. - The manager skips `on_store_failed()` for TRANSIENT errors only (EINTR, EAGAIN, EBUSY, EMFILE, ENFILE, ENOMEM). ENOSPC, EIO, EACCES and errno-less failures, including the short-write error from #66278, still count, as before. - No change to the BackpressureDetector API or to tiers that don't report an errno. ## Validation New tests: the errno table in a new `test_io_errors.py` (it tests the new `io_errors.py` module); thread pool keeps the first failing errno and the FS tier reports ENOTDIR/ENOENT from a real failed store/load, in `test_fs_tier.py`; and two cases in `test_backpressure.py`. manager.py reverted to main (34c6538): $ pytest tests/v1/kv_offload/tiering/test_backpressure.py -k "transient or capacity" FAILED ...test_transient_failures_do_not_activate_pressure[24] # EMFILE FAILED ...test_transient_failures_do_not_activate_pressure[11] # EAGAIN FAILED ...test_transient_failures_do_not_activate_pressure[4] # EINTR 3 failed, 3 passed With this PR: $ pytest tests/v1/kv_offload/tiering/test_backpressure.py -k "transient or capacity" 6 passed $ pytest tests/v1/kv_offload/tiering/{test_io_errors,test_backpressure,test_fs_tier,test_tiering_offloading}.py 214 passed ## Detail

title: [Attention][DCP] Sparse MLA DCP: CuTe DSL A2A reduce and DCP ShardQ (Kimi K3.1 6/6)
summary: <!-- markdownlint-disable --> ## Purpose Last split (6/6) of Kimi K3.1: sparse MLA optimizations for decode context parallelism (DCP). Splits 1-5 are merged (#66030, #66028, #66037, #66532, #65685), so this diff is only the DCP part. Nothing here changes behavior without DCP. Changes: - **CuTe DSL direct A2A LSE reduce (SM100).** Same buffers and signal protocol as the CUDA op, 2 launches instead of 4. - **DCP ShardQ.** Extends the TP ShardQ from #63956 to DCP == TP (FlashInfer sparse MLA, SM100). Prefill rows push their MLA and indexer pages into a symmetric-memory workspace (`vllm/v1/attention/ops/dcp_shardq`), and each rank then handles a slice of the tokens with all heads over the gathered context. Prefill rows skip the query all-gather, LSE combine and top-k merge; decode rows stay on the DCP path. The workspace holds `max_model_len` tokens (plus one page per request). A step that doesn't fit runs on the DCP path as on `main`; no scheduler changes. Controlled by `attention_config.sparse_mla_shard_q` (on by default, same as TP ShardQ); needs an fp8 indexer K cache. - **nvfp4_ds_mla + DCP** is now accepted; its chunked-context gather reads the local context. - **FlashMLA sparse:** DCP can gather up to 128 query heads, and long fp8 mixed batches run in chunks. - The indexer metadata no longer syncs to read DCP-local lengths back from the GPU. - Kimi K3.1 DSA layer hooks for DCP ShardQ. Related: #65555 is the ROCm DSv4.1 ShardQ indexer. ## Test Plan / Results Kimi K3.1, real weights, 2 × 4 GB300, TP = DCP = 8, fp8 KV cache, fp8 indexer, a2a DCP backend, interleave 1, no sp

summary: ## Overview `has_quark()` decides whether vLLM may select its MX-FP4 emulation kernels, but it imports only the top-level `quark` package, which loads nothing but its version, while those kernels import `quark.torch.kernel`. title: [Bugfix][ROCm] Fix the query scale of the ll4mi FP8 MFMA paged attention
summary: ## Overview With `VLLM_ROCM_FP8_MFMA_PAGE_ATTN=1` and an fp8 KV cache, ROCm paged attention returns wrong output for GQA 5-16 on gfx942 and gfx950: Qwen3-14B-FP8 scores 0.02 on GSM8K. The ll4mi mfma16 kernel quantizes the query with an inverted scale, and only lane 0 holds the query maximum. This PR fixes both. The bug dates from #22222. #68863 removes the mode instead; the two PRs are mutually exclusive. ## Claims - `q_scale` is the dequantization scale `q_max / 224` and multiplies the QK scale, as `k_scale` does. `scaled_vec_conversion` stores `fp8(q / q_scale)`, so `q_scale = 224 / q_max` with `scale2 /= q_scale` multiplied every logit by `(q_max / 224)^2`. - `warpReduceMax` reduces with `__shfl_xor`, so every lane holds the warp maximum. With `__shfl_down` only lane 0 did, and the other lanes quantized and rescaled their query elements with smaller, different maxima. - Nothing else changes. `warpReduceMax` has one caller, and its result is read only under `MFMAType::Fp8`. The f16 MFMA path, the auto KV cache and GQA 1-4 (mfma4) give bitwise-identical output before and after on gfx942. ## Validation MI325X (gfx942), `_rocm_C` built from `153dc0464` with and without this patch. title: [Perf][Model Loader] Prefetch the node's share under EP and read whole tensors with pread
summary: <!-- markdownlint-disable --> ## Overview **Stacked on #68351**: the first commit is #68351's; review the rest ([this PR's own diff](https://github.com/anish-shanbhag/vllm/compare/fix-prefetch-node-local-split...prefetch-ep-aware)). Auto-prefetch skips any checkpoint that does not fit in 90 % of available RAM. Under expert parallelism with the EP weight filter (on by default with #68491), a node reads only the shared tensors plus its own ranks' experts, often a fraction of the checkpoint. DeepSeek-V4-Pro is 805 GiB, and on nodes with ~800 GiB free it gets no prefetch at all, even though a DEP16 node reads 256 GiB of it. Kimi K3.1 Pro is 1454 GiB, and a DEP16 node reads 503 GiB of it. This PR gates on what the node reads when whole shards do not fit, prefetches just those bytes, and then hands the loader tensors read with `pread` instead of views of the file mapping when the rank uses tensors whole. Checkpoints that fit still get #68351's whole-shard split. summary: ## Overview Opt-in ROCm prefill path for DSA indexers under decode-context parallelism (`DCP > 1`). title: [DCP][Performance] Add Shared-DCP peer-addressable decode data paths
summary: # [DCP][Performance] Add Shared-DCP peer-addressable decode paths Depends on #50005. ## Summary This PR introduces Shared-DCP for bounded single-node decode. Shared-DCP represents selected DCP intermediates as peer-addressable distributed GPU objects with stable storage, explicit ownership, `local_view` / `peer_view`, and device-side synchronization. DCP already shards state and combines rank-local results. This PR changes how selected decode intermediates are stored and consumed: producers can write directly into the consumer's final layout, or consumers can load owner shards directly through CUDA VMM peer mappings, without first materializing a complete tensor through a collective. The PR covers four decode-time communication points: | Boundary | Shared-DCP path | | --- | --- | | Query AllGather | Fused RoPE/FP8 producers store query shards directly into each consumer-local inbox | | Top-K candidate AllGather | Stable-TopK loads owner-local candidate shards directly through local and peer views | | LSE AllGather | Output producers store each destination's LSE shard directly into that output owner's VMM allocation | | Output ReduceScatter | Output producers store destination head shards into the same owner allocation; the owner performs the final local LSE correction and accumulation | DeepGEMM is unchanged. ## Shared-DCP performance vs baseline The primary full-stack comparison uses the final clean #50009 source for both arms. summary: # [DCP][Kernel] Add Shared-DCP consumer-direct Top-K Depends on #50005. ## Summary This is the focused Top-K extraction of Shared-DCP. DCP already distributes data across ranks. For sparse-indexer candidates, this PR uses an owner-sharded object: ```text DeepGEMM owner-local scores -> local Top-K candidate shard -> publish one owner-local CUDA VMM object per rank -> stable-TopK consumer directly loads rank-major local/peer shards -> global Top-K indices ``` The existing bounded path instead materializes a complete candidate tensor on every rank: ```text local Top-K candidate shard -> pack -> candidate AllGather -> complete local candidate tensor -> stable-TopK ``` The new path removes that materialization boundary. The data still crosses GPU boundaries and synchronization is still required, but the consumer reads the owner-sharded physical layout directly. DeepGEMM is unchanged. ## Scope and runtime contract - opt-in `VLLM_DCP_TOPK_VMM=1`, default off; - bounded decode rows 16 through 128; - one owner-local candidate allocation per DCP rank; - rank-major stable-TopK peer consumption; - device-side publish/wait/ack epochs for CUDA-graph replay; - eager VMM workspace initialization before memory profiling and capture; - exact rows=32 activation marker without first-seen-shape logging in the hot path.
