title: GroundAnything: Reconciling Parallel Decoding with Precise Visual Grounding at Flash Speed
summary: Autoregressive (AR) grounding models serialize spatial predictions, introducing sequential latency and imposing a causal order on output tokens. We view grounding as visual evidence extraction: objects, locations, and spatial relations are jointly constrained by the image and query, yet their dependencies do not imply an intrinsic left-to-right generation order. This distinction makes bidirectional diffusion a natural fit, allowing spatial hypotheses to emerge in parallel and be jointly refined through iterative denoising. We introduce GroundAnything, a 4B-parameter grounding foundation model that reconciles fast parallel decoding with precise localization through blockwise denoising. Training combines grounding pretraining from public datasets and dedicated data engines, direct AR-to-diffusion conversion with joint AR and diffusion objectives, supervised fine-tuning, and GRPO-based reinforcement post-training. Across 30 grounding benchmarks, our autoregressive variant, GroundAnything-VLM, establishes a new overall state of the art among similarly sized models at 72.42%, remaining competitive with GPT-6 Astra (71.35%). With entropy-guided decoding, GroundAnything also surpasses the prior state of the art at this scale, averaging 61.75% versus 53.32% for the fast MTP-based LocateAnything model. We further explore decoding strategies, showing that an optional self-speculative mode achieves a 4.51$\times$ speedup over the AR counterpart with a 0.74 percentage-point drop in COCO F1mIoU. Infrastructure experiments show that progressive inference optimizations translate parallel

title: Beam Model Technical Report
summary: Beam is a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 501.3B total parameters and 23.4B active parameters, specifically built and optimized for coding, reasoning, and agentic workloads. Beam delivers frontier level reasoning, while requiring 3-4x less inference compute than many models of its class. Pretrained on 23.8T diverse, curated, high-quality tokens, Beam features a 1M-token context window achieved through a novel two-stage midtraining phase, built on verifiable, correctness-anchored data. Post-training leveraged a large-scale, fully asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) campaign across 10.5K GB300 GPUs, generating over 100M rollouts over 4 weeks of training. We believe this is one of the largest scale RL runs conducted by any open lab to date. Across our evaluation suite, capabilities continued to improve as we increased RL compute, with no sign of a plateau. Supported by deep hardware-model co-design, FP8/NVFP4 quantization, and a 1.93B-parameter speculative decoding drafter (DFlash 2), Beam maximizes serving throughput with efficient, flexible deployment. Averaged across conversation turns and harm categories, Beam refuses or pivots on 88.9% of harmful requests while complying with 81.5% of harmless requests, achieving the highest refusal/pivot rate on harmful requests among open-weight models on the Pareto frontier.

title: Efficient and Robust Drafting with Multi-Token Prediction
summary: Speculative decoding has emerged as a critical technique for accelerating Large Language Model (LLM) inference by decoupling generation into a drafting phase and a parallel verification phase. A crucial challenge is therefore designing a drafter that is both lightweight and accurate enough to approximate the predictions of the target model. We present a highly optimized Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) architecture that extends existing backbone LLMs to efficiently produce high-quality drafts. Built around a single shared drafting head, our approach features three core architectural optimizations: target activation injection to anchor semantic planning, zero-copy KV-cache cross-attention to bypass prefill compute and reduce memory overhead, and an efficient clustered vocabulary projection to reduce the cost of full-vocabulary decoding. Testing these improvements with the Gemma 4 model family, our G-MTP shows out-of-the-box speedups for both large server-side setups (up to 3.1$\times$) and smaller models targeting memory-constrained on-device environments (up to 2.3$\times$ on H100 and up to 2.2$\times$ on a smartphone GPU). In addition, we present parameter-efficient fine-tuning recipes for G-MTP that keep the drafter aligned with the backbone LLM under domain shift, requiring up to 1.83$\times$ fewer target forward passes than tuning only the backbone.

title: Supportive Token Revealing for Fast Diffusion Language Model Decoding
summary: Discrete diffusion language models can generate text efficiently by updating multiple masked positions in parallel, but this parallelism introduces a quality-latency trade-off. Aggressive decoding may commit mutually dependent tokens too early, while conservative decoding requires many denoising steps. Existing methods address this tension by deciding which tokens are safe to reveal using confidence or dependency criteria. However, avoiding unsafe commits does not necessarily make the remaining masked sequence easy to decode, since uncertain tokens may depend on masked tokens, creating a bottleneck for denoising steps. We propose AXON, a training-free module that can be added on top of existing parallel decoding strategies for diffusion language models. Rather than replacing the base decoder, AXON monitors the remaining uncertain masked tokens and intervenes only when their current state suggests that additional context is needed. It then shifts the criterion from which tokens are safest to reveal to which confident reveals would best support later denoising. AXON selects anchors, confident masked tokens that uncertain positions attend to, using attention, uncertainty, and confidence signals. Experiments on reasoning and code-generation benchmarks across multiple diffusion language models show that AXON improves the quality-latency trade-off of existing parallel decoders, often reducing the number of function evaluations while maintaining or improving accuracy.

title: Raptor: Rejection-aware Adaptive Tree based on Speculative Decoding
summary: Tree-structured speculative decoding accelerates vision-language models (VLMs) by verifying multiple candidate continuations in parallel. However, long visual contexts increase the cost of speculative computation, making candidate coverage and redundant expansion important considerations beyond tree topology adaptation. We propose Raptor, a training-free framework that uses rejection feedback to jointly regulate candidate coverage and drafting effort. Our key insight is that acceptance length alone cannot distinguish insufficient candidate coverage from excessive deep expansion, and these conditions require different allocation decisions. Raptor therefore extracts complementary rejection-aware signals to characterize speculative progress, frontier coverage, and redundant expansion. These signals jointly guide bounded, momentum-smoothed updates of tree depth, branching width, and drafting budget, together with execution control that limits unnecessary drafting and progressively restores expansion when appropriate. Extensive experiments with two VLMs across seven multimodal benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of Raptor, achieving up to 2.39x average speedup over autoregressive decoding.

title: Next-Latent Prediction Transformers Learn Compact World Models
summary: Transformers replace recurrence with a memory that grows with sequence length and self-attention that enables ad-hoc lookups over past tokens. Consequently, they lack an inherent incentive to compress history into compact latent states with consistent transition rules. This often leads to learning solutions that generalize poorly. We introduce Next-Latent Prediction (NextLat), which extends standard next-token training with self-supervised predictions in the latent space. Specifically, NextLat trains a transformer to learn latent representations that are predictive of its next latent state given the next token. Theoretically, we show that these latents converge towards belief states, compressed information about the history necessary to predict the future. This simple auxiliary objective injects a recurrent inductive bias into transformers while leaving their architecture, parallel training efficiency, and inference unchanged. NextLat effectively encourages transformers to form compact internal world models with coherent belief states and transition dynamics -- crucial properties not guaranteed by standard next-token prediction alone. Empirically, across benchmarks in world modeling, reasoning, planning, and language modeling, NextLat demonstrates significant gains over standard next-token prediction and other baselines in downstream accuracy, representation compression, and lookahead planning. Furthermore, NextLat enables variable-length self-speculative decoding, accelerating inference by up to 3.3x in language modeling. NextLat offers a simple yet effective paradigm for

title: SGAR: Feed-Forward 3D Reconstruction via Sparse Geometry-Guided Attention
summary: Feed-forward models have been very successful in 3D reconstruction with ad hoc attention designs that relate all view patches densely. However, the cost of this dense global attention grows quadratically with the number of views, preventing the model from applying to larger-scale reconstruction settings. In this paper, we argue that most dense attention computations are unnecessary from a classical structure-from-motion perspective: 3D structures stem from geometrically matching regions in 2D. We bring this principle to learning-based feed-forward reconstruction with our Sparse Geometric Attention Reconstruction (SGAR) method. In SGAR, each patch token attends to only a small set of patch tokens from other views, chosen by a lightweight learned key selection module trained to predict cross-view 3D proximity of tokens. Thus, dense global attention is replaced by much more efficient geometric-similarity-guided sparse attention. SGAR is a general method that can be applied to different feed-forward models by fine-tuning. In our experiments, we show that SGAR is the fastest among both state-of-the-art dense and sparse methods and the most accurate sparse one. It runs up to 12-times faster than dense attention at 1,000 views with stable pose accuracy where existing sparse methods fail, and shows the best performance in reconstructing more complete geometries on the same time budget.

title: HiSA: Sparsifying the Hidden Dimension of RoPE Attention in LLMs
summary: Attention in large language models (LLMs) scores every query against every key with a full dot product. We investigate whether this dot product must be computed completely for attention to be effective. We propose Hidden Sparse Attention (HiSA), which keeps the query and key projections intact but only computes a partial dot product, following a static, parameter-free rule set by the token positions: attention becomes sparse in the hidden (feature) dimension, an axis much less explored than token sparsity, rather than over tokens as in almost all sparse attention methods. Based on the structure of rotary position embeddings (RoPE), we decompose keys and queries into parts which can be omitted when computing attention. By training LLMs from scratch with HiSA, we find that this partial dot product does not hurt but improves performance compared with the complete product while computing only about a third of the query-key products. During inference HiSA improves decoding speed and shrinks memory footprint. We also extend HiSA to FlashAttention-3 kernels for training and inference. Finally, we motivate our approach by showing that dense attention learns to suppress the attention score parts that HiSA drops. Code is available at https://github.com/ambroise-b/hisa.

title: DTS: Delta-Based Tile Scoring for Efficient Long-Context Sparse Attention
summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly need to process long documents and codebases, making long-context attention a major prefill bottleneck. Block sparse attention reduces computation by skipping unimportant blocks of the attention matrix, but scoring blocks accurately can itself be expensive. We propose Delta-Based Tile Scoring (DTS), a training-free, content-adaptive tile scoring method for sparse block attention. DTS selects query and key anchors according to local vector changes, using fewer representatives in redundant regions while retaining more detail in heterogeneous regions. To accelerate anchor selection, parallel delta packing partitions the query and key sequences into tile-aligned chunks and performs bounded local scans over these chunks concurrently. The selected tiles are then computed using the original query, key, and value vectors. On LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, DTS keeps average RULER and LongBench scores within 0.10 percentage points of full attention, with RULER evaluated up to 128K tokens. At 128K tokens, DTS reduces measured scoring-pipeline latency by 38% compared with XAttention. On four NVIDIA H100 GPUs, it achieves a 3.3$\times$ prefill speedup over a PyTorch full-attention baseline using FlashAttention-2 at 512K tokens.

title: PCRG: Training-Free Pruning and Caching of Reference Tokens for Video Generation
summary: Reference-to-video diffusion transformers pack the variational autoencoder (VAE) latents of all references and the generated tokens into one full-attention sequence, in which reference tokens make up about half. Because attention cost grows quadratically with sequence length, these tokens take up an even larger share of the attention computation, yet most of them are static, smooth or irrelevant to the output. To accelerate reference-conditioned generation, we propose pruning and caching of reference tokens for video generation (PCRG), a training-free, plug-and-play method that uses two signals the model already computes to assign each reference token to one of three tiers, namely pruned, cached or kept. The first is a low-level redundancy r from VAE latents, since a token whose latent barely changes over time or across its neighbors adds little new content. The second is a high-level importance g from the vision-language-model (VLM) conditioner, where the attention that the prompt and any first or last frames pay to a token tells whether the output needs to read it. Tokens that are not redundant are kept, and redundant tokens are cached if important and pruned otherwise. Pruned tokens leave the sequence before the first step with all rotary position embedding positions unchanged. Cached tokens have their keys and values computed once and reused, and kept tokens are processed as usual. On MiniMax-H3, already distilled to 8 timesteps and quantized to int8, PCRG is 1.57x faster end to end on our V2V-Bench and 1.49x faster on the public VACE-Benchmark, while the quality of VBe

title: Twindex: Index Cache Offloading with Coarse-to-Fine Selection for Long-Context Sparse-Attention Serving
summary: In long-context decoding, GPU memory (HBM) caps how many requests a GPU decodes at once. Sparse-attention models such as Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, DeepSeek V4.1-Flash and GLM-5.2 add an indexer: at every step it scores all past index entries with its own indexer cache, and attention reads the main KV of only the top-k entries. We find that once serving systems move the main KV to host memory, the indexer cache becomes the HBM bottleneck, at 63% of per-request HBM on Qwen and 75% on V4.1 at 1M tokens. Therefore, we introduce Twindex, which keeps only a compact copy of the indexer cache in HBM and the full indexer cache in host memory. At each step, the copy selects a larger candidate set, and the model's own indexer picks the top-k from the original rows of the candidates in host memory. The copy combines the shared component with the compressed residuals, both learned once offline. Twindex changes no model weights and runs inside CUDA graphs. At 1M tokens on modern GPUs, Twindex fits $1.78\times$, $1.62\times$ and $3.03\times$ as many requests as KV offloading alone on Qwen, V4.1 and GLM-5.2, and reaches $1.44\times$, $1.25\times$ and $2.54\times$ decode throughput when host memory does not limit the batch. Every request keeps its own index, and Qwen and GLM requests share prefix main KV in host memory. In our evaluations, mean benchmark scores are at most 3.1% below the baseline's.

title: AURA: AUdio-dRiven streaming Avatar
summary: Current audio-driven video diffusion models can synthesize realistic talking-head videos but generally require dozens of diffusion denoising steps over multi-second video chunks, making them unsuitable for streaming applications such as voice assistants and virtual avatars, where low-latency and online causal generation are required properties. AURA generates video chunk by chunk with a rolling KV cache, requiring only the audio of the current chunk to start generating, rather than a multi-second audio look-ahead like bidirectional models. It comes in two sizes: AURA 1.3B streams 576p video in real time on a single GPU (20.7 fps for a 16 Hz playback rate), making it suited to interactive avatar applications, and AURA 5B streams 720p video at 9.7 fps. Our two-stage distillation pipeline first aligns the causal student with the teacher, by training it to match the teacher's trajectories with fewer diffusion steps and a chunk-wise sliding window causal attention mask, then applies Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) with backward simulation to close the remaining quality gap. On standard talking-head benchmarks, AURA 1.3B runs 23x faster than its own bidirectional teacher and reaches a quality comparable to TalkVerse at a lower resolution, and AURA 5B matches its TalkVerse teacher at 720p while running 17x faster. To support reproducibility and further research on streaming avatar generation, we release the weights of both models along with a dataset of 30K synthetic videos and their precomputed teacher trajectories.

title: STEPQuant: When and Where Errors Matter in Delta-Rule Recurrent State Quantization
summary: Linear attention replaces growing KV caches with fixed-size recurrent states, yet these persistent states can become a substantial memory bottleneck under concurrent serving. Directly quantizing recurrent states to low precision often leads to severe accuracy degradation, as quantization errors propagate through successive state updates. We discover that the impact of these errors depends on two complementary dimensions: temporally, errors in long-lived memory can persist across many decoding steps; spatially, errors in different key rows affect model outputs differently, while state magnitudes vary substantially along both rows and columns. Motivated by these observations, we propose STEPQuant, a spatial-temporal post-training quantization framework for Delta-rule recurrent states. STEPQuant allocates precision according to error magnitude and memory lifetime, and jointly fits key-row and value-column scales based on state distributions and key-row impact on output error. Experiments on Qwen3.8-27B and Kimi-Linear-48B-A3B-Instruct across both long- and short-generation benchmarks show that STEPQuant closely matches FP32-state accuracy under a nominal 6-bit budget and outperforms uniform INT8 in its 4-bit configuration. Integrated into SGLang with optimized GPU kernels, 6-bit STEPQuant achieves over 5x recurrent-state compression and reduces total serving memory by up to 68.7%. Our code is available at https://github.com/Dreamer-Toby/STEPQuant.

title: Aggron: Aggressive Compression of Agentic KV Caches during Head-of-Line Stalls in the Request Queue
summary: LLM agents run long, multi-turn programs whose contexts grow at every step, and serving them is limited by KV cache capacity. To alleviate this limitation, systems use context compression techniques, which typically wait until the KV cache crosses a large threshold and then summarize large spans of history at once, either in the background while the agent progresses or on the critical path. These summarizations can be done using the same model running on the same engine, or using the same or a different model running on extra hardware. When running on the same engine, summarization competes with the requests being served for both compute and memory capacity. To maximize the cost-effectiveness of summarization, this paper presents a new serving system called {\em Aggron}. Aggron summarizes agentic requests at every turn and selectively summarizes only certain parts of the KV cache. As a result, Aggron retains accuracy and keeps summarization requests lightweight. Moreover, Aggron launches summarization requests from a separate {\em Summarization Queue} while the corresponding agentic request whose KV cache we want to compress is stalled in the main request queue due to head-of-line stalls. The Summarization queue utilizes compute and memory capacity left over by the head-of-line stalls in the main queue. Further, to maximize efficiency, the server issues summarizations only when it predicts that they can complete before the corresponding agentic request will finally execute. In our evaluation, we compare Aggron to state-of-the-art asynchronous summarization. At high load, Ag

title: TriAxialKV: Toward Extreme Low-Precision KV-Cache Quantization for Agentic Inference Tasks
summary: Agentic workloads have emerged as a major workload for LLM inference. They differ significantly from chat-only workloads, requiring long-context processing, the ability to handle multimodal inputs, and structured multi-turn interactions with tool calling capabilities. As a result, their context exhibits structure that can carry different importance along three key axes: temporal recency to the current turn, modality such as text or image tokens, and semantic role such as user queries, tool calls, observations, or reasoning. These axes capture distinct token behaviors and lead to different sensitivities to KV-cache compression. However, existing KV-cache quantization methods are typically homogeneous or exploit only heterogeneity on a single dimension, such as temporal proximity or modality, overlooking the interactions among them. To this end, we introduce TriAxialKV, a novel mixed-precision KV-cache quantization scheme that assigns each token a triaxial tag, calibrates per-tag sensitivity, and allocates INT2/INT4 bit-widths under a fixed memory budget. We implement TriAxialKV as an end-to-end serving system, comprising calibration, mixed-precision quantization and memory management, and custom fused Triton decode kernels. When using Qwen3-VL-32B-Thinking as a computer-use agent operating the OSWorld, TriAxialKV matches the accuracy of SGLang with BF16 KV cache while supporting 4.5$\times$ KV cache capacity and achieving 30% higher end-to-end throughput, when running on real GPU systems.

title: Storing the Gemma 4 K=V Cache Once: Exact Global-KV Memory Savings in a Paged Serving Engine with Unchanged Attention Kernels
summary: In the global attention layers of Gemma 4 31B, the value is the normalized key projection, and the key is the value scaled by a fixed weight, with rotary position encoding on one quarter of its dimensions. The Gemma 4 report states that this design reduces the global KV cache by up to 37.5%, but the open serving engines that we checked still store a full key and a full value: 1,024 values per KV head and token. We store one 640-value row instead, exact in real arithmetic, and an unchanged paged attention kernel reads it through two overlapping strided views as its key cache and its value cache. In a vLLM prototype with the 16-bit 31B model, the outputs are bit-identical to an emulation of the same arithmetic on the stock cache, 2 of 432 final answers differ from the stock engine (within its run-to-run noise), and the steady decode KV memory per request falls by a factor of 1.34 to 1.40 at 32K to 64K tokens. On a prefill/decode pair of two A100 GPUs with NIXL transfer and CPU offload, a decode engine with a full 15 GiB pool ran 1.38 times the stock decode tokens per step for 16K-token prompts (repeated to 0.06%) and 1.24 times for 8K-token prompts; a model of the vLLM block pool predicted both ratios to within 1% (the engine was 0.7% to 0.9% higher) and matched the change between them. The eager decode throughput rose by 1.30 and 1.11 times, and on this path the compact engine gave the same output tokens as the emulation for 8 prompts at batch 1. The run-time prototype makes an eager step 4% to 9% slower at equal batch, and the method does not yet stack with an 8-bit KV cach

title: Online Temporal Rotations for 2 Bit KV-Cache Quantization in Video Diffusion Transformers
summary: Video diffusion transformers reuse key--value (KV) caches across denoising steps, which quickly becomes a bottleneck for long video generation. We find that quantizing temporally distant cache vectors leads to a large range and high quantization error, but that nearby video tokens in the KV-cache share a persistent pattern per channel. These patterns also vary across videos, motivating rotations that are adapted to each video's unique cache. We propose Temporal Rotation Quantization (TRQ), a method that rotates frames in the cache that are adjacent in time before quantization. For each block of temporally adjacent cache vectors, TRQ fits an orthogonal transform that maps the block's per-channel means to a vector that is close to a constant across channels. To keep the quantization format lightweight, we parameterize this rotation as a tree of $2 \times 2$ planar rotations, each stored with only two bits, followed by a fixed Hadamard transform shared across all blocks. The rotations are fit without gradients or changes to model weights, and we prove that a simple greedy fit is globally optimal for our 'mean-flattening' objective. The transforms are fit online for each new video, and we release fused Triton kernels to make this process efficient at inference. At 2-bit precision and matched compression, TRQ improves VBench subject consistency over the state-of-the-art method QVG from 90.38 to 92.02 on LongCat-Video-13B and from 86.33 to 87.61 on HY-WorldPlay-8B, as well as improving other metrics.

title: UnStep: Training-Free Acceleration of Causal Video Diffusion with Fewer Steps Than Distillation
summary: Distilling bidirectional multi-step video diffusion transformers into few-step causal models has become a common approach for streaming video generation. While these few-step students are significantly faster than the teachers they are distilled from, they remain slow for real-time generation. In this work we present UnStep, a training-free wrapper that accelerates few-step causal video models at inference by running them with fewer diffusion transformer (DiT) steps than during distillation and limiting the temporal window retained in the attention KV cache. We propose two inference-only mechanisms to recover quality lost by step reduction and attention windowing: renoising the generated latent frames to a near-clean level and reusing the existing clean-cache pass to refine them, and applying truncated SVD to the DiT attention value and output projections. We also accelerate inference with a quality-preserving runtime stack for the DiT and VAE decoder, including more efficient attention calls and KV indexing, fused Triton RoPE with cached coefficients, and VAE decoding with optimized memory layout, precision, and convolution kernels. By reducing computation and optimizing the runtime stack, UnStep sets a new throughput regime for causal video diffusion, by running substantially faster than current methods, reaching 50 FPS on a single H100 without quality loss, and 77 FPS on GB200, all without retraining.

title: AscMLA: Unlocking FP4 Efficiency for Long-Context MLA Decoding through Asymmetric Scaling
summary: Long-context decoding repeatedly reads a growing KV cache. FP4 reduces cache storage and traffic but needs block scaling to handle its limited dynamic range. Applying FP4 to multi-head latent attention (MLA) requires reconciling different K/V scaling requirements on a shared latent. Existing approaches address this mismatch through dequantization or separate encodings, adding execution or storage overhead. We present AscMLA, which combines asymmetric K/V scaling with pipelined scale delivery to process a single FP4 payload directly. AscMLA uses 38.2% less cache memory than FP8 and achieves geometric-mean speedups of 1.35x over TRT-LLM's FP8 and 1.26x over CAKE's NVFP4 MLA kernels.

title: FrontierReplay: Split-Free Exact Prefix Caching for Hybrid Language Models
summary: Hybrid language models combine self-attention with recurrent layers whose in-place state updates restrict prefix reuse to exact saved positions. Saving states on a coarse grid wastes reusable prefixes, whereas existing fine-grained exact caches must cut the prefill forward pass at each mid-prompt checkpoint, adding scheduler steps that outweigh the reuse gains under load. We observe that across multi-turn chat, agent loops, document question answering, and tree search, prefix reuse almost always ends at structural boundaries predictable in advance, such as turn ends and known branch points. We present FrontierReplay, a prefix caching system that materializes exact checkpoints at these boundaries without cutting the prefill. While the forward pass runs uncut, FrontierReplay logs a short window of recurrent-layer inputs and invokes a cross-layer, state-only replay kernel to build the target state 6-37x cheaper per token than full recomputation without host synchronization. A frontier-aware retention policy prioritizes active anchors and proven branches while lending dead checkpoint slots to the attention KV cache. Across diverse hybrid architectures, model scales, and workloads, FrontierReplay delivers clear gains over existing exact caches, lowering median time to first token (TTFT) by 16-89% (up to 8.9x), raising 80% service-level objective (SLO) capacity by up to 1.73x, and improving goodput by up to 4.26x (3.67x at larger scales). Compared with approximate replay methods, FrontierReplay delivers up to 1.54x higher goodput while preserving exact task accuracy, avoiding the

title: BlockJack: Cross-Tenant Redirection Fault Attacks on Paged KV Cache Address Translation in LLM Serving
summary: Large language model (LLM) serving frameworks accelerate inference by retaining previously computed states in a key-value (KV) cache. Paged serving frameworks such as vLLM organize this cache through block tables analogous to OS page tables, which map each request's logical KV blocks to physical KV blocks, forming a software-managed address translation layer. Although fault attacks such as Rowhammer have exploited OS page tables to redirect memory accesses, prior fault attacks on LLMs have largely targeted the data plane, i.e., model weights or KV-cache contents, leaving KV-cache mapping unexplored. We present BlockJack (i.e., Block Hijack), the first KV cache address-translation fault attack in LLM inference. By corrupting block-table entries, BlockJack redirects a request's KV cache reads to blocks assigned to another tenant's request without modifying model parameters, prompts, or cached KV states. It achieves both confidentiality violation (victim information appears in attacker responses) and integrity violation (attacker-supplied context steers victim answers). We study paged KV cache mappings in vLLM and formally characterize when redirect targets are predictable. Across seven models spanning the Qwen, Llama, Gemma, and Phi families, a faulted mapping exposes victim context. For the integrity attack, we examine how topic proximity, intra-topic divergence, and model behavior shape redirected responses. On a 248-scene medical benchmark, the integrity attack causes up to 41.1% of responses to recommend less urgent care, while still appearing consistent with the victim's

title: Characterizing High Bandwidth Flash for LLM Serving
summary: Large language model (LLM) serving requires substantial memory to store model weights and KV caches. Agentic workloads compound this pressure through repeated interactions over growing contexts, making it important to retain KV cache for reuse. High-bandwidth flash (HBF) offers a way to expand accelerator memory capacity for LLM serving, but its access costs and limited write endurance complicate its use. We evaluate HBF for high-throughput agentic serving across system design and scheduling choices to understand when additional capacity improves serving performance and energy efficiency. We introduce an HBM-HBF-host hierarchical storage system and buffered cache-aware scheduling, and use trace-driven simulations to analyze their effects on performance, energy consumption, and HBF write lifetime. Across the evaluated workloads, the fastest HBF-augmented systems reduce completion time by 21.1-86.9% relative to HBM-only systems. Modeled energy savings reach 62.4%, with benefits depending on the workload and weight placement. Buffered cache-aware scheduling extends estimated HBF write lifetime from 0.99 to 13.63 years in the evaluated configuration. These results demonstrate the importance of coordinating data placement and scheduling in serving LLM with HBF, positioning HBF as an actively utilized lower-level memory tier rather than passive storage.

title: Thinking in Streams: Proactive Spatial Reasoning with Vision-Language Models
summary: Recognizing when a requested spatial condition holds in streaming video can require maintaining and updating spatial knowledge across changing viewpoints. We study this capability through proactive spatial reasoning, where a model receives a query in advance and determines whether and when to respond as the stream unfolds. We introduce ProSpace-Bench, comprising nine tasks across object, camera, and scene reasoning, and ProSpace-Train for supervised training. To support spatial decisions, we propose ProSpace-VLM, which injects explicit geometric encodings estimated causally from incoming frames into intermediate VLM layers, using the existing KV cache as spatial memory and spatial token selection for efficient streaming. Experiments reveal a substantial gap between VLMs and humans, while ProSpace-VLM improves timely responses and correct abstention over fine-tuned baselines. Analyses examine how ProSpace-VLM represents previously observed spatial information across changing viewpoints.

title: Ask in the Crowd: Differentially Private LLM Inference via Dummy-Augmented Shuffling
summary: Large language models are increasingly deployed as LLM-as-a-Service (LLMaaS), where user queries are sent to remote LLMs for inference, raising severe privacy concerns about the exposure of sensitive user inputs. Differentially private inference mitigates these risks by injecting noise into input embeddings. However, existing methods struggle to balance privacy and utility, as stronger privacy protection often leads to substantial accuracy degradation in LLM inference. In this work, we propose DP-SPD, a differentially private LLM inference framework that protects user queries by hiding the real query among client-generated dummy queries. All queries are randomly shuffled before being sent to the server, preventing direct identification of the user's true intent. To improve inference efficiency, we exploit the shared-prefix structure among queries and reuse transformer key--value (KV) caches during decoding. We analyze the privacy guarantee of DP-SPD and evaluate its utility on classification and generation tasks, as well as its privacy protection under QIA, EIA, and GPT-based attacks. Experimental results show that our method achieves strong inference-time privacy protection and near-plaintext utility while improving inference efficiency through shared-prefix KV-cache reuse.

title: MedPsy: State-of-the-Art Small Medical Language Models for Efficient Edge Deployment
summary: Medical language models promise expert clinical support, but the strongest open-source LLMs remain too large for private edge-device deployment, while compact medical models still trail substantially on knowledge-intensive and real-world healthcare tasks. Reasoning models that fit edge memory budgets can produce long reasoning traces, increasing sequential decoding, end-to-end latency, energy consumption, and KV-cache memory pressure. We present MedPsy, a family of text-only 1.7B and 4B medical language models designed for edge deployment, targeting this accuracy-generation-efficiency trade-off. Our recipe combines a synthetic medical data pipeline over biology, medicine, and health seeds with chain-of-thought targets from a 235B medical-focused LLM teacher; a four-stage post-training curriculum comprising two SFT stages followed by two RL stages with hard-sample mining; and an edge deployment evaluation spanning multiple GGUF quantization variants and real-device inference on laptop and smartphone hardware. On seven closed-ended medical benchmarks, MedPsy-4B surpasses MedGemma-1.5-4B by 19.34 points and matches MedGemma-27B while being 6.75x smaller; MedPsy-1.7B outperforms MedGemma-1.5-4B by 11.42 points despite being less than half its size. On HealthBench-Hard, MedPsy-4B surpasses MedGemma-27B by 15.33 points, while MedPsy-1.7B surpasses it by 11.66 points despite being ~16x smaller. Beyond accuracy, MedPsy reduces average response length by 1.7x (1.7B) and 3.2x (4B) versus its Qwen3 backbones, while Q4_K_M quantization preserves the aggregate score within 1 point of BF

title: DeepEdu-F: A Framework for Efficient and Scalable Agentic LLMs in Vietnamese Education
summary: Cloud AI assistants send student data to foreign servers, conflicting with data-sovereignty laws such as Vietnam's Decree 53, and are not grounded in the national curriculum, so they often hallucinate on local content. Self-hosting an open model keeps data on-premise but faces two costs that weight quantization does not remove. An AI tutoring session revisits the same long material every turn, so once prefix caching removes the prefill cost, decoding over a growing KV Cache dominates response time; and grounding the tutor in local knowledge by fine-tuning is too costly to repeat as that knowledge changes. We present DeepEdu-F, a framework for the Vietnamese AI tutor DeepEdu with two components. LastSet selects the critical KV Cache entries once per turn from the question's attention, decodes the whole turn from that set, and keeps the full cache so later questions can select again. REPAIR (Reliable Evidence-based Playbook Adaptation and Insight Revision) curates a verified playbook from past interactions instead of updating weights. LastSet decodes up to 3.1x faster than dense decoding at a 256k-token context, faster than four sparse baselines, with accuracy close to full attention. Compared with ACE (ADD), REPAIR raises final accuracy from 70.0% to 80.5% on Formula and from 53.6% to 59.7% on FiNER, while mean task/scenario goal completion across AppWorld's normal and challenge splits increases from 9.28% to 16.28%.

title: Reinforcement-Aligned Probabilistic Weather Forecasting with Discrete Tokens
summary: Global medium-range weather forecasting must not only generate ensembles efficiently to characterize uncertainty in future states, but also serve downstream applications such as extreme-event warnings and cross-sphere coupled simulations. We introduce WeatherCraft, a framework that unifies probabilistic generation and reinforcement learning alignment through discrete weather tokens, bringing the GPT-style pretraining--post-training paradigm to global medium-range weather forecasting. A multiscale tokenizer represents atmospheric states as a coarse-to-fine token hierarchy, while a Transformer models causal dependencies across time and scale and predicts tokens within each scale in parallel. Direct sampling generates diverse ensembles, and exact token log-probabilities enable Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to maximize downstream task rewards without differentiating through evaluators or coupled models. On the ERA5 benchmark, WeatherCraft's eight-member ensemble mean reduces day-15 normalized RMSE by 17.6% relative to the strongest evaluated deterministic baseline and, with KV caching, achieves an approximately $18\times$ inference speedup over GenCast. Direct fair-CRPS adaptation improves ensemble probabilistic skill, while reward-based post-training improves forecasts of persistent land temperature extremes and coupled ocean heat extremes. This work establishes discrete autoregressive modeling as a general foundation for scalable, task-alignable Earth system foundation models.

title: Do Thinking VLMs Need to Keep Looking at Long Videos? Write It Down, Then Look Away
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) reason about long videos over hundreds to thousands of tokens. Every decoding step re-reads the key-value (KV) cache of the entire video. Must the model keep looking while it reasons? In LookAway, the model first writes timestamped notes on what the question needs and then puts the video away. Once the notes close, the inference engine hides the video's KV cache for the rest of the response. Across both hybrid and pure-attention VLMs, dependence on the video is concentrated early in the response. On Qwen3.6-27B, writing notes preserves accuracy better than free reasoning at the same withdrawal step. Replacing them with another video's notes harms accuracy, whereas keeping the video visible alongside the model's own notes adds no significant benefit. Without additional training, LookAway nearly matches full-video thinking accuracy at 0.12-0.13 times its modeled decode cost. To shorten this initial look, we fine-tune the model on its own correct LookAway responses. Reinforcement learning then rewards correct answers while penalizing KV reads. The trained model puts the video away after a median of 66-68 tokens. Across three held-out benchmarks, it writes more tokens than an identically trained full-video model yet reads only 27-35% as many KV positions at matched accuracy.

title: RoCoKV: Accelerating LLM Inference Serving through Uncertainty and Redundancy Aware KV Cache Compression
summary: KV cache compression is critical for large reasoning models, where most of the cost comes from long generated reasoning traces rather than the input prompt. These traces often contain redundant and low-utility tokens due to looping, self-verification, and corrections. However, such tokens may still receive high attention scores, making it difficult to remove them without harming the reasoning process. We propose RoCoKV, a KV cache compression method designed for large reasoning models. RoCoKV introduces two key components. First, uncertainty-guided adaptive pruning adjusts the compression strength based on the model's confidence, allocating more memory during uncertain phases and applying stronger pruning when the model is confident. Second, redundancy-aware token selection reduces the impact of tokens that are highly similar to recent reasoning content, encouraging the model to retain more informative and diverse tokens. Beyond the algorithm, we co-design RoCoKV with the serving stack: we develop fused three-phase CUDA decode kernels and integrate them into vLLM as a drop-in plugin that preserves its paged KV layout and CUDA graph capture, turning algorithmic savings into real end-to-end speedups. Extensive experiments across three reasoning benchmarks and two reasoning models demonstrate that RoCoKV consistently improves reasoning accuracy under constrained KV cache budgets, achieving higher accuracy compared to state-of-the-art KV cache compression methods. For DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B in vLLM, RoCoKV achieves a 1.27X speedup and 38% higher throughput on AIME25, the

title: Visual Jev: Accurate and Efficient Decisions from Shared Visual Context
summary: Applications increasingly ask multiple closed-choice questions about the same image, requiring accurate probabilities and efficient inference. We present Visual Jev, a visual decision model combining LM-head candidate readout, answer-supervised post-training, and independent question branches over a shared visual prefix. On held-out test images from four benchmarks, task SFT raises the 4B model's macro accuracy from 83.4% to 88.5% and error-discrimination AUROC from 0.834 to 0.890. Its macro accuracy exceeds the hosted Jev and OpenAI Decisions APIs by 2.77 and 5.06 percentage points, respectively, with the lowest NLL. We further show that better accuracy and calibration do not ensure reliable decisions. Fixed confidence thresholds exceed target error rates, and simply reordering options changes 17% of the model's accept-or-review decisions on SNLI-VE. At 32 questions per image, shared-prefix inference reduces amortized time per question from 20.5 to 5.6 ms, a 3.7x speedup over batched full sequences on one RTX 5090. Engine-level prefix caching reduces KV memory to 24.3% of that used by our custom shared-prefix path.

title: TripleKV: Predict, Prefetch, Protect -- KV Cache Management for AI Agents
summary: LLM agents alternate between inference and tool execution, repeatedly reusing their growing context across calls. Under high concurrency, their combined key-value (KV) cache working set can reach hundreds of GiB, far exceeding GPU memory capacity. As idle KV cache blocks are evicted to slower storage tiers, returning agents incur expensive retrievals that stall inference. To address this problem, we present \emph{TripleKV}, a three-tier KV cache management system that hides the delays of these retrievals. %exploits tool execution to hide these delays. In agentic workloads, the KV blocks needed by the next inference request are known in advance; only the time of their reuse is uncertain. TripleKV uses a tool-aware latency predictor to estimate when each tool call will complete and prefetches the required KV blocks from SSD into host DRAM ahead of time. Unlike GPU prefetching, this avoids reserving scarce GPU memory and interfering with concurrent inference requests. To further improve DRAM utilization, TripleKV eliminates duplication of GPU-resident blocks in DRAM, and introduces a victim-cache mechanism that refills blocks from SSD upon their eviction from GPU memory. Across data, web, and coding agents, TripleKV reduces the fraction of requests requiring critical-path SSD reads from 45--76\% to under 10\%. It also reduces P95 time to first token (TTFT) by up to 49\% compared with vLLM extended with DRAM and SSD KV-cache tiers, and achieves 1.5-7$\times$ lower P95 TTFT than recent agent-aware systems.

title: Berth: SLO-Preserving GPU Sharing Without New Preemption
summary: Inference services keep GPUs reserved for their worst-case load, and most of that capacity sits idle. Filling it with best-effort work such as training is the obvious remedy, and latency is why it rarely happens: on a shared GPU, a request that must finish within milliseconds finds the best-effort job's kernels running or queued ahead of it. Spatial sharing cannot evict them, temporal sharing gives the request only its turn, and hardware partitioning protects it by idling what it does not use. Systems that keep both the SLO and the utilization have reached inside the stack (rewriting kernels, patching the driver, instrumenting the framework), which the operator of a closed GPU stack cannot do. This paper argues that reaching inside is unnecessary. The time-slicer built into commodity GPUs already preempts a running kernel within a fraction of a millisecond and switches the moment a context runs out of work; what it lacks is priority, and priority can be created from outside by controlling what the best-effort context has to run. Berth is a user-space system built on this observation: a preloaded shim feeds the best-effort job to the GPU only when no request needs it (feed control), a declared deadline reference extends the rule to continuous-batching LLM engines, and a shortened best-effort time slice, set without privileges, bounds what a long kernel can cost. Berth changes no application, framework, kernel or driver. Across 31 scenario points with MLPerf SLOs and 13 baselines, Berth meets SLOs within a few percentage points of running alone, above every baseline, with 2.7

title: Kameleo: In-Situ Activation-Precision Selection for Bit-Serial LLM Accelerators
summary: Weight-only quantization keeps the activations of large language models (LLMs) in a higher-precision format, pushing the on-chip inference cost to the activation arithmetic. Bit-serial, variable-length accelerators offer a promising path to reduce this cost by lowering activation precision while preserving model quality. They process only the mantissa bits that each layer needs. The length has to be chosen per layer and operator, and today it is chosen by offline calibration: a search driven by the perplexity of the full model on a representative dataset. The search is repeated for every model and workload, and its result degrades silently on other data. This paper presents Kameleo, an accelerator that selects the activation precision at runtime, on the accelerator, from the data it is processing. Kameleo replaces the global perplexity by a local proxy that compares the output of each GEMM at reduced and at full precision. It exploits the fact that a bit-serial datapath produces this comparison almost for free, because the reduced-precision result is an intermediate state of the full-precision computation. Two passes over the first tokens of a workload set the precision of every GEMM. On four LLMs and seven datasets, Kameleo stays within a 1% perplexity budget at a 2.11-2.34x reduction of prefill cycles on the matrix multiplication unit (MXU), close to the reduction of configurations calibrated offline on the evaluation data itself. Calibrated configurations transferred to other data, in contrast, often violate the budget. The selection hardware adds only 3.7% to the accele

title: Posterior Matching Distillation
summary: Diffusion distillation accelerates image and video generation by compressing a pretrained teacher's iterative sampling process into a few network evaluations. Distribution-based methods achieve this by matching the student's output distribution to the teacher's. This matching is often driven by reverse-KL objectives, whose mode-seeking bias favors dominant teacher modes at the expense of diversity across samples. We introduce Posterior Matching Distillation (PMD), a new member of the distribution-based distillation family that combines mode-covering posterior sampling with any-step generation. At zero population loss, PMD recovers the teacher's full posterior of clean images at each trained noise level. Its stochastic student supports any-step sampling budgets within the trained timestep grid without further training. To learn these posteriors, PMD matches exponentially reweighted averages of student samples conditioned on a fixed noisy state to corresponding teacher posterior means. Under Gaussian corruption, exponentially tilted posterior mean is a single teacher evaluation at a shifted input. We prove that, matching tilted means over an open neighborhood uniquely identifies the full posterior. PMD thus supervises the entire conditional distribution through a family of mean constraints, without any auxiliary student-score network. Experiments on SDXL and FLUX.2 [klein] 4B demonstrate that PMD achieves the best FID among 4-step methods on both models, while maintaining competitive or leading performance across prompt-alignment and perceptual-quality metrics.

title: VSpark: Speculative Decoding for Autoregressive Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Our aim is to accelerate autoregressive vision-language-action models (VLAs), which generate robot actions one token at a time. Speculative decoding makes this possible: a lightweight draft model proposes several tokens at once, and the VLA verifies them in a single pass, accepting only those that match its own predictions, so decoding remains lossless. The speedup, however, is limited in robot control, where many different tokens encode nearly the same motion and a draft close to the correct action is still rejected. To address this, our approach, VSpark, is built upon three design choices: (i) rollouts collected with calibrated action noise, which expose the draft to a wider range of robot states; (ii) feature alignment, which trains the draft to match the VLA's hidden features rather than its output tokens alone; and (iii) continuation reuse, which keeps the predictions the VLA has already computed along rejected drafts as candidates for the next verification step, instead of discarding them. On four VLAs with different action tokenizers and four manipulation benchmarks, VSpark achieves 1.28x to 2.10x speedup while keeping the VLA's decoding lossless.

title: CompoundingKernel: Self-Improving from Zero to First
summary: We present CompoundingKernel, a self-improving agent system that writes GPU kernels by search. As of 2026-11-11, its generated kernels rank #1 on the public L1, L2 and Quantization boards of SOL-ExecBench (NVIDIA B200). They have held #1 on L1 since 2026-10-27, albeit a short loss on 2026-11-07. All 235 problems have a site-verified correct kernel; on the 209 public-board problems they are 4.40x faster than the benchmark's reference baseline. The search starts from zero: agents get each problem's PyTorch definition but no reference kernels or official scores. A per-problem archive outside the model holds every correct kernel and its lineage. An LLM controller reads it, picks a parent or a new design, and gives each parallel child agent one direction. Checks outside the model decide correctness. At equal wall time, it beat a coded UCB style tree on 35 of 38 problems by making 2.4x as many correct attempts. Over a thousand agents ran at once, and one warm restart fix raised their evaluation rate 3.6x. We find that the rate of reliable measurements, not the number of agents, limits how far such a search scales. Our code and kernels are available on URL.

title: NarrowSpec: Draft Hidden Width Need Not Match the Target in Speculative Decoding
summary: Speculative decoding is widely used to speed up generation in large language models (LLMs), with a small draft model proposing tokens that one forward pass of the target model verifies. Draft models that read the target's hidden states, such as DFlash and EAGLE-3, typically inherit the target's hidden width. We show that the draft's whole residual stream can run at half or a quarter of that width while largely preserving acceptance. For DFlash, which borrows the target's vocabulary projection, the trained output adapter folds into it, giving one narrower projection with logits unchanged up to floating-point rounding. We test two drafter families, DFlash and EAGLE-3, on two targets, Qwen3-8B (NVFP4) and GPT-OSS-20B (MXFP4), in SGLang on a B200 and a DGX Spark (GB10). At batch size 1 and temperature 0, narrowing the draft to half or a quarter width speeds up end-to-end decoding by 1.06-1.12x on B200 and 1.13-1.44x on GB10. The speedup holds at larger batch sizes. From batch 32 to the largest batch each GPU fits, narrowing reaches up to 1.21x on both GPUs, and no narrow draft is slower than full width.

title: [Bugfix][Core] Keep the aligned sliding-window prefix hit when dropping the EAGLE block
summary: ## Purpose Before: in `SlidingWindowManager.find_longest_cache_hit`, when no full window of cached blocks is found, the cached run at the start of the prompt is used as the hit. With EAGLE and `alignment_tokens > block_size`, that run is aligned twice. It is re-aligned by its length *before* the EAGLE block is dropped, then the EAGLE block is dropped and the result is aligned again. The first alignment is wrong for EAGLE: the run already ends at a block that is aligned *after* the drop, so the hit loses up to one alignment unit. Example: block size 2, `alignment_tokens=6`, sliding window 20, EAGLE on, blocks 0-10 cached and block 11 not. The run ends at block 9 (aligned for EAGLE: 9 * 2 % 6 == 0). The hit should be blocks 0-8 = 18 tokens, but the function returns 12 tokens. After: the first re-alignment is removed. Without EAGLE it was a no-op, because the run always ends at an aligned block. With EAGLE the drop lands on an aligned length. The existing re-alignment after the EAGLE drop is kept. This only changes how much of a cached prefix is reused (a shorter hit was still correct). It does not change model outputs, so no model eval is included. Not a duplicate: I searched open PRs and issues for sliding-window / EAGLE / alignment prefix-cache fixes. The closest, #51295, fixes the EAGLE drop in the hybrid coordinator, not this fallback path in `SlidingWindowManager`, which is unchanged on main. ## Test Plan ```bash pytest tests/v1/core/test_single_type_kv_cache_manager.py tests/v1/core/prefix_cache \ tests/v1/core/test_prefix_caching.py tests/v1/core/test_kv_cache_utils.py

title: [Core] Decode states at prefix-match boundaries for hybrid prefix caching
summary: <!-- markdownlint-disable --> ## Overview Hybrid prefix caching: keep the Mamba state at the last `prefix_match_unit` boundary a request's decode crossed and cache it when the request finishes, so the next turn of a multi-turn or agentic session resumes less than one unit before the previous end instead of at the last Mamba block boundary. summary: ## Summary This is an exploratory prototype for changing scheduler policy without redeploying vLLM. It separates the startup-time `max_num_seqs` resource capacity from a live `max_num_running_seqs` admission cap. The prototype adds: - scheduler get/update methods for the live cap - EngineCore and EngineClient utility-RPC plumbing - dev-gated `GET /v1/runtime_config` and `PATCH /v1/runtime_config` endpoints - validation and scheduler/API tests ## Motivation Inspired by operator feedback that inference-engine tuning knobs are almost exclusively startup flags: https://x.com/skeptrune/status/2094620791732330889 `max_num_seqs` currently has two responsibilities: it sizes static buffers/compiled graphs and it initializes the scheduler concurrency limit. This draft tries splitting those responsibilities so the resource envelope remains immutable while policy inside that envelope can change live. ## Semantics tried here - `--max-num-seqs` remains the startup allocation capacity. - `max_num_running_seqs` can change from 1 through that capacity. - Lowering below the current running count uses drain-down semantics: existing requests continue, but replacements are not admitted until the running count falls below the new cap. - Raising is allowed only up to the startup capacity. - Lowering does not reclaim GPU memory or resize CUDA graphs. - Updates run in EngineCore through the existing serialized utility path, so scheduler mutation occurs at an engine iteration boundary. - The HTTP surface is under `VLLM_SERVER_DEV_MODE`; this draft is not proposing a stable production endpoint yet. title: [Doc]: Docs use CLI flag names that `vllm serve` does not register
summary: ### The doc issue Several pages document `vllm serve` options with the underscore spelling (e.g. `--hf_overrides`) while the options are registered under the dash-separated spelling (e.g. `--hf-overrides`). `vllm serve` parses its arguments with `FlexibleArgumentParser`, which rewrites underscores in long option names to dashes before the options are looked up, so both spellings are accepted: ``` --hf_overrides == --hf-overrides --tokenizer_mode == --tokenizer-mode --config_format == --config-format --load_format == --load-format ``` The underscore spellings were therefore not broken commands. The issue is that they are inconsistent with the rest of the docs and with the option names that `vllm serve --help` prints and that the generated CLI reference lists. title: [Perf][Kernel] Coalesce K_Buffer loads and co-schedule head blocks TRITON_MLA (upto 1.7x gain at kernel level)
summary: ## Overview Optimized `_fwd_grouped_kernel_stage1` in `vllm/v1/attention/ops/triton_decode_attention.py` by co-scheduling head blocks on `grid[0]` for L2 KV cache locality and loading `K_Buffer` in row-major `[BLOCK_N, BLOCK_DMODEL]` layout for 128-bit vectorized coalescing and bank-conflict-free shared-memory writes. Prior to this PR, `_fwd_grouped_kernel_stage1` scheduled grid as `(batch, head_groups, NUM_KV_SPLITS)`. in MLA, the latent KV head is same for all query heads - but for this grid, for all query head_groups were being scheduled in strided manner since grid scheduler traverses batch dimension first. Secondly, `K_Buffer` was being loaded from global memory with `[BLOCK_DMODEL, BLOCK_N]` as page tile where `BLOCK_DMODEL` being contiguous dimension was being loaded in strided manner ## Claims * **Consistent `TRITON_MLA` decode kernel speedups across GPU architectures** (18 `(batch, seq_len)` configurations, `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V2-Lite` geometry): * **NVIDIA H100:** **1.06x–1.71x** speedup (`1.49x–1.71x` across long-context and batched decode shapes). * **NVIDIA A100:** **1.05x–1.47x** speedup across batched and long-context decode shapes (`1.41x–1.47x` at `bs=128`). * **NVIDIA L40S:** **1.06x–1.38x** speedup across all 18 tested shapes. * **H100 Nsight Compute on `64q1s8k`:** * **L2 cache hit rate** increased from **55% -> 74%** (reducing DRAM throughput from **36.35% -> 2.88%**). * **Shared-memory store bank conflicts** eliminated (`4.4-way` / `8.06%` penalty -> **0**), reducing dynamic shared memory per block from **63.49 KB -> 56.32 KB**. * **Minimal, portable

summary: ## Overview `MEGA_MOE_MXFP4_SM90` advertised only SwiGLU, so `--moe-backend deep_gemm_mega_moe` on Hopper rejected Kimi K3.1's SiTU activation while constructing the experts: ``` NotImplementedError: DeepGEMM MegaMoE mxfp4 experts support ['swiglu'], not 'situ'. ``` SM100's `MEGA_MOE_MXFP4` already accepts `situ`, and the only thing that makes the SM90 variant distinct is its hidden-state staging (FP8 with one FP32 scale per 128, versus SM100's packed per-32 UE8M0). SM90 SiTU support lives in the DeepGEMM kernel, not in vLLM, so simply widening the frozenset would move the failure downstream: an installed DeepGEMM without the SM90 SiTU branch rejects it in its C++ host code (`DG_HOST_ASSERT(activation != "situ")`), which surfaces as an opaque launch error. `deep_gemm_supports_sm90_situ()` probes for the `situ_beta` parameter that [DeepGEMM#62](https://github.com/vllm-project/DeepGEMM/pull/62) adds to `fp8_fp4_mega_moe`, following the same signature-probing pattern this file already uses in `_kernel_fuses_shared_experts`. The probe is false on the DeepGEMM revision pinned in `cmake/external_projects/deepgemm.cmake` today, so construction raises a clear `NotImplementedError` naming the missing kernel. **This PR does not change behavior on the current pin**; it takes effect once DeepGEMM#62 is merged and the pin is bumped. title: [Attention][DCP] Add opt-in FlashInfer fused DCP A2A + LSE combine for MLA
summary: <!-- markdownlint-disable --> ## Overview Adds opt-in `--dcp-comm-backend flashinfer` for MLA. The per-layer DCP output exchange and LSE merge then run as one FlashInfer kernel, `decode_cp_a2a_lse_reduce` from flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#6483. Today that is an all-gather plus a reduce-scatter with `ag_rs`, or four kernels with the opt-in `a2a`. `ag_rs` is the default unless a model selects `a2a`. This stays a draft until a FlashInfer release includes flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#6483 (vLLM pins 0.7.4). It replaces #61922, which targeted the older FlashInfer API. ## Claims - **NCCL symmetric-memory backend.** The flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#6483 kernel reads peer buffers and synchronizes through NCCL's device API (NCCL window, LSA pointers). Its workspace therefore has to be PyTorch symmetric memory on the NCCL backend. FlashInfer's other comm kernels do not need this. PyTorch fixes the backend once per process, so with `flashinfer` the worker selects NCCL before anything allocates. Under the NCCL backend: - rendezvous goes through the group's NCCL communicator, so each group creates it up front (about 0.5 GiB per GPU per group); - symm-mem all-reduce and the custom all-reduce MNNVL buffers rendezvous on the device group instead of Gloo, so they stay enabled. On main they silently turn off under `TORCH_SYMMMEM=NCCL`. Defaults and the CUDA backend are unchanged. The backend alone does not change speed: `a2a` on the NCCL backend is within 0.4% end to end. - **Performance** on 8x H100, TP8/DCP8, CUDA graphs, batch 1. title: [ROCM][KVConnector][MoRIIO] Add WRITE-mode consumer timeout
summary: ## Purpose Fixes the consumer half of ROCm/mori#655 and the hang in #59114. **The #59114 hang is only fixed when `write_recv_timeout` is set below the client timeout.** With the 540s default and that report's ~400s client, the client gives up first, and its abort stops the timer. In MoRIIO WRITE mode the consumer parks a request in `WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS` until the producer's `write_done` arrives. If the producer dies that never happens: the request waits until the client gives up, nothing is logged, and `/health` stays 200. This adds a per-request receive timer on the consumer scheduler; at the deadline the request is failed instead of wedging. It complements ROCm/mori#670 (merged), which fails the producer-side transfer on a QP error but still tells decode nothing. Config: `kv_connector_extra_config["write_recv_timeout"]` (seconds, default 540, finite and > 0, validated at startup) and `write_recv_max_timeout` (default 3 x `write_recv_timeout`, not below it). Documented in `docs/features/moriio_connector_usage.md`. Not a duplicate: the other open MoRIIO timeout PRs cover the prefill side (#51301, #56465) or the handshake (#63856). ## Scope: this fails the request, it does not free the blocks RDMA writes are one-sided, so a passed deadline does not prove the producer's NIC has stopped; releasing a block could let a late write corrupt another request. Blocks stay held until a real `finished_recving` (lifecycle split in #59382): a timed-out request keeps its transfer mapping, so a late `write_done` (a slow producer) still frees its blocks. title: [ROCm][Bugfix] Fix precision loss in asymmetric int8 linear layers on ROCm
summary: ## Overview On ROCm, asymmetric int8 (W8A8) models run through `TritonInt8ScaledMMLinearKernel`, which subtracts the activation zero-point term only after the matmul result has been rounded to bf16, and that loses most of the output precision. summary: ## Overview Add encoder CUDA graph support to the Qwen3-Omni audio tower, which Qwen3-ASR also uses. title: [Model Loader] Bound fastsafetensors peak memory with the 0.4 fit planner
summary: ## Purpose `--load-format fastsafetensors` stages a whole shard per rank in device memory before distributing it, so peak load memory tracks the checkpoint's shard layout rather than the memory actually available. Where a shard is large relative to free memory, the load runs out of memory on a model that otherwise fits. fastsafetensors 0.4 provides a fit planner for exactly this: whole-file loads while headroom is ample, per-file chunk budgets declining as the device fills. Its budget is caller-supplied by design (`parallel_loader.py`, 0.4.0): > **The caller picks the number — it knows what else lives on the device and, > under broadcast loading, must pass the same value on every rank (e.g. > all-reduce(MIN) of each rank's free memory)** so the plan stays identical > across ranks. This PR computes that budget from free device memory, agrees it across ranks with all-reduce MIN, and passes it — with `use_chunk_budget_as_allocation_size` for how chunks are sized, `accumulate_resident` for whether the consumer's memory grows during the load, and `BudgetInfeasibleError` handled for a plan that cannot be satisfied. It raises the dependency floor from `fastsafetensors >= 0.3.3` to `>= 0.4`, which is where the planner lands. ## meta-models/Muse-Glimmer-30B Public checkpoint, 55.5 GiB in 2 shards: largest shard 46.52 GiB, largest tensor 2.505 GiB. summary: ## Purpose Part of #54477 (direct weight reload), follow-up from #64418 / #68038. Under direct reload, every weight update ends with `finish_reload`, which reruns cold-start post-load processing for every module. title: [RFC]: Load plan — an engine-neutral API for sharded weight transfer
summary: # Motivation. Weight transfer engines that move sharded bytes themselves (`nccl_m2n`, sharded RDT/NIXL) need to know, for every tensor the trainer sends, **which part this rank needs** and **where in live memory it goes**. `load_weights` can't tell them: it takes full tensors and shards them internally. Today each engine works this out on its own by reaching into reload internals: - **NCCL M2N** (#51520, #60934, #62853, #60949, #63216) matches parameter names (`resolve_parameter_destinations`) and uses a hand-written hook for experts (`resolve_sharded_weight_target`). Anything else is a full tensor through `load_weights`. - **Sharded RDT** (#43375) bakes an op chain with `FakeRDTTensor` in a layerwise meta dry run and scatters on background threads. The dry run keeps it off direct reload (#64336). Two merged or in-flight pieces make one shared answer possible: - **#63215 / #63256**: every `WeightSource` declares its tensors once in `ParamMeta` (HF name, dtype, shape, owners, placements), identically on every trainer rank. - **#54477** (direct reload): each update views every tensor back to its checkpoint layout in its own storage, `load_weights` writes in place, and post-load processing (PWAL) reruns at finish. Storage never moves. **Goals.** One `plan_loads(model, metadata)` for every engine; the model's loaders stay the only source of truth for sharding; results equal a cold start, checked byte for byte in CI; anything the plan can't express falls back to `load_weights`. **Non-goals for now.** Online quantization, EPLB, per-update subsets of names, rollback, staging buffe

title: [Model] Add masked_token_ids to never sample given tokens
summary: ## Purpose Some token ids must never be sampled: the `lm_head` rows past the tokenizer (padding, so the logits exist but decode to nothing; see #13175) and, for multimodal models, placeholder tokens that are meaningless without their media. Today the only options are per-request `allowed_token_ids` (very slow with a large allow-list) or patching `compute_logits`, which RL frameworks do (e.g. verl, [`monkey_patch_compute_logits`](https://github.com/verl-project/verl/blob/453954b3/verl/workers/rollout/vllm_rollout/utils.py#L117-L145), added in verl-project/verl#7038). RL makes this worse than plain inference: training perturbs the untrained rows and a sampled OOV token feeds back into the policy. This adds an engine-level `--masked-token-ids` (`ModelConfig.masked_token_ids`): - The model runner (`GPUModelRunner.sample()` and the standalone CPU runner) sets those logits to `-inf` once, on the full-vocab target logits, after the batch-sharded all-to-all and before the grammar bitmask and the sampler. Draft heads with their own vocab and TP-sharded logits are not touched. - Draft tokens that hit a masked id are always rejected by the lossless rejection samplers, since the target gives them probability 0. The lossy methods (`synthetic`, `fly`) can accept draft tokens regardless of the target logits, so they are rejected at config time. - The ids are validated against the vocab size at startup. - Prompt logprobs are unaffected. title: [RFC]: Partial-block prefix caching as the default path for every KV cache group
summary: ### Motivation. - Groups in a hybrid model want different block sizes. Prefix caching wants small blocks for fine-grained hits, but for state groups it wants the ability to checkpoint every few hundred tokens. - A prefix-cache hash covers a whole block, so a hit rounds down to a block boundary, and across groups to the LCM of their block sizes. - Main's sub-block hits (#46384) only partly fix this. They need an aligned Mamba group, a sliding-window group with larger blocks turns them off for the whole model, and every mid-block hit copies the tail block. ### Proposed Change. Prefix-cache hits should be able to land inside a block for every KV cache group. A block carries one hash per hash unit, the cache maps each hash straight to its block, and a hit that ends mid-block either extends that block or forks it. Making partial-block hits the default path is what allows a different block size per group. Implemented this way it is a superset of the current full-block approach, which is the case where a block is one hash unit. Not measured yet. #### Design **Hashes.** The prefix cache indexes hash units, not blocks. A block gets one hash per `h` tokens it holds, and the map takes each hash straight to its block. Every prefix-cacheable group's block size is a multiple of `h`, as today. **Hits.** A hit is the longest prefix, a multiple of `h`, at which every group can resume. This is the only mode: the model-wide gate and the LCM fallback are removed. When a group's block size equals the hash unit, it degenerates to today's scheme: one hash per block, and every hit on a block bound

FlashInfer's MLA API multiplies a tensor `bmm1_scale` by log2(e) inside the call (an extra op, about -1.2% decode throughput measured earlier), and it has no precomputed `bmm1_scale_log2` input yet, so plain serving keeps host floats at no cost. summary: ## Purpose An FP8 KV cache on MLA models (DeepSeek V2/V3/V3.2, Kimi, GLM) now uses the checkpoint's KV-cache scales. On main, no checkpoint `k_scale` / `v_scale` / `q_scale` reaches an `MLAAttention` layer (except the Kimi-K2.5 special path), so every MLA model runs its FP8 KV cache at scale 1.0. Part of RFC #54477 (tracker row 29). summary: ## Overview DiffusionGemma batches mix causal requests (prompt and commit) with bidirectional requests (denoise). On SM100-family GPUs, vLLM had no fast backend for these batches: - FlashInfer rejected the model. - The default backend, FA4, fails at startup because its per-request causal mask is SM90-only. This PR runs the mixed batches on FlashInfer TRTLLM-Gen and makes that the default for text-only serving (`--language-model-only`) on SM100-family GPUs. title: [ROCm][Kernel] Pick the split of `top_k_per_row_decode` per row on the device
summary: ### Purpose `torch.ops._C.top_k_per_row_decode` takes about 100 µs for short decode rows of wide logits, even rows no longer than k, which only need their own indices. On MI300X/MI325X, with logits at least 200,000 wide (the sparse-attention indexer case), main splits every row into 10 blocks and merges their 10·k candidates, whatever the row's length: | rows × seq_len (k = 2048, width 262,144, FP32, MI325X) | main | this PR | |---|---|---| | 8 × ≤ k | 104 µs | 5 µs | | 8 × 2–4K | 42 µs | 20 µs | **Root cause.** A block whose chunk holds fewer than k live logits pads its k candidates with `-FLT_MAX`. For a row with `seq_len <= k`, almost all of the merge's 10·k candidates are then the same value. The merge is a radix select: on every pass those ~19k identical candidates fall into one histogram bin, and their shared-memory atomics serialize (about 100 µs on MI300X). Rows slightly longer than k pay a smaller version of the same cost, plus the merge of 10·k candidates for a row that one block would finish faster. The split cannot be decided on the host: `seq_lens` lives on the device and the call is captured in CUDA/HIP graphs, so one captured graph has to be correct and fast for any lengths. The new split is ROCm-only, because it was only measured on MI300X/MI325X. CUDA keeps the fixed split. The PR also fixes wrong indices for wide strided logits, on every platform (see below). ### Change On ROCm, the split-work path (`csrc/sampler.cu`, `numColumns >= 200000`) now launches `topKPerRowDecodeSplitWork` on a `(rows, maxBlocks)` grid that depends only on the number of rows and t

title: [Bugfix][KVConnector] Split MLA kernel rows larger than the NIXL block into dense pages
summary: #### Overview The NIXL connector registers a KV cache group incorrectly when the model runner picks a larger kernel block for that group than the block size NIXL picks across all groups. This PR registers such rows as dense NIXL pages when their layout allows it, and rejects the rest with an actionable error. #### Root cause - The runner selects a kernel block per KV cache group from that group's backends (`prepare_kernel_block_sizes`). - NIXL selects one block size from the backends of *every* group (`_sync_block_size_with_kernel` → `select_common_block_size`), and applies one ratio (`_physical_blocks_per_logical_kv_block`) to all of them. - When a backend in another group (e.g. a drafter's) only supports smaller blocks, a group can keep a kernel block (e.g. 128) larger than NIXL's (64). Its view is `[num_blocks, H, 128, C]`, so `stride(0)` spans two NIXL pages while NIXL's `num_blocks` is doubled. Registration then either: - raises `AssertionError: KV cache view cannot be partitioned into NIXL regions` (e.g. kernel 256 vs 64), or - silently registers whole storage rows when `num_blocks * block_stride` happens to match the storage span (e.g. kernel 128 vs 64, two layers per tensor). Transfers then address the wrong bytes. This affects any attention type, not only MLA. #### Example `--block-size 128`, an MLA group whose backend supports `MultipleOf(16)`, and a drafter group whose backend only supports 64. title: [Bugfix][Attention] FULL-graph decode follows reloaded KV scales or refuses the update
summary: ## Purpose FULL CUDA-graph decode either follows a weight update that changes the FP8 KV-cache scales, or the update is refused. Without this, decode replays graphs that captured the startup scales as host values and silently uses the wrong ones (RL flow: dummy start, then real weights). Stacked on the MLA reload-follow and FlashInfer bmm-scale PRs. Part of RFC #54477 (tracker rows 29 / 38). **Device scales where the kernel takes them** - Standard FlashInfer trtllm-gen decode, FP8 KV cache: precomputed fp32 `bmm1 * log2(e)` (FlashInfer's `bmm1_scale_log2`) and `bmm2` device tensors, so the kernel adds no op. Always on. - FlashInfer XQA decode and FlashInfer MLA sparse (DeepSeek V3.2, GLM-5.x): device scales when weight updates are enabled (`weight_transfer_config` set). Both APIs turn tensor scales into kernel scales with extra ops (XQA divides, MLA multiplies by log2(e)), so plain serving keeps host floats. MLA dense already does this (previous PR). - All of these are refilled in place after every load by `AttentionImplBase.process_kv_scales_after_loading(layer)`, which standard `Attention` and composite backends now call too. **FA4 1.0 descale** - FA4 skips the descale tensor for a per-tensor scale of 1.0 (saves three copy kernels per layer and step). With `weight_transfer_config` set it now keeps the tensor, so FULL graphs follow a later KV-scale update instead of refusing it. Without it, the skip still marks the scale frozen and a changing reload is refused. **Refusal where they don't** - Decode paths that keep startup scales set `frozen_kv_scales` (`"full_graph"`: host
