title: [Bugfix] Direct reload: resolve LoRA base_layer names in the update completeness check
summary: Suggested title: [RL][Model Loader] Enable LoRA under direct reload ## Purpose Part of the direct weight reload RFC (#54477). With LoRA enabled, the default `VLLM_RELOAD_MODE=auto` reloaded layerwise. Under `VLLM_RELOAD_MODE=direct`, a tied-embedding model failed at finish with `the update did not load 1 parameters ... ['lm_head.weight']`. Root cause: LoRA wraps layers after cold start, so live parameters are named `x.base_layer.weight`, while `load_weights` reports plain names (`BaseLayerWithLoRA.load_weights` forwards to the base layer). Direct reload compared these two spellings in three places: - **Completeness check:** the tied `lm_head` alias could not be resolved through `embed_tokens.base_layer.weight`, so the tied head counted as missing. - **Params-kept check:** wrapped layers never matched the recorded checkpoint names, so the check silently skipped them. - **Sleep-preserve patterns:** level 2 sleep matches them against live (wrapped) names, and the completeness check now does the same. Changes (`reload/direct.py`): - One `_unwrapped` helper maps a live name to its cold-start name. Every name comparison goes through it. - `direct_reload_enabled` no longer refuses LoRA in `auto` mode. The docs drop "LoRA, in `auto` mode only". **Depends on #68978 for LoRA on MoE models.** Expert weights from plain checkpoint names are skipped on LoRA-wrapped `RoutedExperts`. Until #68978 lands, such an update fails at finish in direct mode (layerwise silently kept the old experts). title: [Bugfix][Muse] Keep MegaMoE expert storage across direct weight reloads
summary: ## Purpose Muse Spark with MegaMoE experts (`--moe-backend deep_gemm_mega_moe`) does not survive a direct weight reload (`VLLM_RELOAD_MODE=direct`). `MuseSparkMegaMoEExperts.finalize_weights` ran only once, because later passes returned early once `_transformed_l1` was set. It also gave up the checkpoint storage it was handed: - **Native NVFP4 / BF16 layouts:** after DeepGEMM's transform, the checkpoint parameters were set to `None`, so a reload has nothing to load into. - **TRT-LLM (hybrid TEP) NVFP4 layout:** `.data` was rebound to freshly shuffled tensors. The rerun was skipped, so after a reload the kernels read checkpoint-layout bytes. - **Derived tensors:** the post-expert gamma and the hybrid decode scales (`_input_global_scale`, `_g1_gate`, `_g1_up`, `_g2_scale`) were rebound, never refilled, even though captured CUDA graphs read them. What this PR changes: - `finalize_weights` repacks on every post-load pass and writes into each parameter's own storage with `replace_parameter`. - The DeepGEMM operands are views built from those parameters, not cached copies. - Derived tensors are refilled in place with `refill_derived`, so captured graphs keep their addresses. - Kernel-format loads (`weights_already_processed()`: weight-cache IPC, kernel-format in-place reload) skip the repack, behind one guard. - Steady-state memory is unchanged. Before, the transformed tensors replaced the freed checkpoint tensors; now they are copied back into the checkpoint storage. A reload transiently needs one layer's transformed copy. By design, `finalize_weights` is no longer idempotent. I

title: [Bugfix] Keep KV-cache scale defaults under dummy loading
summary: ## Purpose With `load_format=dummy`, the dummy loader writes random values into the attention KV-cache scales. A checkpoint without KV-cache scales never overwrites them, so after a dummy start and a weight sync (the usual RL startup) the engine still differs from a real start. This PR makes dummy loading write the values a real start has. Part of the direct weight reload work (#54477). **Root cause.** `DummyModelLoader` fills every parameter and persistent buffer through `initialize_single_dummy_weight`, which writes random values unless the tensor sets `dummy_weight_value`. A checkpoint without KV scales never holds the attention scales: - `q/k/v/prob_scale` (`KVCacheScaleParameter`) are created as `-1.0`, the sentinel that post-load processing reads as "not loaded, use the default". After a dummy load they hold a random value instead. - `_q/_k/_v/_prob_scale` are persistent buffers registered at `1.0` by `set_default_quant_scales`. With an unquantized KV cache, post-load processing never rewrites `_k_scale` and `_v_scale`, so they keep the dummy value. - Compressed-tensors `q/k/v_scale` are created as `1.0` and used directly as the scales, with zero points at `0.0`. A checkpoint without a `kv_cache_scheme` never writes them, so with an FP8 KV cache the random value becomes the scale. - Inkling registers its own `k_scale` / `v_scale` buffers at `1.0`. A weight sync from such a checkpoint never writes these tensors, so the dummy values survive it. Layerwise reload hid this by recreating the scales on every reload. Direct reload writes in place, which exposed it. **Fix.** E

summary: ### Motivation. The Rust frontend is planned to become the default for `vllm serve` (#68784). One item there is to make sure front-end CI coverage runs with both front-ends. For multimodal requests, this coverage does not exist today: no Buildkite job sends an image, audio or video request to a server running the Rust frontend. The Rust frontend has cargo tests for its own logic against a scripted engine, and `llm-multimodal` checks its preprocessing against HF reference outputs, but nothing checks Rust frontend + real engine + real model against the behavior of the Python frontend. Running the existing multimodal tests against the Rust frontend found three bugs that users would hit after the switch: 1. **Qwen3-ASR engine crash.** Two audio clips of different lengths in one batch crash the engine. Since #68099 the model expects `audio_feature_lengths` to stay on the CPU, and the Rust frontend's `qwen3_asr` spec (in `llm-multimodal`) does not mark the field `keep_on_cpu`. #60970 reported a similar crash for the same model and path in production. 2. **Media on private hosts is refused.** The Rust frontend refuses image URLs that resolve to loopback or private addresses, with no way to allow them; the Python frontend fetches them. Users loading images from an in-cluster object store cannot use the Rust frontend (#65348). 3. **Phi-3.5-vision prompt differs from HF.** The Rust frontend tokenizes the rendered prompt in one pass; HF's processor tokenizes each text segment around an image separately, each with a BOS. title: [LoRA][MoE] Match plain checkpoint names on LoRA-wrapped experts
summary: ## Purpose A LoRA-wrapped `RoutedExperts` only matched PEFT-style names (`experts.N.gate_proj.base_layer.weight`), because the expert mapping baked the `base_layer.` prefix into the checkpoint-name patterns. title: [RFC]: DP pause/sleep correctness: coordinator latch, request admission, device-idle completion, and sleep/pause layering
summary: ### Motivation. Pause and sleep are the control plane RL post-training stands on: every weight sync is a pause → (trainer work) → sleep → wake → resume cycle. This RFC tracks four separable problems on that path. They are one topic: **what each call claims versus what it actually guarantees.** | # | Problem | Status | |---|---|---| | 1 | Coordinator's `engines_running` latches `True`; drain can only time out | **Fixed** — #51481 (merged) | | 2 | Per-mode request admission during pause was specified (#32103) but never implemented | #51488 (draft) | | 3 | Pause completion is CPU-only: the future resolves while the device is still busy — and in DP the pause path itself manufactures the GPU work it fails to wait for | #52914, #52957 (in review) | | 4 | `sleep` embeds request-fate policy (`mode`, default `abort`) that belongs to `pause`, and the pause→sleep flow runs the quiescence consensus twice | #53082 (draft, the end-state implementation) — seeking consensus | --- **1. The coordinator latch (fixed by #51481).** After a pause, a single request arriving from a front-end set the DP coordinator's `engines_running` to `True` permanently: `True` was a *prediction* made when forwarding a wake, while `False` was an *observation* requiring the engines to actually step — and paused engines never step, so `wave_complete` was never produced and `True` had no path back. `wait_for_requests_to_drain` could then only reach its 300 s timeout, and the stale `True` published to front-ends made them skip the `FIRST_REQ` notification, so after `resume` nothing woke the engines. title: [Feature][HiSparse] Reuse GPU Main KV buffers across prefill layers
summary: ## Overview Multi-turn agents often append a short tool result or user message to a long, cached conversation. A prefix hit saves the work of recomputing those tokens, but their Main KV still occupies memory across the model's layers. A dedicated prefill worker can therefore run out of device memory to admit another request while it has only a handful of new tokens to compute. This PR implements layerwise Main KV offload for sparse MLA prefill as proposed in #48203. The prefill worker keeps long-lived Main KV in local pinned DRAM and reuses device buffers across layers. The goal is to admit more concurrent requests within the same device memory budget. ## Claims - The producer keeps indexer KV on GPU and reuses a configurable number of GPU Main KV buffers across layers. The scheduler accounts for those buffers per compatible KV layout. - With a 4,096-token prefix hit and a 16-token append, each layer loads 4,096 history rows and writes back the 16 new rows. Requests sharing the same physical prefix page load it once per layer. Attention still uses its usual top-k selection. ## Validation CPU regression tests cover buffer accounting, shared prefixes, writeback acknowledgement, DMA descriptor lifetime, ordering when two layers reuse a buffer, and NIXL descriptor mapping. CUDA end-to-end validation is pending. The target is GLM-5.3 with FP8 Main KV and a BF16 correctness control, compared with an all-GPU baseline of the same dtype. The serving comparison will measure admitted concurrency, throughput and p95 time to first token at a fixed GPU memory budget. [Setup and workload]

title: [Perf][KV Connector] Batch Mooncake transfer descriptors across matching regions
summary: ## Overview Batch the producer-side address calculation in Mooncake's `_build_transfer_params` across consecutive transfer regions with the same layout. This extends #62478, which vectorized the calculation across blocks within each region. ## Claims On an H200 host CPU, building the descriptors for 49 matching regions and 64 contiguous blocks took **74 µs**, down from **415 µs**. A single-region call took **46.1 µs**, up from **43.3 µs**. **The GLM-5.3 FP8 serving measurements did not establish a reproducible TTFT, TPOT or throughput improvement.** A short, fully cached Qwen3-8B burst completed faster on two runs. title: [Quant] Fit online LUT-B codebooks with exact DP in a fused Triton kernel
summary: <!-- markdownlint-disable --> ## Overview Online LUT-B quantization (`--quantization lut_b_moe`, #62759, #67267) now fits codebooks the way the compressed-tensors LUT-B fitter does (vllm-project/compressed-tensors#996): exact weighted k-means by dynamic programming instead of Lloyd iterations. The fit runs in one fused Triton kernel on CUDA. On `zai-org/GLM-4.7-Flash` (one B300) online quantization takes 76 s, down from 403-451 s on `main`, with 5-7% lower reconstruction error. ## Claims - `quantize_lut_b` runs these steps: 1. block exponents from the circular cut of the block amax phases; 2. the exact weighted 1D k-means codebook of each 8x64 tile, snapped to E4M3; 3. one round (`num_scale_rounds=1`) of moving each block exponent by up to +-2 against that codebook, then refitting the codebook and keeping it only if the error does not grow. - This is the CT fitter's default ("CD0"). The PyTorch path gives exactly the same raw codebooks as CT's reference DP on test tiles. - Relative squared reconstruction error on GLM-4.7-Flash experts drops from 3.39% (Lloyd on `main`) to 3.17%. - On CUDA, one single-warp Triton program fits each tile; its output matches the PyTorch path. - CPU and ROCm use the vectorized PyTorch DP. - The exact zero entry for tiles that contain zeros is kept, as before. ## Validation All on one NVIDIA B300. **Tests** at b26583e50e, `chg run -g=1 -- .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/kernels/moe/test_lut_b_moe.py -q`: ``` 10 passed, 7 skipped, 17 warnings in 8.63s ``` The 7 skips need a Rubin (SM107) GPU. `test_quantize_gpu_matches_cpu` is new and takes 3.59

title: [Bugfix][Core] Make EncoderDecoderCacheManager slot release idempotent
summary: ## Purpose For encoder-decoder models (Whisper, Voxtral), the encoder cache budget silently stops being enforced after the first decode step. `EncoderDecoderCacheManager.allocate()` runs **once** per request — encoder scheduling short-circuits on every later step (`scheduler.py:1528-1542`, `num_computed_tokens > 0`). But `Scheduler._free_encoder_inputs()` runs on **every** step from `update_from_output` (`scheduler.py:1795-1796`), and its enc-dec branch (`scheduler.py:2144-2148`) calls `free_encoder_input()` whenever `num_computed_tokens > 0`. Two things made that per-step call non-idempotent: 1. `EncoderDecoderCacheManager.free_encoder_input()` credited `num_free_slots` unconditionally, with no reference guard — unlike the base class, which checks `self.cached`. 2. `EncoderDecoderCacheManager.get_cached_input_ids()` returned `set(range(len(request.mm_features)))` unconditionally, so the `if not cached_encoder_input_ids: return` early-out in `_free_encoder_inputs` (`scheduler.py:2129-2131`) never fired. title: [Metrics] Report vllm:iteration_tokens_total for each chunked prefill
summary: ## Purpose Fix `vllm:iteration_tokens_total` reporting for chunked prefill. The V1 implementation currently records this histogram from frontend `IterationStats`. Prefill-only chunks do not produce request outputs, so those model executions are not observed. When the final prefill chunk produces the first output token, the frontend reports all computed prompt tokens together in that iteration. For example, a request with a 10-token prompt, `max_tokens=2`, and a 4-token chunk limit is currently represented approximately as: ```text [11, 1] ``` The first sample combines all 10 prompt tokens with the first generated token, even though the prompt was processed over three separate model executions. This PR moves iteration-token accounting to scheduler stats, where the actual number of input tokens in every model batch is available. The same request is then reported as: ```text [4, 4, 2, 1] ``` This intentionally defines each histogram sample as the number of model input tokens scheduled for one model execution: - Each chunked-prefill execution is reported when it occurs. - The first generated token is an output of the final prefill execution, not an additional input to that execution. - A generated token is counted when it is fed back into a subsequent decode execution. - The final generated token is never fed back and is therefore not counted as model input. - Zero-token scheduler steps are excluded because they do not execute a model batch. title: [v1][kv-transfer] Prioritize remote KV polling in scheduler
summary: Add an experimental scheduler path to prioritize remote KV transfer admission and polling before scheduling regular decode work. In disaggregated prefill/decode deployments, a decode request that needs remote KV blocks can sit behind already-running decode steps. Since the KV connector only starts or observes transfer progress when a scheduler step reaches the connector metadata path, this can inflate TTFT by one or more decode-step boundaries even when the actual NIXL transfer is short. This change adds an opt-in environment flag, VLLM_KV_TRANSFER_PRIORITY_POLL, that makes the scheduler run a KV-transfer focused step when all of the following hold: - KV transfer is enabled for the scheduler. - There is active decode work in the running queue. - A waiting or skipped request has KV transfer parameters. - The scheduler is not paused. When enabled, the scheduler skips regular running-request decode scheduling for that step and scans waiting/skipped requests for remote KV transfer candidates. Non-KV candidates are preserved by moving them to the step-local skipped queue, while KV candidates may be admitted into WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS so the connector can start or poll the remote load. This is intentionally gated because it trades decode throughput for lower TTFT. In Qwen3-30B-A3B FP8 disaggregated tests, the policy reduced TTFT by roughly 13-19% for concurrency >= 2. The best observed point was concurrency=4, where TTFT improved by ~19% with negligible ITL impact and slightly higher system throughput. title: [Kernel][ROCm] Use naive block assignment for WNA16 MoE
summary: ## Summary ROCm GPTQ/AWQ WNA16 MoE currently always calls `moe_align_block_size`, even when a very small decode batch activates only a sparse fraction of the expert pool. vLLM's unquantized Triton MoE path already avoids that overhead with a naive assignment mode in this regime. In naive mode, each program handles one routed token/expert pair. Lane zero is valid and the remaining `BLOCK_SIZE_M - 1` lanes are masked. The change is model-agnostic: it does not dispatch on model name, hidden size, expert count, or other Ling-specific geometry. ## Performance evidence A fresh matched current-main A/B on AMD Radeon 8060S / Strix Halo (`gfx1151`) compared upstream `75231eff2` with this PR's `df4c60d38`. title: [Bug][KV Offload] cudaHostRegister can leave mixed pinned/unpinned TP ranks
summary: ## Summary CPU KV offload can start a tensor-parallel group in a mixed pinned/unpinned state because each rank independently calls `cudaHostRegister` for its own process VA of the shared mmap and failures warn-and-continue locally. ## Observed behavior Across two independent TP=2 hosts, each with 2x RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs, repeated starts produced both: - both ranks pinned; and - mixed starts where one rank failed registration and continued unpinned while the other rank remained pinned. The pinned rank carried the expected page-table bookkeeping asymmetry: 96 MiB/GPU for a 48 GiB region (`48 GiB / 4 KiB * 8-byte PTE`). Synchronized transfer performance is then bounded by the unpinned rank while the pinned rank still pays the bookkeeping cost. ## Desired invariant A TP group should never serve with mixed host-registration state. Registration needs a coordinated all-rank outcome: - every rank pinned; or - every rank consistently follows the same configured fallback/failure policy. A rank-ordered registration transaction with a mapping fence removes simultaneous registration as a source of nondeterminism. If any rank fails, successful ranks must unregister exactly once before the group makes one coherent policy decision. ## Policy question Current behavior preserves availability by allowing local unpinned fallback. Changing every failure to a startup error could break valid deployments whose regions cannot be pinned (for example, the large-region failure discussed in #51080). The durable fix therefore needs an explicit compatibility decision: coherent all-unpinned fallbac

title: [Misc] Warn when EAGLE/MTP speculation costs a large prefix-cache hit
summary: ## Purpose EAGLE-style speculation (including MTP) cannot reuse the KV of the last matched block: the drafter runs one token ahead of the verified prefix, so `KVCacheCoordinator` drops one drop-unit off every affected group's prefix-cache hit. That is correct and intentional — see the discussion in #38182 and the design doc attached to #17137. The problem is that nothing tells the operator. On hybrid Mamba/GDN models the KV cache manager enlarges the attention block size to keep page sizes uniform, so the one-block drop costs **thousands of tokens per request** instead of a nominal 16. The result is a large, silent `gpu_prefix_cache_hit_rate` drop that looks exactly like a regression, and gets reported as one repeatedly: - #38182 — 92% → 71% on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, 16 comments of rediscovery before a maintainer confirmed it is expected behaviour, not a bug - #47194, #43559, #50188 — separate reports that start from the same surprise This PR adds a startup warning when the computed drop is much coarser than the configured block size, and stays quiet when fine-grained partial hash hits already shrink it. ### Why a warning rather than a fix The drop itself is required for correctness. #50438 proposes lookahead-aware prefix-cache hashing as the real mitigation; until that lands, the behaviour is here to stay and the only gap is that it is invisible. This is deliberately a UX-only change: no scheduling, allocation, or cache behaviour is touched. ### Implementation notes Two functions in `vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_utils.py`: - `eagle_prefix_cache_drop_tokens()` computes the worst-case pe

title: [RFC]: Suffix decoding on GPU (`suffix_gpu`) — GPU-resident suffix decoding compatible with async scheduling
summary: ## Summary Suffix decoding gets the best acceptance lengths among model-free drafters on repetitive and agentic workloads, but the in-tree implementation (`method="suffix"`, #25784, from Arctic Inference) is CPU-side and rejected by the async-scheduling whitelist. This RFC proposes `suffix_gpu`: a GPU-resident suffix drafter that follows the same device-state drafter contract as `ngram_gpu` (#29184), so suffix decoding composes with async scheduling — no host sync on the draft path, drafts come from the previous step's device sampled ids. The in-tree diff is small (config + a proposer wrapper + runner wiring + unit tests, ~500 lines). The drafter core (suffix automaton over device tensors, cross-request global index with background rebuilds, fused Triton kernels, CUDA-graph capture) lives in a standalone package ([SuffixGPU](https://github.com/zip95297/SuffixGPU)), imported lazily — vLLM works without it installed, same pattern as the CPU suffix method's `arctic-inference` dependency. ## Motivation - #38069 asked for n-gram/suffix speculative decoding in the new runner under the condition that it stays compatible with async scheduling; it went stale, but the gap is still there. - Async scheduling is on the way to being the default. `method="suffix"` forces `--no-async-scheduling` today (`config/vllm.py` whitelist: "async scheduling is only supported with EAGLE/MTP/Draft Model/NGram GPU/DSpark"), giving up CPU/GPU overlap exactly where spec decode helps most: high-concurrency TPOT. - The reason is structural, not incidental: the CPU suffix tree needs the committed host token

title: [RFC]: Layerwise KV Cache Transfer for MooncakeStore with Session API Optimization
summary: ### Motivation. ### Background As model context windows continue to scale (128K → 1M+ tokens), the KV cache has become one of the dominant memory and bandwidth consumers in LLM serving. vLLM already supports layerwise KV cache transfer through connectors such as `LMCacheConnector` (PR #16625) and `OffloadingConnector` (RFC #19854), which use per-layer hooks to overlap KV cache transfer with model forward computation. In the distributed KV cache ecosystem, `MooncakeStoreConnector` provides a shared KV cache backend across GPU nodes via RDMA. However, the current MooncakeStore connector transfers all layers' KV data in a single bulk operation per request — it performs the full load before the first attention layer and submits the full save after the last layer. This design misses the opportunity to pipeline transfer with per-layer computation and suffers from increasing metadata overhead as models grow deeper. ### The Key Explosion Problem A straightforward layerwise transfer approach would extend each KV block key with the layer index to distinguish data belonging to different layers. With N layers and M blocks per layer, this transforms the key space from M keys to **N × M** keys. This explosion in key count directly impacts: - **Lookup performance**: Each prefix cache hit check must scan N × M candidates per block, linearly increasing latency. - **Master server overhead**: Each layer’s block-keys lookup requires a master RPC. - **Backend scheduling cost**: The store's internal metadata index grows proportionally. The same problem has been noted by RFC #33398 (Layerwise KV

title: [Bugfix][Model] Reuse CUDA segments when loading Inkling expert weights
summary: ## Purpose Fixes #51205. The NVIDIA Inkling w13 loader dropped the previous CUDA scratch tensor before allocating the next one. While `GPUWorker.load_model()` applies `max_split_size_mb=20`, this leaves fully free 20 MiB allocator segments that cannot satisfy the next smaller upload. CUDA reserved memory therefore grows while allocated memory remains flat, which can exhaust lower-memory GPUs or livelock the loader in allocator retries. This change chains the CPU `narrow()` view and `.to(param.device)` operation so the previous CUDA tensor remains alive until the next allocation completes. The tensor layout and destination copies are unchanged. Thanks to @brocktice for documenting the allocator interaction and suggested fix in [this issue comment](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/51205#issuecomment-5216204535). Duplicate check: on 2026-08-12, no open PR referenced `#51205`, and no open PR matched the Inkling loader / max-split allocator keywords. AI assistance disclosure: OpenAI Codex assisted with root-cause validation, test implementation, H200 A/B execution, and PR drafting. The human submitter reviewed every changed line and the attached evidence before submission. ## Test Plan ```bash CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=7 .venv/bin/python -m pytest \ tests/models/inkling/test_moe_weight_layout.py::test_moe_w13_upload_reuses_cuda_allocator_segments \ -v -s CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=7 .venv/bin/python -m pytest \ tests/models/inkling/test_moe_weight_layout.py -v .venv/bin/pre-commit run --files \ vllm/models/inkling/nvidia/moe.py \ tests/models/inkling/test_moe_weight_layout.py ``

title: [Bugfix] Fall back to native rotary when flash-attn is installed but fails to load
summary: ## Purpose `ApplyRotaryEmb.__init__` guards the optional flash-attn rotary import with `suppress(ModuleNotFoundError)`. That covers a *missing* module, but not an *installed but unloadable* one: when the `flash_attn` C extension cannot be loaded, Python raises `ImportError` — the parent class — which escapes the narrower guard and aborts engine startup during model loading. `ApplyRotaryEmb` is constructed by `RotaryEmbedding.__init__` (`rotary_embedding/base.py`), so this guard runs when loading essentially any model that uses RoPE — not just the VL models that call it directly. A broken optional dependency therefore takes down startup for everything. The common trigger is mundane: rebuild or upgrade PyTorch without rebuilding flash-attn. `flash_attn.ops.triton.rotary` resolves fine, then loading `flash_attn_2_cuda` fails on a moved/removed `c10` symbol: ``` ImportError: .../flash_attn_2_cuda.cpython-312-x86_64-linux-gnu.so: undefined symbol: _ZN3c104impl3cow23materialize_cow_storageERNS_11StorageImplE ``` This PR distinguishes the two cases rather than widening the guard blindly: - `ModuleNotFoundError` — flash-attn simply is not installed. Stay silent; this is the normal, expected path and its behaviour is unchanged. - any other `ImportError` — flash-attn is installed but broken. Fall back to native **and** emit `logger.warning_once`, so the user learns their flash-attn is unusable instead of silently running the slow path. A plain `suppress(ImportError)` would fix the crash but hide a genuinely broken install, which I believe is why the narrow exception type was requeste

title: test(prefix cache): pin two mamba "align" + EAGLE prefix-cache defects
summary: Tests only, no production change. Three properties of mamba `align` + EAGLE/MTP prefix caching, pinned as executable assertions so a fix can be judged against them. CPU only: drives the KV-cache manager through the existing `make_kv_cache_manager` / `make_request` harness. No model execution, no GPU. ``` 11 passed, 7 xfailed ``` **How to read the table.** A test that **passes** on `main` is pinning behaviour as it is today — it goes red if that behaviour changes, intentionally or not. A test marked **xfail** is asserting the behaviour we want and does not get it; it carries `xfail(strict=True)`, so CI stays green now, and when a fix lands the test XPASSes and `strict` turns that into a failure — the marker has to be removed together with the fix. The EAGLE drop costs a whole block, not one hash unit `tests/v1/core/prefix_cache/test_eagle_mamba_drop_cost.py` — block 16, hash unit 4, producer caches 48 tokens (three whole blocks), consumer shares all 48. `prefix_match_unit` exists so the drop costs one hash unit rather than one cache block. title: [Bugfix] Correct TRTLLM NVFP4 SiTU output scale
summary: ## Summary - centralize the TRT-LLM NVFP4 MoE `g1_scale_c` calculation - avoid folding `g1_alphas` into the SiTU output scale when the kernel already receives it through `output1_scale_gate_scalar` - use the same calculation during initialization and post-load processing - add focused coverage for gated SiTU and non-SiTU scaling ## Root cause The backend selected the gate/up scale solely from `is_act_and_mul`. For SiTU, that folded `g1_alphas` into `g1_scale_c` while also passing the same value separately to the kernel as `output1_scale_gate_scalar`, applying the gate scale twice. SiTU should pass only the cloned `a2_gscale` as the output scale; conventional gated activations keep the existing product. ## Duplicate-work check No open vLLM PR or issue was found for the TRT-LLM NVFP4 SiTU double-scaling bug. title: [Bugfix][Structured Output][Spec Decode] Validate accepted blocks before commit
summary: ## Purpose Fixes #43338. Structured-output requests using speculative decoding must satisfy this commit invariant: > Request history and grammar state advance through the same longest > grammar-valid token prefix. Any rejected suffix remains schedulable for > resampling. At `main@4666a8ba9ed5d271bf751cf1384cab2d2dcc0cfa`, the scheduler appends the verifier's accepted token block to request history before `StructuredOutputGrammar.accept_tokens()` checks the block. Prospective grammar masks reduce the chance of an invalid token, but they cannot establish the commit invariant when one accepted block crosses either of these state transitions: 1. deferred grammar activation at the end of model reasoning; 2. grammar termination before the final accepted token in the block. The invalid suffix is therefore already visible in request state when `accept_tokens()` rejects it. Depending on the serving path, that produces an invalid structured response or terminates the request with `FINISHED_ERROR`. This PR validates accepted multi-token structured-output blocks before `Scheduler._update_request_with_output()` mutates request history. It uses the non-advancing `StructuredOutputGrammar.validate_tokens()` interface, commits only the valid prefix, and leaves the existing post-commit path as the sole grammar-state advancement operation. ### Resulting behavior - Reasoning content through a deferred end marker remains unconstrained. - Tokens after the marker must form a valid grammar prefix. - Blocks sampled after reasoning has ended are validated in full, including suffixes that follow gram

title: [Bug] Cross-node TP CUDA-graph replay deadlocks with NCCL 2.28.9 (fixed by NCCL 2.30.4) — watchdog "RPC call to sample_tokens timed out"
summary: ### Your current environment 2× NVIDIA DGX Spark (GB10, SM12.1), connected back-to-back over 200G RoCE. vLLM TP=2 across the two nodes, `mp` distributed executor backend. NCCL 2.28.9 (as shipped). DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731. ### 🐛 Describe the bug With CUDA graphs enabled, serving deadlocks within the first 2–3 requests: a CUDA-graph replay containing NCCL collectives hangs on the cross-node link. The engine watchdog eventually fires with: ``` RPC call to sample_tokens timed out ``` after which the server must be killed. With `--enforce-eager` the identical setup serves indefinitely, which isolated the hang to captured-graph NCCL collectives (not the collectives themselves — eager NCCL is fine under the same traffic). **Root cause / resolution data point:** upgrading NCCL 2.28.9 → **2.30.4** fixes the deadlock with graphs re-enabled; nothing else changed. So this is the NCCL graph-capture bug class, not a vLLM logic bug — but vLLM can save users days here. Related: #41725 (same watchdog signature). ### Suggestion - Document the NCCL ≥2.30.4 requirement for multi-node CUDA-graph capture over RoCE (or gate/warn: if `torch.cuda.nccl.version() < (2,30,4)` and world spans nodes and cudagraphs enabled, log a prominent warning suggesting `--enforce-eager` or an NCCL upgrade). - The watchdog message could surface "likely collective hang inside CUDA graph replay; try --enforce-eager" as a hint — `sample_tokens timed out` sends users to the sampler, which is innocent. _Checked before filing: #41725's thread has no NCCL-version discussion; this adds the missing root-cause data point. title: [Feature] Allow random dataset to use --dataset-path for realistic token sampling
summary: ## Motivation When benchmarking speculative decoding, the acceptance rate of draft tokens depends heavily on the token distribution of the input. Currently, the `random` dataset in `vllm bench serve` generates purely random token IDs, which do not represent real-world text distributions. This can understate the effectiveness of speculative decoding in production. On the other hand, the `sharegpt` dataset uses real conversation prompts but does not support `--input-len` to control input length, making it impossible to run benchmarks with a fixed input length using real text. SGLang's benchmark tool already supports this via `--dataset-name random --dataset-path <sharegpt.json> --random-input-len 8192`, which samples tokens from ShareGPT and truncates/repeats them to the requested length. ## Proposal Allow `--dataset-name random` to accept `--dataset-path`. When provided, the random dataset samples token IDs from the file and truncates/repeats them to fill `--random-input-len`. File format is auto-detected from the extension: - `.json` → ShareGPT format (conversations array) - `.jsonl` → one JSON object per line with a "prompt" field - `.txt` → plain text, one line per entry No new CLI arguments are needed. When `--dataset-path` is not provided, the random dataset behaves exactly as before (purely random token IDs). ### Usage ```bash vllm bench serve \ --dataset-name random \ --dataset-path /data/ShareGPT_V3_unfiltered_cleaned_split.json \ --random-input-len 8192 \ --random-output-len 1024 \ --max-concurrency 32 \ --num-prompts 32 ``` ### Why not use existing options? - `--da

title: [Bug]: Triton MoE and block-FP8 GEMMs mishandle the K tile — an out-of-bounds weight read, and wrong scales when a tile spans two quantization groups
summary: ## Summary Two Triton GEMMs used by quantized MoE serving get the K tile wrong, and in both cases a sibling code path already does it correctly. 1. **`fused_moe_kernel_gptq_awq` reads the packed weights out of bounds.** The kernel builds `k_mask` whenever `K` is not a multiple of `BLOCK_SIZE_K` and applies it to the scale load and to *both* zero-point loads, but the weight load itself is unmasked, so the last K iteration reads past the end of the weight tensor. The sibling `fused_moe_kernel` masks the identical load. The numbers that come back are multiplied by a scale that *is* masked to zero, so the arithmetic result is unaffected — this is a memory-safety bug, not a numerical one. 2. **`w8a8_triton_block_scaled_mm` can pick one scale for a tile that spans several quantization groups.** `_w8a8_triton_block_scaled_mm` reads a single scale pair per K tile, indexed by `(k * BLOCK_SIZE_K) // group_k`, which is correct only when `BLOCK_SIZE_K` divides `group_k`. Nothing enforces it, and the comment above the default config states the requirement inverted — "BLOCK_SIZE_K must be divisible by block_size[1]" — which is exactly the configuration that breaks. The fused-MoE launcher clamps this (`BLOCK_SIZE_K = min(BLOCK_SIZE_K, min(block_shape[0], block_shape[1]))`); this one does not. Neither is caught today because the shipped defaults stay inside the safe range: `w8a8_triton_block_scaled_mm`'s default config sets `BLOCK_SIZE_K = block_k`, and `test_fused_moe_wn16` only uses `k` values of 128 and 1024, which are multiples of every `BLOCK_SIZE_K` the untuned path picks. title: Fix for Issue 52413: causal_conv1d Alignment Specialization Race Condition
summary: ## Purpose Fixes issue #52413: Alignment specialization on causal_conv1d metadata pointers forces inference-time JIT compiles; raced shared-cache writes produced silent all-NaN outputs. **Problem:** - Triton kernels allowed alignment specialization on dynamic metadata pointers that change per-request - This caused unnecessary inference-time JIT recompiles - Concurrent JIT cache writes led to corrupted kernels producing silent all-NaN outputs (data corruption) **Solution:** Added dynamic metadata pointers to `do_not_specialize_on_alignment` in both `_causal_conv1d_fwd_kernel` and `_causal_conv1d_update_kernel` decorators to prevent alignment-based specialization. ## Test Plan - [x] Added regression test `test_causal_conv1d_metadata_ptrs_not_alignment_specialized()` that validates kernel decorators keep metadata pointers in alignment exemption list - [x] Test command: `.venv/bin/python -m pytest -v --noconftest tests/kernels/mamba/test_causal_conv1d_jit_metadata.py` - [x] Verified fix doesn't break existing kernel signatures or math - [ ] Full causal_conv1d test suite on Linux with CUDA (`.venv/bin/python -m pytest -v tests/kernels/mamba/test_causal_conv1d.py`) ## Test Results - [x] Regression test **PASSED**: `test_causal_conv1d_metadata_ptrs_not_alignment_specialized` - [x] No compile errors in modified files - [x] Code changes verified to be minimal and isolated to kernel specialization metadata only - [ ] Full functional test suite pending (requires Linux CUDA environment) --- <details> <summary>Essential Elements of an Effective PR Description Checklist</summary> - [x] T

title: [Test] Add a prefix-caching x tool-calling gate
summary: ## Purpose Agentic deployments run prefix caching and tool calling together — repeated system prompts and tool definitions are exactly the prefix a cache is meant to reuse — yet no test exercises the combination: the per-parser tests never boot an engine, and the tool-calling e2e tests never enable prefix caching. A regression that only appears when the cache engages is invisible today. Adds `tests/tool_use/test_prefix_cache_tool_calling.py`, which boots the same tool-calling server with prefix caching off and on and asserts (1) a well-formed, schema-conformant tool call in both configurations, and (2) that under the caching configuration the cache was *actually exercised* (`vllm:prefix_cache_queries` and `vllm:prefix_cache_hits` non-zero, and zero in the control arm). Assertion 2 keeps the gate honest: a cache that never engaged would pass while proving nothing. title: [Documentation]: Clarify FileStore vs TCPStore security behavior by executor and version
summary: ### Description The current vLLM security guidance warns that PyTorch distributed TCP initialization can create a TCPStore listener on all interfaces, including in single-host deployments, and appropriately recommends firewall and network isolation: https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/usage/security/#notes-on-pytorch-distributed That warning is important, but the documentation no longer makes the configuration and version boundary clear after these changes: - #50999 switched local `MultiprocExecutor` and `UniProcExecutor` rendezvous to `file://` / `torch.distributed.FileStore`, eliminating the TCP rendezvous listener for those paths. - #51635 retains TCPStore when ROCm AITER custom all-reduce is enabled because that integration currently requires it. - Multi-node and ordinary data-parallel configurations continue to use TCP rendezvous. Released versions from before #50999, including v0.27.1, still construct a `tcp://<loopback>:<port>` rendezvous URI for local executors. A loopback address in that URI should not be taken as proof that the TCPStore server is bound only to loopback; operators can still observe a wildcard listener on the selected port. Could the security and distributed-deployment documentation add a concise version/configuration matrix covering: 1. The default store for local `UniProcExecutor` and `MultiprocExecutor`. 2. The store used for multi-node and data-parallel deployments. 3. The ROCm AITER custom all-reduce exception. 4. The first vLLM release containing #50999. 5. title: [Bugfix] Encode special tokens found in text for MistralCommonBackend in multimodal processors
summary: ## Purpose Fixes #50706 vLLM crashes at engine startup for Mistral3/Pixtral models whose tokenizer resolves to transformers' `MistralCommonBackend`. Per transformers' `AutoTokenizer` resolution, this happens whenever `mistral-common` is installed (`is_mistral_common_available()`) and the model's `model_type` (`mistral`/`ministral`/`mistral3`/etc) is mapped to `MistralCommonBackend` in `TOKENIZER_MAPPING_NAMES` — whether or not the checkpoint ships more than one tokenizer format plays no part (h/t @hmellor for the correction). Affected checkpoints include e.g. `nvidia/Mistral-Medium-3.5-128B-NVFP4`, `mistralai/Mistral-Medium-3.5-128B`. `MistralCommonBackend` never encodes special tokens (e.g. `"[IMG]"`) found in plain text. During dummy multimodal input profiling (run at engine startup to size the encoder budget), `PixtralProcessor` counts a mismatch between the placeholder in the templated text and the encoded ids and raises: ``` ValueError: Mismatch in `image` token count between text and `input_ids`. Got ids=[0] and text=[1]. ValueError: Failed to apply PixtralProcessor on data={'text': '[IMG]'} with kwargs={'truncation': False, 'return_tensors': 'pt'} ``` `InputProcessingContext.get_hf_processor` now swaps in a `MistralCommonBackend` subclass (`with_placeholder_token_support`) that resolves known special-token strings found in text back to their ids, scoped only to the tokenizer instance handed to HF processors — never used for general/user-prompt tokenization. title: [Feature]: Add torch.compile support for SiglipEmbeddingModel
summary: ## 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch Please add vLLM `torch.compile` support for the standalone `SiglipEmbeddingModel`. title: [Bug] Streaming input: zero-token continuation crashes EngineCore (Invalid request status: RUNNING) — client-triggerable via temperature>0 chat sessions
summary: ## Summary A streaming-input (resumable) session **kills the entire engine** (`EngineDeadError`) when a continuation turn produces **zero output tokens** — i.e. the model samples a stop token as the very first token of the turn. The scheduler then finds the resumed request still marked `RUNNING` in the waiting queue and raises, taking down `EngineCore` and every concurrent request on the server. This is a follow-up to #52471 (streaming-input depth costs); splitting the crash into its own issue because it is a distinct correctness/availability bug with a clean trigger. ## Severity The trigger is **ordinary chat traffic**: multi-turn sessions with temperature > 0 (the default for conversational serving; e.g. gemma-4's own `generation_config.json` ships `temperature: 1.0`). A zero-token stop-finish is a normal, per-turn sampling outcome, so a long enough conversation hits it with high probability — and one unlucky sample from one user crashes the shared engine for everyone. We observed **9 engine deaths across 5 fresh instances and 4 configurations**. ## Traceback (v0.25.1, deployed) ``` File ".../vllm/v1/engine/core.py", line 1304, in _process_engine_step outputs, model_executed = self.step_fn() File ".../vllm/v1/engine/core.py", line 547, in step_with_batch_queue scheduler_output = self.scheduler.schedule(self._should_throttle_prefills()) File ".../vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py", line 981, in schedule raise RuntimeError(f"Invalid request status: {request.status}") RuntimeError: Invalid request status: RUNNING ``` The traceback is entirely within `EngineCore` → `Scheduler`

title: [Feature]: Low-overhead asynchronous early-exit checks & KV-cache reclamation for Continuous Batching
summary: ### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch Problem Statement In high-throughput production environments running long-context agent loops or strict JSON-enforcement pipelines, models frequently burn a significant portion of generation cycles on post-plateau tail-tokens (e.g., polite wrappers, redundant formatting) after the core semantic task is complete. While stop_strings and custom LogitsProcessor hooks exist, evaluating them per-step in Python introduces severe bottlenecks: CPU-GPU Sync & GIL Contenter: Per-step synchronous callbacks disrupt the execution loop, create heavy interpreter friction, and degrade throughput at scale (batch size > 64). Even in Python-heavy orchestration stacks, this creates unacceptable micro-lags. KV-Cache Bloat & Fragmentation: Finished or logically complete sequences linger in the active batch until the explicit stop token hits or max tokens are reached, occupying precious blocks in PagedAttention and artificially inflating latency for concurrent requests. An Economic Perspective In high-volume enterprise deployments (e.g., fintech, customer ops, logistics), long-context generation loops routinely burn 20–30% of output tokens on post-plateau tail generation. For enterprise clients processing tens of millions of requests monthly, this translates to hundreds of thousands of dollars in wasted infrastructure costs annually, plus artificial latency inflation due to occupied KV-cache slots. title: [Feature]: Support per-request dynamic LoRA scale
summary: ### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch Currently `LoRARequest.lora_scale` is fixed at request creation and baked into the CUDA graph / kernel as a scalar. This prevents: - same-adapter requests in one batch from using different strengths; - adjusting LoRA strength mid-generation. A real ASR service works around this by baking scale into separate adapter copies (one slot per scale). This wastes slots and limits scale to discrete presets. **Proposal:** Add `LoRAScaleState` — a per-request `UvaBackedTensor` (`[max_num_reqs]`) following `SamplingStates`, passed to the LoRA kernel along with `token_to_req`. Effective scale = `base_scale * request_lora_scales[token_to_req[token_idx]]`. No per-token memory, CUDA-graph-compatible. **Evaluation (real adapter + WER A/B):** | Condition | CN mean \|B-A\| | EN mean \|B-A\| | | --- | --- | --- | | off (noise floor) | 0.022% | — | | 1.0 pre-fix | 17.184% | — | | 1.0 post-fix | 0.038% | 0.028% | - 4 adapter slots → 1 slot. - Arbitrary continuous scale values. - Two bugs found & fixed: CUDA graph captured the scale-free kernel variant (`tl.constexpr`), and the all-ones buffer wasn't refreshed. ### Alternatives - **Baking scale into separate adapter copies** (current workaround) — consumes one adapter slot per scale, limited to discrete presets such as `LORA_SCALES=0.5,0.7,0.9,1.0`. - **Storing a per-token scale array** — would require more GPU memory (e.g. 128 KB per batch vs 1 KB per request) and does not follow vLLM V1 persistent-batch style. ### Additional context - Full per-test-set breakdowns and logs are available on request. - Happy

summary: ### Your current environment <details> <summary>Environment</summary> ```text vLLM: 0.27.1 Container image: vllm/vllm-openai:v0.27.1-x86_64-ubuntu2404 GPU: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (sm_120) CUDA: 13.0.2 PyTorch: 2.13.0+cu130 FlashInfer: 0.6.16.post3 Model: Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 Engine: V1 Scheduler: async scheduling (implicitly auto-enabled by v0.27.1 for this MTP configuration) Input mode: text-only ``` </details> ### 🐛 Describe the bug In vLLM 0.27.1, `SpeculativeConfig.max_model_len` is consumed by the V1 GPU model runner. When the running sequence exceeds the configured drafter limit, the drafter is supposed to be skipped. Instead, the runtime continues to schedule and verify speculative slots. The server command does not include `--async-scheduling`. This is intentional: in vLLM 0.27.1, `async_scheduling` defaults to `None`, and the V1 configuration automatically enables async scheduling for supported MTP/EAGLE-style speculative decoding. The actual affected deployment therefore uses the async scheduler. With the affected path, the target model continues to process `num_speculative_tokens=2` draft slots after the effective drafter limit is exceeded. The drafts are rejected, so the metrics continuously show drafted tokens with 0% acceptance. This adds unnecessary target-model verification work and lowers long-context decode throughput. The eligibility check also uses the batch-wide `common_attn_metadata.max_seq_len`. Therefore, one over-limit sequence makes speculation stop for every request in the same GPU batch, including otherwise eligible short requests. Related

title: [RFC]: Extensible GEMM Epilogue Contracts for Residual, Norm, and Gated Activation Fusion
summary: ### Motivation. vLLM has mature linear-kernel selection and several compiler fusion passes, but the kernel interface and the graph-fusion interface do not yet share one typed contract for fusing a producer GEMM with adjacent residual, normalization, scaling, quantization, or gated-activation work. Today a provider is generally selected to produce the linear output, after which model code or a compilation pass applies downstream operations. This leaves two recurring gaps: 1. a provider that can evaluate a valid epilogue while accumulators are still in registers cannot advertise that capability through the same selection path; and 2. correctness constraints around reduction domains and tensor-parallel collective boundaries are encoded in one-off fused modules/patterns instead of one fail-closed contract. This RFC proposes an optional `GemmEpilogueSpec` understood by linear-kernel providers and compiler rewrites. It is not a request to fuse every decoder block or to require one backend. A provider may accept a spec only when it can implement the exact shape, dtype, reduction, aliasing, and distributed semantics; otherwise vLLM uses the existing unfused path. The initial target is the common Transformer structure in which GEMMs are interleaved with residual addition, RMSNorm-style normalization, scaling/quantization, and SwiGLU-like gated activations. Diffusion/omni models are a downstream consumer, but the abstraction belongs in vLLM's kernel boundary if it is sufficiently generic. ### Proposed Change. #### 1. title: [Core] Make the shm message-queue busy-wait window configurable
summary: ## Purpose `SpinCondition` busy-waits for `busy_loop_s` after each read before parking on its zmq notification socket, hardcoded to `1`. This makes that window configurable via `VLLM_SHM_BROADCAST_BUSY_LOOP_S` and **keeps the default at `1`**, so behaviour is unchanged for every existing deployment. The right value is a property of the hardware, not of vLLM. On a discrete-GPU server the current default is a good trade: a spinning core is thermal noise and the saved wake-up is free latency. On packages where the CPU and GPU share one power and thermal budget, it is not — the core held at max clock is taken out of the GPU's headroom. The window also interacts with step rate in a way that is easy to miss: `1s` is far longer than the gap between engine steps under load, so it never expires during a generation and the reader spins from the first token to the last. The idle case it was added for (#19036) is the only time it lapses. ## Evidence Measured on 4× NVIDIA GB10 (DGX Spark), GLM-5.2, TP=4 + DCP=4, 8 concurrent decode streams. `py-spy` attributes **98.3%** of the rank-0 worker's on-CPU samples and **99.9%** of `EngineCore`'s to this busy-wait: ``` sched_yield (vllm/distributed/utils.py:48) wait (shm_broadcast.py:203) <- the busy_loop_s branch acquire_read (shm_broadcast.py) dequeue (shm_broadcast.py) worker_busy_loop (multiproc_executor.py) ``` Only rank 0's node is affected — remote workers take `MessageQueue.recv()` and block in zmq — so the cost lands on the node that also runs the API server and the scheduler. title: [Bugfix] Pad the MiniMax-M3 decode index tile to a power of two
summary: ## Purpose Fixes #49157. `_decode_index_score_kernel` derives its lane tile directly from the head count: ```python BLOCK_SIZE_HQ: tl.constexpr = num_idx_heads * BLOCK_SIZE_Q hq_offsets = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE_HQ) ``` `tl.arange` requires a power-of-two extent, so decode fails to compile whenever `num_idx_heads * BLOCK_SIZE_Q` is not one: ``` ValueError: arange's range must be a power of 2 ``` `num_idx_heads == num_kv_heads`, which is not a power of two for every TP split — e.g. 96 query heads over 6 KV heads. The prefill kernel is unaffected because it puts the head dimension in the program grid, so the head count never becomes a `tl.arange` extent there. This rounds the tile up to the next power of two and bounds the head dimension in the existing `q_mask`, which already guards every load, score and store indexed by `hq_offsets`. The trailing lanes are masked out, so results for the real heads are unchanged. ## Test Plan `test_decode_index_topk_correctness` hardcoded `num_idx_heads = 2`, which is a power of two, so it could never reach this path. It is now parametrized over `[2, 3, 6]` and checks the kernel against the reference implementation already in that file. ```bash pytest tests/kernels/attention/test_minimax_m3.py::test_decode_index_topk_correctness -v ``` ## Test Result | | failed | passed | |---|---|---| | before | 12 | 6 | | after | **0** | **18** | The 12 failures are exactly the `num_idx_heads` 3 and 6 cases; the `2` cases pass either way. title: [Core] Add configurable sleep to shm broadcast busy loop
summary: ## Summary This adds a configurable, bounded sleep to the shared-memory reader's existing busy branch: - `VLLM_SHM_BROADCAST_BUSY_SLEEP_S=0` is the default and preserves continuous polling. - A positive finite value sleeps for that duration after `sched_yield()` on each busy-path check. - Negative, NaN, and positive/negative infinity values fail at `SpinCondition` construction. - The existing one-second busy/idle transition and ZMQ notification path are unchanged. The variable is excluded from compile factors because it changes runtime scheduling, not generated code. ## Why this is not duplicating #52814 #52814 makes `busy_loop_s` configurable. With a short value, the reader leaves the busy branch and parks in ZMQ during active decode. This PR controls a different dimension: the polling interval *inside* the busy branch. A positive value keeps the reader on the SHM polling path during the existing busy window, while bounding how frequently it checks. This provides an intermediate CPU/latency tradeoff for deployments that want to avoid a ZMQ park on every active decode step. I described this distinction and the supporting measurements in [the #52814 discussion](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/52814#issuecomment-5335995192) before opening this draft. The two controls are orthogonal and could coexist if maintainers find both useful. ## Validation ### Unit and repository checks ```console VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE=cpu .venv/bin/python -m pytest \ tests/distributed/test_shm_broadcast.py -q # 35 passed ``` ```console .venv/bin/pre-commit run --files \ vllm/distributed/device_c

title: [Bug]: causal_conv1d Triton kernels round BF16 products before FP32 accumulation
summary: ## Environment - vLLM current main: `5a4c8d99242e9e069b604d0e9b969e77f7dd501d` - Reproduction base: `1a5b3bbe62e754990cc34a8e90799d34a7467ab9` - GPU: NVIDIA H200, compute capability 9.0 - PyTorch: `2.11.0+cu130` - CUDA: `13.0` - Triton: `3.6.0` ## Bug Both Triton causal-convolution kernels accumulate into FP32 but multiply the input/history and weight while they are still BF16: ```python acc += matrix_x * matrix_w ``` The affected sites on current main are in `vllm/model_executor/layers/mamba/ops/causal_conv1d.py`, in `_causal_conv1d_fwd_kernel` and `_causal_conv1d_update_kernel` (currently lines 455 and 1061). The BF16 product rounds before it reaches the FP32 accumulator. The official `causal-conv1d==1.6.2.post1` CUDA implementation converts both weights and inputs/history to `float` before the multiply-add. Its forward kernel builds `float weight_vals[]` and `float x_vals[]`; its update kernel does the same before `out_val += weight_vals[j] * x_vals[j]`. The minimal correction is: ```diff - acc += matrix_x * matrix_w + acc += matrix_x.to(tl.float32) * matrix_w.to(tl.float32) ``` at both sites. BF16 convolution history and output remain BF16. This does not change recurrent-state dtype or routing semantics. ## Exact reproduction A deterministic BF16 width-4 fixture compares the public APIs against a sequential reference. The reference evaluates each BF16-operand multiply-add in FP64 and rounds once to FP32 after every tap, which exactly models FP32 FMA: BF16 operands have eight significant bits and the FP32 accumulator has 24, so FP64 represents the intermediate exactly. title: [Docs]: Clarify Mamba cache mode comments in hybrid block-size alignment
summary: ### Description The comments in `Platform._align_hybrid_block_size()` describe the `mamba_cache_mode == "all"` branch as "With prefix caching" and the other branch as "Without prefix caching": ```python if cache_config.mamba_cache_mode == "all": # With prefix caching, align to mamba chunk size for kernel perf ... else: # Without prefix caching, use minimum block size that satisfies # both backend alignment and mamba page size compatibility ``` This is misleading because `mamba_cache_mode="align"` also operates with prefix caching enabled. When prefix caching is enabled, Mamba models may use either `"all"` or `"align"`; when it is disabled, the mode is normalized to `"none"`. The `else` branch therefore covers both `"align"` (prefix caching enabled) and `"none"` (prefix caching disabled), rather than only the no-prefix-caching case. ### Suggested clarification Describe the branches in terms of the Mamba cache modes instead of whether prefix caching is enabled. For example: ```python if cache_config.mamba_cache_mode == "all": # In "all" mode, align to the Mamba chunk size for kernel performance ... else: # In "none" and "align" modes, use the minimum block size that satisfies # both backend alignment and Mamba page size compatibility ``` No runtime behavior change is intended. ### Additional context - File: `vllm/platforms/interface.py` - Observed at commit: `5a4c8d99242e9e069b604d0e9b969e77f7dd501d` - The comments were introduced in #37467. - Related documentation work: #46778. This issue was prepared with AI assistance and reviewed by the submitter.

title: [RFC]: Internal State Checkpoints for Mamba Align Mode
summary: # [RFC]: Internal State Checkpoints for Mamba Align Mode ## Motivation. `mamba_cache_mode="align"` stores recurrent states at reusable Mamba block boundaries. Today a state can only be committed at the end of a model forward, so a prefill that crosses its last reusable boundary must be split: ```text forward [0, 7680) -> cache state@7680 forward [7680, 8000) -> running state@8000 ``` The second call repeats the full model only to obtain an intermediate recurrent state. A checkpoint-capable recurrent kernel can do both in one call: ```text forward [0, 8000) -> checkpoint state@7680 -> running state@8000 ``` This RFC adds `support_internal_checkpoint` to `MambaSpec` and derives checkpoint states from the scheduled prefill range. The optimization is enabled only when support is explicitly declared; all other configurations keep the current split behavior. ## Examples Notation: ```text B Mamba block size CP@N checkpoint after token N RUN@N private running state after token N ``` ### Aligned prefill For `B=4`, a six-token prefill can cross the reusable boundary at position 4 in one model forward: ```text tokens [0-------------4-----6) forward [0-------------------6) state ZERO ---> CP@4 ---> RUN@6 ``` ### Non-final chunk For `B=4` and `prompt_len=20`, a scheduler chunk ending at 10 does not need to be clipped to 8: ```text prompt [0-----------------------------20) chunk [0-------------8-----10) forward [0-------------------10) state ZERO ---> CP@8 ---> RUN@10 ``` ### Chunk ending on a Mamba boundary A chunk ending at 12 needs no internal checkpoint: ```text chunk [0-------------

title: [Bugfix][ROCm] Fix num_tokens inflation for 2-D (M-RoPE) positions from the MTP drafter
summary: ## The fix `RotaryEmbedding.forward_static` flattens `positions` **before** deriving `num_tokens`. When positions arrive 2-D — `(3, N)`, as the MTP drafter of a multimodal model passes them, where 3 is the number of rope dimensions, not tokens — `flatten()` makes `num_tokens = 3N` and the next line `query.view(num_tokens, -1, head_size)` fails on a query that holds N tokens. This makes speculative decoding (MTP) completely unusable on multimodal M-RoPE checkpoints in this code path, and the failure is actively misleading: - **under torch.compile** it surfaces as a dynamo fake-tensor error — `TorchRuntimeError: RuntimeError when making fake tensor call ... call_method view ... shape '[3*s18, -1, 256]' is invalid for input of size 2048*s47` — which reads as a compiler/quantization problem and sends debugging in the wrong direction (int8/compressed-tensors combinations were suspected for two days before the rope was isolated); - **in eager** it is concrete: `shape '[6144, -1, 256]' is invalid for input of size 4194304` — 6144 = 3 × 2048, the rope-dim inflation. ## Repro Multimodal M-RoPE checkpoint with an MTP head (e.g. the official `Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B`, a `Qwen3_5MoeForConditionalGeneration` VLM whose text config carries `mtp_num_hidden_layers: 1`), served with: ``` vllm serve <model> --tensor-parallel-size 2 \ --speculative-config '{"method": "mtp", "num_speculative_tokens": 3}' ``` → engine init fails at `determine_available_memory` with either error above. Without `--speculative-config` the same model serves fine (the drafter is what passes 2-D positions). ## The change

title: [ROCm][Perf] Tune Triton W4A16 dense GEMM tiles for gfx90a (104 CUs)
summary: ## Purpose — why this change exists The Triton W4A16 dense GEMM's tile table routes gfx90a into its **MI300 branch, tuned for 304 CUs**. An MI210 has 104. At decode widths that starves the card: with `BLOCK_N=64`, a narrow-N layer launches only **80–96 workgroups onto 104 CUs** — fewer than one per CU — while the SMs sit idle. Shrinking `BLOCK_N` for the gfx90a narrow shapes raises that to 320–384 workgroups and lets the card actually fill. This is the same class of issue as any large-SI tile table being reused for a small-SI part: the dispatch is legal, so nothing fails — the kernel just runs at a fraction of the achievable rate and nobody notices. ## Measured (2× AMD MI210, gfx90a, wall clock over the production `triton_w4a16_gemm`) | shape | M | stock | tuned | speedup | |---|---|---|---|---| | q_proj | 1 | 62 | 83 | **1.34×** | | q_proj | 8 | 61 | 83 | **1.36×** | | o_proj | 1 | 55 | 80 | **1.45×** | | o_proj | 8 | 55 | 80 | **1.45×** | | gate_up | 1 | 146 | 166 | **1.14×** | | gate_up | 32 | 152 | 178 | **1.17×** | (µs per call, lower is better; decode-relevant shapes are M=1..32.) ## Scope Tile constants only for the gfx90a narrow-width rungs — no kernel-body changes, no API change, other architectures' tiles untouched. Measured on ROCm 7.14 / MI210; MI250X (same gfx90a, 2× CUs per package) inherits the same branch and is expected to benefit at M=1..8 where the per-CU launch count is still the binding constraint.

title: [ROCm][Perf] W4A16 gfx90a: extend the narrow-tile rung to M<=16
summary: ## Purpose Stacked on #52975 (the gfx90a narrow-tile ladder). That ladder bounded its narrow tiles at M<=8, straight from the M=1/M=8 search. Measuring the in-between points shows the bound was premature. ## Measured (2× AMD MI210, GB/s of int4 bytes, median of 31, interleaved) | shape | M=9 | M=12 | M=16 | M=24 | |---|---|---|---|---| | gate_up | **1.44×** | **1.45×** | **1.37×** | 0.79× | | q_proj | **1.40×** | **1.38×** | **1.39×** | — | | o_proj | **1.43×** | **1.40×** | **1.41×** | — | The rung stops at 16 because M=24 regresses: past that the narrow tile stops buying occupancy and only costs reuse. ## Where it overlaps the magic-bias path (#52983) `_use_magic_bias` keys on BLOCK_M <= 16, so M=9..16 picks the fast dequant up automatically on this rung. The two effects were measured apart, because the headline hides opposite mechanisms: | shape | new/old | tile alone | magic-bias alone | |---|---|---|---| | gate_up | 1.44× | 0.97× | **1.49×** | | q_proj | 1.40× | **1.30×** | 1.08× | | o_proj | 1.43× | **1.33×** | 1.07× | On gate_up the tile change alone is slightly negative and the whole win is the dequant; on the narrow shapes it is mostly the tile. ## Deliberately not the fp8 W8A16 ladder This kernel keeps its own searched N >= 16384 split rather than adopting the fp8 kernel's (M, N)-keyed ladder: fp8 decode costs ~4.5 VALU ops per weight against int4's ~19, and decode cost is what sets the occupancy-vs-reuse crossover. M=24 above is the direct evidence — fp8 wants a wider rung there; this kernel regresses.

title: [Bug]: `set_splitting_ops_for_v1` early return skips the empty-splitting-ops guard — breakable cudagraph + `cudagraph_mode=PIECEWISE` + spec decode silently rejects every draft
summary: `CompilationConfig.set_splitting_ops_for_v1` returns early when the compilation mode is not `VLLM_COMPILE`, which skips the guard that would otherwise disable piecewise cudagraphs for an empty `splitting_ops`. The resulting configuration — piecewise cudagraphs with attention *inside* the graph — silently produces wrong results for any batch whose per-request query length differs from the captured one. Speculative decoding is the case where that happens in practice, and the state is reachable in stock vLLM via `VLLM_USE_BREAKABLE_CUDAGRAPH` (auto-enabled for several architectures). ## The early return ```python def set_splitting_ops_for_v1(self, all2all_backend, data_parallel_size=1): if self.mode != CompilationMode.VLLM_COMPILE: if self.splitting_ops is None: self.splitting_ops = [] return # <-- skips everything below ``` The guard that is skipped: ```python elif len(self.splitting_ops) == 0: if self.cudagraph_mode == CUDAGraphMode.PIECEWISE: logger.warning_once( "Piecewise compilation with empty splitting_ops does not contain " "piecewise cudagraph. The guard itself is correct; it is simply not reached. ## Why the resulting state is unsound With `splitting_ops=[]` the attention op is inside the captured region. title: [Discussion] Tiered SWA/Mamba checkpointing (HBM tail + store periodic) + recompute backfill for divergent hybrid prefix hits
summary: # Issue Draft **Title:** [Discussion] Tiered SWA/Mamba checkpointing (HBM tail + store periodic) + recompute backfill for divergent hybrid prefix hits **Labels:** `discussion`, `kv-cache`, `hybrid-models` --- ## Context This builds directly on #52773 and is motivated by the same class of problems documented in #45238, #45702, and #52959. **#52773** proposed `get_hybrid_backfill_tokens(request, num_computed_tokens) -> (num_local, num_external)` — when Full Attention's prefix survives deeper in HBM than Mamba/recurrent state, ask the connector to backfill the missing state from the external store instead of discarding the FA hit (draft PR #52774, measured 80× cost gap). **#45238** showed that align-mode Mamba retains only ~1 checkpoint per request (at the tail), so when that position lands in request-unique tokens, all reuse drops to 0% — including perfectly matched FA blocks. Periodic SWA/Mamba checkpointing to the external store** — HBM stays O(1) per request (tail only, as today), but the connector periodically checkpoint

summary: ### Your current environment <details> <summary>Relevant environment</summary> ```text vLLM source: main at d626108 Python: 3.12.14 prometheus-client: 0.25.0 prometheus-fastapi-instrumentator: 8.0.0 FastAPI: 0.136.3 Starlette: 1.6.0 ``` This issue is isolated to the ASGI metrics endpoint and is not GPU- or model-dependent. </details> ### 🐛 Describe the bug Upper-layer schedulers and resource managers, such as llm-d and aibrix, rely on the `/metrics` endpoint to retrieve selected vLLM resource-utilization metrics for placement, routing, and scaling decisions. The default HTTP exposition implementation provided by `prometheus_client` supports repeated `name[]` parameters so these consumers can request only the samples they need. vLLM currently does not preserve this default capability. Every filtered request instead returns the full, potentially large metrics payload, forcing the server to serialize and transfer unrelated samples and the caller to receive, parse, and discard them. With frequent scheduler polling or many vLLM instances, this wastes substantial network bandwidth and CPU resources on both sides. The `/metrics` endpoint ignores the `name[]` query parameter supported by `prometheus_client` for returning selected metric samples. title: Exclude model field from ModelConfig.compute_hash()
summary: ## Purpose ModelConfig.compute_hash() includes the model field (HF name or local path). This causes cache misses when the same model is loaded from different paths: vllm serve /data1/Qwen3-8B --tensor-parallel-size 1 vllm serve /data2/Qwen3-8B --tensor-parallel-size 1 Both instances compute different config_hash solely because self.model differs, so Instance B cannot reuse Instance A's compiled cache. Although both instances refer to the identical model, they compute different config_hash values solely because the model field differs. As a result, Instance B cannot reuse Instance A's compiled cache, leading to redundant compilation overhead. hf_config already contains all the necessary information to uniquely identify a model's architecture and configuration. We have tested this change on: Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B Tensor parallel sizes 1 and 2 In all cases, the computed hash remains consistent across different model paths (e.g., /data1/Qwen3-8B vs /data2/Qwen3-8B), while still correctly producing unique hashes for genuinely different models. ## Test Plan ## Test Result --- <details> <summary> Essential Elements of an Effective PR Description Checklist </summary> - [ ] The purpose of the PR, such as "Fix some issue (link existing issues this PR will resolve)". - [ ] The test plan, such as providing test command. - [ ] The test results, such as pasting the results comparison before and after, or e2e results - [ ] (Optional) The necessary documentation update, such as updating `supported_models.md` and `examples` for a new model. </details>

title: [Performance] MooncakeConnector emits one RDMA descriptor per (layer, block) — but with the unified paged KV layout a block's layers are contiguous; page-level descriptors give up to 19x faster PD transfers
summary: ## Summary On vLLM ≥0.26 the KV cache pool is a **single unified allocation** (`num_segments=1`): every layer's cache tensor is a strided view over one storage, with block stride equal to the pool page size, and **one physical block's data for all layers lives contiguously inside one page**. `MooncakeConnector`'s sender, however, still iterates **per layer region**, emitting one transfer descriptor per `(layer_region, block)`. For a hybrid-attention model (DeepSeek-style, 43 layers / 5 KV groups) this shreds a physically contiguous page into ~61 tiny descriptors (avg ~16 KB, compressed layers contribute sub-KB fragments), and a 1M-token prompt produces **254k descriptors per rank**. Transfer throughput then becomes descriptor-count-bound and collapses with prompt length, while the underlying data was contiguous all along. The existing coalescing path (`_can_coalesce_block_transfers`) can never fire on this layout: its gate requires `transfer_len == region.block_len`, but with the unified pool `block_len` is always the full page (~1.04 MB here) while a single layer's per-block payload is 0.8–100 KB. We instrumented the gate in production: **668/668 evaluations returned False for exactly this reason** (block-id runs themselves were nearly perfectly contiguous, offsets all zero). ## Environment - vLLM 0.26.0, TP=4 (symmetric PD), `--block-size 256`, `--kv-cache-dtype fp8` - Model: DeepSeek-V4-Flash (43 layers, 5 KV cache groups: full-attention + MLA compressed + sliding-window + GDN state) - `MultiConnector` with `MooncakeConnector` (kv_producer/kv_consumer), RDMA (RoCE, 2×200

title: [Docs] Document 7 undocumented kv_cache_dtype values
summary: ## Summary `docs/features/quantization/quantized_kvcache.md`'s `kv_cache_dtype` options list covers 3 of the 17 values `CacheDType` (`vllm/config/cache.py`) actually supports. This documents 7 of the remaining 11: `fp8_inc`, `fp8_ds_mla`, `int4_per_token_head`, `int8_per_token_head`, `fp8_per_token_head`, `nvfp4`, `nvfp4_4over6`. title: [Bugfix] Avoid accelerator lookup for CPU compile-cache paths
summary: ## Summary Restore the per-device compile-cache isolation introduced by #38962 without reintroducing its CPU startup regression. Both regular and AOT compile-cache paths now include the device index: ```text rank_0_0_dev0 rank_0_0_dev1 ``` Device-index selection is handled by the platform abstraction: - Platform.current_device_index() returns the current accelerator index when available and otherwise falls back to 0. - CpuPlatform.current_device_index() always returns 0 without querying torch.accelerator. CPU cache paths therefore use rank_<rank>_<dp_rank>_dev0. ### Why #38962 fixed compile-cache collisions when multiple engines in one process use different accelerator devices but share the same rank and data-parallel index. Inductor artifacts can contain device-specific stream references, so loading an artifact compiled for another device can fail with errors such as: ```text CUDA driver error: invalid argument ``` Its unconditional use of torch.accelerator.current_device_index() also caused CPU-only startup to fail: ```text RuntimeError: Cannot access accelerator device when none is available. ``` #53304 reverted the change to restore CPU execution, but that also removed the per-device cache isolation. This follow-up restores the device suffix while moving device-index lookup behind current_platform. CPU avoids accelerator lookup entirely, while accelerator platforms retain separate cache directories for each active device. ### Implementation - Add Platform.current_device_index() with a safe fallback when no accelerator is available. - Override it in CpuPlatform to return

title: [Docs] Clarify the cache_salt trust boundary and quantify its cost
summary: Follow-up to #39082, which merged earlier today. Three additions to the cache salting section, all small and independent — happy to split or drop any of them. **1. Where the salt must come from.** The merged text covers salt unpredictability but not its origin, and `cache_salt` is an ordinary request-body field. In a self-hosted deployment the caller writes it, so an adversary who sets their own salt to a victim's value recovers the shared blocks and the timing signal returns. Entropy does not help there — the adversary is not guessing the value, they are supplying it. This also disambiguates one merged line. "Set `cache_salt` on every request" does not say who sets it, and a reader who takes it as client-side guidance builds exactly the configuration the section is warning about. **2. Verifying isolation.** A misconfigured salt is hard to see from latency alone, since a cross-tenant hit and a same-tenant hit are indistinguishable by TTFT. The paired assertion matters: a test that only checks "different salt, no reuse" also passes when prefix caching is off entirely, or when the salt reaches nothing and no request ever hits. **3. A number for the efficiency cost.** "Salting reduces cache efficiency" is the line operators have to size a decision against. Measured on A100-SXM4-80GB with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct over a 2119-token shared prefix, read from `vllm:time_to_first_token_seconds`: 32.8 ms cached vs 149.6 ms uncached, about 4.6x. title: [Bug]: torch.compile cache key does not include num_speculative_tokens, causing compiled-graph collision across different speculative-token counts
summary: ### Describe the bug When serving the same model with speculative decoding and varying `num_speculative_tokens` (e.g. sweeping `k=7, 9, 11`), vLLM reuses a `torch.compile` artifact compiled for one value of `k` for a different value of `k`. Because the compiled Inductor graph embeds concrete tensor sizes, loading the wrong artifact triggers a runtime stride/size assertion failure: ``` AssertionError: expected size 7==9, stride 5120==5120 at dim=0 ``` The failure is order-dependent: the first `k` to compile populates the cache, and any subsequent `k` that happens to share the same cache directory loads the stale graph and crashes. Values that happen to be launched on a clean cache work fine, which makes the bug very non-obvious. ### Root cause vLLM computes the `torch.compile` cache key in `VllmConfig.compute_hash()`, which delegates to `SpeculativeConfig.compute_hash()`: - `vllm/config/vllm.py`: `VllmConfig.compute_hash()` appends `self.speculative_config.compute_hash()`. - `vllm/config/speculative.py`: `SpeculativeConfig.compute_hash()` currently only hashes: 1. Whether the method uses auxiliary hidden states (`eagle3`, `extract_hidden_states`, `dflash`, `dspark`). 2. The draft model config hash, when (1) is true. 3. `eagle_aux_hidden_state_layer_ids`, if present. **`num_speculative_tokens` is not included in the hash.** Since `num_speculative_tokens` changes the target verification batch size (e.g. query length `1 + k` in many backends) and therefore the concrete shapes seen by Inductor, it must be part of the cache key.
