title: [Fix] disaggregation: fix HiSparse spec PD transfer on PP>1 prefill
summary: ## Bug HiSparse + speculative decoding + PD disaggregation on a `--pp-size > 1` prefill fails on the first request: every non-last pipeline stage raises ``` ValueError: HiSparse spec PD transfer requires an appended device-only draft KV buffer ``` inside `send_kvcache` (mooncake), killing that stage's transfer thread. All subsequent PD requests hang at 0 completions while `/health` stays 200. ## When it happens Mooncake PD with a spec-decoding decode engine and hisparse. Only the last prefill PP stage owns a draft runner, so non-last stages register `num_draft_entries = 0`; `send_kvcache` derives the host-backed vs device-only boundary in the receiver's `dst_kv_ptrs` from the local stage count and raises when it is 0. Any model whose weights exceed one node's HBM at the target TP forces PP>1 on the prefill (GLM-5.3 FP8 at TP8: 88.5 GB/GPU > 80 GB HBM), so production-shaped topologies hit this on the first request. The current CI does not reach this path (the hisparse PD test runs PP=1 with a dense prefill and no spec), and this is the destination-side boundary suggested during #37771 review. ## Fix The decode receiver ships its registered draft-entry count over the mooncake registration wire (one field appended after `dst_draft_rows_dcp_collapsed`, i.e. frame `msg[22]`; absent for peers that predate it), and `send_kvcache` takes the host-backed/device-only boundary from the destination's registration, falling back to the local count when the field is absent. title: [Fix] kernel_plugins: Let the K3.1 verify megakernel serve its own request buckets
summary: ## Motivation With `--enable-nvidia-megakernel`, the Kimi-K3.1 host binding built the verify megakernel's weights view with `request_batches=(1, 2, 4)` for Q8 (8 draft tokens). The megakernel serves 1 to 8 requests per verify (`served_request_batches` in `sgl_nvidia_mega.kimi_k31.verify_contract`). However, its graph check (`kimi_k31_verify_dsa_binding.can_run_graph` → `request_capacity(batch_size, built.request_batches)`) refused 5 to 8 requests against the host's tuple. So any TP16 DFlash verify with 5 to 8 running requests fell back to SGLang's eager path. summary: <!-- Thank you for your contribution! Please follow these guidelines to enhance your pull request. If anything is unclear, submit your PR and reach out to maintainers for assistance. Join our Slack community at https://slack.sglang.io to discuss further. --> ## Motivation On AMD with the default `aiter` attention backend, EAGLE/MTP `target_verify` for non-MLA models runs on the legacy Triton `extend_attention_fwd`. That kernel has no split-KV: each request's long paged KV is walked by one program, so at agentic context lengths it runs far below HBM bandwidth. The faster `unified_attention` verify path from #23146 already exists, but it is only taken when `SGLANG_USE_AITER_UNIFIED_ATTN=1`. That variable also moves prefill and decode to Triton `unified_attention`. With one-token KV pages (the default) that makes 16k-token prefill chunks over long contexts tens of times slower on MI300X. With `--page-size 16` the variable is usable, and the InferenceX MI325X Qwen3.5 recipe sets it, but prefill and decode then leave the aiter kernels, which costs TTFT and throughput (397B table below). This PR is the target-verify half of decoupling the EAGLE paths from that variable. #40872 (approved) is the draft_extend half; the two are independent and merge cleanly together. The #40872 thread already points at this gap: with #40872 alone, NEXTN decode on Qwen3.5 drops below no-spec decode at ~11k context, and the cause is target verify still on `extend_attention_fwd` (554 us per call at 11k vs 14 us on `unified_attention`). This PR is that follow-up. On Qwen3.5-122B-A10B-FP8 at TP2 on 2x MI

title: [Perf] gc: Run full collections in lockstep across DP-attention ranks by default
summary: [by Claude Code] ## Motivation With DP attention, every scheduler gathers with all the others once per step (the MLP-sync gather), so a pause on any one rank stalls every rank at the next gather. CPython's full (generation-2) garbage collection is such a pause, and each rank's collector starts one on its own allocation counts: the ranks pause one after another, so a collection cycle costs up to one pause per rank instead of one. We measured this serving DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with PD disaggregation on Vera Rubin, with decode on 32 attention-DP ranks (DEP32), Python 3.12, launched through `sgl.Engine`, which does not run the HTTP server's post-warmup `/freeze_gc` (#49412 proposes that separately). Over one hour of steady load, a per-rank stall tracer showed: - Every ~9.3 minutes, each decode rank ran one automatic full collection of 240-350 ms, scanning ~1.3M long-lived objects (375 were frozen). - The 32 collections landed one after another in a 30-72 s window. That is ~8.5 s of all-rank stall per cycle, ~1.5% of decode time, concentrated in ~10% of the run. - Removing those stalls from each request's timeline (time-uniform sample of ~105k requests) raises per-user decode speed (1000 / TPOT p90) by 3.0%. `--gc-freeze-on-idle-secs` (#50883) freezes only after idle periods, which a continuously loaded decode server does not have, and does not line ranks up. The first revision of this PR added `--gc-dp-lockstep-steps N` (off by default). title: [Perf] [NVIDIA] deep_select: Opt-in multi-wave cluster top-k for long-tailed rows
summary: [by Claude Code] ## Motivation DeepSelect's bf16 top-k sends a batch to a cluster kernel only when the batch fits in one wave of some cluster tier. A larger batch goes to the one-CTA-per-row kernel. That kernel runs every row at once, so its time is set by the longest row in the batch. The DeepSeek-V4.1 decode indexer hits this case. With DSpark (6 verify rows per request) and 40 requests per rank, each index layer runs a top-512 over 240 rows. On a Vera Rubin GPU (SM107, 212 SMs) the widest one-wave tier is the 2-CTA cluster with 106 rows, so all 240 rows go to the one-CTA-per-row kernel. Agentic decode batches mix very different context lengths: in the samples below, the longest row is 2.6-6.3x the mean row. The cluster kernel already launches one cluster per row, and the hardware starts the next row's cluster as an earlier one retires. Run over several waves, its time follows the total row length instead of the longest row. ## Modifications - New opt-in env `SGLANG_DEEP_SELECT_MULTIWAVE=1`. It sends bf16 top-k batches with more rows than every one-wave tier, and at most `_MULTIWAVE_MAX_ROWS` = 512 rows, to the cluster tier with the most rows per wave (the 2-CTA tier on SM107), which then runs over several waves. Batches that fit a one-wave tier, short rows (`vocab_size <= 16384`) and every other dtype or signature dispatch exactly as before. - Off by default: on uniform row lengths the one-CTA-per-row kernel wins (numbers below), so whether it pays depends on the workload's context mix. - `_precompile` reads the env once per signature and passes that tier's module to `_C

title: [Perf] eplb: Compute the dispatch map's first match with scatters instead of a loop over replica slots
summary: [by Claude Code] ## Motivation `compute_logical_to_rank_dispatch_physical_map` runs on every rank at every EPLB rebalance. Inside `_nearest_expert_dispatch`, `first_match` walks the replica slots one at a time. For each slot it runs several elementwise ops on full `[layers, logical experts, ranks]` tensors, so its cost grows with the largest replica count of any expert. title: [Perf] disaggregation: Admit DSpark PD-decode batches without waiting for the in-flight forward
summary: [by Claude Code] ## Motivation With the overlap scheduler, a PD decode server admits newly transferred requests in `get_new_prebuilt_batch`. Unless `_nonblocking_admit_in_scope()` holds, the schedule stream first waits for the whole in-flight forward (`schedule_stream.wait_stream(forward_stream)`). The admission work (seed, filter, merge, KV allocation: a few dozen small kernels and copies) then sits between that forward and the next one. The non-blocking path already exists: the seed runs on the forward stream after the in-flight forward, and the rest runs on the schedule stream without the wait. Today only EAGLE takes it, under the megakernel runtime switches. Under DP attention, one rank's admission delays all ranks. We profiled 8 ranks of a DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash DEP32 PD decode on Vera Rubin (DSpark, 40 running requests per rank). On those ranks, a step that admits requests runs about 45 small serialized ops (about 1% of the step) before the draft forward. Every other rank then waits for it at the draft's first MoE all-to-all. Each rank admits on about a quarter of steps, so at 32 ranks nearly every step has an admitting rank. That costs every rank about 1% of the step. DSpark's seed (`build_dspark_disagg_draft_input`) builds the draft input from the last token and the seq lens, and writes both into the FutureMap. It reads nothing back to the host. It uses neither hidden states nor DSA top-k indices, the two inputs that keep some EAGLE requests on the blocking path. So the existing non-blocking path applies to DSpark unchanged. ## Modifications - `_nonblocking_admit_in_sc

title: [Perf] reject_sampling: Vocabulary-tiled block-verification accept
summary: ## Motivation With `--speculative-use-block-verification`, `chain_speculative_sampling_triton` runs one program per request. That program scans a full vocabulary row for the residual mass of every drafted prefix it tries, then walks the vocabulary twice for the final token. At small batch a few programs do all of this serially while the rest of the GPU idles. #48949 tiled the final-token pass for chain verification only; block verification had no tiled path. ## Modifications Block verification with fp32 `p`/`q` now runs on three vocabulary-tiled Triton kernels in `python/sglang/kernels/ops/speculative/reject_sampling.py`: - `_block_split_mass_kernel`, grid `(requests, num_slots - 2, cdiv(V, BLOCK_REDUCE))`: one `BLOCK_REDUCE` tile of the residual mass `sum(max(r_i * p_i - q_i, 0))` of one prefix. - `_block_split_tile_kernel`, grid `(requests, cdiv(V, 4096))`: the accept decision, then the sum and the largest prefix-scan element of one 4096-token tile of the selected row. - `_block_split_final_kernel`, grid `(requests,)`: the accepted-draft stores, then the classic CDF walk over tile sums, rescanning only the tile where the CDF crosses the coin. The outputs (`predicts`, `accept_index`, `accept_token_num`) are meant to be bitwise identical to `speculative_sampling_classic_kernel` on the same uniform samples: - the kernels use the classic launch's `BLOCK_REDUCE`, `BLOCK_V` and `num_warps`; - each load keeps the classic address form (the mass kernel unrolls the prefix row as a constexpr), so Triton picks the same register layout and summation order; - tile sums are accumulated

title: [Perf][DSA]: Cut MTP decode overhead with live-length-bounded replay metadata and a greedy-draft argmax exchange
summary: ## Motivation With MTP on DSA models (GLM-5.x, DeepSeek-V3.2), every decode step pays costs that scale with `--context-length` and the vocab rather than with the live work: - The replay metadata kernels launch one program per 128 columns of the context-wide page table: 8193 per row at the default 1M context. - The MTP draft-decode replay precomputes into a full-width scratch table, then copies it into every step backend. - Each greedy draft step all-gathers `rows x vocab` logits only to take an argmax. ## Modifications - **[DSA] Bound the replay metadata kernels by the live KV length.** - Adds bounded variants of the decode, target-verify and draft-extend replay metadata kernels (`kernels/ops/attention/dsa_metadata_bounded.py`). - Each request gets at most `min(budget / rows, 256)` programs, which stride over its live column blocks. - The grid depends only on (rows, width, budget), so it stays CUDA-graph safe. - Outputs are bit-identical to the unbounded kernels. - Used on CUDA with kpool 1 and without KPool metadata fusion. - **[DSA] Write the MTP draft-decode replay metadata in one bounded launch.** - `DeepseekSparseAttnMultiStepBackend` writes each step backend's graph metadata straight from `req_to_token`, in one bounded launch for up to 4 steps. This replaces the precompute + full-width copies. - Draft steps seeded with the draft-extend top-k no longer run their DeepGEMM schedule refresh, which they never used. - Enabled per captured bs, only when the step backends' tables match. - **[Spec] Greedy EAGLE drafts: exchange vocab-shard argmax partials instead of gathering

title: [Perf] sampling: Warm up the FlashInfer sampling module at server startup
summary: ## Motivation The startup warmup requests set `temperature` to 0. `SamplingParams` changes this to `top_k=1`, so the batch is `is_all_greedy` and the sampler runs `torch.argmax`. The warmup does not call FlashInfer sampling, so `get_sampling_module()` does not load the FlashInfer `sampling` module. The first user request that sets top-k, top-p, or min-p loads the module. If `flashinfer-jit-cache` is not installed (the Docker default is `INSTALL_FLASHINFER_JIT_CACHE=0`), FlashInfer compiles `sampling.cu` with nvcc during that request. We observed a 60 s stall on the first request without this change. ## Modifications The warmup requests now send `top_k: 2` in place of `temperature: 0`. This applies to the `/generate` warmup, the VLM chat warmup, and the PD disaggregation warmup. The sampler then calls `top_k_top_p_sampling_from_probs`, and the module loads before the server is ready. ## Accuracy Tests Not applicable. The change does not touch model code, and the server discards the warmup outputs. ## Speed Tests and Profiling Not measured. ## Checklist - [ ] Format your code according to the [Format code with pre-commit](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#format-code-with-pre-commit). - [ ] Add unit tests according to the [Run and add unit tests](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#run-and-add-unit-tests). - [ ] Update documentation according to [Write documentations](https://docs.sglang.io/developer_guide/contribution_guide.html#write-documentations). - [ ] Provide accuracy and speed benchmark results according to [Test

title: [Fix] [AMD] dsv41: Fix wrong TP4 wo_a output from hipBLASLt's strided bmm on ROCm 7.2
summary: ## Motivation With the ROCm 7.2 torch wheel (`lmsysorg/sglang-rocm:v0.5.22-rocm724-mi35x-20261025`, torch 2.11.0+rocm7.2, HIP 7.2), DeepSeek-V4.1 TP4 target verify returns a wrong wo_a output at 289-294 rows on MI355X, on every layer (relative error 1.4 against an fp32 reference). DSpark verifies 6 rows per request, so a 49-request verify batch hits it. The DSpark draft takes the same route. `_wo_a_bf16_bmm_token_major` (#46176) has hipBLASLt write the bmm straight into the token-major layout through a strided `out=`. The hipBLASLt bundled with that wheel picks a stream-K kernel at these row counts that miscomputes the strided destination; the same GEMM writing a packed result (the einsum) is exact. The ROCm 10 build of the same day (`v0.5.22-rocm10-mi35x-20261025`, torch 2.11.0+rocm10.0.0, HIP 7.15) is exact at every row count, so the change applies before HIP 7.15 only (`_STRIDED_BMM_OUT_OK`, the gate #45193 uses). ## Modifications Before HIP 7.15, TP4 verify rows 9-384 go through `_hip.wo_a_verify_matmul`: - MXFP8 wo_b (the gfx950 default): the packed einsum plus one fp8-grid quant launch over both groups, written straight into wo_b's token-major fp8 + ue8m0. This replaces the strided bmm plus wo_b's own quant with the same traffic and launch count. `_launch_fp8_grid_quant` also takes a `[M, G, K / G]` input read through its strides; 2-D callers keep their tiles and addresses. - bf16 wo_b and the DSpark draft: the einsum copied token-major at the 6 broken rows only (`_WO_A_VERIFY_STRIDED_BMM_BAD_ROWS`, the measured failure set); main's strided bmm everywhere else. - CUDA

title: [Feat] PD: Add Mooncake host-only KV staging for decode
summary: ## Motivation In disaggregated serving, allocating decode GPU KV slots before remote transfer completes reserves device capacity for requests that are not yet ready to decode. This PR enables Mooncake to use the native decode Host-receive path. Incoming prompt KV is received into the HiCache Host pool, and GPU allocation is deferred until restoration admission. Decode prefix caching is not required. ## Modifications - Register native Host-pool buffers with Mooncake and publish Host destinations through the existing transfer metadata. - Extend native buffer export to support uncompressed MLA and shared-index DSA, while retaining the existing MHA/GQA/MQA path. - Reuse native allocation budgets, pool transfer descriptions, and HiCache loading queues to batch H2D restoration. - Reuse native completion events and cross-rank acknowledgment before admitting restored requests. - Preserve memory ownership during cancellation, transfer failure, and rebootstrap until outstanding local copies and remote writes are drained. Enable Host-only staging on decode with: ```bash --disaggregation-decode-host-receive-threshold 0 --disaggregation-decode-retraction-backup host_pool ``` The default threshold of `1` retains the existing receive behavior. Host-pool capacity is configured through the existing HiCache options. ## Accuracy Tests Evaluated GLM-5.2-FP8 using the official SGLang evaluation scripts and scoring logic. Both modes used temperature `0`, an output limit of `8192` tokens, and concurrency `32`. | Benchmark | Baseline | Host-only staging | |---|---:|---:| | GSM8K, thinking enabled

title: [Feat] pp: Add CPU-staged Gloo transport for pipeline parallelism
summary: ## Motivation TDX / Confidential Computing (CC) deployments that require host-memory PP communication need a selectable `GPU → CPU → Gloo → CPU → GPU` path while retaining their existing TP backend. The tested upstream baseline (`16eb87c06fca`) does not expose this PP path. This PR adds `--pp-transport gloo`, stages PP payloads through owned CPU buffers and restores received tensors to CUDA. Default transport selection and TP collectives are preserved. The existing PP tensor send path does not automatically stage CUDA tensors on the CPU for Gloo. In the tested environment, explicitly creating Gloo process groups and sending CUDA tensors directly triggers `gloo::IoException: writev ... Bad address`. This PR adds GPU-to-CPU staging on send and CPU-to-GPU restoration on receive so that PP payloads can travel through Gloo. A matched end-to-end comparison on two H20 hosts exercised Qwen3.5-35B-A3B with cross-host TP1/PP2, NEXTN and full decode CUDA graphs. The unmodified upstream default NCCL path completed eight serial warmup requests but failed to complete the concurrency-4 warmup block within the common 180-second limit. A second control using the PR implementation at the time with default NCCL also exceeded the limit: its first serial warmup block eventually took 184.01 seconds. Gloo completed all 32 warmup requests and 48 measured requests. Its measured output token sequences matched across repeats and concurrency settings. title: [Perf] [NVIDIA] muse-spark: Fuse the o_proj all-reduce into the attention boundary
summary: Rebased on main after #45112. cc @Fridge003 @BBuf ## Motivation - At decode and DFlash verify, each Muse Spark layer runs the o_proj all-reduce and the attention-boundary kernel (post-norm, gated residual, pre-norm) as two kernels. - For at most 16 rows on B300 TP4, this PR does the all-reduce inside the boundary kernel. It saves about 1 us per layer, over 62 layers per step. ## Modifications 1. `o_proj` skips its all-reduce when the fusion applies. 2. The boundary kernel stores each rank's bf16 partial into every rank's push workspace with unicast stores. It then sums the four partials in fp32 in rank order, the same order as the 1shot push all-reduce, so the result is bit-exact. 3. The reduce reuses the cluster path of `muse_spark_all_gather_norm_residual` and adds an optional fp32 router output. New op `communication.muse_spark_all_reduce_norm_residual`, with a KernelSpec. The model calls it with the boundary's `jit_kernel_kwargs()`, like the FFN all-gather. 4. title: Fix dp-attention + speculative decoding crashes in flashinfer MLA backend
summary: ## Motivation Running MLA models (e.g. DeepSeek-R1) with `--enable-dp-attention` together with NEXTN/EAGLE speculative decoding on the flashinfer backend crashes during CUDA graph capture / prefill. Plain dp-attention (no spec) and plain spec (no dp-attention) each work; only the combination breaks. Verified fixed on 4-node A100*8 **tp32 / dp4 / ep32** DeepSeek-R1-0528-bf16. ## Root causes Two independent upstream changes exposed latent invariant violations in the MLA backend: 1. **PR #20978** ("pad max-num-requests in decode cuda graph") made the max capture batch size round **up** to a multiple of `attn_tp_size` under dp-attention. title: fix: shrink --hicache-size budget for SIDECAR draft host pool
summary: ## Motivation When `--hicache-size` is set (fixed GB budget for host-side KV cache) and a SIDECAR draft model is registered, the draft model also gets a host-side KV pool that must match the target's token count (for 1-to-1 index sharing in L2 transfers). However, the draft's per-token byte cost can be **larger** than the target's (e.g. quantized target + bf16 draft), causing the combined target+draft host memory allocation to **exceed** the user-specified `--hicache-size` budget. In practice this causes the server to OOM on startup. For example, with a quantized 27B target + bf16 1.5B draft at TP=4: - Target host pool: 7.60 GB/rank - Draft host pool: 9.50 GB/rank - **Total: 17.10 GB/rank** — far exceeding the 4 GB `--hicache-size` cap ## Modifications Add `_adjust_hicache_size_for_draft()` in `kv_cache_builder.py` which: 1. Computes the per-token byte cost of both target and draft device pools via `_device_pool_size_per_token()`, which derives the cost from pool geometry (head_dim, head_num, layer_num, dtype for MHA; kv_cache_dim, layer_num, dtype for MLA) rather than `get_kv_size_bytes()`, since the device pool may be in post-capture mode where buffers are not yet allocated. 2. Shrinks the budget by the factor `target_spt / (target_spt + draft_spt)` so the total (target + draft) stays within the user's `--hicache-size` cap. 3. Reduces both `hicache_size` and `hicache_ratio` (the latter needed because post-capture pools have zero allocated buffers, so sizing falls back to the ratio). 4. title: Eliminating IPC Overhead with Free-Threaded Python
summary: # Proposal: ThreadedEngine — Eliminating IPC Overhead with Free-Threaded Python ## Motivation SGLang's serving runtime is architected around three core components — **TokenizerManager**, **Scheduler**, and **DetokenizerManager** — each running as a separate OS process. They communicate via ZMQ IPC sockets and shared memory. This multi-process design was originally necessary because CPython's Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) prevents true parallelism across threads. This architecture incurs measurable overhead: 1. **Serialization cost**: Every message crossing a ZMQ boundary must be serialized (`send_pyobj`) and deserialized (`recv_pyobj`). For text-only workloads the payloads are small, but for **multimodal workloads** (images, audio), CPU-side preprocessing produces large intermediate representations that must be copied through shared memory or serialized across the IPC boundary. 2. **Memory duplication**: Multimodal tensors (e.g., image embeddings) processed by the TokenizerManager must be wrapped in shared memory (SHM) or copied before the Scheduler can access them. In a single-process model, these tensors could be passed by reference — zero copies, zero SHM bookkeeping. 3. **Latency**: Each IPC hop adds scheduling jitter and context-switch overhead. In latency-sensitive serving scenarios (e.g., real-time vision-language assistants), these micro-delays accumulate. CPython 3.13t introduced experimental free-threaded builds (PEP 703), and **CPython 3.14t** stabilizes this further. title: [Fix] pd: Fail a prefill room whose KV transfer never ends (default off)
summary: ## Motivation On the prefill side of PD disaggregation, the only deadline on a sender covers `KVPoll.Bootstrapping`. Once decode has bootstrapped, a room in `WaitingForInput` or `Transferring` has no deadline. If its transfer never finishes, the room holds its KV forever. We hit this on a PP8 disaggregated prefill with the Mooncake backend. One prefill worker stopped sending KV. 36 in-flight rooms never reached `Success` or `Failed`, and KV pool usage stayed at 0.96-0.99. The worker admitted no new request for the remaining ~9 minutes of the run, until it was stopped. Nothing was logged as an error. We did not capture where the sender stalled, and a small 2-node attempt to reproduce it did not stall. So this PR does not fix a root cause. It adds a backstop that turns a permanent stall into failed requests and freed KV. A second gap is the Mooncake transfer worker. It waits on a chunk's device events (`wait_event` for an early send, `indices_event` for the async index copy) with a blocking `synchronize()`. If that wait never returns, every room queued behind it on the same worker waits too. An abort that arrives during the wait cannot free the worker either. ## Modifications New env `SGLANG_DISAGGREGATION_TRANSFER_TIMEOUT` (seconds, default `0` = off). - **Sender poll** (`CommonKVSender.poll`): a room still `WaitingForInput` or `Transferring` this long after its last chunk was queued is failed. `CommonKVManager.fail_transfer_on_timeout` records the reason and tells decode, then the scheduler frees the KV through the existing transfer-failure path. title: [Feat] platforms: Let OOT platforms provide breakable graph backends (3/3)
summary: ## Motivation SGLang lets users choose a graph backend independently for decode and prefill. Both phases can select `breakable`, where one model forward is captured as multiple device-graph segments separated by operations that run eagerly. Today, selecting `breakable` always constructs SGLang's built-in `BreakableCudaGraphBackend`. An out-of-tree platform can provide a full decode graph backend, but it has no equivalent way to provide its own breakable graph implementation. The platform must patch SGLang or inherit CUDA-specific code, even when it already supports segmented graph capture on its device. This is the final PR in a three-part series: 1. [PR 1](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/49402) introduced the device-neutral `BaseGraphBackend` and `BaseBreakableGraphBackend` contracts. 2. title: [Perf] disagg: Send each PP prefill stage's last KV chunk when its forward ends
summary: ## Motivation With PD disaggregation and a PP prefill server, a stage sends a request's last KV chunk only when it processes that request's result. Results travel the PP output ring, so the result reaches a stage `pp_size - 1` micro-batches after the stage's own forward. The stage's KV is already final when that forward ends. Until the ring catches up, every stage keeps the request's KV locked, and the decode hand-off waits for the ring as well. The target layout is a decode without PP (decode PP 1), where every prefill stage sends its own layers early. With a PP-matched decode only the last stage can send early (the other stages' decode peers read their aux from them), so the gain there is minimal. ## Modifications The new env flag `SGLANG_ENABLE_PP_PD_PREFILL_EARLY_SEND` is off by default. It applies to `event_loop_pp_disagg_prefill` with the Mooncake backend, PP > 1, and only on layouts a token-exact check covered (see Accuracy Tests): no MLA, and no transferred per-request state (`_PP_PD_EARLY_SEND_STATE_TYPES` is empty, so Mamba, SWA and DSA layouts are out). Other layouts keep the regular path. - **Non-last stages.** Right after launching a micro-batch, the stage hands the last chunk of every request that finishes in it to the transfer worker. The forward's launch event rides on the sender (`_early_send_wait_event`), and the worker waits on it before reading. These stages send without aux: `send(..., send_aux=False)` leaves the aux index out, and the Mooncake worker writes the aux only for a chunk that has an aux index and only on the request peer (main's KV-shard rul

title: [Perf] [NVIDIA] qsa: FlashInfer prims-ts sparse decode attention backend (opt-in)
summary: ## Motivation On SM100-class GPUs the QSA (Qwen4-Exp) decode path gathers the selected K/V rows into a page-aligned scratch (`fused_kv_prepare`, 33 pages of 64 tokens per request) and then runs FlashInfer's dense trtllm-gen paged decode over the copy. Every selected byte is read from the pool, written to the scratch and read again, and the scratch takes about 550 MB per GPU at 256 rows. FlashInfer 0.7.4 ships `QTokenKvBlockSparsePagedTSWrapper` (prims-ts, CuTe-DSL, SM100/SM103/SM107): a sparse decode kernel that takes the indexer's block ids and the request page table and reads the selected blocks in place, one launch per layer plus a split-KV reducer, no gather and no scratch. This PR wires it into `QwenSparseAttnBackend` behind an opt-in flag. The default path is untouched. ## Modifications - New server argument `--qsa-decode-attention-backend {auto,flashinfer_sparse}` (default `auto` keeps today's path) in `arg_groups/fields/exec_.py`, `arg_groups/field_order.py` and the server-arguments doc. - New `layers/attention/qsa/flashinfer_sparse.py`: `FlashInferSparseDecode` plans one wrapper per (batch size, layer) over the flat `[slots, Hkv, D]` pool viewed as HND pages, keeps a full-width Int32 page table for eager batches (the CUDA-graph table passes through), pads eager batches above the graph range to a small bucket ladder with inactive rows, and returns `[rows, Hq * D]`. Workspaces stay under 1 MiB each. - `qwen_sparse_attn_backend.py`: `forward_decode` tries `_try_flashinfer_sparse_decode` first. title: [Fix] speculative: Feed every accepted token to the penalizers
summary: - Speculative decoding fed the penalizers only the last output token of each request per verify round. A round can commit several tokens, so frequency, presence, and repetition penalties and `min_new_tokens` counted one token per round. - `Req.penalty_cumulated_len` records how many output tokens the penalizers have seen. `ScheduleBatch.cumulate_penalty_output_tokens()` now feeds every output token past it, with each token's batch row as `req_indices`: one token per request after a decode step, a variable number after a verify round. Retract resets the length, since the re-prefill batch starts its penalizers from zero. - `ScheduleBatch.prepare_for_decode` makes the one call, before it branches on the speculative algorithm, so plain decode, EAGLE, NGRAM, STANDALONE, DFlash, and DSpark share it. The per-algorithm calls in `eagle_prepare_for_decode` and `spec_prepare_for_decode` are gone, and the penalizers' `req_indices` is now required. - Behavior change under speculative decoding: penalties count every accepted token. Two approximations stay as before: draft rows of one round share the penalties as of the round's start, and under overlap scheduling the round in flight is fed on the next round. - Behavior change without speculative decoding, under overlap scheduling: the first decode step no longer feeds the prompt's last token to the penalizers when no output token is committed yet. - Measured on NGRAM with `min_new_tokens=24` and a prompt that ends early: 59 output tokens before, 26 after, 26 without speculative decoding. summary: ## Motivation Main's DFLASH worker can plan a verify length per request and run a packed ("compact") verify since #46190. title: [Feature] Free-Threaded Python (3.14t / nogil) Support for SGLang
summary: ## Motivation CPython 3.13 introduced an experimental free-threaded build (PEP 703) that removes the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL). CPython 3.14t is the first release where this build is stable enough for production use, and the ecosystem of packages with free-threading wheels is growing rapidly. vLLM has demonstrated ([vllm-project/vllm#28762](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/28762)) that a large-scale CUDA-accelerated serving framework can run under a free-threaded interpreter. SGLang shares a similar dependency footprint and architecture. Enabling free-threaded support would unlock true CPU-level parallelism in the Python layer — benefiting the tokenizer manager, scheduler, HTTP server, disaggregation controller, and other asyncio + thread-pool components that today serialize behind the GIL. This RFC tracks the dependency readiness, identifies the internal code changes needed, and proposes a phased plan to make `uv pip install sglang` work out of the box in a clean Python 3.14t environment on Linux x86-64 (CPU and CUDA). ## Background | Term | Meaning | |---|---| | **3.14t** | The free-threaded (no-GIL) CPython 3.14 build, identified by the `t` suffix in the ABI tag (`cp314t`). | | **cp314** | The regular (with-GIL) CPython 3.14 build. | | **Stable ABI** | A subset of the CPython C API that is ABI-compatible across Python versions (PEP 384). Extensions built against the stable ABI only need one wheel per platform, not one per Python minor version. | | **`Py_GIL_DISABLED`** | The compile-time macro set in free-threaded builds. C extensions must check this to us

title: [RFC] Agent-Aware KV Cache Phase 1 for Agentic Workloads
summary: ## Summary This RFC proposes Phase 1 of agent-aware KV cache support in SGLang. The goal of this phase is to add a minimal, backward-compatible metadata path for agentic workloads so workflow information can flow from the API layer into runtime requests and KV cache nodes, and optionally affect radix cache eviction. This is intentionally a foundation/prototype phase, not a full workflow-aware cache system. ## Motivation Current KV cache eviction policies such as LRU, LFU, and SLRU treat requests mostly independently. That works well for standard chat/completion workloads, but it misses reuse opportunities in agentic workflows, where requests often share: - repeated prompt prefixes across planner/tool/worker steps - parent/child step relationships - short-term reuse after tool calls - workflow-level TTL or reuse intent Without workflow-aware signals, cache entries that are likely to be reused by upcoming steps may be evicted too early. ## Proposal Phase 1 introduces: - an optional `agent_hints` field in OpenAI-compatible requests - propagation of `agent_hints` through the internal request pipeline - lightweight workflow DAG tracking in the scheduler - radix cache node annotation with workflow metadata - a new optional radix eviction policy: `agent_aware` Initial `agent_hints` fields include: - `workflow_id` - `agent_id` - `step_id` - `step_index` - `total_steps` - `parent_step_id` - `children_step_ids` - `tool_name` - `expected_tool_duration_ms` - `cache_ttl_ms` - `shared_prefix_hash` - `reuse_hint` ## Scope Phase 1 is intended to cover: - request schema support - metadata p

title: [RFC] Decouple the SWA sidecar page size from the full-attention page size (DSv4, Hybrid Models)
summary: ### Checklist - [x] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed. - [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed. ### Motivation #### Summary Allow the sliding-window-attention (SWA) KV sidecar pool to use a physical page size that differs from the full-attention pool's `page_size`. Concretely, add a `swa_page_size` so a hybrid model can keep `page_size = 256` for full layers while paging the SWA sidecar at 128. #### Motivation For hybrid models (full-attention layers + sliding-window layers), SGLang splits the KV cache into a full pool and a SWA sidecar pool. Today the sidecar inherits the full pool's `page_size` (paged SWA mode requires `page_size == 256`). A sliding window only keeps the most recent `W` tokens. When the sidecar is paged coarser than the window, capacity is rounded up to whole pages, and both the SWA KV pool and any per-page state pools are over-allocated. With a 128-token window paged at 256, that is ~2x over-allocation of the SWA-side pools — memory that could otherwise be effective KV token budget. The page size cannot simply drop to 1: attention/state kernels require a kernel-friendly granularity. 128 is such a granularity, and halving the sidecar page (256 → 128) removes the rounding waste while staying kernel-compatible. #### Proposal Introduce a distinct `swa_page_size` for the sidecar, independent of the full pool `page_size`. title: [Perf] [AMD] minimax-m3: Default page_size to the 128-token sparse block on ROCm

With `page_size == 128` a selected sparse block is exactly one allocator page. The sparse prefill attention then derives each block's slots from one base slot (`PER_PAGE_SLOTS` in `flash_with_topk_idx.py`), and the decode sparse kernel reads the block as one contiguous page (`PAGED_CONTIG` in `topk_sparse.py`), instead of looking up 128 `req_to_token` entries. It fails on main (`KeyError: 'page_size'`), and it also fails on a variant that overrides an explicit `--page-size`. title: [Fix] deepseek_v4: Capture decoder-tail graphs at startup, never on a step a DP rank skips
summary: ## Motivation A DeepSeek-V4.1 prefill server can hang on its first busy prefill steps after startup. This happens with DP attention (attention TP 1), `--moe-a2a-backend megamoe`, `--cuda-graph-backend-prefill breakable`, and decoder SWA bounded replay. Every DP rank stops. After 300 s, DeepGEMM's MegaMoE grid-sync timeout traps and the GPUs report Xid 43. A restart doesn't help: the next cold start can hang the same way. How it happens: 1. With MegaMoE and no DP gather in the graph, `prefill_graph_tolerates_sum_len()` lets each DP rank replay the prefill-graph bucket of its own token count. 2. The decoder replay tail (#45059, #45107) takes one of two forms, depending on the bucket: - In buckets of at least `SGLANG_DSV4_DECODER_TAIL_GRAPH_MIN_PREFILL_TOKENS` (2048), it runs as an eager break, `_tail_layers_in_prefill_graph`. The break replays row-bucket graphs of its own. - In smaller buckets, the tail layers, MegaMoE included, are recorded inline in the prefill graph. 3. The break captures a missing row-bucket graph on first use. `RowBucketGraphRunner._record` calls `tp_group.barrier()` before it captures. 4. Take a step where one rank's bucket is at least 2048 and another's is below 2048: - The first rank waits in the gloo barrier. - The second rank has already launched MegaMoE and waits in its grid sync for the first. - Neither can move. #45881 guards one variant of this: an idle rank, which never reaches the break. title: [Fix] dflash: Apply request penalties under DFLASH and DSPARK
summary: ## Motivation Fixes #46752. With `--speculative-algorithm DFLASH` or `DSPARK`, `repetition_penalty`, `frequency_penalty`, `presence_penalty` and `min_tokens` have no effect. Two causes: 1. `spec_prepare_for_decode` never cumulates penalty output tokens for the DFLASH family (only `eagle_prepare_for_decode` does), so penalizer state stays at identity. 2. DFLASH verify and its fast-path checks read `acc_linear_penalties`, which `SamplingBatchInfo` doesn't have, instead of the `acc_additive_penalties` / `acc_scaling_penalties` that `copy_for_forward()` produces. The dense fallback also scaled a zero buffer, which drops `repetition_penalty`. ## Modifications - `spec_prepare_for_decode`: cumulate in the `is_dflash_family()` branch, as EAGLE does. It stays per branch so EAGLE doesn't count twice. - `apply_dflash_verify_logits_adjustments`: apply `acc_additive_penalties` and `acc_scaling_penalties` broadcast over the verify block, as EAGLE verify does. The scheduler always hands workers a `copy_for_forward()` copy, so these buffers are the only way penalties arrive. The grammar fallback now applies only the vocab mask. - `_can_skip_verify_logits` and `verify_logits_adjustments_are_noop` now see the accumulated buffers, so penalized batches take the eager verify path. This also covers the DSPARK block-accept estimator gate from the issue, which uses the same check. - `test_dspark_sampling_accept_graph.py`: its fake `sampling_info` had the nonexistent `acc_linear_penalties` field; it now has the two real ones. Penalties keep EAGLE's relaxed spec-decoding semantics (see Not covered).

title: [Feat] cp: Let zigzag CP keep a batch with a request shorter than 2 x cp_size
summary: ## Motivation `ZigzagCPStrategy.can_apply` turns context parallelism off for a whole EXTEND batch as soon as one request in it extends by fewer than `2 x cp_size` tokens, because zigzag cuts each request into `2 x cp_size` blocks and such a request leaves some of them empty. The batch then takes the non-CP path: every rank runs the full chunk eagerly, outside the prefill CUDA graph the server was sized for. A one-token health check or an exact repeat of a cached prompt arriving beside a chunk of fresh prompts is enough to trigger this, and on a server whose memory is sized for the CP prefill graph it can run out of memory. ## Modifications - `ZigzagCPStrategy.allow_short_requests()`: an opt-in, off by default. Once called, `can_apply` keeps an EXTEND batch on CP when its longest request extends by at least `2 x cp_size` tokens, so every rank still owns at least one row; shorter requests in that batch get empty zigzag blocks on some ranks. It is meant for prefill attention backends that run zero-length blocks correctly. MIXED batches keep the per-request rule, and a batch where every request is short still leaves CP, as before. - Nothing in this repository calls it, so default behaviour is unchanged. A model or backend integration that has verified its attention kernel with empty pieces calls it once at setup. - Unit cases in `test/registered/cp/test_cp_strategy_unit.py` for the four combinations: a short request beside a long one with and without the opt-in, a batch of only short requests, and a MIXED batch. ## Accuracy Tests - `test/registered/cp/test_cp_strategy_unit.py -

title: [Feat] logprob: Return an input candidate selector's weights with the prompt logprobs
summary: Stacked on #51899 (the input candidate selector pull request; this one is opened against its branch); merge that one first. This pull request adds only the second half: the selector's weights travel with the prompt logprobs to the client. ## Motivation An input candidate selector lets a request replace the plain top-k of its prompt logprobs with candidates of its own choosing, and it can attach a weight to each candidate (for example, a sampling probability). Until now those weights were computed and dropped inside the forward. A client that asked for candidates had no way to learn how they were chosen, so a weighted candidate set could not be reproduced or corrected on the client side. ## Modifications - **Forward.** `LogitsProcessorOutput` gains `input_top_logprobs_weights`: per sequence, `[rows, k]` float32 host spans of its selector's weights, pinned when the chunk ran on borrowed graph-pool memory. The prefill CUDA graph runner keeps them in its trimmed output. `None` when the batch has no selector request. - **Scheduler.** `SchedulerLogprobResultProcessor` gathers a request's spans across prefill chunks into `ReqLogprob.input_top_logprobs_weights`, a `[rows, k]` float32 array with one row per non-null entry of `input_top_logprobs`; the sampling token's row is dropped, as it is for the top logprobs. A forward that returns no weights for a request with a selector raises `RuntimeError` instead of answering with plain top-k rows. - **Transport.** `BatchTokenIDOutput` and `BatchStrOutput` gain `input_top_logprobs_weights` (`None` unless a request of the batch has weights).

summary: ## Motivation On Hopper, Inkling 2 Small runs TP8/EP8 with no MoE a2a backend: every rank sees all tokens, runs the 48 of the 384 routed experts it owns (a contiguous id range), and each MoE layer ends in an all-reduce. title: [Feat] scheduler: Report where an ignore_eos request's first stop token would have ended it
summary: ## Motivation With `ignore_eos`, the scheduler keeps decoding past every stop token and the response never says where the reply would have ended. A client that wants the valid prefix of a fixed-length generation has to rebuild the stop set itself (EOS, the tokenizer's additional stop tokens, `stop_token_ids`), and that copy can drift from what the scheduler actually checks. This PR makes the scheduler record where the first stop token would have ended the request, and reports it on every length finish as `meta_info.finish_reason.ignored_stop`. Example, `max_new_tokens=64, ignore_eos=true`, EOS sampled as the second output token: ```json "finish_reason": {"type": "length", "length": 64, "ignored_stop": {"position": 2}} ``` The same request without a stop token at or before `max_new_tokens` reports `"ignored_stop": null`. Other finish types never carry the key. ## Modifications - **Scheduler** (`python/sglang/srt/managers/schedule_batch.py`, `req_types.py`, `dllm/mixin/scheduler.py`): under `ignore_eos` the stop-token check in `Req._check_token_based_finish` now runs too. Its first match records `Req.ignored_stop_token_len`, the output length at which the same request without `ignore_eos` would have stopped; nothing else changes, decoding continues to `max_new_tokens` and the output keeps every token. Every `FINISH_LENGTH` (the dLLM context-limit one included) passes the value on, and `to_json()` emits `ignored_stop` as `{"position": L}` or `null`. title: [Perf] rust-server: Decode each chunk's own bytes for byte-level BPE tokenizers
summary: ## Motivation The Rust server's detokenizer shards decode every stream through dynamo-tokenizers' `DecodeStream`, which on each step re-decodes all ids since its last complete text and moves its offsets only when the text grew and does not end in U+FFFD. A stream whose text never completes, such as a run of skipped special tokens or stray bytes that keep the text ending in U+FFFD, never moves them: each token costs O(output length) and the request O(n²). That work runs on the shard thread that serves every request hashed to it, and with more shards the single from-scheduler dispatcher blocks once that shard's bounded inbox fills. One such stream makes the other requests on the server wait behind it. ## Modifications - **Byte tables** (`tokenizer_manager/byte_tables.rs`, new). For a Hugging Face `tokenizer.json` with a `ByteLevel` decoder and a BPE model, build every id's bytes at startup, with special tokens kept and skipped: a token's characters map back through the inverse of the GPT-2 byte-to-unicode map, an added token's content is its own UTF-8, and an id that only `tokenizer_config.json` declares uses its decoded text when that text holds no U+FFFD. - **Startup check.** Every id, three ids past the vocabulary, and 512 random sequences weighted to added tokens and tokens that split characters must decode to the tokenizer's own text for both `skip_special_tokens` values. title: [Fix] disaggregation: A prefill request without a decode reservation yields its storage prefetch to a bootstrapped one
summary: Stacked on #51882 (a parked optimistic prefill yields its KV when a bootstrapped request is blocked on KV); this pull request must not land before it. ## Motivation A prefill engine with a storage (L3) tier keeps what a request read from storage, host staging and an anchor pin, from the moment the read commits until the request is admitted. Requests that still wait in the bootstrap queue, or optimistic requests without a decode reservation, can hold all of that budget. A request that already holds its decode reservation then parks on `anchor-lock cap reached` or on the staging limit and cannot load its own storage hit, while the holders wait for a reservation the decode side cannot give until the bootstrapped request finishes. Both sides wait until a disaggregation timeout fires. Synthetic example: request X gets its decode reservation. Request H arrives, reads its storage hit into staging, and waits in the bootstrap queue behind X. When X reaches the prefill engine its hit cannot commit because H holds the anchor budget. X times out and H is served after it. ## Modifications - Parked storage hits commit in scheduler order, bootstrapped requests first (`BufferModePipeline.order_parked_hits`). - While the hit of a bootstrapped request cannot commit, one request without a decode reservation gives up its prefetch per scheduler pass and starts its lookup again (`yield_storage_prefetch`, called from `get_next_disagg_prefill_batch_to_run` when storage is enabled). title: [Fix] disaggregation: A parked optimistic prefill yields its KV when a bootstrapped request is blocked on KV
summary: ## Summary With optimistic prefill, a PD prefill worker can finish a request before its decode worker has reserved memory for it; the finished KV then stays with the request ("parked") until the decode reservation arrives. A request that already holds its decode reservation (bootstrapped) can be refused prefill KV because parked requests hold the pool, while those parked requests wait for the decode memory the bootstrapped request already holds. Neither side moves until a PD timeout fails one of them. This change lets one parked request give its KV back in that case. ## Symptom & Reproduction - **Symptom:** a PD pair with `--optimistic-prefill-attempts` > 0 and long prompts stalls: the prefill worker's waiting queue holds a bootstrapped request, the prefill KV pool is held by parked requests, and no forward runs until the PD timeout fails one of them. - **Reproduction (two requests, one prefill + one decode worker, a KV pool sized for about one prompt):** send request A; its prefill finishes and parks because decode has not bootstrapped it yet. Before this change the pair waits until a PD timeout; with it, A yields on the next transfer-queue scan and B is served. ## Root Cause A parked request gave its KV back only when no request row was free (the existing row rule). With long prompts the KV pool fills before the rows run out, so the rule never ran and nothing released the parked KV. ## Fix - `Scheduler.get_new_batch_prefill` records in `prefill_admissi

summary: ## Motivation A request that asks for input (prompt) logprobs with `top_logprobs_num = K` gets, at every prompt position, the K most likely tokens. Some consumers of prompt logprobs want a different set of K candidates per position, for example K tokens drawn from the model's next-token distribution at that position, or K tokens fixed by the caller. The choice depends on the logits of the position, so it has to be made where the prompt logprobs are computed, inside `InputLogprobProcessor`, where the row of logits exists; after the forward only the top K is left. summary: ## Motivation When a request finishes in a step, the scheduler releases its KV, radix and PD sender state synchronously and only then serializes and enqueues its final output. title: Perf [AMD] replace triton gdn with fly dsl gdn packed when applicable
summary: On ROCm, GDN packed decode can call AITER's `flydsl_gdr_decode` instead of the Triton packed kernel. The default stays Triton. ## Summary - `SGLANG_USE_HIP_GDN_PACKED_DECODE_BACKEND=aiter` selects the FlyDSL path. Any other value, including the default `triton`, keeps the Triton packed decode. - The hook is inside `TritonGDNKernel.packed_decode`. ReplaySSM decode stays on Triton. - Q, K, and V are strided views of the post-conv `mixed_qkv` row. Nothing is copied into separate Q/K/V tensors. - A launch the kernel does not cover logs once and falls back to Triton. The adapter also stays on Triton when `flydsl_gdr_decode` is missing or does not zero padding rows. Graph replay pads with a negative cache index, and those rows have to come back as zeros. - The two kernels are not bit-identical. Triton rounds beta to the activation dtype. FlyDSL keeps beta in fp32 and uses a fast-math exponential. The registered test compares them with a tolerance over several chained steps. Covered launches match the Triton kernel's assumptions: `scale == head_k_dim ** -0.5`, `dt_bias` in the activation dtype, int32 cache indices, K a multiple of 64, V a multiple of 32, and the state in fp32 or bf16. ## Server ```bash export SGLANG_USE_HIP_GDN_PACKED_DECODE_BACKEND=aiter export SGLANG_USE_AITER=1 export SGLANG_USE_AITER_UNIFIED_ATTN=1 export SGLANG_ROCM_GDN_ONLINE_MXFP4=1 export ROCM_QUICK_REDUCE_QUANTIZATION=INT4 python3 -m sglang.launch_server \ --model amd/Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B-Quark-MXFP4 \ --host 0.0.0.0 --port 5060 --tp-size 8 \ --trust-remote-code \ --attention-backend aiter \ --kv-cache-dtype

title: [Fix] custom-ar-v2: Build the communicator during CUDA graph capture
summary: ## Motivation With FlashInfer AllReduce fusion on, which is the default for NemotronH at TP>1, the first large burst of traffic after startup stalls every TP rank for about 7.5 s on H100. `CustomAllReduceV2.obj` is a `cached_property`. Building it loads the `communicator` JIT module, which on a cold JIT cache means an nvcc compile. With fusion off, the captured decode graphs run their all-reduces through this class, so the compile happens during CUDA graph capture at startup. With fusion on, the captured layers use the fused all-reduce, and nothing builds the communicator until the first eager all-reduce that needs it. That happens mid-serving: here, the embedding all-reduce of a large prefill. One rank compiles while the other three wait on the JIT build lock. `py-spy` stacks of all four schedulers during the stall: ``` _build_lock (sglang/kernels/jit/utils/compile/loader.py) load_jit (sglang/kernels/jit/utils/compile/loader.py) _init_communicator (sglang/kernels/ops/communication/all_reduce.py) WorkspaceLease.get_communicator (symm_workspace.py) CustomAllReduceV2.obj (custom_all_reduce_v2.py) CustomAllReduceV2.custom_all_reduce (custom_all_reduce_v2.py) ... VocabParallelEmbedding.forward (vocab_parallel_embedding.py) ``` This is likely the "c=128 drop with fusion on" reported in #50021. ## Modifications - `custom_all_reduce_v2.py`: `capture()` builds `self.obj` before capturing. `GroupCoordinator.graph_capture()` enters it on every rank at startup, so the communicator is ready before serving, whatever the captured graphs use. The disabled path is unchanged. - New CPU unit

It is the first in-tree backend to consume the request-scoped `kv_hints` from #51088. title: Perf [AMD] all-reduce tuner for graph and eager mode
summary: ## Motivation This is a significant modification of [#34838](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/34838), which introduced `python/sglang/auto_tune/allreduce_tuner.py` as item 4 of the auto-tuner roadmap ([#13363](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/13363)). That PR established the idea and the file: time the all-reduce backends and write the best one per message size to a JSON table. It kept to four backends, derived the sizes from the model config, timed eager calls only, and ran from a `--allreduce` flag on the auto-tune main flow. What is kept from it is the shape of the output and the place in the tree. What is new here is a second timing mode for CUDA graphs, a selection file that names who competes, cross-rank agreement before entering any collective, and the synchronisation needed to keep eight ranks from wedging in a timing loop. The entry point is a standalone torchrun module that starts no server and loads no model. Which all-reduce backend is fastest depends on the message size, the hardware, and whether the call is replayed from a CUDA graph. New all-reduce implementations keep landing (another custom all-reduce, another QuickReduce codec, FlyDSL INT4), and the only way to know where each one wins is to time them against each other on the machine before a model is started. The tuner is the tool for that: it opens the kernels the selection names, times them at the sizes you list, and writes the winner per size. ## Workflow Commands, example output for each mode, and the stack-dump guide are in [`python/sglang/auto_tune/README.md](https://github.co

title: [Fix] [AMD] attention: preserve DCP LSE through prefill graph wrappers
summary: ## Motivation ROCm DCP MLA attention returns an `(output, LSE)` pair, but its two call sites in `forward_mla_rocm.py` did not mark that return shape for the prefill graph attention wrapper. title: [Perf] disaggregation: Vectorize staging gather/scatter for aligned KV buffers
summary: ## Motivation The staging gather/scatter kernels read KV buffer addresses from a pointer table on the device. Triton cannot infer alignment from a loaded pointer, so the KV side is lowered to scalar loads and stores. In the PTX for the current kernels, the payload moves one element at a time, and scatter also uses 8 KB of shared memory that the vectorized version does not need. The KV buffers are 16-byte aligned in practice. The kernel just has no way to know. ## Modifications - Add an `ALIGNED_16` specialization to the gather and scatter kernels. When it is on, the row bases get a `tl.multiple_of(..., 16)` hint and Triton emits vector loads and stores. For scatter, the hint covers the fused and persistent kernels; the per-page scatter kernel keeps generic addressing. - Check the KV buffers once when Mooncake or NIXL registers them (`kv_buffers_preserve_16_byte_alignment`, called from `build_staging_kv_buffer_info`). The result is stored with the buffer info, so transfers do not rescan the buffer list. - On each transfer, only the staging buffer address is checked (`_can_use_aligned_staging_copy`), because it can start at any ring offset. The strides and head offsets come from the buffer shape, so the registration check covers them. If any check fails, the transfer uses the generic kernel, same as today. Nothing changes when staging is disabled, and nothing changes for buffers that fail the checks. ## Test New test file: `test/registered/kernels/ops/kvcache/test_disaggregation_staging_buffer.py` - Gather and scatter give bit-exact results on both the aligned path and the ge

title: [Fix] rl: One tensor weight payload per engine rank under pipeline parallelism
summary: ## Motivation `update_weights_from_tensor` sends one CUDA-IPC payload per TP rank and each scheduler rank reads `serialized_named_tensors[tp_rank]`. With `pp_size > 1`, stage 1's rank r opens the same handle as stage 0's rank r: it gets stage 0's parameters, which it does not own and skips, so later stages are never updated. Two consumers on one IPC handle also break producer-side refcounting (#8203 saw it as OOM). ## Modifications Payloads are now one per engine rank in world-rank order: producers emit `tp_size * pp_size` copies and each rank reads entry `tp_size * pp_rank + tp_rank`. The list stays flat, so trainers that already send one bucket per engine GPU need no change, and `pp_size == 1` behaves as before. ## Tests New unit test `test_weight_payload_per_engine_rank.py` covers the index and the payload count - 3 of its 4 cases fail without the fix. summary: ## Motivation #43463 launches the QSA indexer's decode MQA-logits TileLang kernel with a fixed number of CTAs per row, each striding over the row's 64-key groups. title: [Perf] cosmos3: optimize Sim-Bimanual kv cache management
summary: Motivation Cosmos3 Nano Sim-Bimanual repeatedly concatenates text, history, and current KV during inference, and rebuilds history after each clean-frame commit. This adds memory traffic, allocation overhead, and temporary KV copies, especially with full history. Related issue: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/48144 ## Modifications - Reuse request-local, per-layer `[text | history | current]` KV buffers across denoising steps. Only clean frames commit history. - Preallocate full-history capacity for each request and reject requests exceeding the configured history limit. - Preserve sliding-window sink/recent retention using one scratch buffer sized for a single layer's recent-window K/V (**48.125 MiB total** in this benchmark), reused across all 36 layers. Full history requires no scratch storage. Overlap compaction with subsequent computation through per-layer CUDA events, with stream cleanup on normal and exceptional exits. ## Accuracy Tests - Both full and sliding modes produce **bit-identical BF16 latents and all 901 decoded RGB frames** compared with the original KV implementation. - Targeted unit suites: **217 tests and 116 subtests passed**. Coverage includes history retention, clean/noisy KV separation, request isolation, stream ordering, and exception cleanup. - Pre-commit checks passed. ## Speed Tests and Profiling Tested on one **RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition**, Intel Xeon Gold 6444Y, PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130. title: [Test] rust-server: Verify disconnect aborts an admitted unary prefill
summary: ## Motivation In prefill/decode disaggregation, a client such as a router can lose its connection to a prefill server before any response byte arrives. The prefill server should then stop work on the request it already admitted, so the client needs no abort of its own for it. The Rust frontend already behaves this way: when the connection closes, the server drops the request's handler, and the generation's guard (`impl Drop for Generation` in `rust/sglang-server/src/api_server/handlers/generate.rs`) sends the scheduler `AbortSource::Guard(rid)` for a request intake has accepted. No test in the native API tests closes a real connection on an admitted unary request, so nothing pins that a closed TCP connection actually reaches that guard. ## Modifications Test only, one file: `rust/sglang-server/src/api_server/http/native_api.rs`. New test `closed_connection_aborts_admitted_unary_prefill`: - builds a disaggregation `CoreHandle` and serves `routes()` with `axum::serve` on a `127.0.0.1:0` TCP listener; - writes a unary prefill `POST /generate` (with `bootstrap_host`, `bootstrap_port`, `bootstrap_room`) over a raw HTTP/1.1 socket and accepts it at intake; - checks that no response byte arrives while the request is admitted, then closes the socket; - requires the scheduler's abort channel to receive `AbortSource::Guard` naming the request's rid within five seconds, and nothing after it. ## Accuracy Tests Not applicable: no change outside the test module. title: [Fix] scheduler: Keep chunked prefill cuts on the QSA compress grid
summary: ## Motivation With `--disable-radix-cache` on MI355X (gfx950), Qwen3.8-Flash-Next aborts during chunked prefill. The failing check is `torch._assert_async((prefix_lens % ratio == 0).all())` in `_qsa_build_write_plan` (`qwen_sparse_attn_backend.py:654`), which ROCm reports as `HSA_STATUS_ERROR_EXCEPTION ... code: 0x1016` in `_assert_async_cuda_kernel<bool>`. Compressed QSA keys every `qsa_compress_ratio` (4) tokens, so a chunk cut short of its prompt must end on a multiple of 4. Two cuts of a new request end anywhere here: 1. **Exact chunk fill** (gfx95; for hybrid models like this one, only while prefix sharing is off) bills prompts at their raw length. Two 7,827-token prompts leave 730 of a 16,384-token chunk for the third. `_select_prefill_admission` floors this cut to `truncation_align_size`, but nothing put the QSA ratio there, and since #48399 exact fill has no off switch. 2. **`add_one_req_ignore_eos`**, taken by `ignore_eos` requests when the radix cache is off, cut without `truncation_align_size`. `sglang.benchmark.serving` sends `ignore_eos` by default. This PR puts the QSA ratio into `truncation_align_size` and floors the ignore-EOS cut to it. The other half is a continuation's cut in `add_chunked_req`, at the free-memory cap, which can be any count with the radix cache on or off: #44076 floors it to `truncation_align_size`. The remaining caps on a chunk (page-billed admission, the shortest-prefill-first limit, the PP dynamic chunk size, the unified-memory budget) are page-granular, and `QSATokenToKVPool` requires `page_size % qsa_compress_ratio == 0`. summary: ## Motivation The non-MLA NHD batch-prefill path in the aiter backend copies the whole of q on every layer (`q.contiguous().view(...)`) although `mha_batch_prefill_func` does not need it contiguous; this PR hands the kernel a view, with the helper #47822 added for the unified call site. title: [Perf] dsa: Skip unused FlashMLA schedules for packed prefill
summary: ## Motivation When DSA selects `flashmla_kv`, eager metadata initialization builds the legacy unpacked split-KV schedule for the expanded query rows. Token-packed prefill builds a different schedule inside `flashmla_kv_token_packed` and returns before the unpacked attention call. For a batch whose layers all pack successfully, the legacy schedule is never consumed. This is particularly relevant to long chunked prefills on SM100/SM103 (including Kimi-K3.1, where token packing is enabled by default). Avoid that unused planner invocation without changing the packed kernel or the legacy fallback. ## Modifications - Defer only for ordinary eager `EXTEND` batches using `flashmla_kv` with packing enabled, prefill CUDA graph disabled, no two-batch overlap, and no custom eager-metadata hook. - If packing rejects a layer, construct the same unpacked schedule using the batch's expanded/clipped sequence lengths, `seq_len_q=1` and padded prefill head count. Store it in that batch's metadata and reuse it across later fallback layers. - Keep the existing eager schedule lifetime for non-packed prefill, mixed batches, decode, verify, draft extend and graph paths. No new flag, native planner, or cross-batch cache. ## Accuracy Tests Added a regression to the existing eager DSA metadata CPU test. title: [Perf] tokenizer_manager: Drop the prompt token list once a single request is dispatched
summary: ## Motivation `GenerateReqInput.input_ids` stays a Python `list[int]` for the whole request, because `ReqState.obj` holds the request until it finishes. With long agentic prompts (0.5-1M tokens) at high concurrency, the tokenizer manager process holds tens of millions of list elements in the young GC generations. Every gen0/gen1 collection walks all of them, about 8-9 ns per element, so the process stalls for 0.2-0.5 s per collection. Clients see these stalls as mid-stream gaps in the token stream. A PD decode gateway hits this hardest: it serves the full prompt of every in-flight request for the whole length of its decode. ## Modifications - `TokenizerManager.generate_request`, single-request path: after `_send_one_request`, `obj.input_ids` is set to `None`, so the prompt list is freed by refcount instead of living in the young GC generations until the request finishes. The scheduler already has its own `array('q')` copy. - The release is skipped while something reads `obj.input_ids` after dispatch: request logging at `--log-requests-level` 2 or 3, `--export-metrics-to-file`, request dumps (`dump_requests_folder`) and crash dumps (`--crash-dump-folder`). These keep the original list, so their output, dump loading and multimodal requests are unchanged; such deployments keep today's GC behavior. - Nothing else reads `obj.input_ids` after dispatch (the OpenAI chat path reads it only before dispatch; batch requests are unchanged). - Native HTTP `/generate`: the streaming response holds `request` until the request finishes, and `request.json()` caches the parsed body on it. title: [Fix] [AMD] unified_cache: Release a stashed chunk's window rows once its forward is processed
summary: > **Known issue, do not use yet (2026-11-21).** A CPU model on the real cache path shows that the deferred release can free a window another request has just taken over: a short request whose prompt is a prefix of a chunked one re-homes the stashed chunk's window rows, and the release that runs after the forward then frees those pages while the tree still holds them. Releasing at once behind a wait for the forward (the first version of this PR) or behind the WAR barrier does not do this. The PR stays a draft until this is fixed or it goes back to waiting for the forward. With `SGLANG_OPT_UNIFIED_CACHE_FREE_OUT_OF_WINDOW_SLOTS=1` and the WAR barrier off (its default on ROCm), a stashed prefill chunk's out-of-window SWA rows are retired at once but released only after the forward still storing them has been processed, without making the scheduler wait for that forward. ## Motivation Stashing a prefill chunk retires its out-of-window SWA rows and clears their full -> SWA mapping on the scheduler's stream. Under the overlap scheduler that chunk's forward is still running, and the aiter unified-attention path resolves the mapping in every sliding layer's KV store, so the later layers store those tokens at the padding slot and read stale rows. A prompt longer than one chunk then keeps wrong sliding-layer KV for all but the tail of each non-final chunk. It stays in the radix cache, the host tier and the PD transfer, and nothing is logged. title: [Fix] sgl-router: Learn the KV block-hash mode from published events
summary: ## Motivation `--policy cache_aware` (including `--dp-aware`) never matches the prefix cache of hybrid-SSM models with EAGLE-family speculative decoding (EAGLE / EAGLE3 / NEXTN), and silently falls back to least-load routing. Root cause: the engine and the router disagree on the KV block-hash mode. - **Engine:** `unified_tree_core.py` sets `self.is_eagle = params.is_eagle and TREE_STATE not in self._family_slot_ids`. The router now uses it as the source of truth for the query hasher: - `block_size_oracle.rs`: new `observe_bigram`. The observed mode overrides the `speculative_algorithm` guess for `is_bigram()` / `hash_config()`. It's first-wins across workers. title: [Fix] hicache: Move NIXL pages that are not whole O_DIRECT blocks
summary: ## Motivation Refs #45563. With a NIXL file plugin and O_DIRECT on (the default), every transfer's address and length must be whole 4 KiB blocks. DSA models' host pages are not: GLM-5.x has 3,316,736 B KV pages and 667,392 B indexer pages. Such a pool fails `is_stride_page_aligned(4096)` and falls back to copy mode. Copy mode's staging slots are exactly one page long, so the kernel refuses (EINVAL) every transfer and NIXL leaves empty files behind. The L3 then either never produces a usable hit or, with older NIXL, restores all-zero KV. ## Modifications **Copy mode (any layout, any pool).** Under O_DIRECT, each staging slot is padded to whole 4 KiB blocks. A write copies the page into the start of its slot and NIXL writes the whole slot; a read fills the slot and copies only the page's bytes back. This is the same approach as #42491 for hybrid pools, applied to both the v1 (KV) and the v2 (hybrid) staging buffers. **Zero-copy for `page_first_direct`.** When NIXL will open files with O_DIRECT, `MLATokenToKVPoolHost` and `DSAIndexerPoolHost` place their pages at a 4 KiB-multiple stride, so `HiCacheNixl` keeps zero-copy instead of falling back to copy mode: - **Allocation (`alloc_padded_pages`):** one allocation of `page_num × stride`, exposed as the usual `(page_num, ...)` tensor through a strided view. The view keeps the allocation's CUDA host-registration ranges, so `destroy()` still unregisters them. - **Who decides:** `get_storage_page_align(layout, allocator_type)` asks the backend. summary: ## Motivation On a hybrid model (Mamba, gated delta rule), a cached prefix can be resumed only at a node that holds a recurrent state. title: [Perf] moe/humming: Reduce host overhead in prepare_buffers
summary: ## Motivation `HummingRunnerCore.prepare_buffers` runs on every Humming MoE forward. It calls `get_buffer_metas` twice: once inside `_workspace_shapes` to size the two workspaces, then again to slice them. title: [Fix] epd: Honor caller mm_hashes under zmq_to_scheduler and mooncake
summary: ## Motivation An external KV-aware router can send `mm_hashes`, one hash per image. Join our Slack community at https://slack.sglang.io to discuss further. --> ## Motivation [Foundry](https://github.com/foundry-org/foundry) persists CUDA graphs across restarts. The first start (`save`) archives the captured graphs, their kernels and the device-memory layout. title: [Fix] distributed: Give the attention-TP subgroup a PyNCCL communicator under attention DP
summary: ## Motivation Without attention DP, the attention-TP group is the TP group, which has a PyNCCL communicator. With attention DP, `initialize_model_parallel` builds a separate attention-TP subgroup with `use_pynccl=SYNC_TOKEN_IDS_ACROSS_TP or enable_symm_mem`, normally false. title: [Bug] Gemma 4 FA4 image masks ignore sliding_layers_only on full-attention layers

This report is based on code inspection and the reviewer finding at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/51778#discussion_r4642747893; a full-model FA4 accuracy run has not been performed. ### Proposed fix Carry the `sliding_layers_only` policy in FA forward metadata and omit the image `mask_mod` / corresponding aux tensors on non-windowed layers when it is set. title: [Feat] distributed: Exact reduce-scatter for deterministic inference
summary: ## Motivation With `--enable-deterministic-inference`, `GroupCoordinator.reduce_scatter_tensor` does not call a reduce-scatter. It runs an all-reduce on a clone of the input and keeps this rank's slice. The comment gives the reason: the reduction order must not depend on the receiving rank. The cost is that every rank takes part in reducing the whole tensor to keep `1/tp` of it. This change gives the same bits without the all-reduce. Each rank receives only its own rows from the other ranks and adds them in the order the all-reduce would have used. It is off by default. The flag is `--enable-exact-reduce-scatter`. We first built this for sequence-parallel prefill in a fork of v0.5.23, where the reduction was an all-reduce followed by a slice. On main that path already uses a reduce-scatter, so we did not touch it. The deterministic path is the place on main that still pays for a full all-reduce. ## How it works 1. `all_to_all_single` sends chunk `j` of each rank's tensor to rank `j`. Rank `r` then holds the `tp` versions of its own chunk. 2. `reduce_order.fold` adds those versions in the all-reduce's order. A floating-point sum depends on the order of its additions. The order is not assumed. `reduce_order.py` finds it by asking the all-reduce. - Every rank fills a tensor with a chosen constant and the ranks all-reduce it. This is repeated for a fixed set of probe values. The probe values are chosen so that any two addition trees give different bf16 sums on at least one probe. summary: [Fix] [Intel] disaggregation: Compute Mooncake transfer addresses in uint64 ## Motivation On Intel XPU, two Mooncake transfer paths kill the prefill transfer thread the first time they run: ``` File ".../disaggregation/mooncake/conn.py", line 2036, in process_layer_tp_aware src_page_base_addrs = src_layer_ptr + prefill_page_indices * src_kv_item_len OverflowError: Python int too large to convert to C long RuntimeError: Transfer thread failed because of Python int too large to convert to C long. The NIXL connector already does the same for this reason (`nixl/conn.py`, `_pack_stride_descs`). - Every operand is non-negative and the result is a device address, so the values are unchanged on CUDA. - Add `test_sliced_draft_address

title: [Fix] [XPU] graph: make sgl-kernel scratchpads graph-safe with shared workspace and dual compatibility
summary: ## Motivation On XPU, `sgl_kernel` internal scratchpad allocators (MoE's `_get_moe_ws` and GDN's `_get_gdn_workspace`) use module-level dictionary caches. When capturing an XPU Graph at smaller batch sizes, the device memory pointers of these initial buffers become baked into the captured command lists. If a subsequent eager or larger forward pass triggers buffer expansion, the references to older buffers are dropped, allowing PyTorch's caching allocator to recycle their physical memory for other active tensors. Subsequent graph replays then overwrite those newly allocated buffers, causing silent memory corruption. This PR introduces a robust, capture-aware, and dual-compatible scratchpad buffer management layer for Intel XPU: 1. **Graph Capture Mode**: All captured graphs (Decode Full, Prefill Breakable/Full) and layers share dedicated static graph workspaces via narrow slicing, keeping physical device pointers immutable and completely isolated from eager execution. Retired buffers from in-graph reallocations are retained for the graph lifetime. 2. **Zero-Break `torch.compile` Integration**: Custom ops (`sgl_xpu::get_moe_ws_op` and `sgl_xpu::get_gdn_ws_op`) support dynamic shapes (`SymInt[]` / `SymInt`) without graph breaks when models combine `torch.compile` and XPU Graph. 3. **Lifecycle & GC Safety**: Tracks active graph owners with `weakref.finalize` reference counting so scratchpads are safely released when all runners exit, without leaking memory or invalidating co-existing backends. 4. **Dual Compatibility**: Automatically bypasses patching if `sgl-kernel-xpu` define

title: [Perf] deterministic: Launch a fixed number of Triton decode blocks for large split budgets
summary: ## Motivation In deterministic mode, Triton decode attention gets much slower than in normal mode as the batch grows: on MI350X, gpt-oss-20b reaches 0.33x of normal-mode throughput at 64 concurrent requests and 0.21x at 256. The cause is the split budget. For batch invariance, deterministic mode fixes the decode split size at 256 tokens and sizes the budget for the longest possible request (512 splits for gpt-oss's 131k context). The kernels launch one block per split of that budget, so for a 1k-2k-token request about 99% of the blocks do no work, and the waste grows with the batch. This PR lets the grouped decode kernel run fewer blocks than splits, each block looping over the request's own splits: enough blocks to cover the GPU, and at least 32 per request and head tile. In deterministic mode the merge also stops at the request's split count instead of walking the empty tail. Every split is computed and merged in the same order as before. **Impact** - Deterministic gpt-oss-20b: 0.33x / 0.21x -> 0.63x / 0.50x of normal mode at 64 / 256 requests; gpt-oss-120b +63% / 2.1x. Any model on Triton decode attention in deterministic mode benefits, more with a longer context limit. - Normal mode is bitwise unchanged, including MLA with its core-count-sized split budget: checked against main on MI350X for MLA and GQA shapes at batch 1-64, at 0.98-1.05x main's kernel time. In deterministic mode GQA results are bitwise the same as today; on MLA shapes the merge's early stop can move them by a few ULP, and they stay batch-invariant. ## Modifications - `decode_attention.py`, `_fwd_groupe
